The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.
Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.
Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.
Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”
A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.
Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.
After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.
A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.
Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.
Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).
Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.
Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu, where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.
After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).
He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

Indian men’s Kabaddi team booked its place in the semifinals of the Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship with a dominant 48-20 victory over Tanzania at the Veer Savarkar Stadium in Ahmedabad.
India produced a strong all-round display, registering 30 raid points and 10 tackle points while inflicting six all-outs on Tanzania. The visitor managed 15 raid points and five tackle points, with no all-outs.
Neeraj Narwal led India’s raiding effort with 12 points from 16 raids, including six bonus points. Naveen Kumar and Shivam Patare also made valuable contributions, finishing with nine points each. Naveen scored nine raid points from 11 raids, while Patare also collected nine raid points from 11 raids.
India’s defence was equally effective, with Shubham Shinde leading the way with five tackle points. Deepak added three tackle points, while Pravesh Malik contributed two.
For Tanzania, Juma Sultania was the standout performer, scoring 13 points from 20 raids, including nine bonus points. However, India’s collective effort ensured it remained in control throughout the contest.
The win secured India’s place in the semifinals of the inaugural edition, which will be played on Friday at 8:30 p.m., keeping its campaign firmly on track for the title. India will next face Sri Lanka in the last group-stage contest on Thursday at 8:30 p.m.

Singapore and Indonesia set up a task force to combat haze from illegal burning
Indonesia and Singapore have agreed to work together to tackle illegal land burning, which has caused a toxic haze across Southeast Asia
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia and Singapore agreed Tuesday to cooperate more closely to combat the illegal burning of land that has contributed to a toxic haze that has blanketed multiple cities across Southeast Asia in recent weeks.
Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan met with Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir in Jakarta and said afterward that the two countries agreed to establish a task force to strengthen enforcement under existing regulatory powers, and to consider new ones.
The haze comes primarily from western Indonesia where forest and peatland fires often are started to clear land for farming. While such fires are common during the dry season starting in April, this year’s are the worst on record, partly because of hotter and drier weather attributed to the El Niño weather pattern.
“El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but the burning of the forest and land is caused by human actions," Balakrishnan said in a joint press statement. “We have a responsibility to ensure the health of all the citizens of Indonesia and Singapore. Therefore, I hope that the Indonesian and Singapore governments will work together to overcome this challenge.”
The haze in Southeast Asia has triggered health concerns and ignited a public backlash from Singapore, Malaysia and other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Singapore recently announced it had sent warning letters to 10 Indonesian companies that may have been linked to forest fires.
Nasir added that Indonesian authorities also have taken law enforcement actions resulting in hundreds of individuals and more than 50 companies facing legal proceedings. Some of them have been found guilty under Indonesian law.
“Smoke can cross borders, so can money. That is why we must follow the money trail these companies have left behind. Singapore offered to share data on companies linked to the fires, which we welcome as a valuable opportunity,” Nasir said in the joint statement.
The thick haze has turned the skies orange over the Indonesian sections of Borneo Island, and has spread across neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and other parts of Southeast Asia where it has disrupted life and prompted schools to close.
Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry has recorded more than 2,020 square kilometers (780 square miles) of burned land between January and July, while the Nusantara Atlas project estimated that nearly 8,960 square kilometers (3,460 square miles) had burned by the end of August.

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
Goodbye Raila
BBC Africa Eye investigates the killing of three mourners at Raila Odinga’s national farewell
Watch on iPlayer
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

But that doesn’t mean it lacks competency. It has a similar form factor to its Ultra sibling, including the same titanium-reinforced hinge and IP48 weather-resistant rating. For most people, the MediaTek chip inside delivers solid everyday performance, and the camera is surprisingly capable in normal lighting conditions. We like the battery life, but turn-offs include only three promised Android updates and so-so Motorola AI features.
The Moto Watch wouldn’t be our first pick for an Android smartwatch, but if you’re looking for a sleek wearable that accurately measures health metrics, it does the job. Plus, it’s included, so you can try it out at no cost (you can always upgrade later if you need a more capable smartwatch). The Moto Buds 2 Plus earbuds Motorola is adding to this deal feature Bose audio tuning. The Swarovski styling may not appeal to everyone, but hey, you can always regift it.
Motorola isn’t discounting the MSRP, but you can lower the price by trading in an eligible phone or device. For example, you can knock up to $250 or more off an iPhone. In our search, a Pixel 6 in good condition saves $35, while a Pixel 10 could save up to $290. We’re not sure whether the Razr is worth trading in a newer iPhone or premium Android phone, but you can still save money on an older device.

Shopping at Louis Vuitton can feel intimidating, especially for a first-time customer.
The French luxury house, founded in 1854, is known for its handbags, luggage, and signature LV monogram. Even though these pieces are widely recognizable — and worn by celebrities like Emma Stone and Zendaya — many come with price tags in the thousands. For a purchase that expensive, it can be helpful to know what to expect before you shop.
Business Insider spoke with three former Louis Vuitton employees about the most common mistakes they saw customers make. Here's what they said.
Louis Vuitton shoppers shouldn't expect to find discounts at its stores.
Shelley Alvarado, a former sales associate and keyholder manager at a Louis Vuitton location in Topanga, California, said customers would often come into the store and ask if any items were on sale.
"I think that people assumed that there would be sales, and there wasn't a sales section at all. Louis Vuitton never went on sale," Alvarado told BI.
According to Louis Vuitton's website, that is still the case. The brand does not offer discounts on its products.
Waiting too long on limited-edition items is risky.
Eddison Brown, a former Louis Vuitton client advisor in Los Angeles, said he would encounter customers who waited too long to purchase special collaborations and limited-edition drops, ultimately missing their chance.
"If you want something that's a limited drop, you have to be adamant about purchasing that right away because it'll be gone before you know," Brown told BI.
He also recommended building a relationship with a client advisor. These are employees who develop one-to-one relationships with customers, and can be a resource for information about upcoming products.
Choosing price over practicality is a big mistake.
Given the high price of luxury bags, it can be tempting to choose the less-expensive option. However, Dominique Danielle, a former Louis Vuitton employee in the Philadelphia area, said that sometimes meant customers ended up with a bag that didn't actually fit their needs.
"Customers would default to a less expensive option or bag without considering whether it actually fits their lifestyle," Danielle told BI.
Some customers, she said, later returned bags after realizing they couldn't fit everything they needed to inside. She recommended being open to an associate's advice rather than assuming a different size suggestion was an attempt to upsell them.
Thinking a bag will look brand new forever is unrealistic.
A Louis Vuitton purse isn't necessarily supposed to look the same years after you buy it. For instance, Danielle explained that the untreated cowhide trim on bags like the Neverfull and Speedy naturally darkens with use.
"The idea of it is to get darker and show the wear and show just the journey of the bag," Danielle told BI.
Brown also said that aging can add character to a bag, especially when it's passed down through generations.
That said, customers should not treat expensive bags as indestructible.
The former employees all told BI that a high price tag doesn't mean customers should skip proper care and maintenance.
"Making this investment doesn't eliminate the need for care. It actually requires more of it because you have something that's precious and delicate and expensive," Danielle told BI.
Danielle emphasized the importance of storing these luxury items in their dust bags when not in use. Brown also recommended being mindful of exposing bags to rain or severe weather.
Feeling intimidated by the luxury environment is unnecessary.
All three former employees said customers sometimes seemed intimidated by the luxury environment or worried about how associates perceived them based on their appearance.
"I think that they assumed that the salespeople were judging them right when they walked into the store, which wasn't the case at all," Alvarado said.
To help shoppers feel more comfortable in the environment, Brown encouraged them to browse and ask associates any questions they had about any item.

A shouting match between American and Cuban officials broke out on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, with a member of the Cuban delegation calling a Trump official a "liar."
The confrontation unfolded as U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz spoke against the annual resolution condemning the U.S.' decades-long economic embargo against the island country, which is due to be voted on this week. Waltz had taken the podium to argue that member states should not support the measure.
As he detailed years of alleged corruption by the socialist government, members of the Cuban delegation, including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez, began to slam on their designated table and yell for a point of order. U.N. officials then sought to tone down the outbursts.
But Rodríguez walked down the aisle to the head of the General Assembly and yelled to Waltz, “You are a liar!"
Waltz responded, “You understand who you’re dealing with? This is America. Back up.”
The exchange was a break from the diplomatic decorum traditional to the U.N., and it came amid heightened tensions between Cuba and the U.S. as President Donald Trump's administration seeks to force changes to Cuba's political system by increasing its already punishing economic campaign.
Trump, a Republican, announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that affect basic activities such as cooking, the water supply and internet and telephone services.
The Caribbean country, already facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles, is now being pushed to a breaking point.
Cuban officials have also repeatedly stressed that as U.S. officials demand that Cuba open up to private investment, Washington keeps piling on sanctions that stymie the very economic opening it has sought for decades.
Tuesday's outbursts came a week after a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island's government.
Waltz and other U.S. officials have been using these public events and gatherings at the world body to try to persuade U.N. member states to vote on Wednesday against the annual resolution. The measure is aimed at calling out the U.S. government's “maximum pressure policy” against Cuba.
For the past 34 years, the resolution has received overwhelming support. Last year, the vote was 165-7, with 12 abstentions. Argentina, Ukraine and Hungary opposed the measure for the first time.
While such resolutions are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.

On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency. At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé.
For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official.
Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment.
Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.”
Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings.
Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U.S. DOGE Service, that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.”
According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer.
By March 26, the emails show, Lewin still hadn’t accepted the job offer, and had not filed his OF-306, the federal government's standard pre-employment background screening form; without this document, a federal agency cannot lawfully issue a final job offer or consummate an appointment. An HR executive noted in an email dated March 31 that Lewin had not completed the onboarding tasks required to initiate “the security reciprocity process,” which recognizes the transfer of an employees’ security clearance from one agency to another. (A detailing agreement between the GSA and USAID dated February 14—two weeks after Lewin says he began at USAID—specifes that “commencement of the detail is contingent upon the Detailee’s successful adjudication and receipt of any necessary security clearances and other pre-employment screening required by USAID.”)
On March 28, Lewin signed a letter terminating all remaining USAID staff. And as he executed sweeping powers to liquidate all 60 of USAID’s overseas missions and cancel thousands of lifesaving projects worldwide, HR repeatedly followed up with Korzeniewski.
More than a week after Lewin’s appointment, the emails show, a USAID official told Korzeniewski that the agency’s office of security was “unable to issue a USAID ID card to Jeremy Lewin as SEC [the agency’s secure database] did not have a record of Jeremy as an employee.”
“Until you’re onboarded at USAID, you aren’t even in the system,” says Natalia Machuca, a 15-year agency veteran who hired many staff. “You can’t get a badge, get into your computer, or even walk around the building.”
Lewin tells WIRED, “I was a regular government employee with a valid security clearance held by the State Department during this entire period. USAID HR was confused about this paperwork for a period of days, but this issue was cleared up once they were made aware of the dual appointment and my State Department position.”
But according to a top executive in HR, no one from their office saw any delegation documents until late April 2025. As one longtime HR executive at the agency, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said of Lewin: “He was the equivalent of an administrative ghost.”
“I think this creates a huge accountability problem if you have these actors who are making really consequential life-or-death decisions who didn't go through any standard confirmation process,” says Don Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, “or in this case didn't even complete their paperwork to become a formal employee.”
Lewin—who a White House official says submitted all the paperwork required for employment and clearance—provided WIRED with two documents, both dated March 18, 2025. One is an appointment and compensation waiver, signed by Rubio, naming Lewin director of strategy and planning, and stating that he would not be paid “pursuant to, among other provisions of law, 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b).” The other is a standard appointment affidavit naming Lewin USAID’s director of strategy and programs. A signature on the form appears to be Rubio’s, with the title given as “HRO”—usually an abbreviation for human resources officer. The State Department did not answer questions about this document.
To one former senior USAID official, Rubio’s use of 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b)—an obscure provision traditionally reserved for rapidly deploying emergency-response staff to disaster zones abroad—to appoint Lewin looks like a legal contortion.
“It is so unconventional that I’d never seen it used before I got to USAID,” the official said. “It was created for the purposes of scaling up really quickly if there was some outbreak of a virus somewhere and they needed to bring people on, then let them go.”
Brian Feinstein, a law professor at the Wharton School of Business, acknowledged that while using 22 U.S.C. § 2385(b) to appoint Lewin is complex, it appears to him to be legal. “Because Lewin's appointment is consistent with this law regarding USAID personnel,” he says, “his unusual status should not be a factor.”
Outside of this point, legal questions also remain about Lewin’s actions at the agency before he was appointed by Rubio, and his failure to complete the onboarding required to begin his initial detail period at USAID. During this time he was part of a team that issued sweeping orders, including one to then acting administrator Jason Gray to lock all USAID staff worldwide out of email and all communication systems, which could have put many staff’s lives at risk, and to terminate 57 of the agency’s top officials.
David A. Super, professor of law and economics at Georgetown University, describes Lewin’s failure to complete his onboarding as much more than an administrative slip-up. “You can’t just walk in the door of a federal agency and become an employee,” he says. Under federal law, a cabinet secretary can only assign the authority of a Senate-confirmed position such as USAID administrator to a subordinate official—an agency employee or officer who works under the supervision of a higher-ranking officer. These regulations, Super says, are a way for Congress to guarantee that “someone walking off the street should not be given these enormous powers.”
Nina Mendelson, who teaches law at the University of Michigan, agrees. She says the administration appeared to be trying to bypass the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, a federal statute that dictates how temporary vacancies in Senate-confirmed executive branch positions are filled. “The FVRA specifies who may fill in, for a limited time, when a Senate-confirmed post is vacant,” she says. “The possibilities are a first assistant, someone holding another Senate-confirmed post, or a longtime civil servant in the particular agency. Lewin doesn’t seem to have been any one of those.”
Lewin being placed atop USAID came in a specific context. In February 2025, shortly after the arrival of Lewin and other DOGE affiliates at the agency, two dozen current and former USAID employees and contractors sued Musk and DOGE in Maryland District Court. They successfully secured a preliminary injunction on March 18, on the grounds that special government employees—temporary hires from outside USAID and the government—lacked the authority to execute sweeping federal actions. That same day, Rubio delegated powers of the agency’s top job to Lewin.
On March 28, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the Justice Department an emergency stay, pausing the injunction based on the administration’s argument that the actions were taken by Lewin in his role as a federally appointed official. In his declaration, Lewin wrote: “I am not, and have never been, an employee of Elon Musk or USDS,” adding, “I report directly and only to Acting Administrator Rubio” in his role at USAID.
The ruling gave Lewin the green light to fire thousands of career civil service and Foreign Service staff that very day, but the legal battle didn’t end there. The district judge has since allowed thousands of affected employees to sue DOGE and the administration as a group and ordered the government to hand over a trove of internal documents.
Kevin Byrnes, a veteran federal employment law attorney representing more than 170 former and current career USAID staff in a separate suit challenging DOGE’s role in the mass firings, says the fact that Lewin had not completed mandatory onboarding paperwork raises even more questions about the authority of nonconfirmed agency leadership, and potentially exposes Lewin personally.
“If Lewin didn’t even fill out the papers and was not authorized to take these actions, then he could be exposed to personal liability,” says Byrnes, who is asking the court to reinstate all the plaintiffs to their USAID jobs, with back pay.

Turkish parliamentary committee approves defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
A Turkish parliamentary committee has approved a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
ANKARA, Turkey -- A Turkish parliamentary committee approved a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on Tuesday, as tensions between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels grow.
The defense agreement commits the sides to regard an armed attack against one as an attack on all three. It was approved by the foreign affairs committee with the votes of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan ’s ruling party and its allies, despite objections from the opposition.
The agreement now goes to the full assembly for a debate and a vote. No date has been set.
The 16-article Mecca Joint Defense Agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, joint weapons production, technology transfers and intelligence sharing. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, according to the agreement, which was published by Turkish state media.
Ministers from the grouping have already met twice — in Istanbul and in Riyadh — while high-level delegations from the three countries held talks in Tehran on Monday to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war.
Turkish government officials say they are considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, but that the agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.
Ruling Justice and Development Party legislator Fuat Oktay, who heads the committee, urged fellow members to approve the pact, arguing that it aims to increase deterrence and cooperation, does not target other countries and is likely to contribute to peace and stability.
"The agreements our country has signed and to which it is a party are not intended for aggression, expansionism, or the formation of a bloc against third countries,” Oktay said. “On the contrary, our nation is a party to defense agreements aimed at strengthening deterrence, fortifying our region and fostering peace and stability.”
Opposition parties warned the agreement could put Turkish soldiers in harm's way and embroil the country in other nations’ conflicts.
“Will this agreement enhance the security of the peoples involved, or will it create new obligations that entangle Turkey in the wars of other nations?” asked Semra Caglar Gokalp of the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party.
Pointing to conflicts between Pakistan and India and tensions along Pakistan's border with Afghanistan, she continued: “What are the limits of the responsibility Turkey might assume in the face of these challenges?”
The opposition has also criticized the parties for holding meetings before parliament has ratified the pact.

I’ve never listened to a full episode of the Happy Wife Happy Life podcast, hosted by Jordan Myrick and Kendahl Landreth, but I’ve sure seen all the clips.
My Instagram Reels algorithm recently served me, along with 5 million other viewers, a brief rant from Myrick about feeling bamboozled by the health care system. Then, I spent the next hour scrolling through the show’s other snippets on Reels, loving the couple’s snarky banter. Still, I never followed the duo to a different platform to watch the full-length podcasts.
On Monday, Instagram announced plans that might have turned me into a regular listener of the show. Instagram will expand tests in the US that let creators upload long-form content up to 90 minutes and flip a video’s orientation to horizontal. Creators can also link their short clips directly back to full-length videos.
“Our belief here is that entertainment and creativity are not limited to a three-minute video,” Tessa Lyons, vice president of product at Instagram, tells WIRED. She wants to build the “best place for social entertainment” with this overhaul of Instagram video. The social media platform may soon feel like a streaming service, as more viewers watch longer videos on their big screen.
Instagram is also expanding its creator tools for turning Reels into episodic content. “We want to be able to say, ‘Wow, Reece loved episode 3. So, as soon as episode 4 drops, we've got to make sure to show it to him,’” Lyons says. This Reels feature, called “Series,” is already available for some creators in the app, and it's being tested for TV viewing as well.
Instagram is focused on the experience of watching videos on your TV. It's hunting for ways to make that TV experience feel social, like showing your connections what you’ve been watching via the Friends tab. The company also plans to turn your smartphone into a TV remote.
Lyons sees the video-focused update as avoiding one of IGTV’s core mistakes—IGTV was the company’s previous attempt at more expansive content. In that instance, many viewers desperately wanted to flip the screen. IGTV failed to connect with users, in part, because it only allowed vertical videos. Meta discontinued the app a few years after its 2018 launch.
While Instagram’s latest changes challenge YouTube’s TV dominance, they also try to leverage its current strength as a platform for clips. Bite-sized clips, often of two people sitting behind podcast microphones, feel inescapable on social media right now, with many creators using them to boost visibility. Even WIRED’s own podcast now records videos for social media clipping.
Instagram is streamlining a viewer’s potential fandom journey. Rather than viral clips and long-form content existing on different platforms, Instagram is positioning itself as a centralized experience where I can stumble on Myrick’s health care rant in the morning and then open the app on my TV later that night and get a nudge to stream the full podcast episode.
“What we're seeing right now is that a lot of great short-form content is vertical, and a lot of great long-form content is horizontal, and we have the design challenge of figuring out how to make that all work cohesively in one product,” Lyons says. “TV becomes a great destination for watching long-form, horizontal content, and mobile becomes a great place for discovering that content.”

Maharashtra is set to host Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027, one of the state's mega Hindu religious congregations, from October 2026 to July 2028. Held once every 12 years in the twin pilgrimage towns of Nashik and Trimbakeshwar, the event draws millions of devotees who take a holy dip in the Godavari River. Here's all you need to know about the budget, key dates and schedule for the Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2026. The Maharashtra government has approved a comprehensive Kumbh Mela Development Plan worth ₹22,425.39 crore. The information was shared by Union Minister for Tourism Gajendra Singh Shekhawat in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on 27 July 2026. According to the Ministry of Tourism, the proposal received the approval of the Maharashtra Chief Minister at an Apex Committee meeting held on 13 March 2026. According to ANI, the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027 is expected to generate economic activity worth nearly ₹27,000 crore. On 31 July, the report said that the Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Kumbh Mela Authority (NTKMA) and deAsra Foundation launched the next phase of the ANEK (Accelerating Nano Enterprises through Kumbh) initiative on Friday to ensure that local women, street vendors and nano entrepreneurs are equipped to benefit from this once-in-12-year opportunity. "The initiative builds upon a framework developed by deAsra Foundation under its knowledge partnership with NTKMA, which projects that Simhastha Kumbh 2027 could generate nearly ₹27,000 crore in overall economic activity through direct, indirect and induced spending," the report added while citing an official statement. The Nashik–Trimbakeshwar Simhastha Kumbh Mela is one of the world’s largest spiritual gatherings, held once every 12 years on the banks of the River Godavari in Maharashtra. According to the government's description, the event is deeply rooted in the legend of Amrit Manthan and symbolises faith, purity and the eternal cycle of renewal. Trimbakeshwar, home to one of the 12 Jyotirlingas, adds immense religious significance to the region, while Nashik’s rich culture, temples, and ghats reflect its spiritual and historical depth. Ramkund in Nashik and Kushavarta Tirtha in Trimbakeshwar are the region's most significant pilgrimage sites. These sacred ghats are nearly 30 km apart. Ramkund is among the most revered sacred bathing sites and holds particular significance for the Vaishnav tradition. During the Simhastha Kumbh Mela, the site is associated with the observance of Amrit Snan, an important ritual bathing tradition, according to an official release. Kushavarta Tirtha in Trimbakeshwar is a key sacred bathing site for Shaiv ascetics during the Simhastha Kumbh Mela. Situated against the backdrop of the Brahmagiri hills, the site is distinguished by its architectural features and its deep-rooted religious significance. 31 October: The Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Simhastha Kumbh Mela will begin on 31 October 2026. The last day of the Kumbh will be on 24 July 2028. 'Dhwajarohan': The Kumbh Mela flag-hoisting ceremony is scheduled for 12.02 pm on 31 October at Ramkund. (Bloomberg) -- For the past two years, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin have used social media to chronicle their lives on the Villa Vie Odyssey, a cruise ship that was on an around-the-world trip until it ran out of fuel in Cambodia.
Now, their dream voyage appears over. The couple are among hundreds of residents shocked by an order to disembark the ship in Sihanoukville, where the vessel has been stranded because it can’t afford fuel, which Villa Vie Residences claims has as much as quadrupled in price since the Iran War began.
“Lanette’s not happy that she’s getting up but we have six hours to pack our belongings — in Cambodia, in Sihanoukville,” Johan said in a YouTube video on Tuesday, when he disclosed the Odyssey was ordering all passengers to disembark by 2 p.m. that day.
“I don’t want to leave,” said Lanette.
About 200 residents were aboard the 650-passenger ship when disembarkation was ordered, Villa Vie founder Mikael Petterson said in a telephone interview, noting the company is set to cover lodging and local transportation, but not the cost of travel out of Cambodia.
The company “recognizes that this is a difficult and disruptive period for residents, crew members, and employees,” it said in a statement.
The Odyssey’s travails are a microcosm of the damage caused to businesses by the US war on Iran, which this week sent Brent crude over $115 a barrel. It also raises questions over Villa Vie’s investment model: the company sells cabins for permanent residency at prices ranging from under $130,000 to $440,000, plus monthly fees of $2,000 to $10,000, according to its brochure.
The Odyssey began its world voyage in October 2024, and its arrival in Cambodia follows port visits in Thailand. The company was next scheduled to go to Vietnam, though its website outlined ambitious long-term plans for travel to destinations as far flung as Casablanca and the Caribbean, along with Greenland, Madagascar and Melbourne.
But as fuel prices have climbed, so has talk of a looming crisis.
In the two months before the order, Lanette and Johan say residents were repeatedly told the company was short of money, then given hope that investors or other solutions were on the way. When those plans fell through, the cycle began again. Lanette describes the experience as “emotionally exhausting,” and the couple says residents were divided over how to save the ship.
Petterson said residents had balked at a request to contribute toward fuel for the ship’s departure. Villa Vie proposed an extra $500 a month, plus a fuel surcharge, and was seeking financing.
The company said fuel costs had risen from a historical average of about $1,800 per cabin a month to as much as $8,000 in parts of Asia. Fuel pushed monthly costs to $3 million, and Villa Vie is considering a financial restructuring and seeking new funding over the next 60 days.
But for now, many of the Odyssey’s investor-passengers remain in Sihanoukville, a one-time boomtown that during the pandemic saw criminal syndicates seize empty resorts, casinos and condos for use as industrial-scale cyber-scam compounds.
A subsequent nationwide crackdown shut hundreds of illicit operations, driving out victims and syndicate bosses by the thousands, but Sihanoukville remains a ghost of its former self. A recent visit revealed padlocked casinos and abandoned scam compounds lining the coast, flanked by rows of shuttered Chinese restaurants and half-built concrete towers.
“It’s a blessing for Sihanoukville,” said Ayub Yulianto, general manager of the Novotel Sihanoukville Holiday Resort. “The province has suffered from this rather negative perception, so having the cruise people in Sihanoukville hopefully creates a positive impact.”
The Odyssey, itself, never operated at full capacity, according to resident Randy Cassingham, who documented his time aboard the vessel on his Residential Cruising blog where he posted the disembarkation notice.
“I think we probably peaked at around 350, and there were around 200 still active at the end,” Cassingham said in an Oct. 27 update in which he criticized Villa Vie for doing little to help the stranded passengers.
“The cabins were small and sparse, but that was OK: cabins were really our bedrooms and a place to shower,” he said. “But it wasn’t ‘luxury’ — it was promoted, after all, as ‘affordable’ and it was until the company started begging for money.”
For some people who had looked into buying a cabin, news of the Odyssey’s stranding confirmed their decision to wait. One Reddit user said an aunt had planned to sell her home to buy one, but put the plan on hold after family members raised concerns.
Several users also questioned whether the ship’s business model could work without a steady stream of new cabin buyers and payments from current residents.
The ship originally left Belfast, Northern Ireland, for a “continuous” voyage around the world, according to the company’s website. Johan said he and Lanette had hoped to live aboard for 15 years or more, and that they valued their two years at sea but worried about people who had joined recently or invested their savings and retirement income.
Holly Hennessy has been traveling the world aboard the Odyssey with her cat, Captain, narrating their journey on a Facebook page called Captain the Cruising Kitty. Her posts capture their unexpected life ashore, with Captain on a bed at Sihanoukville’s Independence Hotel, where Jacqueline Kennedy once stayed, and riding through the city in a tuk-tuk.
“We’ve had a few months to anticipate this happening; most shipmates have gotten to a place of acceptance,” Hennessy said. “It’s still utterly heartbreaking though.”

Srinagar, Oct 28: The Pashmina Testing and Quality Certification Centre (PTQCC) at the Craft Development Institute (CDI), Srinagar, has recorded a sharp rise in the testing of Geographical Indication (GI) products, especially Kashmir Pashmina, Kani and Sozni embroidered shawls, during the current financial year.
The surge reflects stronger institutional capacity, upgraded laboratory infrastructure and growing demand for authentic GI certification and QR coding.
In a detailed press statement issued here today, a spokesman of the Handicrafts and Handloom Department, Kashmir stated that the testing rate which was 40-45 per day in 2024-25, has now risen to 170 per day in 2026-27. “In 2024-25, PTQCC conducted 13,369 tests at an average of 40-45 tests per day. This rose to 22,351 tests in 2025-26, with the daily average increasing to 75-85 tests. In the current financial year, PTQCC has already performed approximately 21,000 tests.
With another 21,000 tests projected between November 2026 and March 31, 2027, the annual total is expected to reach around 42,000 tests, nearly doubling the testing rate achieved in the previous year,” the spokesman explained. 
To support this expansion, the spokesman further stated that Pashmina Laboratory has been strengthened with advanced equipment, including a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and two High-Resolution Digital Microscopes.
“The Department is in the process of procuring another OFDA 2000 fibre analyser and an additional digital microscope during FY 2026-27 under CAPEX. These additions are expected to further accelerate testing, improve precision in fibre identification and quality assessment and meet the rising demand for GI testing and QR coding of certified products,” he said, adding that those GI Authorised Users who submit hand-spun, hand-woven Pashmina products with Sozni embroidery are being given preferential treatment.
In order to bring greater transparency in GI testing, certification and QR coding at PTQCC, the Department has developed an in-house Online Appointment Token Management System to further streamline the operations across all testing labs of the Department including IICT and QCD (Quality Control Division). “The web application has been developed by the Resource Cell of the department which shall be operational shortly on pilot basis,” he added.
The Directorate is in the process of augmenting additional manpower to operate the machines for which technical staff is being sent to Wool Research Association (WRA), Thane Maharashtra for technical training. “With trained manpower, we shall have more teams in place to conduct tests in PTQCC so that the rising demand for GI testing and QR coding post aggressive media campaign, by GI Authorised Users is met. “The enhanced testing capacity strengthens the authentication of Kashmir’s prized handicrafts, protects the interests of artisans and weavers and builds greater consumer and buyer confidence in genuine GI-tagged products,” the spokesman stated.
Faster and more reliable certification is particularly important for exports and premium domestic markets, where authenticity is a key differentiator for Kashmir Pashmina and related handicraft products, the spokesman concluded.

Japanese tech investor SoftBank has sold another 1.2% stake in Ola Electric through a series of open market transactions between January 6 and October 22, reducing its holding in the electric two-wheeler maker to 11.7%. Its investment vehicle, SVF II Ostrich (DE) LLC, sold 5.55 Cr shares during the period, leaving it with 54.15 Cr shares. The filing pegged its holding before the transactions at 12.9%, calculated using the company’s latest share capital. The SoftBank entity also sold 1.12 Cr rights entitlements during the period, even as Ola Electric looks to raise nearly ₹1,000 Cr through a rights issue to repay debt and fund expansion. SoftBank received 4.33 Cr rights entitlements against the 54.15 Cr shares it held on the October 13 record date, under the issue’s two-for-25 ratio. It sold approximately 25.9% of these entitlements, leaving it with 3.21 Cr as of October 22. Rights entitlements allow eligible shareholders to subscribe to additional shares at the issue price. Shareholders can exercise these entitlements or transfer them to other investors. Selling an entitlement does not reduce their existing equity holding. SoftBank first backed Ola Electric in July 2019 with a $250 Mn investment that valued the EV maker at around $1 Bn. It participated in a subsequent funding round in September 2021, when Ola Electric’s valuation rose to $3 Bn. The Japanese investor has progressively reduced its holding since the company went public in August 2024. In January this year, SoftBank disclosed the sale of 9.46 Cr shares, or a 2.15% stake, through open market transactions between September 3, 2025, and January 5. That disclosure put its holding after the sales at 13.53%. The latest filing calculates the pre-sale holding using Ola Electric’s expanded share capital. Before that, the investor sold another 9.4 Cr shares, representing a 2.15% stake, between July and September 2025. Another Round Of Fundraising Ola Electric is seeking additional capital to stabilise its core electric scooter business while investing in battery manufacturing and energy storage. Its ₹999.74 Cr rights issue opened on October 22 and will close on October 30. It comprises up to 37.03 Cr partly paid-up equity shares priced at ₹27 apiece. Investors must pay ₹16.20 per share on application, with the remaining ₹10.80 payable through a subsequent call. In June, Ola Electric raised ₹780.24 Cr through a qualified institutional placement (QIP), exceeding its initial target of ₹500 Cr. It had earmarked ₹225 Cr from the net proceeds for debt repayment, ₹335 Cr for organic growth, and the remainder for general corporate purposes. Meanwhile, Motilal Oswal Financial Services and Calliope Capital Advisors applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares on the opening day of the rights issue. Motilal Oswal applied for approximately 1.28 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by ANI Technologies, an Ola Electric promoter-group entity. Calliope applied for another 1.1 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by Indus Trust, another promoter-group entity. Revenue Decline Adds Pressure The fundraise comes as Ola Electric steps up investments in battery cell manufacturing and battery energy storage systems while pursuing a broader business reset. This includes shifting towards dealer-operated stores and rolling out more affordable electric scooters. The company’s consolidated operating revenue fell 45% to ₹455 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹828 Cr in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year. Its net loss, however, narrowed 21.5% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr. It is yet to announce its Q2 FY27 results. Ola Electric is also battling to regain ground in the electric two-wheeler market. Its market share fell to 6.5% in September from 7.6% in August. Earlier this month, Goldman Sachs downgraded its recommendation on the stock to ‘Sell’ from ‘Neutral’ and cut its target price to ₹23 per share. Shares of Ola Electric ended today’s trading session 16.775 higher at ₹34.95 on the BSE.

Healthy snacking brand Troovy has raised ₹100 Cr ($10.5 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by existing investor Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its manufacturing capacity and fuel its research and development (R&D) for product development. The D2C brand will also strengthen its distribution across quick commerce and offline channels. Besides, the startup plans to expand its portfolio into categories like namkeen, biscuits and cookies by January 2027, Baranwal said. “We will also launch more products in existing categories and build our R&D capabilities. We’re planning to develop new products with parents, as well as innovators from across the country,” cofounder Mansi Baranwal told Inc42. Founded in 2021 by husband-and-wife duo Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee, Troovy initially entered the market with clean-label ketchup and later expanded into the healthy snacking category. Its portfolio of products includes chips, puffs, sauces, spreads, millet-based pasta, cookies and milk mixes. Chips and puffs are Troovy’s hero categories, together accounting for around 60-70% of sales, as per Baranwal. Troovy Doubles Down On Offline Expansion Marketplaces and quick commerce account for roughly half of Troovy’s sales, while sales from its own website brings in about 30%. Offline retail, which the startup recently entered in Delhi NCR, accounts for close to 6% of revenue. Troovy has begun building its offline distribution network, starting with Delhi NCR and neighbouring areas. It plans to expand into select metro and Tier I markets, initially focusing on Delhi NCR, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, with some presence planned in Punjab and Haryana. Baranwal said the startup is taking a measured approach as it works out its distribution strategy for offline retail. “We’re very much in learning mode. We’re trying to figure out the playbook and experiment with different things,” she said, adding that North India is an important market for chips. The latest fundraise follows Troovy’s $5 Mn Series A round in January this year, led by Fireside Ventures. “Troovy grew 5X in the eight months following our last investment, and that is what made us double down,” said Ankita Balotia, principal at Fireside Ventures. The latest fundraise announcement comes months after the startup came under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s (FSSAI) scrutiny over the use of the word “Healthy” in the names of its Veggie Chips, Ragi Chips and Moong Dal Chips. The regulator said the product names could mislead consumers, despite the products containing other ingredients. Responding to a question on the food regulator’s crackdown, Baranwal said stricter enforcement of food labelling rules could benefit brands that have invested in product formulation and ingredient transparency. “I strongly think that this is great for the sector as well as for consumers and the country at large. These regulations exist for the benefit of the consumer, and tighter implementation is always better from a consumer perspective,” she said. However, she said compliance could add to the costs and operational challenges faced by startups that lack adequate testing infrastructure. “We do a lot of lab testing, and it puts a lot of pressure on startups like us that don’t have the correct infrastructure,” Baranwal said. She added that Troovy was also working to reduce sodium levels in its products and limit the use of ingredients it considers undesirable.

Don't throw away your old Kindle — repurpose it instead
You can probably still read on it, and, with some finessing, you can turn it into a useful display.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Earlier this year, Amazon announced it would be ending software support for older models of Kindle products, much to the dismay of longtime users. Meanwhile, others criticized Amazon for contributing to the global e-waste problem by encouraging customers to upgrade from their functional devices to new models. But starting May 20, the company officially ended support for any Kindle device released before 2013 — meaning customers who had been holding on to their ereaders for more than a decade were now unable to buy, borrow, or download new books on them.
But this doesn't mean you necessarily need to get rid of your trusty ereader, even if it is one of the affected models. There are ways to maintain your existing library, load new ebooks through alternative methods or completely rework the device by hacking the display for novel uses. So what should you do with an old, outdated Kindle? Here are some options that do not involve throwing it away.
Is my old Kindle obsolete?
The Kindle first debuted in 2007, and Amazon has since released dozens of models of tablets with paper-like screens for reading books and other media. As of this year, devices that came out in 2012 or earlier are no longer supported by Amazon. Affected models include the very first Kindle, Kindle 2, Kindle DX, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4, Kindle Touch, Kindle 5 and the first version of the Kindle Paperwhite. At the time of the announcement, Amazon told Engadget the decision affected only about 3 percent of its active users and cited updates in technology for making the change. "These models have been supported for at least 14 years — some as long as 18 years — but technology has come a long way in that time," the company said.
So, will a 14-year-old Kindle still work? Yes, technically your device won't immediately be bricked. You can continue reading books you have already downloaded, as long as you remain logged in. Don't deregister or reset the device, or you will be locked out. Meanwhile, your Amazon account and Kindle library remain fully accessible on other devices and apps, including mobile Kindle apps, the desktop version of Kindle and its web browser counterpart. Devices from 2013 and later, including recent Kindle Paperwhite models, the seventh to twelfth generations of the entry-level Kindle and premium devices like Kindle Voyage (released in 2014) will still be able to download new purchased or borrowed content as usual.
Can I still read with my outdated Kindle?
Although older models will now be unable to download new purchased or borrowed books, that doesn't mean you can't read anymore on a pre-2013 device. If you want to keep your outdated Kindle for reading, you can certainly continue using it and loading it with new content, despite lacking software support.
The easiest way to do this is by sideloading — using a USB data cable to directly import files rather than Amazon's "Send to Kindle" feature, which loads content virtually via email or app transfer. To do this, first, download Calibre to your computer. This open-source tool is designed for formatting and transferring ebooks between devices. It also allows you to send personal documents and other PDFs to Kindles. As a side note, many books are available for free as PDFs on internet repositories like the Internet Archive's Open Library and Project Gutenberg. Be sure to keep a backup of PDFs on your computer in case you lose access to files on your Kindle device.
What else to do with an obsolete Kindle?
Perhaps you've updated to a new ereader, but still want to find a use for your old Kindle. There are a number of relatively easy hacks to repurpose a Kindle. Its display uses power very slowly, so it can last a long time on a charge, making it a great option for electronic clocks, calendars and other dashboards. To do that, you'll need to set up an external home server with a micro computer like a Raspberry Pi. Set it to run a companion script, which you can download for free on GitHub, to format your data into a simple grayscale image. Your Kindle then automatically wakes up on a timer, downloads that fresh image over Wi-Fi, and displays it.
If, despite all these options, you still want to get rid of your old device, don't forget to wipe it clean before doing so. To do that, perform a factory reset by going to "Settings," and "Reset to Factory Defaults." You can then check local options for e-waste disposal to get rid of it, or ship it back to Amazon. And if you're looking to get something new to replace it, Amazon offers 20 percent off to people affected by the recent changes to software support. If you want to ditch Amazon entirely, you can consider a number of ereader alternatives from companies like Boox and Kobo.

The Franklin County board of elections building at 1700 Morse Street in central Columbus, Ohio, is an early voting site for next week’s midterms. It is also located in the middle of the large Somali American community that was targeted by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s Operation Buckeye last December. The campaign was designed, the agency said, to find “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens.”
The result was a paltry number of arrests, months of sustained harassment, and a lingering feeling that ICE agents could return at any minute, especially around election time.
“Here in central Ohio, our early voting location is located in a neighborhood that's been the hardest hit by ICE, and it's an immigrant community neighborhood,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with the 614 ICE Watch group and the Ohio Good Neighbor Network, tells WIRED. “So we knew that that neighborhood was at risk and that people were going to be going to vote there, and a lot of the community there, like our Somali community that can vote, our Latino community, they walk to the location.”
Baiman’s group is responding to the threats from the Trump administration to target immigrant communities during the midterms. Dozens of volunteers are already patrolling near early voting sites in Columbus every day, Baiman says, and the figure will rise to around 250 on Election Day. They have been trained to document, record, and report any sightings of federal immigration agents, sharing the information in dozens of Signal and WhatsApp groups.
“We teach people that they have to observe the behavior. We show them what to look out for, what does ICE look like, this is the type of uniform that agents wear, these are the types of vehicles that they drive,” Baiman says. “We show them examples so that they can get familiar with what they might see.”
These efforts are being repeated in towns and cities across the country. WIRED spoke to a dozen people taking part in this effort, whose groups are working together to combat what they see as an existential threat to American democracy. Central to this response are training sessions run by massive national groups like Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Indivisible, as well as local groups like Living United for Change in Arizona and NorCal Resist, that have created massive groups of people who can document and record what ICE is doing, understand voters rights, and in many cases, prepare for worst-case scenarios.
Officially, the Department of Homeland Security has said that it has no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on Election Day. “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED, but added: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”
For the past six months, President Trump and his allies have declined to rule out possible deployments to voting locations during the midterms, even though they would be illegal under federal law. When asked in May if he would deploy the National Guard or ICE during the midterms, Trump said: “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections.”
“Why are there objections to sending ICE officers to polling places?” Todd Blanche, then acting attorney general, said in July. “Illegals can’t vote.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.
Some election experts simply don’t believe it will happen: “ICE and troops will not be at the polls,” David Becker, a former Justice Department trial attorney who is now head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said at a recent media briefing. “It won't happen. If it happens at all, it will be isolated. It will be accidental. It just won't happen.”
But for organizations on the ground interacting with voters in communities that have been targeted by ICE during Trump’s second term in office, the reality feels very different. Hundreds of different groups are part of the fight against possible ICE intimidation at the polls, and they are all working in coordination with each other.
“I've been up and down this state, in and out of Reno, in and out of Las Vegas, into our rural counties, and the number one question I get is about federal agents at polling locations,” Cisco Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, tells WIRED.
Beatriz Lopez, the executive director of Voto Latino, a group encouraging Hispanic and Latino citizens to register to vote, agrees, particularly when it comes to the communities her organization is focused on.
“We know that Latino voters are in the crosshairs of this administration because we know our electorate, our voting bloc, is what's going to shape and determine the elections of so many competitive races,” Lopez tells WIRED. “There is legitimate fear among our community.”
Lopez’s group, like many others WIRED spoke to, will be operating a war room on Election Day, with the specific goal of identifying and debunking viral disinformation that could dissuade citizens from voting. But they are also preparing for more troubling, real-world concerns.
“One of the scenarios that we're anticipating is that at the same time that we're trying to get people out to vote, there might be home raids by ICE in some of these neighborhoods, which has a real chilling effect on people,” Lopez said.
To combat this scenario, groups like 614 ICE Watch in Columbus are organizing patrols in neighborhoods near polling locations. “We send our folks in pairs or in groups. We never want to send anyone alone; we always want to have multiple people there so they can help take control of the situation,” Baiman says, adding that they have trained volunteers in a unique method of de-escalation: “If it starts to get very tense, we teach our folks to hum, to sing, to calm themselves down.”
The goal is not to interact with ICE agents but to document what they are doing so that events can be properly recorded and shared publicly. In January, just days after Alex Pretti was shot and killed in Minneapolis, more than 200,000 people logged into an “Eyes on Ice” Zoom training session, designed to teach people how to properly document ICE activities. Those skills are now being deployed during the midterm elections, Ezra Levin, cofounder of Indivisible, a group founded to stop the rise of authoritarianism in the US, tells WIRED.
On a much smaller scale, Living United for Change in Arizona has been training volunteers to become “constitutional defenders” in person, as the group prepares for next week’s vote. To track ICE activity, the group created a heat map that volunteers use to log and track ICE activity. The map is not available publicly, but WIRED was given access to the website and reviewed hundreds of recorded incidents of ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties.
Groups are also using social media to draw attention to what is happening. Last week in Sutter County, California, six ICE vehicles showed up in the parking lot of the Yuba City board of elections building, where a ballot drop box is located. Following a call from a local resident, NorCal Resist, a mutual aid organization, was able to send one of its trained volunteers and post an alert on Instagram.
“They don't like the attention, [and] when there's more community attention, they do often leave,” Giselle Garcia, programs director with NorCal Resist, tells WIRED.
DHS denied it was conducting immigration enforcement at a polling location, and said its agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation against an illegal immigrant from Mexico. “ICE parked in front of a polling center—with permission from a representative of the center—while waiting for the target to exit the courthouse,” Chandler Rebel, a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.
Much of this work, however, is being done in private, a move Lopez says is necessary to protect the online infrastructure they have put in place over the course of the past two years. Levin said that Indivisible’s leadership team would be hunkered down in an Airbnb in an undisclosed location on Election Day, on alert to deploy their sizable resources wherever they are needed.
Despite the fear that pervades minority communities about what Trump and his federal agents will do next week, every group leader, activist and volunteer WIRED spoke to in recent weeks has repeated one central belief: They are prepared.
“You have all this traditional election protection infrastructure that's really, really robust, but then there is this grassroots infrastructure,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, which combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They've done all this tactical documentation training. They know how to be constitutional observers, and I'm pretty confident that when and if we have an uptick in federal enforcement at the polls, it's going to get documented really, really quickly, and it's going to be beamed out to the world that it's happening.”

Rise and shine, everyone, another busy day is on the way. And it is getting off to a pleasant start here on the Pharmalot campus, where clear blue skies and comfy breezes are greeting us. As for the official mascots, they have finished keeping passersby at bay and are now happily snoozing in their respective corners. As for us, we are firing up the trusty kettle for another cuppa stimulation. Our choice today is Earl Grey, a favorite from our pantry. Of course, you are invited to join us. For the full experience, we are now hawking replicas — take a look. Meanwhile, here are a few items of interest. As always, do keep in touch. We appreciate feedback, criticism, and tips. …
GSK is seeing its return to oncology start to pay off, STAT says. In the past week, a cancer drug picked up an approval for another tumor type, the company unveiled the first data from a global study of a promising next-generation chemotherapy, and a medicine the firm licensed got the limelight in a presidential session at a major oncology conference. GSK is also awaiting another expected approval in the coming weeks for a new lung cancer drug. That said, GSK is still a small player among big drugmakers. Its oncology sales last year were about $2.67 billion, a 43% jump from the year prior, but less than one-tenth of the sales of Merck’s Keytruda alone.
A House lawmaker is investigating whether the three largest pharmacy benefit managers targeted independent pharmacies with audits in retaliation for supporting a bill that would require the companies to adjust payments to the retailers, STAT tells us. James Comer (R-Ky.), who heads the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, late last week sent letters to CVS Caremark, OptumRx, and Express Scripts, claiming that independent pharmacies “experienced an unusual surge in burdensome audits” after many openly backed the legislation he introduced last year.
