India is strong, watch Dhurandhar: Arunachal minister on ITBP chief's China border remark
BJP MLA Balo Raja rejected perceptions of Indian weakness while responding to reports of continuing LAC face-offs. His Dhurandhar reference came amid opposition demands for transparency and the MEA's call for diplomatic and military engagement.
Arunachal Pradesh minister and BJP MLA Balo Raja on Wednesday asserted that India was "very strong" and questioned remarks attributed to ITBP chief Shatrujeet Singh Kapur about continuing India-China border face-offs, urging people to watch the spy thriller Dhurandhar to understand the country's growing intelligence capabilities.
Speaking to reporters in Itanagar, Raja reacted to reports about the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) leadership's remarks on continuing face-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). He said India should not be perceived as weak and cited the country's growing intelligence capabilities to make his point.
"Why make statements like that when you are a DIG? Why perceive yourself as weak? India is very strong. You must have seen the 'Dhurandhar' movie; watch it, and you will see how much India's intelligence capabilities have grown," Raja said.
Raja serves as Arunachal Pradesh's minister for Urban Affairs, Land Management and Civil Aviation. His remarks came amid a political debate following reports that ITBP Director General Shatrujeet Singh Kapur had addressed troops about continuing face-offs at various locations along the frontier in Arunachal Pradesh.
WHAT ITBP CHIEF SAID ABOUT ARUNACHAL BORDER
Speaking at the Himveer Samman Samaroh, an annual felicitation ceremony for ITBP personnel held at the Central Training College (CTC) in Alwar, Rajasthan, ITBP Director General Shatrujeet Kapur recently confirmed that confrontations with Chinese troops were continuing at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border, marking the first official confirmation of ongoing face-offs on the northeastern frontier.
“In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened at several locations in Arunachal, and it continues,” Kapur said at an annual felicitation ceremony for ITBP personnel.
According to the information provided, the confrontations have been ongoing since July, when reports emerged that Chinese troops were denying Indian forces access to key patrolling points along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the Taksing area.
The developments suggest that military friction continued through the BRICS Summit in New Delhi in September, which Chinese President Xi Jinping attended.
Kapur said the ITBP's newly raised Shaurya commandos performed exceptionally well during the confrontations. The commandos specialise in high-altitude warfare.
The ITBP, established in 1962, guards the 3,488-km-long LAC with China. Kapur said the force was raised as a mountain guerrilla force and was assigned border-guarding duties along the Chinese frontier in 2004. He also stressed that the force should not abandon its original role.
OWAISI SEEKS CLARIFICATION FROM CENTRE
On October 24, AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi raised concerns over the situation along the India-China border in Arunachal Pradesh and demanded a comprehensive clarification from the Narendra Modi-led government on reports of Chinese intrusions and alleged restrictions on Indian patrols and civilians.
Owaisi said the reported confirmation by the ITBP director general was a matter of serious concern. He accused the Centre of keeping the country in the dark about developments along the border and said his earlier questions on the issue had gone unanswered.
MEA RESPONDS TO REPORTS OF CONTINUING FACE-OFFS
Earlier, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) clarified the government's position after reports attributed remarks about continuing People's Liberation Army (PLA) face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh to ITBP Director General Shatrujeet Singh Kapur.
During its briefing on Friday, the MEA referred questions about the specific details to the Ministry of Defence and outlined the broader situation along the India-China border.
"Insofar as the specifics are concerned, I would refer you to the Ministry of Defence. As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns. Both sides continue to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation along the Line of Actual Control. The two sides have also agreed to discuss ways to improve understanding of the LAC in appropriate areas for better border management. I would also like to emphasise that the maintenance of peace and tranquillity in the border areas is essential for the overall development of bilateral relations," the MEA said.

India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted
- Published
For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.
The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.
Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.
The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.
Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.
Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.
The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.
The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.
"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."
He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.
In a statement, Meta told the BBC that it may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.
Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.
Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.
The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged ministers to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.
At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.
The Indian Express reported, external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.
The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.
Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.
The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.
Earlier this week, several media outlets reported, external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".
The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.
Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.
Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.
But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".
In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trivedi was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.
Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.
Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra, known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.
For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.
"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.
"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.
Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.
"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.
Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.
Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.
"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.
But that freedom comes with a new vulnerability - dependence on platforms that can restrict their work or cut off access to their audiences.
No one knows this better than Rachita Taneja, the creator of the hugely popular Instagram comic Sanitary Panels.
"My career would not have existed without the internet," she told the BBC. Yet she describes social media as a double-edged sword.
"At the end of the day it's a for-profit endeavour that answers to advertisers," she says.
Taneja says that Meta's compliance with Indian government requests reflects the company's commercial priorities rather than concern for users' rights. Meta declined to comment.
Even cartoonists working in traditional newsrooms face pressure. Adhwaryu says artists may soften captions, avoid certain subjects or think twice before submitting a cartoon. Over time, he says, such self-censorship can become normalised, even without explicit instructions.
Still, cartoonists have found ways to support one another.
When Acharya's Instagram account was first restricted, Taneja drew a stick-figure cartoon in solidarity. "Seeing people on the front lines creating communities, protesting, running campaigns, tirelessly fighting for their own rights and the rights of others is what keeps me going," she says.
Adhwaryu believes satire will continue to adapt. He compares cartoons and humour to a "shape-shifting virus".
"It keeps mutating in response to its environment," he says. "It will find its way."

ఫ్రాన్స్ నిరసనల సందర్భంగా, నిరసనకారులను ఎదుర్కోవడానికి ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఫ్రాన్స్లో నిరసనకారులను అడ్డుకునేందుకు పోలీసులు ‘పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్’ను సిద్ధం చేయడాన్ని చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది కృత్రిమ మేధ (AI)తో సృష్టించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో. ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు అలాంటి స్క్వాడ్ను ఏర్పాటు చేసినట్లు ఆధారాలు లేవు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఈ విషయం గురించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, నిరసనల కోసం ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు ఇటువంటి పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేయడం గురించి ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు లభించలేదు.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఇందులో ఉన్న మనుషుల ముఖాలు, అక్షరాలు అస్పష్టంగా, అసహజంగా ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోని కృత్రిమ మేధ (AI) ఉపయోగించి సృష్టించి ఉండొచ్చని తెలుస్తోంది.
దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వీడియోను AI వీడియో డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో(ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఈ వీడియోను ఏఐతో రూపొందించినట్లు స్పష్టమైంది.
అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోను ముందుగా ‘Jaranor films’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీ అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియో AI ద్వారా చేయబడిందనే లేబుల్ ఇందులో ఉంది. ఈ పేజీ వివిధ ఏఐ వీడియోలను రూపొందిస్తుంది. గతంలో కూడా ఈ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసిన ఈఫిల్ టవర్పై పాలస్తీనా జెండా వీడియో గురించి మేము రాసిన ఫాక్ట్-చెక్ కథనాన్ని ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, నిరసనకారులను ఎదుర్కోవడానికి ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక AI వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

New India Foundation announces shortlist for 2026 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize
The award presentation has been scheduled for December 12 at the Bangalore Literature Festival 2026.
The New India Foundation (NIF) on Wednesday announced the shortlist of five books for the 2026 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize (KCBP), the foundation said in a statement on Wednesday.
The winner, who will receive a cash prize of ₹15 lakh, will be announced in December, with the award presentation scheduled for December 12 at the Bangalore Literature Festival 2026.
“We are delighted with this year’s shortlist. The five books demonstrate the value of rigorous, imaginative non-fiction in deepening our understanding of India and are exceptional in their ability to bring important aspects of the country’s experience into focus,” chair of the jury and political scientist Niraja Gopal Jayal said, according to the statement.
“The NIF Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Book Prize embodies the New India Foundation’s mission to foster high-quality research and writing on all aspects of the world’s largest democracy,” the statement said.
The five shortlisted books for the award this year are “A Man for All Seasons: The Life of K.M. Panikkar” by Narayani Basu; “Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia” by Sam Dalrymple; “Assembling India’s Constitution: A New Democratic History” by Rohit De and Ornit Shani; “A Sixth of Humanity: Independent India’s Development Odyssey” by Devesh Kapur and Arvind Subramanian and “The Secret Master: Arun Kashalkar and a Journey to the Edge of Music” by Sumana Ramanan.
The books examine different aspects of India’s political, constitutional and cultural history including the making of the Constitution, the country’s development since Independence and the partitions that shaped modern Asia.
An eminent seven-member jury, including Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran, former foreign secretary Nirupama Rao and entrepreneur Manish Sabharwal, selected the shortlist.
The statement said the KCBP, instituted in 2018, celebrates original non-fiction works written in or translated into English. Based in Bengaluru, NIF supports original research and scholarship on post-Independence India through fellowships and literary awards, the statement said.

Meta's Waddle World is a Tamagotchi-like AI pet app
But it's only available in the Philippines for now.
Looks like a big part of Meta's AI strategy is to rely on "uwu" and cuteness as a way to get people to use and train its models and agents. The company has released a new Tamagotchi-like AI-powered pet-rearing game called Waddle World, but it's only available in the Philippines for now. If you've ever played Tamagotchi or any other virtual pet game, Waddle World will feel very familiar. You hatch an egg to get a pet, then you have to play with it and feed it to keep you happy. This virtual pet, however, can chat with you and even create illustrated journal entries to illustrate your conversations.
Social media consultant Matt Navarra has posted links to its Apple App Store and Google Play store listings on X. Based on those listings, the game first became available in late September. Waddle World is a 16-bit game that Meta describes as a "daily journal disguised as a pet." You'll be able to write or dictate a journal entry, which the game presents as a way to communicate with your pet. Every time you write in your diary, your pet writes back and draws a little doodle to go with the entry. The responses are, of course, powered by Meta's AI. As Navarra noted, this is basically "Tamagotchi meets ChatGPT."
In addition to the app's journaling features, you can play mini-games to collect points that you can use to buy food and toys for your pet. One mini-game will have you stacking grocery items on top of your pet's head. Another will have you catching falling stars and dodging bombs. The third game will have you spelling words using the jumbled letters on the screen. It's not clear why it has such limited availability at the moment, but it's possible that the company is testing it in the Philippines before giving it a wider release.
Meta already lets you design cute avatars and designate a personality for your Muse agent. It also revealed the "Muse Charm" at its Connect event in September. The Muse Charm, designed to be an AI companion, is an egg-shaped physical device like the Tamagotchi that contains your Muse avatar. It's small enough to be a keychain, created so that you'll have constant access to Muse — or for Muse to have constant access to your environments and experiences. Meta is aiming to release the device in time for the holidays this December.

Festive Rush Comes At A Cost India’s ecommerce sellers are heading into the festive rush with a growing cost burden. While Amazon India and Flipkart have cut commissions to attract more sellers, higher cancellation penalties, platform fees and logistics costs are denting their margins just as festive demand peaks. Meanwhile, subdued discretionary spending and rising logistics costs are adding to their woes. But what’s really happening? Flipkart’s Penalty Shot: Flipkart’s zero-commission push across fashion categories in July has nearly doubled seller onboarding. However, its new penalty structure charges sellers ₹30 for delayed dispatches and another ₹60 for cancelled orders, regardless of order value. This flat fee is hurting smaller sellers and low-value orders, taking the shine off its zero-commission model. Amazon Plays Spoilsport, Too: The ecommerce giant has followed suit. It has revised its cancellation fee structure, linking charges to order value instead of slapping a flat fee. Amazon’s flat tier-based penalty for cancelled orders can go up to 10% of the order value for orders up to ₹10,000, falling to 8% for orders between ₹10,001 and ₹50,000, 5% for orders between ₹50,001 and ₹1 lakh, and 2% for orders above ₹1 lakh. An additional 18% GST applies to these charges. Deliveries Turn Costlier: Rising logistics costs are also adding to the festive-season strain, with Amazon raising closing fees and Delhivery introducing a surcharge on D2C shipments. Flipkart is also considering a revision in seller fulfilment fees. Quick commerce is adding to the pressure, with frequent, smaller shipments increasing vehicle requirements and waiting times at distribution hubs. Sellers In A Tight Corner: The shift to value-linked cancellation fees adds to the cost of doing business on marketplaces, particularly for those operating on thin margins. Sellers have also flagged the difficulty of contesting such charges, saying the process can be cumbersome even when they have evidence of timely dispatch. With penalties, surcharges and logistics costs piling up, here’s how ecommerce sellers are paying the price. Bengaluru-based AI startup Live2.ai has raised ₹130 Cr ($13.7 Mn) in a pre-Series B funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. The fundraise comprises both a fresh issue as well as a secondary component providing partial liquidity to undisclosed early investors. The AI-powered SaaS startup’s board features backers like Sony Innovation Fund, SOSV and Duane Park. The startup, which offers enterprises a SaaS platform that helps them monitor engagement for campaigns across channels, will use the fresh capital to build its AI platform further, strengthen its go-to-market strategy for enterprise customers and global consumer brands and expand regional cloud infrastructure. It also plans to hire across engineering, data science and customer success teams in North America, Europe, Singapore and India. “Brands today are drowning in signals and starved of action. Every conversation, creator post and trend spike is a revenue decision waiting to be made, and most are made too late or not at all. This funding lets us close that gap, with detection, decision and activation running in one governed loop for enterprise customers across North America, Europe and APAC,” said CEO and cofounder J Venkat. Founded by Venkat, Neha Suyal and Yash Arora, Live2.ai’s social intelligence platform monitors brand conversations across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X, and review sites. It combines social listening and trend identification with influencer content auditing, campaign compliance, social publishing, and performance tracking. It also enables brands to convert content into shoppable experiences across channels. The platform’s major differentiator lies in how it runs eight AI agents, including tools for crisis detection, trend identification, campaign auditing and automated responses, with governance controls and human review mechanisms. Live2.ai said its revenue grew fourfold in the past 12 months, with only 10% of its revenue coming from the Indian market. Its clientele includes names like Bonkers Corner, Drools, Enamor, Henkel, Bliscent, among others. Organisations are increasingly turning to AI to automate workflows across functions, and marketing is no exception. Nutanix’s cofounder Ajeet Singh recently launched a new venture Different, describing it as an AI marketing system to automate demand generation. Enterprise players are also acquiring AI startups to bring such capabilities in-house. Global software giant Adobe acquired agentic AI martech startup Rilo last month, while SaaS major MoEngage acquired Aampe to augment its agentic marketing initiatives.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) taunted the Congress party for its dismal show in the MLC elections despite the use of paper ballots, a key demand of Opposition parties in their campaign against EVMs.
The Congress drew a blank in Karnataka while the BJP won five Legislative Council seats in Uttar Pradesh and the Samajwadi Party three as results were announced on Wednesday (October 28) for the biennial elections held in 28 Upper House Constituencies across four States.
"MLC elections in 28 seats across 4 big States — Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar and Karnataka. Elections were held using ballot papers. Guess how many seats Congress won?" PM Modi said in a post on 'X'.
Counting began on Tuesday (October 27) and was still underway in some seats.
Elections to the six teachers' and five graduates' constituencies in Uttar Pradesh, four each in Bihar, two each in Karnataka, and three graduates' and two teachers' constituencies in Maharashtra were held on October 23.

Prep time for Wallabies a challenge - Borthwick
- Published
England coach Steve Borthwick says his players have tried to make most of limited preparation time for their Test against a comparatively battle-hardened Australia.
Borthwick has just finished working with his squad during a three-day training camp before they return to their club sides on Wednesday.
England face Australia in their opening match of this autumn's Nations Championship campaign at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Sunday, 8 November.
While England must balance their international preparations with the demands of the Premiership season, the Wallabies have much more time to focus on forthcoming matches.
Australia have played 10 Tests since July, including matches against South Africa and New Zealand.
"It's a case of doing more of less," Borthwick told BBC rugby union correspondent Chris Jones.
"Identifying the clear priorities and chasing them and not being side-tracked, not deviating from that.
"I think this is one of the challenges, particularly balancing the different stakeholders [the clubs and the national set-up]."

England's preparations have also been affected by the Prem schedule, with players involved in Sunday's fixtures having less time for full squad training.
"We had a session today really that was affected obviously by the fact that we had a Sunday game in Prem Rugby," Borthwick explained.
"Fortunately, we don't have any Sunday games this coming week in Prem Rugby, which I'm pleased about.
"So that should allow players to be recovered in a proper run into the Test match."
Borthwick acknowledged the challenge of balancing club and international commitments, but said playing at the weekend could benefit England.
"They'll go back and play the rugby and in so many ways that will be a positive for us for next weekend," he said.
"The players are match fit at club level, playing regularly at club level, and as long as they don't get injured, then they're all available for selection next week, then that will be positive.
"I'd say on one side, I think it's a real strength of English rugby that the players have such great loyalty and passion for their clubs as we saw very evidently in this last round with the derbies that went on.
"They are team-mates and best of mates the next day for a couple of days [with England] and then they go back to being rivals again until they come back into camp next week."
Borthwick also identified the breakdown as an area where England need to adapt to the demands of international rugby.
He pointed to the recent European fixtures, in which English clubs collectively lost more of their own breakdown ball and won less opposition breakdown ball than teams from other competing nations.
"Part of my job is identify those bits of where I need to bridge from where the players are in Prem rugby to where they are in Test rugby," he said.
"The level of competition [at the breakdown] is at a different level in Test rugby."

United Nations, Oct 28: The head of the UN nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli military strikes this year or last year.
President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the U.S. went to war with Iran on Feb. 28 was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the US carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 “obliterated” the country's atomic program.
During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the U.S. bombed its sites last year.
However, Grossi said that “since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026."
Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week's midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn't immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi's remarks.
Iran maintains that its nuclear program is peaceful. However, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
The UN meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting.
Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
Iran's UN deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the US-Israeli attacks, denouncing their “wars of aggression against Iran” and accusing the US of committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
He never mentioned the IAEA's unanswered questions or the demand to return its inspectors. Instead, he asserted that “Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran.” Israel has never confirmed that it possesses nuclear weapons.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz called Iran a “brutal dictatorship” and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologize to Bahrain's envoy, a council member, for attacking his country.
“We've heard tireless allegations against the United States, ” he said. “What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran's continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations.”
The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.
“Your lies are no good here,” he said.

Partial results from Israel's contentious election show no clear winner
TEL AVIV, Israel — With a majority of the votes counted on Wednesday morning, there was still no clear winner in Israel's pivotal parliamentary election, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was leading his main opposition rival, Gadi Eisenkot in the official tally.
However, the various opposition groups as a whole, including a significant showing by two Arab-led factions, had more votes overall than Netanyahu's right-wing bloc of parties — indicating Israelis had turned out in their numbers to express their dissatisfaction with his government.
Overnight Tuesday both leaders addressed supporters and hailed their early results, somewhat prematurely, each suggesting they had triumphed.
"We made history! The public has voted for change," said Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff who has promised more diplomacy and less extremism.
Netanyahu told supporters, "The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public."
But such a tight race means there could now be weeks of political gridlock.
The winning party needs a coalition of 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Israeli parliament, or Knesset, in order to form a government. The final results will depend on the math and negotiations among broader alliances.
Arab voters make up about 20% of Israel's population, and two Arab-led parties — the socially conservative United Arab List, or Raam, and the left-wing Joint List — could be kingmakers, except that both Netanyahu and Eisenkot and his allies have resisted partnering with them.
According to election officials, Israeli voter turnout on Tuesday was at more than 77%, the highest in more than two decades. Tens of thousands of expatriates flew in from abroad to cast their ballots in the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, with almost two decades in office across multiple tenures, but Israelis are divided over his leadership.
The issues at stake
Many question Netanyahu's ability to keep them safe after the Hamas attack, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Nearly 1,200 people were killed when Hamas attacked army bases, residential communities and an outdoor music rave — and 251 people were taken hostage back to Gaza.
Israelis have been reeling from reports that the government had received repeated warnings from countries in the region that Hamas was planning a major assault on Israel.
What happened in return was an Israeli military onslaught that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, and left most of Gaza destroyed. Today, Israel is fighting back against charges of genocide while Netanyahu faces an international arrest warrant for alleged war crimes.
Israel's wars in Gaza and the region, and its policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many international governments. Public support for Israel in the United States has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters.
Still, many other Israelis are fed up with the world's rebuke over the Gaza war and more than 67 percent of Israelis in a July 2025 poll said they were not very troubled about the suffering of people in Gaza. Netanyahu's supporters have said the wars he has led across the region, from Gaza to Lebanon to Iran, have restored Israel's security.
At Netanyahu's election night party on Tuesday in Jerusalem, giant screens played Hollywood-style videos of soldiers marching, airstrikes blowing up buildings and other destruction. Some clips appeared to show massive explosions of villages in Lebanon, where Israeli destruction of civilian infrastructure has drawn condemnation from human rights groups as potential war crimes, which Netanyahu's government denies.
The videos also repeatedly showed President Trump shaking hands with and endorsing Netanyahu. The two leaders have discussed plans to potentially launch major attacks against Iran, which could take place after U.S. midterm elections. Trump urged Israeli voters to reelect Netanyahu to "finish the job that we started."
Supporters of his Likud party at the event struck a defiant tone. When asked if Israel went too far in the war in Gaza, 24-year-old Ori Hazan replied: "We will keep fighting them, and this is now the ideology, this is the policy. You fight us, we will kill you, OK? That's it."
What comes next
With the race so close, election officials told NPR they expect to finish counting votes — including hundreds of thousands of ballots from Israeli soldiers — by Thursday afternoon.
Then whichever candidate comes out on top will get the first chance to try to form a governing coalition. The party will have six weeks to do that. Both blocs are expected to engage in major horse-trading to try to form a government. This has always been the case as no party in Israel's parliamentary system has ever won outright.
Eisenkot's Yashar party includes figures from Israel's political center and moderate right. The opposition parties he would partner with range from the right and center to the liberal left. He has pledged not to join a government led by Netanyahu.
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, which is part of Eisenkot's bloc, called on X for the bloc to form a coalition with the Arab parties.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't stop with the racism," he said. Even though it would help the Eisenkot bloc win, since the 2023 attack on Israel there's been heightened mistrust of Arab political leaders.
Another possible scenario is if neither side is able to form a government, leaving Netanyahu as a caretaker prime minister, with a repeat election held next year.
Additional reporting by Kate Bartlett.

Tamil Nadu retained the overall title at the 41st National Junior Athletics Championships in Chennai on Tuesday, finishing with 19 gold, 12 silver and 13 bronze medals. Haryana was second with 40 medals and Karnataka third with 25.
The host State added to its tally on the final day through T. Dharanidharan in the men’s Under-20 javelin, Sadhana Ravi in the women’s U-20 triple jump and two wins over 200m. Its men’s and women’s U-20 4x400m teams then won the last two finals at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium.
Sadhana, who had won the long jump earlier in the meet, completed a jumping double with a personal best of 13.22m in the triple jump. She improved on the 13.08m she had brought into the competition. Tamil Nadu’s P. Shrihanisha took silver with 12.28m, while Gujarat’s Hemanshi was third with 12.15m.
Romanian Bedros Bedrosian, the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu’s (SDAT) high-performance coach, sees strength in the state’s jumps group. “There are a lot of talented athletes in Tamil Nadu,” he said, pointing to the first two places in the triple jump. Bedrosian believes Sadhana can go farther but said her progress should be managed carefully. Pushing an 18-year-old too hard, he cautioned, could increase the risk of injury.
Neil Samraj won the Under-18 boys’ 200m in 21.03 seconds, lowering the National Record (NR) of 21.08 set by Abhay Singh in 2023. It was his second NR and gold of the championships, following his 10.45 in the 100m. Telangana’s Lodenge Ramu was second in 21.36 and Maharashtra’s Manas Shinde third in 21.48.
“Actually, 100m is my main event. I don’t concentrate much on 200m. I tried just to see where I stand, and I managed a new NR,” Neil said. He felt more focussed work on the longer sprint could take him below 21 seconds.
Neil said the limited places available to each country for the 2026 Youth Olympics had gone to athletes considered stronger medal prospects, leaving him out despite his wins.
In the women’s U-20 200m, Tamil Nadu’s Bhavana G. lowered the Meet Record twice on her way to gold. She ran 23.93 in the semifinal and 23.82 in the final, ahead of Gujarat’s Kajal Vaja (24.10) and Haryana’s Nancy (24.26). Both times improved on the previous meet record of 24.05.
Tamil Nadu closed the five-day meet by taking the women’s U-20 4x400m in 3:47.43 and the men’s race in 3:10.67. The U-20 NR for the events stand at 3:34.18 for women and 3:05.54 for men; neither mark was broken on Tuesday.
Dharanidharan moves past 76m
Dharanidharan made his intentions clear with his first throw in the men’s U-20 final. His 75.34m was already beyond the 73.42m personal best he had set in June. He went farther on the second attempt, reaching 76.18m, a mark none of the other throwers matched.
The Tamil Nadu athlete followed it with 75.27m on the third throw and then fouled his remaining three attempts. Uttar Pradesh’s Rajat Kumar took silver with 72.44m, while Chandigarh’s Mangal Singh reached 71.21m for bronze. Five competitors crossed 70m, but the lead Dharanidharan established early on held throughout. His winning throw improved his previous best by 2.76m and put him 3.74m ahead of the runner-up.
His season had already taken him from this stadium to a world final. Dharanidharan won the U-20 event at the Indian Athletics Series meeting in Chennai in May with 69.48m, before raising his best to 73.42m at another series meeting in Ludhiana in June. In August, he qualified for the World U-20 Championships final in Eugene with 68.07m, taking the last of the 12 places. He then threw 72.35m to finish sixth, while fellow Indian Ashish Yadav won silver.
Tuesday’s result was his first throw beyond 75m. He placed fifth with 72.04m at the National Junior Federation competition in April, before the wins that followed over the summer.

Assam Police forms SIT to probe killing of five over Guwahati hotel lease dispute
The firing incident happened near Hotel Bilas Inn in Guwahati’s Bora Service area on Monday evening.
Assam Police have constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to probe a firing incident in Guwahati in which five people died. Guwahati Joint Commissioner of Police Ankur Jain will head the six-member team, the police department said in a statement on Tuesday.
The firing incident happened near Hotel Bilas Inn in Guwahati’s Bora Service area on Monday evening, in which the owner of the hotel, Helena Bharali (58), three family members and one other person died.
The other deceased persons have been identified as Debarshi Kashyap (39), Rinika Kashyap (30), Bhudev Bharali (65) and Narayan Das (48).
Deep Dive
Debarshi was Helena’s son, and Rinika was his wife. Bhudev was Helena’s elder brother, and Narayan was their driver, according to the police.

Police arrested prime accused
Police arrested the prime accused, Ghanakanta Gogoi (34), hours after the incident on Monday. Police said he had taken the hotel owned by Helena on lease and, according to the initial investigation, a dispute over the lease led to the firing incident.
According to the police statement, the firing took place at around 9 pm after an argument over the lease and management.
“The hotel owners had entered into a five-year lease agreement with the accused on 10 September 2025, at a monthly rent of approximately ₹1.8 lakh. Following renovation of the property by the accused, disagreements reportedly arose regarding the use of the premises and provision of certain facilities,” police said.
They said both parties had agreed to sit together to resolve the matter, and a meeting was scheduled for Monday evening at the hotel premises.
“A meeting was fixed to resolve these issues, but before it could formally commence, an argument escalated into a physical altercation, following which the accused opened fire on six persons,” police said.
“The accused was subsequently traced to the Basistha Police Station area and brought into police custody. The pistol used in the offence has also been seized,” the statement read.

Pistol seized, empty cartridge cases recovered
Police seized the licensed .32-calibre pistol allegedly used in the firing. Several empty cartridge cases and live cartridges of the same calibre were also recovered from the scene, officials said.
The scene of the incident was secured after the firing, and teams from the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and the Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) were engaged to examine the site and collect evidence.
SIT to conduct comprehensive investigation
Later, on Tuesday afternoon, Assam Police announced the SIT, headed by senior IPS officer Ankur Jain, with Deputy Commissioner of Police (Central) Shambhavi Mishra, DCP (Crime) Debajit Nath, Additional DCP (Central) Viku Achumi, Paltan Bazar police station officer-in-charge Kuleshjyoti Bhuyan and sub-inspector Abinash Das as members.
The SIT has been tasked with conducting a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances leading to the firing, examining forensic evidence and witness statements, and establishing the sequence of events.
Police said the team would also examine other relevant aspects of the case to ensure a thorough and time-bound investigation.

After the incident, the bodies were sent to Gauhati Medical College and Hospital (GMCH) for postmortem, and the principal of the institute, Babul Kumar Bezbaruah, said the report would be handed over to the police soon.
Bezbaruah said that one person, Satyendra Pathak (43), was brought in with several bullet injuries and was undergoing treatment.
Helena’s family members said the bodies would be cremated in Barpeta, at their ancestral home. Police said the bodies would be handed over to the families on Tuesday evening after the postmortem examinations.
The family members said Helena built the business through hard work and that the entire family was involved in it. “She was not the only owner, but she led the business and took major decisions,” they said, adding that they did not sense the danger.
“We knew that there were issues and the meeting was called for that, but we didn’t imagine this could go this far,” they added.

Panos Panay, Amazon's senior vice president of Devices and Alexa, says a couple hundred million people now use Alexa+, the revamped version of the decade-old voice assistant, on its Echo devices. He says people talk to Alexa+ two to three times more than before its AI glow-up, cook with it five times more, listen to music three times more, and create routines twice as much.
To keep that momentum going, Amazon has new Echo products to deliver a richer Alexa+ experience, including minor refreshes on existing hardware and entirely new categories. Announced Wednesday and available for purchase now, they include the Echo Dot ($100), Echo Studio With Home Camera ($250), Echo Show 16 ($500), Echo Time ($200), and the first Alexa Photo Frame ($200).
“I don't think anyone's really doing AI at all in the home, and if they are, they aren't doing it well,” Panay says at an intimate media-only event in New York City. As people have “deeper” conversations with Alexa+, Panay says devices need to be in premium shape—a strategy Amazon has been focusing on after announcing more premium Kindles and Alexa Tablets in early October.
You can see that premiumization in the hardware pricing: The Echo Dot—once the affordable, entry-level $50 smart speaker—now starts at $100. That's higher than the marked-up prices on existing Amazon devices from this summer, which the company blamed on the memory shortage.
Echo Dot
Panay says Amazon has sold more than 100 million Echo Dots, and in 2026 alone, people spent more than a trillion minutes listening to music on the diminutive orb. So, the main goal for the new Dot? Boost the sound. The full-range driver reportedly delivers 50 percent stronger bass performance and crisper vocals.
With four beamforming microphones (up from three) and Amazon's AZ3 chip, Alexa can isolate your voice in a noisy environment and track your commands more effectively. It also has Omnisense like last year's Echo Dot Max, which can sense the environment to, say, detect when you walk into the home and turn on the lights.
The Dot now supports the Matter standard and works as a Thread border router, turning it into a hub for setting up and controlling smart home devices. If you have an Eero router, it can also turn into a Wi-Fi extender.
It comes in four colors, three of which are calming pastels. Amazon's design head Chris Green tells WIRED that's intentional to evoke a calm, softer aesthetic, citing recent data showing nearly half of US adults are stressed once a week. Alternatively, you can buy the Kids Echo Dot, which has the same hardware but in fun designs, plus Amazon Kids+ for age-appropriate content.
Echo Studio With Home Camera
The new Echo Studio is the first Amazon smart speaker with a camera—a feature once limited to Amazon's Echo Show smart displays—allowing Alexa to identify the person making the command (along with voice recognition) for more personalized responses. That's especially important these days as Alexa+ can connect to email or calendar apps and needs to verify who's speaking before divulging personal information.
It also lets you use Live View to check in on your home and monitor pets, or video call friends and family. With no display on the Echo Studio, you'll need to pair it with a Fire TV or use your smartphone to view the camera feed of the person you're calling—as seen in the picture above when Panay used the Studio to Drop In on his dad. This “Drop In” feature will arrive later through a software update.
The camera enables what Amazon calls “Advanced Room Adaptation,” which tunes the sound to the room. Even if you move around the space, the volume will stay consistent. And it can also be used for visual intelligence—just like how you might use your phone to identify an object with Google Lens, you can pick up an object and show it to Alexa through the camera, and it can identify it and answer questions. For example, show a board game you've decided to play and ask Alexa to explain the rules.
While no privacy shutter physically blocks the camera, you can press a button to turn off the mics and camera, and an LED lights up when the camera is on and in use. If you don't want yet another camera in your home, Amazon says you can buy the standard Echo Studio. The speaker is otherwise very similar to the 2025 model and is meant to be the top-end option for folks who want even better audio quality.
Alexa Photo Frame
Digital photo frames are a well-established category now, with companies like Aura and Skylight leading the market. Now Amazon's entering the fray with the Alexa Photo Frame. Yes, you can still talk to Alexa just like any other Echo device, but the 10-inch display will always show your photos—nothing else. The bottom edge lights up when Alexa activates, and you can ask it the weather or to show you pictures of your dog last Halloween.
The caveat is that you need to use Amazon Photos. Once your images are in Amazon Photos, you can choose who and what appears on the frame—even newly captured photos so Mom can see the latest pics from your vacation before she even asks. The display is a semi-matte, anti-glare touchscreen that adjusts brightness based on the room's ambient light, and you can swipe the screen to see more images. Tap an image to play a voice note tied to the picture—that's something you can add in the Amazon Photos app, but a future update will let users add voice notes to images straight on the Alexa Photo Frame.
Smart curation happens in the background to choose the best photos. For example, if you have a lot of vertical images, it will stack them side by side and group familiar faces together. Maybe that means a pic of your kid when they were 8 years old, and the pic on the right of when they're 14. (Though Google has been doing this for years on its smart displays.) Alexa knows to choose pictures of people smiling, and understands timing—you'll be served last year's Halloween pictures around this time of year.
Amazon says it's easy to set up for someone else—like your grandparents—and the frame comes in three styles: black, birch, or walnut.
Echo Time
The other entirely new product is the Echo Time. It's similar in size and sound to the Echo Dot, but with a digital clock screen. No cameras here—it's designed for the bedside table, after all—and the 3.2-inch circular display can dim as low as 0.3 nits (the same as Apple's new HomeView).
It's hardly the first time Amazon has dabbled with clocks on an Echo (see the Echo Spot), and Amazon even sold a bedside sleep tracker before discontinuing it barely a year later.
The Echo Time doesn't track your sleep, but it can help you start a bedtime routine as you wind down. The embedded ultrasonic transducer can detect your breathing to identify when you're in a light sleep stage and gently wake you up within 10 to 60 minutes of your alarm, rather than forcing you out of deep sleep. These “Smart Alarms” are increasingly common on fitness trackers, like Google's Fitbit Air, but the pitch here is that you don't need a gadget on your wrist. Sadly, these features work only for the person closest to the Echo Time; with two people in bed, you'll need two Echo Time units—one on each nightstand.
You can choose from hundreds of clock faces, set up alarms with Alexa+, and ask the assistant to remind you about certain things when it wakes you up—like grabbing lunch from the fridge before heading out. Alexa can play soothing soundscapes to lull you to sleep like a sound machine. And when you wake up, you can tap the top of the device to snooze it (up to four times).
There's a Kids Echo Time with wacky designs and more limited features constrained to Amazon's Kids+ service. Kids can set their own alarms, ask for the weather forecast, and customize clock faces, but the main highlight is Sleep Studio. This connects to content from apps like Calm, Headspace, and Moshi to help kids wind down and fall asleep.
Echo Show 16
Finally, there's the Echo Show 16. Yes, it's a bigger smart display, but Panay says Amazon has redesigned the entire experience from the ground up. This specific model is designed to be wall-mounted, though you can buy a kickstand if you'd prefer. It starts at $500, but Amazon has introductory pricing of $400; the version with the Nanomatte anti-glare display (like the one on the Alexa Tablet Pro 12) costs $550.
It has slimmer bezels, a thinner frame, and an entirely new audio system with eight woofers and two tweeters. The 13-megapixel camera can supposedly identify people from up to 17 feet away, so you won't have to walk really close to the screen to see your personalized information. It also supports night vision, so you can use Live View to check in on your home and still see in the dark.
A full built-in Fire TV experience lets you watch as much content as you want while cooking, or follow along with recipes with Alexa. One big focus of the redesign was letting users prioritize the features they use the most. Want to use it as a smart home controller? There's a dashboard that shows all your controls as your primary “Screen Style.” Parents who prefer to use it as a calendar can set the “Family Organizer” screen as the main display. Or just let it turn into a digital photo frame with the Photos Screen Style.
More unique is the AI-generated interface Amazon is debuting with Alexa+ called “Neo.” Instead of a basic chat transcript like most other chatbots, Alexa+ will create charts, generate images, and offer other visuals to zhuzh up its responses during more complex conversations. (That's something Google and OpenAI have also played up with recent updates to Search and ChatGPT.) These “Cards" will also appear in your Alexa app so you can revisit them at any time.
A Reuters report earlier this year revealed details that Amazon was working on a smartphone, codenamed Transformer, with Alexa+ as the focus of the experience and a generative user interface. “Neo” on the Echo Show 16 gives us a first glimpse of what that might look like, and paired with many of the Alexa+ features introduced on the recent Alexa Tablet Pro 12, it feels like the Amazon smartphone is closer than ever.
I asked Panay point-blank whether Amazon was making a phone, and while he said there was “no intent," he pointed out that all of the new software experiences are “scalable.” He then asked to look at the iPhone Duo I was holding and remarked that it was similar in size to the Surface Duo, which Panay helmed at Microsoft. There may be “no intent” on paper, but it sure seems like he wants to make a phone again.

All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics
- Published
On Saturday, 31 October the Olympic rings will be raised for an event hosted on African soil for the first time as Senegal stages the Youth Olympic Games.
The cities of Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly will host 15 days of competition running until 13 November.
About 2,700 athletes are set to compete across 25 sports, with 153 medal events.
There will also be 10 engagement sports held without medals awarded.
What are the Youth Olympics?
Organised by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the event is an elite multi-sport competition for athletes predominantly aged from 15 to 17.
The aim is not only to inspire young people, but also to promote Olympic values and encourage them to see sport as a vehicle for peace and solidarity.
First held in Singapore in 2010, the Youth Olympics contain several elements of the senior Games but add newer sports, mixed-gender events and cultural activities.
Nanjing, China, staged the second edition in 2014 and Argentina's capital Buenos Aires was the venue four years later.
Dakar was due to host in 2022 before the Covid-19 pandemic forced its postponement.
Since its inception, several participants have gone on to top the podium at the Olympic Games.
South African swimmer Chad le Clos and British taekwondo athlete Jade Jones featured at the the inaugural edition in Singapore and two years later became Olympic champions at London 2012.
American sprinter Noah Lyles claimed 200m gold in Nanjing 12 years ago before winning 100m gold at the Paris 2024 Olympics.
Why is it big news for Africa?
Having the Youth Olympics in Senegal is "monumental" for the continent, according to IOC official Christophe Dubi.
"Africa has hosted many international competitions but this is the first time we have anything labelled with the Olympic rings," he told BBC Sport Africa.
Thierno Cisse, deputy chief operating officer of the Local Organising Committee (LOC), says the whole country feels the weight of the moment.
"We know we are going to be ambassadors for Africa," he said.
"It's really important for us to proudly represent the whole continent and show that Africa has high standards."
There is another link to the top of the Olympic movement.
Zimbabwe's Kirsty Coventry, who last year became the first woman and first African to be elected president of the IOC, previously chaired the coordination commission for Dakar 2026.
Youth unemployment remains a pressing issue across much of Africa, the world's youngest continent, including in Senegal.
While some residents remain sceptical, organisers hope these Games can provide both immediate and longer-term benefits through employment, tourism, volunteer programmes and skills development.
More than 400 young Africans have already received training in event operations, logistics, technology, accreditation and venue management.
"The impact will be much wider," Dubi claimed. "It starts with sports and this is where it will permeate across the continent."
What sports will feature at the Youth Olympics?
Nineteen of the 25 competition sports, including athletics, swimming and more youth-focused events like breaking and skateboarding, are ones which were held at the Paris 2024 Olympics.
Beach handball, beach wrestling, futsal and rowing coastal beach sprints are also included alongside Baseball5 and Wushu Taolu, which are both making their debut at the Youth Olympics.
Baseball5, an urban, simplified version of traditional baseball requiring no equipment, will kick off competition at Dakar 2026 on Friday, 30 October.
Wushu Taolu is a modern Chinese martial art practiced competitively via choreographed sequences and sparring, while the coastal rowing takes place on the sea, unlike traditional Olympic rowing.
Golf, karate and surfing are among the 10 engagement sports staged to encourage participation among locals.
Climbing, hockey, modern pentathlon, paddlesport (canoe slalom and canoe sprint), shooting, tennis and weightlifting round out the events intended to deliver gender equality across the Youth Olympics for the first time.
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
Where will it happen?
Rather than constructing an expensive collection of new venues, organisers have focused on renovating and repurposing existing facilities that can continue serving local communities after the Games.
Dakar hosts athletics, rugby sevens and futsal at the historic Iba Mar Diop complex, while swimming, 3x3 basketball, breaking, skateboarding and Baseball5 will take place at the waterfront Tour de l'Oeuf complex.
Road cycling races will be staged along the Corniche Ouest.
The new city of Diamniadio, being developed south east of Dakar, will serve as the operational heart of the Games.
The Abdoulaye Wade Stadium there will host the opening ceremony and archery competition, with badminton at the Dakar Arena.
The Dakar Expo Centre welcomes gymnastics, fencing, table tennis, judo and Wushu Taolu.
Senegal's Atlantic coastline in Saly provides the backdrop for sailing, triathlon, beach handball and coastal rowing at Saly Plage Ouest.
Culture behind the Games
The Games are also designed as a celebration of Senegalese and African culture.
The mascot Ayo, a young lion, was designed by a student while another chose the name from the Yoruba word meaning joy.
The Dakar 2026 medals feature a lion on one side and a baobab tree on the other, with the images intended to represent both Senegal and Africa's heritage, resilience and longevity.
The official song 'Teranga', the Wolof word for hospitality, is performed by Senegalese artist Mamy Mbaye, and the athletes' village programme includes lessons in traditional sabar and djembe drumming and dance.
The Olympic flame was lit in Athens on 10 September and reached Dakar two days later. Since then it has travelled around 3,600km through all 14 regions of Senegal, with about 450 torchbearers over 30 stages.
The tour ends on 30 October at Place de la Nation in Dakar before the flame lights the cauldron at the opening ceremony a day later.
Nigerian wrestling star Blessing Oborududu and Algerian Olympic gymnastics champion Kaylia Nemour are among those who have been recruited to inspire competitors.
Ambassadors for the Games include Senegal football captain Kalidou Koulibaly, Kenyan marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge and social media star Khaby Lame.
Kipchoge has taken on a particularly significant role, mentoring the refugee team making its debut at a Youth Olympics, having been introduced at the senior Games at Rio 2016.
Six young athletes, identified through trials and development programmes in East Africa, will compete in athletics, judo and taekwondo, and receive education and wellbeing support.
How much is it costing?
Neither the LOC nor the IOC could provide a figure on what the Games will cost when asked by the BBC, but Senegal's government committed to spend at least $60m (£44.8m) as part of the host contract.
There are also loans, thought to have increased to around $90m (£67.2m), being spent on long-term sports infrastructure projects.
The Abdoulaye Wade Stadium, which opened in 2022, cost a reported $270m (£202m).
A post-Games impact report should reveal the ultimate cost, but both the LOC and IOC say the event should be judged by its legacy.
"The Games are opening a whole range of new sports that are not famous here," said Cisse.
"Maybe we'll be able to say in 20 years from now that some champions were discovered."
For Dubi, the ambition is wider than Senegal.
"It's not only about sport. People will be amazed by what they will see."
That may ultimately be Dakar 2026's greatest achievement: not simply bringing the Olympic rings to Africa for the first time, but allowing the world to experience the movement through an African lens.

What are wrong number text scams, and how can you avoid them?
It’s not an honest mistake; it’s the start of an attack on your wallet.
There's a good chance you've gotten a message from a "wrong number" at least once. These follow a familiar pattern: a random number asks a question addressed to a name that's not yours, so you politely respond and say they have the wrong number. Instead of acknowledging this and moving on, they thank you for being so kind and ask if you want to be friends.
While the other person might claim that it's "fate" you met like this, a terrible fate awaits if you continue talking to them. It's the start of a scam, not a friendly person looking for conversation — one of many ways crooks try to take advantage of you being kind.
How a wrong number scam develops
If you continue talking to a "new friend" who contacts you this way via standard text message, they'll eventually ask you to move to another messaging app like WhatsApp or Telegram. There are several reasons for this, including centralizing their communication, avoiding fees associated with SMS in other countries and splitting duties among their teams. Once you connect with a person on a web-based messaging app, they'll begin to develop a "friendship" with you, checking in throughout the day.
These greetings often start with relatively innocuous questions, like asking whether you've eaten. In many cases, conversations take on a "romantic" element. These people will pretend to share in personal matters you mention to them, like the loss of a spouse. The scammers like to send pictures, almost always claiming to be Asian women living in major US cities as entrepreneurs.
They'll often hint at being wealthy by showing luxury purses or mentioning that they just got done golfing at a fancy course. After a short period of "normal" conversation, the scammer will bring up some mention of investing in cryptocurrencies, often mentioning that some member of their family has made a ton of money by doing so.
From here, they'll goad you into signing up for a (legitimate) crypto exchange platform, if you don't already use one. They'll show you screenshots of the gains you can supposedly earn by investing in their platform and pressure you to take advantage.
What happens if you try to withdraw
If you go along with their asks, the scammer will guide you through buying real crypto and then "investing" it in a platform they claim they've made huge returns on. In reality, you're sending money to their crypto wallet that you'll never see again. But a single transaction won't be the end. They'll show you fake "growth" results and encourage you to "invest" more. They'll go even further, too, often urging you to take out a loan or borrow cash from friends to put even more in.
Typically, the scam goes on until you want to get your money out. If you try to withdraw a lot, they might say there are taxes and fees to pay — which you can conveniently only cover with new deposits, not the money already supposedly in the account. Once they don't think they can deceive you any longer, they may send you a nasty message blaming you for losing your money or making fun of you for falling for the scam. Then they cut off all contact, and there's very little chance of getting your money back given the nature of crypto.
While it's an awful feeling to realize you've been fleeced, these con artists might not even stop there. Earlier this week, I got a random Telegram message from someone claiming to be a victim of these scams. They mentioned that they had been given a "list" of other victims and that one of them knew a "hacker" who might be able to help folks recover their money — with no cost unless it's successful.
As you probably guessed, this is a follow-up scam. Anyone contacting you who claims to be a lawyer, detective or similar is trying to take further advantage of you and steal even more of your money. You're more likely to be targeted if you post about being a victim online, though apparently these scams are common enough now that randomly messaging people about recovery is a viable strategy.
Staying safe from these scammers
This scam might sound silly if you're careful about online security and generally refrain from engaging with messages from unknown numbers. Even when I've intentionally engaged with these scammers to better understand how they work, I found their messages incredibly bland and annoying. However, they're depressingly effective.
Americans lost over $1 billion to romance scams in 2025, so con artists aren't going to stop anytime soon. And the people who send money aren't the only victims — many of these scam organizations operate by tricking people with fake job ads, then capturing them and forcing them to work under threat of extreme punishment. It's an upsetting situation from every angle.
The best advice to stay safe, which you should share with those in your life who aren't as tech-savvy, is to be skeptical of everything online. Assume everything is phony until you have clear proof that it's legitimate. Recognizing the patterns of common scams is also vital; these almost always play out in the same way, so knowing what's coming before it develops gives you the upper hand.
For instance, it's worth considering anything involving gift cards, and virtually everything with crypto, a scam. Gift cards are a favorite for fraudsters because they're gone instantly and can't be traced. Crypto obviously has legitimate uses, but it's utilized by bad actors against people who don't know any better.
It's also a good idea to limit the amount of information you share about yourself online, especially in public forums. Anything people know about you is something they can exploit to falsely connect with you. Also consider switching away from Telegram to another messaging platform. While I used to get most "wrong numbers" via SMS, they usually come via Telegram now — and might even start with a voice message, which could trick someone more easily. Unfortunately, you can only prevent non-contact numbers from messaging you on Telegram if you pay for the Premium subscription.
When you get a "wrong number" message, it's best not to respond, unless you have the time or energy to verify their identity or motivations. Android and iPhone both have a feature to report messages as spam, which should appear at the top of the conversation when you get a message from an unknown number. You can also forward suspicious messages to 7726 (SPAM) and your mobile carrier will investigate it.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."
