Quick Answer
Apple’s new iPad mini features IP67 water resistance, an Acoustic Display with no grilles, a lighter body, and an 8.5-inch 60Hz OLED display with nano-texture options. Powered by the A20 Pro chip, it adds a landscape front camera, fast charging, and Pencil support. However, it lacks ProMotion, starts at $699/Rs 82,990, and comes in only two colors.
Apple has taken the wraps off a new iPad. This one is an iPad mini, and it comes with perhaps the most radical overhaul of Apple’s smaller tablet. The new iPad mini – which is being referred to as the iPad mini (A20 Pro) – comes with a truckload of new features, some of which have never been seen on any other iPad (including the Pros). Of course, it is also more expensive than ever before (such are the expensive memory times we live in), but is it worth sinking bucks in? Here are twelve things we think you should know about Apple’s new smaller iPad:
Table of Contents
First iPad with IP67 rating
Dust and water resistance have finally – FINALLY – come to the iPad. The new iPad mini comes with IP67 dust and water resistance, making this the first Apple tablet that can survive a spell in the rain or even a fall in the water. The iPad just got pool and beach friendly!
First iPad with an “Acoustic Display”: Look ma, no speaker grilles!
The new iPad mini is also the first to come with no speaker grilles at all. Apple says that its latest tablet has an Acoustic Display, which has specially designed woofers that are “paired through the display” for better bass and volume. There are also tweeters between the glass and aluminum enclosure for better highs. That’s some very impressive audio tech right there. What’s more, it comes with a sealed enclosure that enables the iPad mini to be dust- and water-resistant. Not many openings on this one!
The biggest display on an iPad mini – and the first OLED display on a non-Pro iPad
The new iPad mini comes with an 8.5-inch display, which is the largest seen on an iPad mini. The earlier generations of the tablet had 7.9-inch displays, while more recent ones had larger, 8.3-inch displays. It also comes with a higher resolution, 2316 x 1512, as compared to 2266 x 1488 of the previous iPad mini, although both have the same pixel density (326 ppi). The new iPad mini is also the first non-Pro iPad to sport an OLED display. In the past, the iPad Pros had what Apple calls a Tandem OLED display. That said, the display on the iPad mini is different from those on the Pros – the iPad Pros have an Ultra Retina XDR display, while the new iPad mini has what Apple has termed a Super Retina XDR display.
First iPad mini with TWO display options (and a “polishing cloth” in the box too!)
The new iPad mini actually gives consumers two display options. While the base 128 GB storage option has a “regular” display, the 256 GB and 512 GB variants also come with a “nano texture display glass” option, similar to those seen on the iPad Pro models. What’s more, those who go with this option will also get a “polishing cloth”. Such perks.
Not ProMoted to ProMotion: Bigger, brighter display…but STILL with a 60 Hz refresh rate
The iPad mini comes with a larger and brighter (600 nits) display than on the previous iPad mini (500 nits) and even the iPad Air M4 (500 nits), but, surprisingly, comes with the same 60 Hz refresh rate display that is seen in most non-Pro iPads. The new iPad mini does not come with a ProMotion display, which enables higher and lower refresh rates. No ProMotion for the new tablet in this regard. Pun intended.
Bigger display, but still smaller and lighter than the previous iPad mini (only slightly heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max)
Rather remarkably, even though the new iPad mini comes with a larger display than the previous iPad mini, it is actually more compact and even lighter as compared to its predecessor. It is slightly shorter (195.3 mm vs 195.4 mm), less wide (132.6 mm vs 134.8 mm) and slimmer (5.4 mm vs 6.3 mm) as compared to the previous iPad mini. Making this possible are incredibly thin bezels – 24 percent thinner than on its predecessor. At 255 grams, the new iPad mini is also the lightest iPad ever (the previous mini was 293 grams) and is only a feather heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (249 grams) and even the iPhone Duo (255 grams). This is the easiest iPad to carry, by a mile, for miles (pun intended).
Driven by the latest iPhone chip, with differences across storage models
The iPad mini runs on the same processor that we have seen on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Duo – the A20 Pro. Interestingly, however, there are subtle differences between the processors on different storage variants. The 128 GB and 256 GB storage variants come with a chip with a 5-core CPU and 3 efficiency cores, while the 512 GB variant has a 6-core CPU and 4 efficiency cores. The processor on the 128 GB and 256 GB variants also has a 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512 GB one has a dual 16-core Neural Engine. We are not too sure what difference those make in everyday performance, but if you are a spec and high-performance chaser, then the 512 GB iPad mini might be the one for you.
A better front camera, and now on the landscape side
The new iPad mini has a similar rear camera to that of the previous one – a 12-megapixel camera with f/1.8 aperture – but the front-facing camera, or “selfie and video call” camera, is very different. While it has the same megapixel count (12) as its predecessor, it has a larger aperture (f/2.0 as compared to f/2.4) and, most interestingly of all, is now on the landscape edge rather than the portrait one. Apple has almost always shown the iPad mini being used in portrait mode (apart from when gaming), so this is a significant change.
Compatible with both Apple Pencils
The new iPad mini plays fine with both Apple Pencils, the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the Apple Pencil Pro, making this pretty much a proper sketching, scribbling tab.
No smart connector, so don’t expect Apple keyboard covers
The new iPad mini has no smart connectors (those tiny metallic dots) on its side or back, so in spite of the bigger display and powerful specs, we do not expect to see keyboard covers from Apple for this one.
Fast charging comes to a non-Pro iPad (but the bundled adapter is a slow one)
While its battery life remains at the classic “up to 10 hours of surfing the web on Wi-Fi or watching video”– that is an iPad standard, the new iPad mini comes with support for fast charging. This enables it to get charged up to 50 percent in about half an hour with a 35W or higher adapter. Mind you, you will need to shell out extra bucks for that adapter, as the one that comes in the box is a 20W USB-C Power Adapter.
Also Read: Apple iPad mini (A20 Pro) vs Apple iPad mini (A17 Pro)
Kinda pricey: Priced close to the iPad Air 11 (M4)
The new iPad mini is the most expensive iPad mini ever released by Apple. The iPad mini (A17 Pro) started at USD 499 (Rs 49,900 in India), but the new iPad mini starts at a much higher USD 699 (Rs 82,900 in India). That places it incredibly close to the iPad Air (M4), which comes with a bigger display, a desktop-level processor, and an official price tag of USD 749 ( Rs 89,900 in India), but which is often available at lower prices.
And one more thing…ONLY TWO COLORS
The iPad Mini has generally had a wide range of color options. The 2021 iPad mini and the iPad mini (A17 Pro) had four color options each – space grey, blue and starlight, as well as blue for the A17 Pro and pink for the 2021 edition. The new iPad mini has, however, trimmed the product color palette – it is available in just two shades: midnight and starlight. Hopefully more colors will come along soon!

New Delhi: Private hospitals in India will soon be required to upload their tariff structures and other details to a central government portal, allowing patients to compare costs and make informed treatment decisions, according to two officials familiar with the plan.
Hospitals will have to upload their charges, available specialities, registration details and grievance officer contacts to the government portal under the Clinical Establishments Act (CEA), as part of a plan to improve transparency in hospital billing and grievance redressal.
The Centre, however, has no immediate plans to enforce uniform price ceilings or to step into tariff regulation, according to the officials.
Mint reported on 12 October that Union health secretary Punya Salila Srivastava had directed states and Union territories to ensure healthcare service rates were prominently displayed at hospital reception desks.
The proposed central portal marks the next step, requiring private hospitals to upload their complete tariff cards online so patients can access pricing information before visiting a facility.
Information asymmetry can lead to opaque billing, inflated prices for consumables and arbitrary charges during medical emergencies, potentially pushing households into debt. The risk is significant in India, where the private sector accounts for nearly 70% of outpatient care and 60% of inpatient care. Income disparities across states further compound the problem.
Government replies in Parliament, including figures from the Union health ministry, put the number of private hospitals in the country at 43,486-44,100.
In 2022-23, Indian households spent ₹3.83 trillion on healthcare out of pocket, accounting for 43.4% of total health expenditure, showed the health ministry’s National Health Accounts (NHA).
“The platform will force complete transparency on what hospitals are charging patients for various procedures and clinical services. But right now, we are saying hospitals should transparently display their charges,” said one of the two officials on condition of anonymity.
The platform will serve as a public directory where healthcare establishments must submit accurate administrative and pricing data for access by both the government and the public, the official added.
However, "the statutory provisions of the current law—the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010—do not empower the Centre to impose fixed fees or penalize non-compliance directly,” said the second official.
Medical care costs vary widely by geography and local cost structures, making standard caps impractical.
Hospitals for transparency
Private healthcare providers welcomed the bid for transparency but maintained that public disclosures must reflect clinical complexities and infrastructure variations.
“As healthcare becomes increasingly specialized and personalized, transparency initiatives should continue to balance cost visibility with clinical realities, ensuring that patients receive meaningful information while preserving the quality and continuity of care,” said the spokesperson of Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Ltd in response to Mint’s emailed queries.
Fortis Healthcare said it “supports transparency in healthcare pricing" and "will comply with all applicable requirements as and when notified”.
Dr Aashish Chaudhry, managing director, Aakash Healthcare Pvt. Ltd, a super-speciality hospital in Delhi, said the portal should be supported by clear, standardized reporting guidelines, a simple digital interface and a practical implementation timeline.
“Transparency should empower patients without creating unnecessary administrative burdens that could take healthcare professionals away from their primary responsibility of delivering quality care,” Chaudhry said.
Mint's queries emailed to the spokesperson of Union ministry of health and family welfare, director general of health services (DGHS), Max Healthcare Institute Ltd, Manipal Health Enterprises Ltd and Yashoda Healthcare Group remained unanswered. Medanta declined to comment.
Not enough
Health experts, meanwhile, suggest regular audits, especially of hidden charges at private hospitals.
“It (the latest move) ensures transparency and informed choice. There should be no scope for hidden costs. However, other avoidable costs due to unnecessary tests and treatments will not be covered by this measure,” said K. Srinath Reddy, former president, health policy think tank Public Health Foundation of India.
Periodic audits of hospitals should combine technical, financial and social audits to ascertain benefit, safety, cost optimization and patient satisfaction, Reddy added.
The plan in the current form would be helpful, but may not be enough, according to Anant Bhan, a global health researcher. “Just publishing tariff structures on a website, which might not also be accessible to all patients (in rural areas, for example), can end up being inadequate. The government needs to step up its responsibility to ensure effective governance for stricter, uniform implementation of the CEA,” Bhan added.

Vikings are last unbeaten team as Chiefs lose - NFL week seven
- Published
Week seven of the NFL left one unbeaten team standing and few - if any - would have picked them out at the start of the season.
The Kansas City Chiefs were beaten at defending champions the Seattle Seahawks while the San Francisco 49ers also suffered their first loss.
But the Minnesota Vikings marched on to maintain their 100% record, and there were also big wins for the Cleveland Browns and Denver Broncos.
Here are the biggest stories from Sunday's games in the NFL.
Seahawks show championship pedigree
Kansas City and Seattle have not only won three of the past four Super Bowls, they came into week seven with this season's best offence and best defence respectively, in terms of total yards.
Sunday's primetime match also marked the return of Kenneth Walker, the Most Valuable Player in last season's Super Bowl, to former team Seattle after joining the Chiefs in the off-season.
The running back has made a stunning start with Kansas City, leading the NFL in rushing yards per game (133) after six weeks, but Seattle's defence was determined to show why they became known as 'the Dark Side' during last season's championship run.
They stifled Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs, restricting Walker to 36 yards from 14 carries as KC tied for their fewest points in a game with Mahomes as their starting quarterback.
Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold also continued to lean on Jaxon Smith-Njigba, with last season's offensive player of the year claiming 150 receiving yards and a touchdown, while new running back Emanuel Wilson finished with 100 rushing yards and a score.
The Seahawks ran out 20-3 winners to improve their record to 4-3, while the Chiefs are now 5-1.
Purdy blots copybook
Brock Purdy went to the top of the all-time list for career passer rating last week but did not hit his normal high standards as the San Francisco quarterback was frustrated by the Atlanta Falcons.
The hosts forced four turnovers, including two Purdy interceptions, as they won 29-20 to inflict a first loss on the new Super Bowl favourites.
The 49ers are 6-1 while NFC West rivals the Los Angeles Rams - the pre-season favourites - got back to winning ways.
The Rams are 3-4 after winning 35-21 at the Las Vegas Raiders, where Matt Stafford became the first player to lead two teams for touchdown passes.
Last season's MVP previously set the franchise record for the Detroit Lions before joining the Rams in 2021.
They next face the Los Angeles Chargers, who are the last remaining winless team after the Miami Dolphins won 28-25 at the New York Jets.
Vikings stretch surprise run
For the first time in the NFL, two divisions will go into week eight with all four teams having a record better than 50%.
One of those is the NFC North, topped by the Minnesota Vikings. Before the season, half the NFL was considered to have a better chance of winning the Super Bowl.
But they are the last undefeated team at 6-0 after coming from behind to win 16-10 at home to the Indianapolis Colts.
Their defence has been one of the league's best, Will Reichard is yet to miss a kick and - although their offence is yet to catch fire - the Vikings keep grinding out victories.
Including the end of last season, Kevin O'Connell's team are on an 11-game win streak, but they face a test at divisional rivals Detroit next week.
After naming new signing Kyler Murray as their starting quarterback, the Vikings traded JJ McCarthy four weeks ago and he impressed on his first start for the New York Giants on Sunday, leading them to a 27-21 win in overtime at the Houston Texans.
Elsewhere in the NFC North, Jessie Bates kicked a field goal as time expired to hand the Detroit Lions a 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers.
Only three field-goal attempts have been missed from inside 35 yards all season and Green Bay rookie Trey Smack missed two of them on Sunday.
Watson keeps Browns on top
All AFC North teams also have at least four wins, with the Pittsburgh Steelers kicking off Sunday's action by beating the New Orleans Saints 16-10 in the NFL's first game in France.
The Cleveland Browns (5-2) then regained top spot after Andre Szmyt made his third game-winning kick in four weeks to claim a 27-24 win at the Tennessee Titans.
Deshaun Watson was booed by Cleveland fans in pre-season but has now led five game-winning drives this season and is beginning to look like the player he was at Houston, which convinced the Browns to sign him on a fully-guaranteed deal in 2022 worth $230m (£172m).
Their other divisional rivals went head-to-head. The Baltimore Ravens had to manage without quarterback Lamar Jackson for a third straight game and led the Cincinnati Bengals 13-0 at half-time.
But the Bengals stormed back to win 35-13, with Joe Burrow throwing for four touchdowns and 292 yards as the Ravens suffered a second straight loss.
Baltimore have not set a return date for two-time MVP Jackson (ankle) and have a tough trip to the Buffalo Bills next week.

Broncos back near their best
The Denver Broncos earned the top seed in the AFC Conference last season but, although they beat Buffalo in the divisional round, the win was overshadowed by a late injury to Bo Nix.
A broken ankle meant the Broncos had to do without their starting quarterback the following week as the New England Patriots denied them a spot in the Super Bowl.
Over their first six games of the season, some questioned whether two off-season surgeries had impacted on his ability to run the ball, which had been a valuable weapon for Denver. Nix had also struggled with his arm.
But the third-year quarterback responded in style, rushing for a 62-yard touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals - the longest QB run since 2022.
Nix finished with 222 passing yards and a touchdown pass as the Broncos won 30-16 to go 5-2 in the AFC West behind Kansas City, who they host next week.

That funny taste in your tap water may be a harmless nuisance—or it may be cause for serious concern. Either way, you can do something about it by installing a reverse osmosis (RO) water filtration system in your home.
Stand-alone RO systems and pitchers sit on your countertop and generally require manual refilling from the tap. You’ll save space and avoid the hassle of constantly refilling the unit by installing an under-sink or under-counter model that connects directly to your plumbing lines. Either way, RO systems aren’t cheap. But for some homeowners, they may be an invaluable investment.
Featured in this Article
What Is Reverse Osmosis?
Osmosis is the movement of molecules—usually water—through a semipermeable membrane that blocks larger particles like salts and sugars from passing through. After osmosis, the concentration of particles on both sides of the membrane ends up in equilibrium. It’s how plants get water from the soil, and it’s how your kidneys filter junk out of your blood.
While osmosis is a spontaneous phenomenon that happens naturally, reverse osmosis requires pressure to force water through a membrane in the other direction, effectively removing all of those compounds from the water to render it pure. It’s how salt is removed from seawater to make it drinkable, and it’s one way tap water can be purified in your home.
RO differs considerably from traditional filtration systems, which rely on physical barriers, typically activated carbon, to manually capture particles that pass through. Eventually, these filters become saturated with sediments and other matter and have to be replaced. While carbon filters are fairly blunt, able to capture larger particles of at least 0.1 microns in size, RO systems have a much finer-grained membrane that captures contaminants on a microscopic level (typically down to 0.0001 microns).
Carbon filters can make your water taste and smell better, but with RO you are getting much, much cleaner water than what that inexpensive Brita filter can muster. (That said, RO can’t capture everything, and carbon filters are still useful for capturing certain volatile organic compounds through adsorption. Most RO systems also have an additional carbon filtration system included.)
Note that two types of RO systems are available: Tanked RO systems filter water slowly (albeit passively, without electricity) and sequester it in a (rather large) tank under your sink. Today, tankless RO systems are more popular, processing water on demand but requiring electricity to keep things flowing expeditiously. Tankless systems are considerably more expensive due to their inherent complexity.
What Are the Real Risks of Contaminants in Water Today?
“US tap water is safe for most people most of the time,” says John Voll, an industrial water treatment veteran and the founder of Tap & Air, a website that monitors water and air quality for hundreds of municipalities. “The problems are local, not universal.”
The first step to understanding your personal risk is to gauge whether your own water is up to snuff by simply looking up its most recent data report online. The Safe Drinking Water Act requires community water systems to publish an annual report on the quality of water they’re delivering, due by July 1 each year.
These are heady documents, so to keep things simple, Voll says to keep your eye on three key pollutant metrics: lead, nitrate or arsenic, and PFAS (so-called forever chemicals popular in nonstick cookware and other products). While the first two are serious issues, they’re fairly rare today. PFAS, however, are a particularly significant problem across the country. Voll says that 98 of the 200 largest US cities have at least one PFAS compound detected in their water supply. Reverse osmosis systems can handle them—as well as lead and other compounds. Carbon filters usually can’t.
“Most people don't need RO,” Voll says, “but some households clearly do, and the way to tell is to read your own water report first.”
What Are the Drawbacks of Using an RO System?
RO systems come with a host of downsides, but most are related in some fashion to cost.
- RO wastes water: The particulars of RO technology have historically meant it requires a large amount of unprocessed tap water to create a small amount of purified water, sometimes up to 4 gallons or more of tap to 1 gallon of clean water (called the pure-to-drain ratio). In recent years that number has dramatically shifted, with 4 gallons of tap water producing up to 3 gallons of clean water, or a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio.
- Filters are costly: RO systems can require up to six different filtration cartridges that must be replaced every year or two, depending on use. Much like printer ink, these costs can be easily overlooked when making your initial purchase. Plan to spend $50 to $200 annually on replacement cartridges, but check prices before you buy.
- RO can strip “good” minerals from your water: Calcium, magnesium, and potassium are all unable to pass through the RO membrane. RO systems also remove fluoride from your water, which many users may not desire and which dentists abhor. Some RO systems can remineralize water and/or raise the pH level of the processed water thanks to additional cartridges—but these, of course, mean further expense on replaceables.
- Plan for professional installation (and additional financial outlays): I try not to DIY too much when there’s even a remote potential for a water leak, so I get a plumber involved for installations like these. And since most RO systems require their own faucet, you’ll need to prepare to have a new hole drilled into your countertop for your tap if you don’t already have one available.
Do You Need an Under-Sink RO System?
Based on my analysis of my city’s water report, no I don’t really need an RO system, as there’s nothing hazardous to worry about. However, as the linked report notes, our water supplier uses chloramine as a disinfectant, and drinking that chloramine-treated water straight from the tap has a slight but noticeable, off-putting taste. This is exacerbated by the extreme hardness of the water; this part of Texas is basically built on top of nothing but limestone, and the resulting amount of calcium carbonate in the water can add a slightly bitter flavor, as well.
For me, RO is all about the way the water tastes. Any lingering contaminants that are removed along the way are just a bonus.
I tested the Waterdrop X12 for this story, hiring a plumber to remove a well-aged unit under the sink and replace it with this more capable one. The job was done in less than an hour.
Under-sink RO filters are separate from your existing plumbing, and most use three color-coded lengths of tubing to tie into it. One connects to your incoming water supply through an adapter valve, one clips into your wastewater drainpipe via an included fitting, and one connects to the faucet. I am confident I could have made these connections on my own—especially since I was replacing an existing system—but I’ve seen how even a small water leak can lead to devastating problems and was happy for the peace of mind that professional oversight supplied.
Once installed and powered up, the X12 launches a 35-minute priming process designed to flush the filters before first use. It seems like an awfully long time for the sink to run, and it is. If you have some way to capture and use all this extra water, plan ahead to collect it. After the session completed (it stops automatically), I was ready to start sipping from the tap.
The X12 is exceedingly simple to use. Tap the LED-equipped button on top of the faucet to start or stop the flow of water, or twist the same button to dial in the number of ounces you want to dispense (up to 999) before depressing it. This way, you can drop your 64-ounce Stanley Quencher in the sink and walk away without having to wait around or worry about an overflow, with a digital timer first offering a measurement of your water’s current TDS (total dissolved solids), then counting down the ounces as they’re dispensed. The good news is that you won’t have to wait long: The X12 blasts water out of its spigot faster than my kitchen sink does—a far cry from the sad dribble of H2O my old RO system provided.
The unit can also be switched into one of two alternate operating modes, including an energy-saving mode (which quiets the device) and “flow mode,” which is designed for high-use households. Both require pressing certain button combinations on the filtration unit. I have used the device in all three modes, and (contrary to other reviews I’ve seen) I’ve never found it to be noisy at all, even though it’s located just 20 feet from my bed.
As for the water, it tastes great. The remineralization feature and pH adjustment (to about 7.5, which I confirmed with a pH test strip) give the water a pleasant tang while avoiding any harshness or chemical flavors. Unfortunately it doesn’t come out particularly cold, which means having to add non-RO ice to the glass to chill it down. First-world problem, I know.
I was especially pleased to discover that the X12 has one of the best water efficiency rates in the business, with a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio (3 gallons of pure water production to 1 gallon lost). Replacement filters (three are needed in total) are sold à la carte for $30 to $160 each.
For an even more powerful version—ideal for larger households—consider the Waterdrop X16, which uses the same cartridges and offers the same features as the X12. WIRED editor Kat Merck, whose municipal water supply does contain PFAS, has had one installed for a year and a half without any maintenance or reliability issues.

Evidence from photojournalists on the scene confirms Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of the new White House ballroom and saluting officials visible far behind and to the left side of the helicopter.
In mid-to-late October, a video spread purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump waving to and saluting nobody on the White House South Lawn prior to boarding his helicopter, Marine One.
For example, Democratic commentator Harry Sisson said the footage (archived) highlights how Trump is experiencing increasing "mental decline."
The clip shows Trump walking toward Marine One — the call sign officials use when a president flies on a special fleet of helicopters — waving toward his left, continuing to walk and then waving, saluting and waving again in a slightly different direction, also off to his left. At the end of the clip, he salutes a Marine and boards the aircraft.
Numerous social media users and other left-leaning commentators shared the video and iterations of the rumor, including former cable news hosts Don Lemon and Joy Reid, as well as fellow progressive voice Adam Mockler. All three have prominent presences on YouTube.
Similarly, The New Republic initially reported, "Trump, 80, Wanders Off While Waving and Saluting to No One." The publication displayed that headline as an image on social media.
In sum, while the clip is authentic, meaning it displays no signs of artificial-intelligence manipulation, evidence shows Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of his new White House ballroom, which has replaced the demolished White House East Wing. He was also saluting and throwing smaller waves to other darkly-dressed officials positioned far behind and to the left side of the helicopter. Therefore, the above social media posts miscaptioned the video.
Fox News broadcast the same live moment leading up to the moment in question, helping to confirm the date this occurred, Oct. 19, as well as providing a clearer look at two or more darkly-dressed individuals standing next to a white fence whom the president appeared to salute (pictured below, to the left of Trump).
(Fox News)
Snopes contacted Lemon, Reid and Mockler to ask if they wished to address this matter but did not receive responses prior to publication. The New Republic declined to comment, but said it updated its report to include a new headline and other updated information. We also emailed the White House to ask if a spokesperson wished to respond to people sharing the false claim. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Reputable media-licensing website Getty Images hosts several photos with text captions providing more information about the moment in question. For example, a picture of Trump waving (shown at the top of this article) is captioned, "U.S. President Donald Trump waves to people working on building the new ballroom as he departs the White House on October 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C." Other photographs show the ballroom construction happening behind Trump and people working on the project both on the ground and up high.
(Brendan Smialowski via Getty Images)
One of Getty's captions says the picture below shows a construction worker giving Trump a thumbs-up sign as Marine One prepared for takeoff.
(Chip Somodevilla via Getty Images)
The Associated Press' image-licensing website also provides more data, including a photo of the ballroom construction from the White House South Lawn, a glimpse of both the White House and ballroom construction from the Washington Monument, a view of Marine One flying over the work zone on the same day, and Trump giving a similar acknowledgement to workers with a fist sign last week.

'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

Large parts of Sudan's capital lose power after drone attack
A drone strike hits a major power substation in Sudan's capital, leaving large parts of the city without electricity for over 12 hours
SHENDI, Sudan -- Large parts of Sudan’s capital were without electricity for more than 12 hours Tuesday after a drone strike on a major power substation, according to an electric company official.
The attack left hospitals and bakeries dependent on generators and limited water supplies across Khartoum.
The state-run Sudanese Electricity Distribution Company acknowledged “serious damage and technical faults” to the distribution network and several main stations and power lines but didn't explain the reason in a statement. It apologized to residents across Khartoum state for repeated and prolonged outages.
A company official, speaking to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said a drone attack hit the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman, on the outskirts of Khartoum. He said it is the second to hit the station this year, blaming it on the country's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The RSF has been at war with the Sudanese military for more than three years. Sudan’s war began in April 2023, when simmering tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in Khartoum and spread across the country.
Deadly drone attacks across Sudan have been carried out by the two rival forces. But those attacks have become rare in Khartoum since the Sudanese military took control of the capital in May 2025, after years of brutal fighting between the military and the RSF.
The U.N. has expressed concern over the use of drones across Sudan, saying they have been killing civilians, including children, and are disrupting essential services.
The official who spoke to AP said technical teams are still assessing the damage, describing the strike as major. He estimated that 60% of power supply in the capital could be affected, predicting that water stations will be most affected.
A resident living near the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman said he heard a drone shortly before the blast.
“At around 4:30 in the morning, on my way to dawn prayers, I heard the sound of a drone very close by, and just moments later a huge explosion, and the power went out,” Abdel-Hafiz Abdel-Mutaal told AP. “I saw fire burning at the transformer station.”
The city descended into darkness after sundown.
Adel Ali, a resident of south Khartoum, said he was without power and water for 17 hours.
“My main concern is how to preserve my insulin supply which needs a fridge,” Ali, a diabetes patient, said. “Life without electricity is totally paralyzed, and a bread crisis is emerging as many bakeries have shut down.” He said this would drive the price of bread even higher.
The electricity company, in its statement, said power rationing would be longer than usual in all areas until repairs are finished. It did not say when that would be. Technical teams were working around the clock to restore power, it added.
The conflict has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the true toll is likely higher. Over 67% of the country's population is dependent on aid, while 825,000 children face acute malnutrition.
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, or IPC, a global food crisis monitor warned last week that the “deteriorating humanitarian situation” across greater Darfur and Kordofan states is worsening, with food insecurity putting these areas at risk of famine.
In a joint statement, over 30 countries including the United States, United Kingdom and the European Commission, urged parties to the conflict in the country “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability" initiative on Sept. 30.
Fox News reported the 90-day requirement on Oct. 25 and quotes department spokesperson Sean Parnell throughout the article. Though Parnell shared the report on X that day, he has not confirmed the 90-day requirement.
In October, a claim circulated online that the Pentagon had announced an initiative called FORTRESS that would require military bases in the U.S. to be able to operate for at least 90 days without relying on civilian power, fuel, water or supply lines.
For example, one Facebook user who made and posted a video about the alleged measure wrote (archived):
The Pentagon just Built a 90- Day Survival Plan.
Under FORTRESS (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability), every major U.S. military base is being ordered to operate for 90 days with no civilian power, fuel, water, or supply chains, using portable nuclear reactors, microgrids, and stockpiles. The military is hardening itself for a grid-down war. Civilians are on their own.
Snopes readers contacted us to ask about the initiative, while similar posts about FORTRESS and what it entails also circulated on Instagram and Reddit (archived, archived).
FORTRESS is a real Department of Defense initiative and social media posts detailing what it involves are broadly accurate. The acronym stands for "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability." Though the measure itself is new, it also includes some energy and manufacturing-related programs that already exist within the DOD.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced FORTRESS during a speech in Quantico, Virginia, on Sept. 30. His speech and a department memo released that day describe the initiative as an "insurance policy" for the United States.
On Oct. 25, Fox News reported more details about the measure (archived), mainly saying it would require U.S. military bases to "keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support."
Fox News reported Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell has led the initiative. Parnell is quoted throughout Fox's report, which he posted to X (archived) that day. His posting of the article, however, does not explicitly confirm the 90-day operating requirement. Therefore, we've rated this claim mostly true.
Snopes contacted the DOD for official confirmation of the 90-day requirement and any additional information it could provide about the FORTRESS initiative. We await a reply to our inquiry.
FORTRESS merges existing DOD programs
The Sept. 30 department memo says FORTRESS would focus on five pillars: "Energy independence; supply-chain and defense-industrial base resilience; a strategic defense reserve; installation hardening and cyber resilience; and resilience in space and spectrum."
Hegseth explained the changes the initiative would bring as follows (at 32:07):
Every major military installation in America is going to generate its own power independent of the civilian grid. If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage or by any means, our bases stay lit. Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark.
We're bringing our critical supply chains home: the rare earths, the specialty metals, the semiconductors, the propellants mined in America, refined in America, built in America by American workers.
We are building long-overdue strategic reserves deep enough to fight through disruption. Think munitions, fuel, medicine, blood. Deep enough that if the world's supply lines break, and in a real war they're going to break, America keeps fighting anyway.
We're hardening every installation on American soil against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones.
And we're securing the high ground and the airwaves, our satellites, our spectrum, our ability to see, to navigate and to talk to one another.
Fox News reported that a "central concern" that FORTRESS would address is the military's reliance on the civilian power grid. Under the first pillar of "energy independence," Fox News said the measure would see the U.S. military developing its own sources of power such as "portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids."
Around a month before the DOD made FORTRESS public, the department had already announced five vendors to build and operate nuclear microreactors at Fort Benning, Georgia; Fort Bragg, North Carolina; Fort Campbell, Kentucky; and Fort Drum, New York; and Fort Hood, Texas, as part of the Janus Program.
That program aims to supply U.S. military bases with "the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids," according to the DOD, and seeks to build at least 20 microreactors.
FORTRESS would reportedly also use another existing DOD program — the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network — to identify domestic factories that could switch to manufacturing for the military in a crisis even if normal supply chains are disrupted.
Hegseth said during his Sept. 30 speech that FORTRESS was not meant to spread concerns about war on American soil. Rather, he said (at 33:56):
We'll make certain that America cannot be starved out, shut down or cut off. A fortress is not a place where you hide from. It's a ground you stand on, the foundation you fight from, the strength that lets you reach anywhere in the world, precisely because you are fully prepared at home.
It is unclear how the initiative would affect civilian disaster preparedness. Writing in The Wall Street Journal on Oct. 9, Tim Echols, who has served on the Georgia Public Services Commission since 2011, suggested the initiative could benefit consumers. Echols wrote that "the learning curve for building nuclear is paid for by the government" through microreactors for U.S. bases, whose technology could also apply to civilian power grids.
Echols also suggested that lessening demand for electricity in cities that provide substantial power to military bases would allow those power companies to retire older units and replace them with more-efficient ones.
Conversely, the user who made and posted the aforementioned Facebook video suggested FORTRESS would leave civilians "on their own" by taking away investment from shared resources.
The U.S. government provides disaster preparedness advice for civilians on Ready.gov.

Rama Rao Malla, the son of a farmer from Anakapalli, went on to earn a B.Ed., an M.Sc. and a Ph.D. in biochemistry from Andhra University. During Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Prof. Malla, of the Department of Life Sciences at the Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management (GITAM) (Deemed to be University), is leading research to develop a blood test for one of the most aggressive forms of breast cancer.
The first graduate in his family, Prof. Malla has been a teacher for more than three decades. He joined GITAM early in his career in 2001 and, after completing postdoctoral work at the University of Illinois College of Medicine, returned to set up the university’s cancer research laboratory in 2011. He has guided 14 doctoral scholars and completed several projects on breast cancer, with four more under way, he says.
His current research focuses on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which lacks the receptors for oestrogen, progesterone and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), the targets of certain cancer therapies. Patients are treated mainly with chemotherapy, to which many develop resistance. TNBC accounts for 10% to 15% of breast cancers, he says, and is increasingly being diagnosed in women in their mid-30s and 40s. Mammography may miss small tumours, particularly in younger women. “If we can identify this cancer at an early stage, we can successfully eliminate the tumours by surgery,” he says.
The project, titled “Exploring Serum Exosomal microRNAs as Minimally-Invasive Biomarkers for Early Diagnosis of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer”, has been sanctioned under the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)’s “Follow-on Nischayak Anveshan” Extramural Grants programme, with Prof. Malla as the principal investigator. He says the project has an outlay of more than ₹2 crore over three years.
The study will examine exosomes, nanosized vesicles released by cells, including tumour cells. Their microRNA content can reflect that of the cells from which they originate. The researchers will compare serum samples from patients with early-stage TNBC, provided by the Mahatma Gandhi Cancer Hospital & Research Institute (MGCHRI) and the GITAM Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (GIMSR), with samples from healthy women. Sequencing and digital polymerase chain reaction (PCR) will be used to identify candidate microRNAs, and a machine-learning model will be trained to distinguish patients with early-stage TNBC from healthy individuals. The ultimate objective is to develop a kit-based test.
“We hope we can achieve something after three years that will be useful for society,” he says.
The co-investigators are P. Kiranmayi, P. Vasudevaraju, A. Krishna Chaitanya and M. Srivenkatesh of the GITAM School of Science; K. Viswa Kalyan of GIMSR; and V. Muralikrishna of MGCHRI.
The World Health Organization advises that any abnormal breast lump should be examined by a health professional, even if it is painless.

While the Friday after Thanksgiving has traditionally been the busiest shopping day of the year, Black Friday deals have gradually spread well beyond the day. First came Cyber Monday, then Cyber Week. Now, early Black Friday deals kick off before November has even started. The tricky part for early birds is knowing what’s a genuine deal and what’s likely to go even lower when Black Friday arrives.
The Reviews team at WIRED tracks prices on our favorite gadgets year-round, and we only highlight deals on devices we have tested that we’d be comfortable recommending to friends and family. Some of these picks may be cheaper for Black Friday, but these are the discounts that have caught our eye so far.
The best trackers for anyone with an iPhone; you can use them to keep tabs on your keys, luggage, bike, or whatever else you worry might go missing. Each AirTag location is marked clearly in the Find My app. The battery should last you a year, and we have a guide on how to replace your AirTag battery. Just please don’t use them to track people. This is the lowest price we have seen on the single tag, but it drops this low pretty frequently.
For Apple fans with an iPhone or MacBook, the Apple AirPods Max 2 are the best over-ear headphones. They offer great sound quality, effective noise cancellation, and good transparency modes. They are usually a little too pricey for our tastes compared to Sony and Bose options, but at $100 off, they look more tempting. Before you pull the trigger, they will likely drop by at least another $30 for Black Friday.
If you want to pair wireless earbuds with your iPhone and enjoy a seamless, feature-rich experience, you should snag the AirPods Pro 3. They are comfy, boast top-notch active noise cancellation, and can even translate some languages in real-time. That said, they are at this price often enough that I hesitate to call it a great deal, and they will likely drop by another $20 for Black Friday.
With a great camera, solid performance, and super slick software features, the Pixel 10 Pro is an excellent Android phone. It also has proper Qi2 support for fast wireless charging, but more importantly, the magnets inside make it easy to attach to docks and chargers. Its bigger sibling, the Pro XL, has been my daily driver for most of the last year, and it has served me well. It has frequently dropped to this price before, but I still think it’s a good deal. Best Buy has the best prices at the time of writing, at $699 for the Pro and $849 for the Pro XL, but they may dip lower for Black Friday.
This is one of our favorite 3-in-1 chargers for keeping your iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch charged up from a single outlet. The unique feature is its height adjustability, enabling it to pull double duty as a tripod for shooting video or FaceTime calls with family or friends. It has been on sale (close to half price) for a while now, but has never been lower than $60 at Best Buy. Snap it up while you still can.
Gadgets are too boring. I want more anthropomorphized devices in my life. Ugreen simply added a wee robot face to this wireless charger that changes its expression based on the charging status. I immediately like it more than all my old faceless chargers. The charging pad supports Qi2/MagSafe and tilts up to 70 degrees to reveal a second pad to charge AirPods or other wireless earbuds. It even has a USB-C port for a third gadget. At 40 percent off, this is the lowest price I’ve seen.
My pick for the best budget Wi-Fi router dips down to this price fairly often, but it’s a great deal for a Wi-Fi 7 router with four antennas, a 2.5-Gbps WAN, a 2.5-Gbps LAN, and three gigabit LAN ports. It’s only dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), so there’s no 6 GHz option, and performance is limited, but for a small home with modest demands, this is a tough price to beat.
I always associate Black Friday with footage of excited shoppers struggling to carry huge TVs out of big box stores. The reality is most Black Friday TV deals are on terrible models you should never buy. But this deal on LG’s 55-inch C6 OLED TV caught my eye. At $400 off the regular price, it is the cheapest it's ever been. The sale price on the 65-inch also makes it a better option than the entry-level LG B6 we just reviewed. Just make sure you pair it with a streaming device and disable the tracking.
This security camera records video at up to 2K at 30 frames per second, offers a 150-degree field of view, and connects directly to your Wi-Fi network. The Tapo app can detect motion (person, pet, vehicle) and enables you to set activity zones and privacy zones. The two-way audio is okay, and there’s a built-in alarm function. You can also slip a microSD card in for local recording. It lacks HDR, but it still earns a spot in our best outdoor security cameras guide. It has bounced between $90 and $65 for the last year, but it’s now down to $60.
It may not be one of the best video doorbells you can buy, but at this sale price, Blink’s latest wired doorbell is the cheapest option worth considering. It delivers reasonably good 2K footage and passable two-way audio, though it’s definitely less responsive than some other options on the market. If you want person detection and cloud storage, you’ll also need to spring for the subscription (from $3 a month). The battery version is also on sale at $39 ($41 off).
Permanent outdoor lights are a great way to avoid having to get up the ladder every holiday season. They offer simple white lighting, different colors, and also holiday-themed lighting effects. Eufy’s lights aren’t the brightest, but they hold up well against the competition and support Matter, so you can tie them into any smart home ecosystem. All lengths are on sale, but the 200-foot string has the best discount and is at its lowest price ever.
If you like to run an organized household, the best digital wall calendars are sure to appeal. You can use them to sync your digital calendars, create lists of chores, and plan your family meals. The Everblog HomeCal is our pick for folks who can’t stomach another subscription. It also works like a digital photo frame if you upload your snaps, and you can log into apps like Netflix and Spotify on it. This is the lowest we’ve seen it drop so far.
One of the best Dyson vacuums, the V15 Detect Absolute has two heads: a Digital Motorbar for carpets and rugs, and a Fluffy Optic for hard floors. This deal bundles it with the car cleaning kit and knocks $290 off the MSRP. Not only is that a third off, it’s cheaper than the regular V15 Detect on sale, but you get three additional accessories: a mini soft dusting brush, a stubborn-dirt brush, and a quick-release extension hose. This Dyson Week deal is available until October 31. Our favorite hair dryer, the Dyson Supersonic Nural Hair Dryer, is also on sale at $330 ($70 off).
A good laptop docking station lets you convert your laptop into a desktop for a comfier experience when you’re working from home, and this compact beauty from Belkin is one of our top picks. GaN technology (gallium nitride semiconductors, a faster, more compact alternative to silicon) lets Belkin pack more ports than you can shake a USB-C cable at, including 96-watt power delivery, three 4K display ports, a gigabit Ethernet port, and more. This deal equals the lowest price we’ve seen.
Learning about the wildlife in your garden can be a lot of fun, and the best smart bird feeders are an ideal way to see which feathered friends are in the area. The thoughtfully designed Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 has a removable 1.5-liter dual-hopper seed reservoir, is easy to clean, and boasts a solar roof to keep the camera charged up. It snaps 8-megapixel photos, captures 4K video, and includes a nifty AI bird-identification feature. We’ve seen it on sale before, but never this low.

New Delhi: The Himachal Pradesh Drugs Control Administration has asked patients and the public to stop using specific batches of medicines declared ‘not of standard quality’ (NSQ) by the central drug regulator, according to the two senior government officials familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by Mint.
The alert follows the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's (CDSCO) September 2026 report, which flagged 330 drug samples nationwide as sub-standard. Of these, 92 originated from Himachal Pradesh manufacturers.
State health authorities confirmed that 70 of the 92 failed critical efficacy parameters—specifically assay and dissolution tests—while 22 showed minor defects, such as labelling issues. To enforce compliance, the state has ordered 96 pharmaceutical facilities to halt manufacturing, either entirely or across specific sections, pending corrective actions. The state accounts for roughly a third of India's domestic drug supplies alongside large export volumes.
Himachal Pradesh is home to over 650 pharmaceutical manufacturing units, largely based in Baddi. About 70% of these are micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and 15-20% are large companies. The state accounts for about 35% of India's total domestic drug formulations, meaning every third drug on a chemist's shelf in India originates from Himachal Pradesh.
Widely prescribed medicines flagged
According to the CDSCO’s website, several widely prescribed medicines manufactured across Solan and Baddi in Himachal Pradesh were declared NSQ after failing critical active ingredient tests:
- Aspo Pharmaceuticals’ Namik-MR tablets, indicated for muscle pain or spasms failed in its aceclofenac content.
- Multiple respiratory formulations were also flagged, including Pharma Roots Healthcare’s AX Cold syrup, prescribed for allergic cough and congestion, which failed ambroxol hydrochloride levels.
- Similarly, Alventa Pharma’s Healtuss LS and Ultra Drugs Formulations’ Cufcott LS, both bronchodilator and expectorant syrups indicated for productive cough and asthma-related airway congestion, failed tests for ambroxol hydrochloride and levosalbutamol.
- Saar Biotech’s K-Coff-D syrup, used to treat dry cough, nasal blockage, and allergic cold symptoms, was cited for deficient phenylephrine hydrochloride content.
- In the topical analgesic category, Cent Cure’s Gone Gel, applied for joint pain, musculoskeletal aches, and sprains, failed the required standard for methyl salicylate.
State cites high volumes
“The volume of substandard samples must be evaluated in proportion to the state’s massive manufacturing output. Himachal Pradesh contributes to approximately one-third of domestic supplies, besides exporting big volumes of drug formulations,” Himachal Pradesh health secretary Ashish Singhmar said, pointing out that the state’s share of failed samples actually declined from 34% in July to 28% in September.
State drug controller Dr. Manish Kapoor said, “The drugs control administration, Himachal Pradesh, maintains a zero-tolerance approach towards the manufacture or distribution of substandard medicines and every effort is being made to ensure strict compliance of regulatory requirements. Following procedures laid down under the law, not only are the licences to manufacture drug formulations suspended/cancelled by the DCA HP, but at parallel, legal action(s) are also taken by the jurisdictions from where samples get drawn for the purpose of analysis/testing.”
“The enforcement is an ongoing administrative check-and-balance: these 96 actions particularly are not entirely on the latest NSQ list. It is an ongoing process where facilities are halted either due to NSQs or when other deficiencies are found during inspections. Increased detection is a positive indicator that our regulatory mechanism is strengthening," he added.
Dr. Kapoor also pointed out that drugs often degrade after leaving factories. "There are multiple stress factors in the distribution chain—storage conditions, temperature, humidity, and rough transport—that can cause quality failure. We cannot exclusively blame only manufacturers."
Queries sent to the health ministry and the Drugs Controller General of India on Tuesday remained unanswered at the time of publishing. Queries sent to Aspo Pharmaceuticals, Alventa Pharma, Ultra Drugs, also remained unanswered, while Pharma Roots Healthcare couldn't be contacted.

Tripurana Vijay is a lanky off-spinner with an uncomplicated action. He gets the ball to drift and dip without losing accuracy for long. Combined with the turn on offer, these qualities make him a tricky bowler to face.
On Tuesday, he offered a glimpse of his skills, claiming three wickets against Chhattisgarh as Andhra looked to take a first-innings lead after posting just 231 in their Ranji Trophy fixture here at the DVR Ground.
For much of his cricketing journey, however, Vijay had little idea about the finer aspects of the game. Hailing from Tekkali in Andhra Pradesh’s Srikakulam district, he started playing cricket on the only cement pitch his town had.
“There is only one net and one cement wicket. There is nothing beyond that. I used to bowl and bat there only. I had no idea about turf wickets,” Vijay told Sportstar.
It was only after joining an academy in Vizianagaram that he encountered a turf wicket and gradually learnt more about the sport he was preparing to pursue professionally.
“I learnt about strength training, fitness, running and everything else. Before that, I only knew how to bowl. I didn’t know much about other aspects of cricket or how professional cricket worked. I got to know all that after joining the academy,” the 25-year-old said.
With the support of his coaches, Vikram Verma and C.D. Thomson, whom he met in Vizianagaram, and his family, particularly his father, Vijay began his journey.
“I started playing cricket because of my father. He used to play cricket and had a lot of interest in the game, but unfortunately, he couldn’t continue,” Vijay said.
“To date, there have been no restrictions from my parents. They have been very supportive of me playing sport. They never told me that I should only focus on my studies or take up a job,” he added.
In four years of senior cricket, Vijay has played 19 First-Class matches, taking 65 wickets. He has also featured in 14 List A matches and 11 T20s – performances that have drawn the attention of selectors and scouts.
At the IPL 2026 auction, Delhi Capitals picked him up for his base price of INR 30 lakh. In May this year, he made his league debut.
“Playing in the IPL is a dream for every player, and representing a team in the biggest tournament in India, alongside the greatest players, is always a great feeling. I worked a lot for it, and by God’s grace, I got the chance,” he said.
In his only appearance, against Rajasthan Royals, Vijay came close to dismissing teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, only for the batter to be dropped off his bowling.
“I was a bit unlucky not to get that wicket, but that’s fine. It’s part of the game, and I’ll just keep working hard and move forward,” he said.

After the IPL, Vijay featured in the Duleep Trophy, where he took five wickets for South Zone in the final his side lost. He subsequently received his maiden India A call-up while attending a Delhi Capitals camp, replacing Vyshak Vijaykumar for the two four-day matches against Australia A.
