The story so far
An initiative launched by Keralam government to make the treatment for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) accessible to more patients is now courting controversy.
SMA is a rare, life-threatening genetic disorder that progressively weakens muscles, severely impairing both mobility and respiratory function. While a complete cure remains elusive, the launch of Risdiplam, marketed as Evrysdi by Roche Pharmaceuticals, the first at-home, oral treatment for SMA, gave hope to thousands of SMA patients. Risdiplam was found to have a significant effect on the progression of the disease, by slowing down motor degeneration, improving physical milestones and stabilising respiratory function.
Risdiplam was launched in India in July 2021, making it the first and only approved drug in the country to manage SMA. But the drug’s astronomical cost made it inaccessible to most families.
Keralam, which has been giving Risdiplam free of cost to eligible children since 2022, made a switch to the less expensive generic version of the drug in October this year . But since then, a section of parents of children living with SMA children have urged the government to switch back to the expensive, branded version.
Last week, when the generic drug was dispensed for the first time at SAT hospital, a Centre of Excellence for Rare Diseases in Thiruvananthapuram, a sticker on the bottle which said “Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials” reopened the branded versus generic debate and a new allegation, that drugs meant for clinical trials were being used on children
How Keralam began SMA treatment
Keralam was the first State to give Risdiplam free of cost through government hospitals in 2022 and an SMA clinic was subsequently opened at SAT hospital. Though initially Risdiplam was given free only to children under 12, in 2026 the government announced an extension of coverage to genetically confirmed SMA Type 2 patients up to age 25, with ₹30 crore allocated in the State budget for this. However, as of now, 109 Type 1 and 2 children with SMA below the age of 12 are being given Risdiplam, free.
Risdiplam, under its trade name Evrysdi, used to cost ₹6.3 lakh for a bottle (current price ₹4.44 lakhs), which the State was getting at a negotiated price of ₹5.4 lakh per bottle. Under the patient assistance programme, Roche used to give 11 bottles free of cost to the State for every four bottles it purchased. The State’s annual requirement was estimated at around 2,500 bottles and the annual financial commitment was around ₹23 crore. The State, therefore, was up against enormous cumulative expenditure as more children became eligible and existing patients required continued treatment.
The decision to switch to generic
A technical experts committee in Keralam met several times to evaluate if the generic alternative, Natsmart, which has all regulatory approvals, and which was ready for commercial distribution in October 2025, could replace Roche’s Evrysdi. Natco Pharma, through a historic Delhi High Court verdict, had won the right to marker the generic alternative of Risdiplam at a dramatically reduced price of ₹15,900 per bottle, against Roche’s Rs. 6.3 lakhs per bottle.
A bottle of Evrysdi on which Roche holds a patent, typically lasts 12 days, meaning the annual maintenance cost for a patient would amount to a crushing ₹60-70 lakh. With Natsmart, the generic alternative, the cost would be under ₹5 lakh. In February 2026, the Keralam government gave the go ahead for Natsmart, and purchase processes were initiated.
What are parents’ concerns?
Parents and advocacy groups including the Cure SMA Foundation of India claim that the branded medication, Evrysdi, has a proven, long-term track record of safety and efficacy, while the new generic version lacks dedicated human bioequivalence or long-term clinical studies specific to paediatric patients. They claim that a sudden switch to an unverified or less effective generic formula could reverse the critical motor and survival progress already achieved by children who are currently stable on the original drug. They have been continuously petitioning the government asking that their children be allowed to continue on Evrysdi.
What do doctors say?
Public health experts have hailed the government’s decision to switch to the generic drug. They say that arguments challenging the efficacy of the generic formulation and alleging a lack of ‘bioavailability’ are entirely unscientific and baseless.
Bioavailability denotes the rate and extent to which an administered pharmaceutical substance enters systemic circulation through the digestive tract. A bioequivalence study normally compares the rate and extent of absorption of the generic with the reference product. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises this as an important way to establish interchangeability. However, bioequivalence studies are not required for every generic medicine. The WHO’s guidance on generic medicines explicitly recognises circumstances in which equivalence studies can be waived. One such circumstance is when the generic and reference products are pharmaceutically equivalent oral solutions containing the same active ingredient at the same molar concentration, subject to the applicable requirements for excipients.
In this case, both products contain Risdiplam. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) approved Natsmart and the regulator’s position is that a bioequivalence study is not required for this particular oral solution. Public health experts also say that the absence of a conventional bioequivalence study does not necessarily mean the regulator approved the drug without adequate evidence. A regulator may accept a scientifically-justified waiver.
Doctors also point out that Natsmart is being prescribed by many premier teaching hospitals in the country and several patients are already using it in Keralam too, for the last five months, without any complaints.
Public health is about maximising access to people, and unless credible scientific evidence demonstrates that the approved generic is less safe or less effective than the original molecule, regulatory approval should remain the primary basis for procurement decisions in publicly-funded health programmes, experts have argued.
The current controversy
The current controversy centres around an alarm raised by parents of children with SMA, after they pointed out that the bottle of Natsmart dispensed to them was labelled, ‘Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials’. Though the authorities clarified later that these were drug sample bottles they were forced to source directly from Natco and not part of the government supply (which was delayed), the issue has become something for Opposition parties, particularly the CPI(M), to latch on to. It has also served to perpetuate fears and misgivings about the generic drug among SMA families.
What is happening at present?
SAT Hospital authorities, who are responsible for the SMA clinic, have now decided to hold a meeting of families to assuage their concerns. They say that several meetings had been held earlier too, to reassure parents about the switch from Evrysdi to Natsmart. However, the new controversy over ‘clinical trial’ drugs may have undone some of the previous work. The labelling issue is clearly separate from the concerns about the switch to generic medicine and the families’ demand for scientific evidence and transparent communication is valid, authorities admit.

Discord public server messages may be soon searchable on Google, but you can opt out
The platform’s Discoverable Servers are about to get a lot more discoverable.
Discord is making a policy change that will further increase the visibility of conversations on its largest public servers. On November 16, the platform's Discoverable Servers will all be getting Server Web Pages. These hubs will display some basic information about the server, including a description and summaries of discussions happening on their public channels. By mid-December, Discord said that messages on posted to those channels could start appearing word-for-word on both the Server Web Pages and in search engine results. Neither the channel summaries nor the individual channel messages will display the poster's username or avatar.
The reason Discord gave for the change is to make it easier for information from these communities to be surfaced in web searches. In other words, you might start seeing Discord pages and messages the same way you'd find a Reddit thread among search hits.
This change is limited to Discoverable Servers, the large communities of at least 1,000 members where no invitation is required to join. Private servers, DMs and Group DMs will remain private. But considering Discord just weathered blowback over its implementation of age verification policies, this decision could raise new questions around how the platform handles privacy concerns.
Server admins for those Discoverable Servers can take action starting now to opt-out channels from being included in their eventual web presence. And individual users can also choose to keep their Discoverable Server posts from being indexed via the Data and Privacy section of Discord's User Settings. In select markets — the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia and South Korea — channel messages will be off by default to honor local regulations, so for those regions users will have to manually opt in to the feature. Teen Discord users are also excluded and do not have the option to turn on channel messages until they are of adult age.

After two months of discomfort, a man in South Korea went to an eye clinic where doctors pulled 11 living, wriggling worms from his eyes. They apparently made the most of their time on the man’s peepers; at the time of extraction, many of the female worms were pregnant. The man narrowly avoided having them spew their loads of living larvae directly into his eyes.
The man in this case was a 71-year-old crop farmer. He told doctors that for the previous two months he had the sensation of having something stuck in both his eyes, which were also red and blurry. When ophthalmologists took a look, they quickly saw the problem: multiple mobile, whitish roundworms. His eyes were not in good shape either, as one might expect. The blood vessels in the membrane over the eye, the conjunctiva, were enlarged, making his eyes look red. And the cells of his cornea—the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye—had eroded, potentially after the helminths’ hanky-panky.
According to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the doctors gave the man a topical treatment to numb his eyes and then began plucking out the worms one by one with fine forceps. They collected 11 adult worms, which ranged in size from 11 to 22 mm.
Examining the worms under a microscope, the doctors identified them as Thelazia callipaeda nematodes, which are widespread across Asia and have also established in parts of Europe. These parasites primarily infest the eyes of cats and dogs but can sometimes make their way into human eyes inadvertently.

Advertising agency Blink Digital India has recently sued Meta and its India entity Facebook India Online Services Private Limited for a compensation of about ₹1,000 Cr over four ‘Meta Business Manager’ accounts that were disabled by the latter on its platform. As per the court’s documents, Blink Digital filed its complaint with the Bombay High Court on September 17 (Thursday). The ad agency is seeking restoration of its accounts and compensation for the disabling of its four accounts. For context, Meta Business Manager is a free backend dashboard that lets businesses and agencies securely manage their Facebook Pages, Instagram accounts, ad accounts, pixels, and team permissions in one place. Advocate representing Meta, Janak Dwarakadas, has been granted time of two weeks to file an affidavit in reply opposing the interim application of Blink Digital. Following which, the court has allowed a week’s time for the advertising company to file rejoinder to Meta’s affidavit. The case’s hearing is set for October 12 (Monday). Blink Digital India, an advertising agency founded in 2009, is headed by Dooj Ramchandani and works with brands on digital campaigns, websites, apps, social media, immersive experiences, games, video and other technology-led marketing initiatives. Some of its prominent clients include KFC, ITC, Star Sports, Vh1, Condé Nast, Moët Hennessy, Viber and Puma. For agencies such as Blink Digital, Meta’s business manager platform serves as an operational layer for managing clients’ advertising infrastructure, while campaigns themselves are created and managed via the Meta Ads Manager. Disabling this resulted in ad campaigns associated with Blink Digital to stop running, also leading to the loss of access to advertising features, including the ability to create or manage advertising activity through the affected portfolio. The development adds on to the growing legal scrutiny of Meta in India in recent times. Most recently, the tech major came under heavy regulatory scrutiny over instances of child sexual abuse content on its platforms. Meta has agreed to report such instances to the central government moving forward. Beyond regulatory hurdles, Meta was also recently sued by media giant Zee over copyright infringement. Zee alleged that users were uploading and monetising its IP content without approval. While the HC has directed Meta to remove the allegedly infringing content, it declined to block the Facebook accounts in question at this stage. Earlier in May, the Delhi HC passed a John Doe order directing Meta to take down multiple Facebook URLs allegedly hosting Zee Entertainment Enterprises Limited’s (ZEEL) unauthorised content.

Geneva – His Excellency Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, today signed several funding agreements totaling € 25.5 million to support critical health priorities.
The agreements include € 4.5 million of funding for the Core Voluntary Contribution Account (CVCA) of WHO; these are fully flexible funds which allow WHO to allocate resources to key priorities outlined in its General Programme of Work. An additional € 15 million will be used to deliver on specific key priorities, such as One Health, the advancement of universal health coverage, and primary health care, communicable and noncommunicable diseases, the medical countermeasure initiative, and the country readiness strengthening through WHO’s office in Lyon.
A large part of the contribution (€ 6 million) is aimed at covering the humanitarian response on several fronts: € 2 million will go towards enhancing mental health initiatives in Ukraine; € 0.35 million is to support the response to the cholera outbreak in Malawi; € 1 million will support WHO’s humanitarian response in Gaza, with an additional € 2 million dedicated to strengthening the technical and human activities of the WHO Office in the occupied Palestinian territory. Finally, € 0.65 million will go to the Contingency Fund for Emergencies, to be used as needs arise.
“As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health. France's financial contributions and agreements, signed today, provide flexibility and align well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, power and perform for health” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.
France’s WHO Framework Agreement for the period 2020-2025 ensures sustainable funding for priority health programmes, aligned with WHO priorities.
Some of the joint 2022-2023 collaboration priorities include the work of the WHO Academy, based in Lyon, stronger health systems towards universal health coverage, health emergencies – in particular the International Health Regulations (IHR) and health emergencies preparedness – and reducing health inequalities.
These priorities align with the France Global Health Strategy 2023-2027, published in October 2023.
“Committed to global health, France supports the WHO’s action in crises and for the benefit of the most vulnerable,” said Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations.
In 2020-2021, the Republic of France contributed over US$ 143 million to WHO, (including assessed and voluntary contributions), with 76% of the contributions in flexible and thematic funds. Flexible funds allow WHO to assign resources when and where they are needed most, ensuring that key priorities are funded, and a better flow of funds, enabling a more agile delivery of WHO’s objectives as per the General Programme of Work.

AI infrastructure startup Simplismart has raised $14 Mn (around ₹133 Cr) in a Series B funding round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC, Micromax, and angel investors. Dallas Venture Capital invested close to $5 Mn in the round, cofounder and CEO Amritanshu Jain told Inc42. Simplismart plans to use the fresh capital to further develop its AI inference platform, deepen partnerships with cloud providers and sovereign AI players, and expand across North America and other global markets. AI inference is the process of running trained models to generate responses or predictions. Founded in 2022 by Jain and Devansh Ghatak, Simplismart builds the software layer between AI models and GPU infrastructure. Its inference engine lets businesses configure how models run based on their speed, cost, and performance requirements, while its orchestration platform manages deployment and scaling across cloud and on-premises infrastructure. “We have spent four years building the software layer between the model and the GPU, helping customers optimise how their workloads are deployed and operated. This funding will allow us to take that platform to more enterprises and cloud providers globally,” Jain said. The funding will also support the development of a dynamic GPU scheduling layer to match AI workloads with available computing capacity across regions and time zones, cofounder and CTO Ghatak said. How Simplismart Makes Money Jain said Simplismart offers three deployment and pricing models: shared endpoints, dedicated endpoints, and bring-your-own-compute deployments. Under the shared endpoint model, customers pay based on token consumption, without a minimum fee. Dedicated endpoints allow customers to rent GPU infrastructure along with Simplismart’s optimisation software, with charges linked to GPU usage and runtime. The bring-your-own-compute model caters to businesses that want to run workloads on their own infrastructure to meet data and regulatory requirements, particularly in sectors such as banking, financial services, and insurance. For its cloud-provider offering, Simplismart works with NVIDIA to help providers deploy and manage AI infrastructure at scale. The startup does not own the computing infrastructure. Instead, its software enables cloud providers to offer managed AI services under their own brands using their existing GPUs. The startup said this offering is already being used by Yotta, with Simplismart powering the serverless inference layer of its Shakti Studio platform. This allows customers to run AI models without managing the underlying inference infrastructure themselves. Around 55% of Simplismart’s revenue comes from the US, with the remainder generated in India, Jain said. Its customers include HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna, and Ema, which use its platform to run video, voice, multimodal, and enterprise AI workloads. Simplismart said its annualised revenue run rate grew 14X over the past six months. Prior to this round, Simplismart raised $7 Mn in a Series A round led by Accel in October 2024. The fundraise comes amid growing investment in India’s AI infrastructure ecosystem. Tata Communications yesterday announced plans to invest $400 Mn to $450 Mn to build 10,000 km of AI-ready connectivity infrastructure across India. The proposed network will connect major data centres and AI hubs to support demand for high-speed, low-latency connectivity.

The 56th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu examines early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, concerns about the reliability of cancer research and challenges in accessing treatment for children with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss how Alzheimer’s disease can affect younger people, the implications of unreliable cancer research, and concerns raised by families over a generic SMA drug.
The episode begins with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and how the condition can present differently in younger people. The discussion looks at changes in memory, behaviour and everyday functioning, and the challenges of recognising the disease when symptoms appear earlier in life.
Another segment examines cancer research articles flagged for suspected links to paper mills. These businesses produce and sell research papers, sometimes using fabricated data, manipulated images or other questionable research practices. The discussion looks at how unreliable publications can undermine scientific progress, affect future research and complicate efforts to assess the evidence behind medical findings. It also highlights the need for careful investigation, as an article being flagged for suspected links to a paper mill does not, by itself, establish research misconduct.
The episode also looks at concerns raised by families of children living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in Keralam over a generic drug used to treat the rare genetic condition. The concerns have brought questions about the safety, quality and effectiveness of medicines into focus. The discussion examines the importance of reliable information about treatment, regulatory oversight and the challenges families face in accessing medicines for rare diseases, where treatment costs can be a significant barrier.
The final segment revisits the history of Alzheimer’s disease through the case of Auguste Deter. In 1901, German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer began documenting the symptoms of Deter, a 51-year-old woman who experienced changes in memory, behaviour and her ability to carry out everyday activities. Her symptoms differed from cases he had typically encountered. After her death in 1906, Alzheimer examined her brain and identified changes that contributed to the understanding of the condition later named after him. The segment explores Deter’s experience and the role of clinical observation and patient documentation in the history of medical research.

India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions
- Published
India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday.
Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors.
Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October.
Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy.
The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.
But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business.
More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition from Musk.
For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution, spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy.
Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed.
This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband.
Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India".
But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs.
"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management.
"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed."
Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note.
The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede.
"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind".
For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available.
While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services.
India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones.
Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise.
All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user.
"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global.
The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.
But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades.
The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors.
Dhirubhai Ambani, the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s.
In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company.
And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence.
"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC.
"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

James Anderson set to continue playing career in Italy with Napoli Knights in the Italia T10 league
James Anderson is now set to captain and co-own the Napoli Knights, one of six teams in the Italia T10 league; after international retirement, England great Anderson continued playing for Lancashire and captained the county this year but Lancashire elected not to renew his contract
Wednesday 28 October 2026 09:04, UK
James Anderson is set to continue his playing career in Italy.
He will captain and co-own the Napoli Knights, one of six teams in the Italia T10 league as the 44-year-old extends his career after being released by Lancashire, his club of 25 years.
Anderson, who played more than 400 times for England across all formats and took nearly 1,000 wickets, is a big name to join the format.
The Italia T10 league is a 10-over-a-side competition, which takes place over 12 days at the Roma Cricket Ground from November 18.
It was created by Nadeem Shahid, a former professional cricketer, and Aamir Akhtar, who helped set up the Everest Premier League in his native Nepal.
High-profile players such as Chris Gayle, Shaun Marsh and Dawid Malan will also feature, joined by members of the Italian national side who impressed earlier this year when they narrowly lost to England at the T20 World Cup.
"The potential for cricket in Italy made it a big draw," Shahid told Reuters. "One of the things that made it attractive is the Italian Olympic Committee beginning to take it seriously after it became an Olympic sport."
He noted: "Tickets will be free for all the matches, and there will be coaching clinics on the sidelines."
Anderson's company, Activate Sport & Leisure, will be involved in some of those clinics, as Italy looks to develop homegrown talent capable of competing at Olympic level by the time of the 2032 Games in Brisbane.
"Of course, we want Napoli Knights to be competitive and challenge for the title, but we also want to contribute to something that continues to grow well beyond the tournament itself," Anderson said.

Justice delayed: Acknowledging women pioneers in science
For a discipline so wedded to reason and fact as science is, it has fiendishly guarded its gender bias. Over centuries, pioneering women in science have been ignored, their achievements overlooked or usurped by male colleagues, their names left out of scientific publications; they have been underpaid and undervalued, denied promotions and advancements in careers, sometimes consigned to housekeeping roles about the office in order to keep their jobs.
In a compilation of such women in scientific research through the ages, Rosalind Franklin would probably be right on top of the list. It was Franklin’s X-ray diffraction image that lore says, was crucial to discovering the DNA’s double helix structure, enabling advances in genetics and molecular biology, with vast applications in medicine. And yet, when the Nobel Prize for Physiology in 1962 was announced, the names on that list were Watson and Crick, shared with Wilkins. It was decades before her true role in this path-breaking discovery came to be known to the world.
Today, Franklin stands testimony to the power of women, as she is representative of the ‘woman wronged by science’, but not just that – her achievements in science (in other fields) have broken new ground that researchers have since travelled on. As we unveil the achievements of women in science, particularly those whom their present refused to acknowledge, it is important to get her story out there, more so since she was vilified and mocked by the very men who benefitted from her work.
At King’s College
Franklin was a British chemist and X-ray crystallographer. In 1951, she joined the team at King’s College London, biophysicists led by John Randall, and Maurice Wilkins as his deputy (who would later share the Nobel prize), that were using X-ray diffraction to study the structure of the molecule, recount Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort, two researchers looking into the past of Watson and Crick to craft their biographies, in an article in Nature.
Franklin, had already been trained in this technique, having used it earlier to study the structure of coal, which she advanced by many lengths with her work. Cobb and Comfort detail in their article: “Franklin was able to exploit a discovery that Wilkins had made earlier — DNA in solution could take two forms, what she called the crystalline or A form, and the paracrystalline or B form. Franklin found that she could convert A into B simply by raising the relative humidity in the specimen chamber; lowering it again restored the crystalline A form.” A B form X-ray image it was that provided great clarity on the actual structure of the DNA.
Photograph 51
The distorted story of Franklin’s role was spread, thanks in good measure, by Watson’s best selling book The Double Helix. In the book, Watson infantilised Franklin, claiming that she did not realise the importance of the photo she took – the life altering, or life-explaining Photograph 51. Let’s refer to what Kings College London records about this photograph: “Photograph 51” is an X-ray diffraction image of DNA taken by Rosalind Franklin, together with her PhD student Raymond Gosling, at King’s College London in May 1952. In fact, the camera was set up to take the photograph on Friday 2 May and it was developed on Tuesday 6 May: as Franklin reported in her lab notebook, the DNA was exposed to X-rays for a total of 62 hours to take Photograph 51.”
Photograph 51 was reportedly infinitely clearer than any of the earlier images, and also with other data from Rosalind’s work during her time at King’s it was possible to make the leap to the double helix structure, notes the college’s website. This entire body of work was key to building the structure of DNA but never properly acknowledged until much later, after her death. Records have it down that James Watson was shown this photograph (without her permission) and it reportedly spurred both him and Francis Crick to attempt to build a model, which was then feted across the world as a path-breaking discovery.
Cobb and Comfort however challenge Watson’s narrative: “[It] contains an absurd presumption. It implies that Franklin, the skilled chemist, could not understand her own data, whereas he, a crystallographic novice, apprehended it immediately.” While implying that the whole story constructed around the Eureka moment from Photograph 51 was probably an exaggeration, they add: “Moreover, everyone, even Watson, knew it was impossible to deduce any precise structure from a single photograph — other structures could have produced the same diffraction pattern... In fact, it was other data from Franklin and Wilkins that proved crucial, and even then, what really happened was less malicious than is widely assumed.” However, malice, wilful sexism, or a casual miss, the fact remains that Wilkins was co-named for the Nobel, while Franklin was not.
On the website of the Rosalind Franklin Institute, set up in Franklin’s honour Professor Patricia Fara, president of the British Society for the History of Science (2016-18), Clare College, University of Cambridge, writes on the life and work of Rosalind Franklin: “Since her early death at the age of 37 [of cancer], Rosalind Franklin has become mythologised as the victim of male prejudice, the unsung heroine who took the crucial X-ray photograph enabling James Watson and Francis Crick to build their double helix model of DNA, and was unjustly deprived of a Nobel Prize. She would neither have recognised nor endorsed this soundbite description. Franklin regarded herself first and foremost not as a woman, but as a scientist, and her DNA research occupied a relatively brief period in her successful career working on a variety of topics. In particular, on top of her famous investigations into DNA, she also made foundational contributions to modern understandings of coal, graphite and viruses.”
Since her death however, Franklin’s story has been freed from the cloisters it was trapped in. It has traversed the mythical seven seas and seven mountains to sound in the corners of the world. Several honours have since been heaped on her, in recognition of her immense contributions to science in a short life. Not least of them, was a 1989 Swedish stamp features an image of the DNA double helix based on Photograph 51.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Tony Blair’s former communications guru, Alastair Campbell, says the UK political system was too quick to revert to overheated rhetoric and polarisation after attacks on MPs, urging politicians to “re-win the argument for democratic politics”.
More than a week after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly targeted in an attack outside her electorate office in northern Victoria, causing her to lose both legs, Campbell said the tenor of political debate in Australia should better reflect Haines’ own approach.
Speaking to the Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast on Wednesday, the commentator said the killings of British MPs Jo Cox, David Amess and former politician Ann Widdecombe had not brought about lasting change in political culture.
“They were followed by everybody saying the right thing about how our political debate culture had to change, about how we had to address online hate and polarisation, all this stuff,” he said.
“But it didn’t take long before we kind of got right back into it. So I think it is about how we genuinely try and generate a different way of talking to each other and about each other now.”
A 43-year-old man has been charged over the alleged attack on Haines and the incident continues to be investigated by police.
The co-host of popular podcast The Rest is Politics, Campbell said Haines’ eventual return to parliament would help bring about change.
“It’s very rare these days that an individual act or incident lasts more than half a news cycle, and so we just move on. I think remembering is so important.
“In a way, the fact that she is still with us and is going to still be part of the political debate, maybe that will help people … that people will see that that is the consequence of the actions that were taken against her.”
A former journalist, Campbell is the author of more than 20 books, including diaries documenting his years working inside 10 Downing Street.
He is due to visit Australia for a speaking tour next month.
Campbell said politicians and the media should reflect on how they speak to everyday people, and why their professions are so poorly trusted.
“It’s made more difficult at the moment because you’ve got Donald Trump in America as the loudest, most talked about politician on the planet, and he represents a lot of the things that I think we don’t want in our politics.
“We’ve got to re-win the argument for democratic politics because it’s under a lot of pressure right now,” he said.
Discussing the rise of populist politics, Campbell said the world was still struggling to grasp the effects of the 2008 global financial crisis.
“If I think of one thing that maybe ties the rise of Trump to Brexit, to the protests that we’re seeing in different parts of Europe, I think is that we haven’t really come to terms with the consequences of the financial crisis, and the sense that there was socialism for the banks who caused it, and austerity for the people, and the people who are still struggling to see their living standards rise.
“That, ultimately I think, is a big driver of what the Americans call affordability, what we call cost of living, just the sense that people don’t feel that they’re able to get on.”
Campbell revealed he occasionally watches clips of Paul Keating’s parliamentary attacks as Australia’s prime minister in the 1990s.
The bestselling author’s latest book is Persevilience: The Word the World Needs Now, published by Allen and Unwin.

Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
- Published
Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".
The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.
Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".
Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.
Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level – meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.
The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.
Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.
Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.
This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.
The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.
Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

For people living with peripheral artery disease (PAD), walking even short distances or doing routine household tasks can become difficult because of leg pain. The condition develops when arteries supplying blood to the legs become narrow, usually because fatty deposits build up along their walls. With less blood reaching the muscles, walking can cause pain, cramps or heaviness that ease with rest. In advanced cases, pain may persist even when a person is sitting or lying down, and poor circulation can lead to wounds that do not heal.
Treatment can be challenging too because movement is an important part of managing PAD, while pain makes it difficult to stay active. Structured exercise, medicines and control of risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and high blood pressure can help manage the condition. When blood flow is severely reduced, procedures may be needed to prevent damage to the feet and legs. PAD can also affect overall cardiovascular health, increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Managing pain
Pain, cramps, heaviness in the calf or thigh that develop during walking and ease with rest are known as intermittent claudication. This happens when narrowed arteries cannot supply enough blood to meet the muscles’ increased needs during activity.
Venu S., consultant vascular surgeon, Prashanth Hospitals, Chennai, says structured walking programmes can help patients gradually increase the distance they can walk. Patients are generally advised to walk until the discomfort becomes moderate, rest until it settles and then resume walking. Sessions commonly last 30 to 45 minutes and take place several times a week, with supervision where possible.
He says patients who follow a structured programme for about three months may be able to walk twice as far, or more, before pain begins. The pace and duration should suit each patient’s ability. Those who find walking difficult may need an adapted exercise programme under medical supervision.
Balaji V., senior consultant, vascular surgery, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai, says quitting smoking, eating a healthy diet, staying physically active and controlling blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol are also important parts of treatment.
Exercise should not mean pushing through severe pain. Pain that does not settle with rest needs medical assessment. Pain in the feet or toes while resting, particularly at night, can indicate a serious reduction in blood flow and requires prompt medical attention.
Diagnosis and treatment
Diagnosis usually begins with a review of symptoms and medical history, followed by an examination of the legs and feet, including checking the pulses. Doctors may measure the ankle-brachial index (ABI), which compares blood pressure at the ankle with that in the arm, to assess blood flow. A Doppler ultrasound scan can help identify narrowed arteries and assess circulation. In patients with severe symptoms or wounds that do not heal, a CT angiogram may be needed to locate the blockage and plan treatment.
Medicines aim to relieve symptoms, slow the progression of arterial disease and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. Antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin or clopidogrel help prevent blood clots. Statins lower cholesterol and help stabilise fatty deposits in artery walls. Medicines to control blood pressure and diabetes are also important. Cilostazol can help some patients with walking-related pain walk farther before symptoms begin, but it is not suitable for people with heart failure. Select patients may need additional medicines to reduce cardiovascular and limb-related risks.
Experts say treatment often needs to continue long term, even when symptoms improve. Patients should not stop or change prescribed medicines without consulting their doctor.
Diabetes can damage nerves and reduce sensation in the feet, allowing cuts and wounds to go unnoticed. It can also affect smaller arteries, making some blockages harder to treat. High blood pressure and cholesterol contribute to arterial damage and the build-up of fatty deposits. Kidney disease can cause calcium to build up in artery walls and delay wound healing. Heart disease can occur alongside PAD because both may result from the same underlying process.
During follow-up, doctors assess changes in walking distance and symptoms and may repeat ABI measurements or Doppler scans to check blood flow. Blood tests can help monitor cholesterol, blood sugar and kidney function.
Preventing complications
When symptoms remain disabling despite medicines and exercise, doctors may consider a procedure to widen the narrowed artery. The decision depends on the location and extent of the blockage, the severity of symptoms and the patient’s overall health.
Angioplasty uses a small balloon to widen a narrowed artery. A stent may be placed to help keep it open. Experts say newer techniques can also help treat complex blockages.
Intravascular lithotripsy uses shock waves delivered through a specialised balloon to modify heavy calcium deposits in the artery, making it easier to widen the vessel. Atherectomy devices can remove fatty deposits in selected cases, while thrombectomy devices are used to remove blood clots. The appropriate method depends on the type and location of the blockage.
For extensive disease, bypass surgery creates an alternative route for blood to reach the affected part of the leg. The choice between a procedure performed through a blood vessel and surgery depends on the blockage, the patient’s condition and the likely benefits and risks.
Pain at rest, wounds that do not heal or gangrene can indicate that the leg is at risk and require urgent medical assessment. A wound that has not healed within two weeks, a cold or discoloured foot, or a black patch on a toe or heel should not be ignored. Sudden, severe leg pain accompanied by paleness, coldness, numbness or weakness is a medical emergency because it may indicate a sudden blockage of an artery.
Regular foot checks are particularly important for people with diabetes, who may not feel an injury developing. Recognising worsening symptoms and seeking timely care can help preserve mobility and prevent serious damage to the feet and legs.

Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.
The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.
“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.
Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.
Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.
The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.
Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.
“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.
Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.
To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said.
Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.

Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according to a study published on Thursday in Science.
The model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an “orchestrator” that organises how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report.
Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient’s symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.
With the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reaching a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the physical exam. Based on what it learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate.
All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an interview.
Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at “working up” the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions.
Assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple-choice questions, the researchers said.
“AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those,” said Dr. Dominic King, the corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, whose team is developing the new technology.
“But of course, that’s not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary.”
The researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do.
“We’re not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We’re also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up,” said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health.
In a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, the researchers will next test the tool’s ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms.

On Sunday, Brazil’s incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the presidential runoff election, making him the President of the South American country for the fourth time. The leftist leader finished second in the first round of presidential elections on October 4, with 45.16% of the vote, while Flávio Bolsonaro was the clear winner, with 47.03% of voters choosing him. But just over 20 days later, the 80-year-old flipped the script and retained his post against all odds. Lula’s win was decisive, with more than 64 million votes compared to just under 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%. According to the Associated Press, analysts credit this turnaround to the additional 14.1 million voters who turned out for the second-round election, including those who had voted for other candidates in the first round. The channel shared pre-written messages for supporters to forward, along with tasks such as amplifying campaign videos and promoting hashtags. The channel’s rapid growth also helped the campaign compete in digital spaces where Bolsonaro’s supporters had been seen as having an advantage. According to BBC Brazil, his round-the-clock digital mobilisation, which used viral videos, hashtags, and a 24-hour livestream on the eve of the runoff, helped counter Bolsonaro's strong digital presence. The campaign clicked, and on October 20, Lula reached 200 million interactions on social media since Oct. 5, while Bolsonaro had 54 million, according to data from the Projeto Brief agency in a study conducted for the local newspaper Estadão. But since the start of the second round, the incumbent’s profiles have received around 111 million interactions, compared with Bolsonaro’s 31 million. The Congress suffered its biggest setback in Karnataka, where the BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four legislative council seats
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday took a swipe at the Congress over its performance in the recent legislative council elections across four states. Congress failed to secure a single victory in polls held across Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra.Taking to X, the Prime Minsiter wrote, "MLC elections in 28 seats across 4 big states - Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar and Karnataka. Elections held using ballot papers. Guess how many seats Congress won?"
Congress Rajya Sabha member Pawan Khera hit back at PM Modi, asking him to demonstrate confidence in the BJP’s prowess by committing to ballot paper voting in all future Lok Sabha and state assembly elections.In a post on X, Khera demanded the suspension of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the restoration of 13.3 crore voters "deleted illegally"."If Narendra Modi is so confident that EVMs have no bearing on election results, let him prove his confidence in the BJP’s electoral prowess through action, not rhetoric," he wrote."1. Commit to conducting all Lok Sabha and upcoming Vidhan Sabha elections by ballot paper going forward.
2. Suspend SIR and restore the 13.3 crore voters illegally deleted from the electoral rolls. 3. Terminate Gyanesh Gupta. 4. Repeal the law that gives life long immunity to Gyanesh Gupta," Khera wrote.
BJP national president Nitin Nabin also took a dig at the grand old party, saying the party would continue to struggle for survival under Rahul Gandhi's leadership. Addressing a gathering during the BJP's ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakta Hatao’ march in Delhi, Nabin said PM Narendra Modi would return to the Red Fort after the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.Nabin also accused the Congress of opposing the cleaning of electoral rolls because it was distressed by efforts to remove alleged infiltrators.“There are voters who have died but whose names remain on the electoral rolls. There are also people whose names appear in the voter lists at two places. There are crores of such voters whose names are registered more than once, while the whereabouts of many others cannot be traced. This is what is called a ‘ghost voter list’,” he said.The remark came after the Congress drew a blank in Karnataka, where the BJP-Janata Dal (Secular) alliance swept all four legislative council seats despite the Congress being in power in the state. The results also saw the Congress lose its sitting Bengaluru Teachers’ constituency to the JD(S).The prime minister's reference to ballot papers comes amid the opposition's repeated allegations of irregularities in electronic voting machines (EVMs) and demands for greater transparency in the electoral process.The Congress suffered its biggest setback in Karnataka, where the BJP retained three seats and the JD(S) wrested Bengaluru Teachers’ from the ruling party.JD(S) candidate A P Ranganath defeated sitting Congress MLC Puttanna by 908 votes, securing 10,810 votes against his rival's 9,902.
The BJP retained the North-East Teachers’, South-East Graduates’ and West Graduates’ constituencies. The results came despite campaigning by chief minister Siddaramaiah, deputy chief minister D K Shivakumar and other senior Congress leaders.In Uttar Pradesh, the BJP won four of the 11 legislative council seats, while the Samajwadi Party secured two, with counting continuing in some constituencies.Bihar saw setbacks for both the Congress and the BJP. Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj Party opened its account in the state Legislative Council after candidate Suresh Prasad Rai defeated sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha by 324 votes in the Darbhanga Teachers’ constituency.
