Bruno Fernandes: Man Utd head coach Michael Carrick and club captain hold clear-the-air talks ahead of Chelsea fixture
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes was an unused substitute in their 3-0 defeat against Bournemouth after being dropped by Michael Carrick; Man Utd head coach will take charge of Saturday's game against Chelsea with Fernandes now in contention after talks on Tuesday
Wednesday 28 October 2026 12:20, UK
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick and captain Bruno Fernandes have met face to face to clear the air, with both vowing to refocus on turning the club's season around.
Fernandes was an unused substitute after being dropped for the 3-0 defeat against Bournemouth on Sunday after he criticised Carrick's tactics following the 4-1 thrashing at Como in the Champions League.
Carrick had described his reasons for dropping his captain as "pure football".
"Picking the team is always a difficult decision," Carrick told Sky Sports. "We've got to make what we feel is the right one for the team to try to get the performance we want."
However, Carrick and Fernandes met at United's training ground on Tuesday, Sky Sports News has been told, for an open and frank discussion, with the head coach satisfied the animosity between them is over, although it is not known if the midfielder apologised for his public criticism.
Fernandes is now expected to be in contention for United's Premier League game against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.
The individual meeting between Carrick and Fernandes was in addition to an all-squad meeting, where there was a renewed determination from all the players and staff that performances have to improve immediately.
There was also a mutual admission, we are told, that there has been a squad-wide underperformance so far this season.
Carrick and the Man Utd players have been given the chance to turn their form around despite the under-pressure head coach thought to be on the brink after Sunday's defeat.
'Fernandes back to his best in training'
Sky Sports News' Danyal Khan at Carrington:
"Bruno Fernandes is absolutely back in contention. From what I understand and what I've been told from sources around Manchester United, Bruno Fernandes has been back to his best in the last 48 hours.
"Now, what does that mean, and how has that come around?
"It was quite out of character, you have to say, for him to come out last week, airing a lot of frustrations after the Como defeat.
"I would also assume that the reaction or lack of by the fans towards him on Sunday, when he's warming up, no shouts of Bruno from around Old Trafford, and then the boos, not just Fernandes, but also the players faced after Michael Carrick had gone down the tunnel.
"What I've been told, Bruno Fernandes has come back to Carrington since Monday. He was here on Monday to receive treatment to maintain his fitness, but since then all has seemingly been back to normal, and that is the message we have received at Manchester United, it is business as usual for everyone involved.
"I imagine he'll have a much bigger part than he did on Sunday against Bournemouth, and he is absolutely back in contention to play for Michael Carrick's side on Saturday."
Neville: Fernandes let himself down - read the room Bruno!
Following the defeat to Bournemouth, Sky Sports' Gary Neville said Fernandes had let himself down.
"Eric Cantona was very unorthodox as a captain," he said. "Roy Keane could sometimes be explosive in his interviews after matches, but they weren't whingers about the tactics, about pressing, or excuse merchants.
"Bruno can't press. To come out and whinge after the game about the manager's tactics, when you've just lost 4-1, and a few thousand fans have paid thousands of pounds to travel over in that far corner and get wet through. I'm sorry, read the room, Bruno.
"This is not a time for whinging, throwing your arms up in the air. This is a time for you to stand up and say, that's not good enough. Be positive. Do something with a positive influence as a captain. But he's not.
"He's gone and basically thrown his manager under the bus the week after [Lisandro] Martinez did the same."
Neville added: "They weren't singing for Bruno Fernandes to come on today, they're backing Michael Carrick. So get in your box. You know where you stand.
"Michael Carrick's won things for the football club on a constant basis, and proven that he can have the humility, the resilience. And Bruno has got that. Bruno has delivered for Manchester United in more ways than any other player in the last 13 years.
"And he's the one player I think you could take back in time, and I think he could play in a Manchester United team in the 90s, in the 2000s because he's massively talented. But he let himself down this week.
"He didn't need to do that, because he's basically stuck the knife into his manager."
What did Fernandes say after Como defeat?
"It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball," said Fernandes.
"But sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work."
Asked if the tactics were to blame for the defeat, Fernandes replied: "That's on the manager and on the staff to see it, it's not on me.
"I just said, I think sometimes we have to be more brave on the pressure, trying to take a risk of getting that press very high and making them uncomfortable - as they did to us."
Sky Sports News reported on October 22 that Fernandes would not be stripped of the captaincy for his comments, but at his pre-Bournemouth press conference the following day, Carrick refused to rule out disciplinary measures against Fernandes.
"The most important thing for me is the team and the dynamics in the squad. It is about the football club. Whatever the situation is, I will always do what is best for the football club," he said.
"If I've spoken to him or haven't... this isn't the time to go into details."
Fernandes was the second United player to publicly criticise the club in October after Lisandro Martinez's comments following the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid.
Martinez said: "I expect more from our technical director [director of football, Jason Wilcox]. We expect more from the top, from upstairs, to bring in more players to compete."
Martinez was not dropped for United's following game, playing 45 minutes of the 1-1 draw at Leeds - but was also benched for the visit of Bournemouth.

Dowman sees red as Arsenal dumped out, but did Arteta go too far?
- Published
Max Dowman is used to grabbing headlines for producing moments of magic but, after being sent off in just his second start of the season as Arsenal suffered a shock loss to Fleetwood Town, the 16-year-old is facing the first test of his short career.
Dowman scored twice as Arsenal beat Ipswich in the previous round of the Carabao Cup and manager Mikel Arteta rewarded him with another start in the last-16 tie at Fleetwood.
And this one was perhaps more of a chance than it looked. Arsenal are currently light on options in the wing with Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke all injured.
But, after being held by Fleetwood during normal time where the Gunners went behind despite having 26 shots and 78% possession, the Premier League champions lost on penalties following Dowman's red card, after a 1-1 draw in normal time.
Arteta gave the youngster a scathing look as he left the pitch and angrily said something to the winger as he went down the tunnel, revealing after the game that it was "something that we discussed already before the match".
The young winger reacted to a heavy challenge by Harrison Neal and, although he did not fully kick out, he made a movement towards Neal with his leg that gave referee Michael Salisbury a decision to make.
It is Dowman's second red card this month after he was also sent off while representing England U19s in the last international break.
"You have to remember he is 16 years of age, he's a kid," former Arsenal midfielder Paul Merson said on Sky Sports.
"He wasn't having the greatest of nights so he's going to get frustrated. He gets the chance every now and then to play for Arsenal.
"He probably feels he should be playing more, he gets the chance tonight, isn't doing too great. It's an old fashioned tackle.
"If that's Viktor Gyokeres he [Arteta] isn't doing that. That's what I don't like. If it's an exprienced international, I don't think he does that. He's a human being.
"He's not the last person to get sent off for Arsenal and he's not the first."
'It was very clear'
"When we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to respect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate. It was very clear." Arteta said following the game.
Dowman is one of best young players in Europe and tough treatment from defenders is something Arteta has previously said that Dowman will have to get used to.
"For me, I'd put my arm round him, it's still 1-1 and you are in the game." Merson said on Sky Sports.
"We all say things in life when you think 'I shouldn't have said that'. For me that's a classic moment where if he could have that back, he'd do it different." Merson said of Arteta's actions.
Former Everton midfielder Leon Osman also believes that it was a lack of experience that played into Dowman's red.
"It was on the far side of the pitch, but from what we saw [Dowman] can't have any complaints." Osman said on 5Live.
"Yes, there were a lot of challenges flying in thick and fast from both teams, and then, there was that moment when a huge challenge came in on him, but as I mentioned earlier they happen so often.
"And you have to know as a good player, people are going to try to kick you at times, and that's what happened.
"It was a poor reaction from him and you hope he learns and he learns quickly."
- Where does Fleetwood beating Arsenal rank in biggest cup upsets? 
  - Published2 hours ago
Nothing to criticise the players for their attitude - Arteta
The surprising loss to Fleetwood, a team 84 places below Arsenal in the football pyramid, was made even worse by the fact that the Gunners' under-21 team had beaten AFC Wimbledon, a side in a division higher than the hosts, on the same night in the EFL trophy.
The first incident of the match came with under two minutes on the clock when the game was stopped for more than eight minutes when a drown was flown above the pitch.
Perhaps Arsenal should have taken that as a warning.
Arteta named an experimental side and gave a debut to 18-year-old Ceadach O'Neill, started 17-year-old Marli Salmon at centre back, 16-year-old Dowman on the wing while goalkeepr Illan Meslier was making his first start for the club too.
But the Gunners boss surrounded that inexperience with seasoned internationals such as Jurrien Timber, Piero Hincapie, World Cup winner Martin Zubimendi, Champions League winner Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres.
All of those players played a huge part in the Gunners winning the Premier League title last season.
However, even after introducing captain Martin Odegaard and £75m signing Bruno Guimaraes from the bench, Arsenal produced a poor performance.
"First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through the next round. The manner that they have done it, and for us a very sad day." Arteta said of the result.
"There is nothing to criticise the players for their attitude, their application. The determination - you could see that was there from the start.
"Even with 10 men, we conceded a really poor goal to start with that gave them some momentum."
The loss in this competition is not the Gunners' first, but it does mean they have not won the League Cup for 33 years.
In 2012, Arsenal lost to League Two side Bradford City on penalties and they were also beaten by Championship side Sheffield Wednesday in 2015 at the same stage too.
With Dowman now suspended, Saka out for around six weeks, Tzolis working to return and Arteta revealing after the match that Madueke was unavailable with an injury, their options in the wide areas for the match with Liverpool on Sunday are looking slim.

New Zealand batter Daryl Mitchell praised India opener Abhishek Sharma for his “world-class hitting” ability, but hoped his side could turn the tide in the remaining two T20Is of the five-match series.

India and China were easing tensions - then a border official spoke out
- Published
For much of the past year, India-China relations appeared to be on a cautious path to recovery.
The two countries have seen ups and downs in their ties over decades - especially over the disputed Himalayan frontier.
But events of the past few days suggest that the thaw which has followed their most recent clashes in 2020 may be more fragile than it seems.
The latest concerns began when India's border police chief said Chinese troops had returned to disputed areas along the Himalayan frontier in large numbers earlier this year, pitching tents several kilometres inside territory claimed by India.
The remarks by Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, director general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), have triggered a political controversy in Delhi.
To begin with, such comments by serving officials are rare. Sensitive border issues are usually addressed by the federal government through its defence or foreign ministries.
At a recent gathering of officers in Rajasthan state, Kapur said face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops had taken place at several locations in the north-eastern state of Arunachal Pradesh and were continuing.
The confrontations began in July, he said, but both sides initially withdrew.
A few days later, Chinese troops returned in larger numbers and pitched tents "around six-to-seven kilometres inside India's perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC)", he added.
The LAC is an ill-defined line separating the areas controlled by the neighbours and India and China have sparred for decades over this disputed 3,440km (2,100-mile) border.
China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet. But Delhi has always rejected the claim, saying the state was an integral part of India.
The dispute is one of the most persistent challenges inherited by independent India from the British colonial rule in 1947. It led to a brief border war in 1962, in which India suffered a humiliating defeat.
More than six decades later, much of the frontier remains undemarcated, with the two countries maintaining overlapping territorial claims.
The region's rugged terrain adds to the challenge: shifting river courses, lakes and snow-covered peaks make it difficult to establish a clear boundary.
As a result, troops from the two sides can find themselves face-to-face along the frontier, sometimes triggering violent clashes and diplomatic tensions.
The last major escalation came in June 2020, when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in Ladakh. At least 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
It was the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975. Indian opposition parties accused the government of losing territory to China - a claim Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has repeatedly rejected.
The clashes triggered a sharp deterioration in relations, disrupting diplomatic engagement and affecting trade and travel. After several rounds of negotiations, the neighbours agreed in 2024 to take steps towards easing border tensions.
They have since moved to restore direct flights and ease visa restrictions imposed after the clashes.
Chinese President Xi Jinping also visited India in September for the Brics summit, his first visit to the country in seven years.
These developments raised hopes of a broader normalisation of ties. But the latest reported stand-offs have renewed questions about how much progress has actually been made on the ground.
After Kapur's comments, the main opposition Congress party once again accused Modi of making concessions to Beijing.
"The prime minister and his entire apparatus remain silent on this grave issue," senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh wrote on X, external.
The Indian government has not explicitly denied Kapur's account that Chinese troops had pitched tents several kilometres inside what India considers to be its side of the LAC.
Foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said last week that "the situation in the border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns".
He said both countries were using military and diplomatic channels to address outstanding issues, but gave no further details.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said that China had "consistently and strictly adhered to relevant agreements" reached with India and it conducted "normal patrol and management activities in the border areas to safeguard territorial sovereignty".
Experts say Kapur's remarks offer a rare glimpse into what they describe as China's increasingly assertive military posture along the disputed frontier.
"This pattern of Chinese probing at various points of the Arunachal Pradesh border has been happening for some time," Shyam Saran, a former Indian foreign secretary who led several rounds of border talks with China in the mid-2000s, told the BBC.
He said such actions were "not enough to result in an immediate war, but enough to sort of create new facts on the ground".
Indian opposition parties have long accused China of extending its presence in both Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, leading to tensions.
Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in China's People's Liberation Army who is now associated with Tsinghua University in Beijing, said both countries had learnt lessons from the 2020 Galwan clashes.
"The two sides should be more careful to avoid this kind of thing from happening in the future," he said, adding that Chinese media had not reported on the latest stand-offs in Arunachal Pradesh.
India and China's tensions also come against the backdrop of a complicated economic relationship.
Despite their differences, the countries remain major trading partners, with bilateral trade, external reaching $151bn last year. But the balance is heavily tilted in Beijing's favour, with Chinese exports to India accounting for about $131bn.
India continues to rely on Chinese imports for machinery, rare earth magnets, electric vehicle batteries and pharmaceutical products.
This dependence means tensions with Beijing can have consequences well beyond the border, particularly for Indian industries and infrastructure projects.
Last week, China also announced restrictions on exports of tunnel-boring machines used in metro rail and highway construction, saying they were intended to protect national security and national interests. Although these curbs were not India specific, they would have a bearing on India's infrastructure push.
"Chinese policy towards India is designed to complicate India's rise, including India's ability to master certain things in advanced technology and manufacturing," Christopher Clary, a professor at the University at Albany in New York, told the BBC.
A similar problem emerged last year when China restricted export of rare earth magnets - widely used in electric vehicles, smartphones, wind turbines and medical scanners.
The move temporarily caused supply problems for Indian industries, highlighting how Beijing's control over key materials can affect global supply chains.
India is now trying to build domestic capacity to produce rare earth magnets, but developing the industry will take time and investment.
For people living along the disputed frontier, the consequences of tensions with China are more immediate.
"Villagers living in some border areas tell us that they cannot access grazing lands because of Chinese intrusion and encroachment. It's not something new, it's been happening for a long time," says Tongam Rina, a senior journalist with the Arunachal Times.
This has created a "sense of insecurity among the people here," she adds.
Villagers usually do not return to those "prohibited" areas for hunting and yak rearing, and they are not sure when they would be allowed again.
The border dispute also has wider strategic implications for Delhi, with a growing realisation that President Donald Trump's focus on expanding economic engagement with China could limit Washington's willingness to back India in any future confrontation with Beijing.
China may have little interest in a full-scale conflict with India but, analysts say, it could see advantages in allowing the dispute to continue.
As China's economic and military power grows, it may calculate that a prolonged stalemate will strengthen its position in any future negotiations.
For India, the latest stand-offs are a reminder that improved diplomatic ties do not necessarily translate into lasting stability along the border.

It is officially the flu season with winter and monsoon seasons creeping in on large parts of the world. There is a need to take precautions and be aware of the risks of the season, particularly at a time when we are hearing of old viruses resurging, or new, never-before heard pathogens rearing their heads, even known microorganisms that cause disease among humans, after a zoonotic spillover.
As in the case of the Shamonda virus. Last week France reported the first human Shamonda virus case, a virus usually circulating amongst livestock. The severely immunocompromised patient died, spurring global public health concerns. While France said there was no health risk as a result of this, there are definitely problems when a new pathogen crosses the barrier. For everything we currently know about the Shamonda virus, read Athira Elssa Johnson’s explainer, here.
She also writes on Melioidosis in India: a potentially deadly infection that may be going undetected. Melioidosis caused by B. pseudomallei which is found in soil and water in tropical and subtropical regions, can cause pneumonia, bloodstream infection, skin and soft-tissue infections, abscesses in organs such as the liver and spleen, septic arthritis and bone infections. It can also affect the kidneys, muscles and prostate.

The story so far:
On October 6, the National Medical Commission (NMC) issued guidelines on advertising and public communication by doctors and hospitals. Intended to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, they cover hospital hoardings, social media and artificial intelligence (AI). Beyond curbing deception, they raise another question regarding how much can doctors and hospitals say to the public about their work and achievements?
What is prohibited?
Claims of “guaranteed cures”, “100% success” or being the “best” are barred. Similarly, fake reviews, manipulated online rankings, misleading celebrity or influencer endorsements, and offers encouraging unnecessary treatment are deemed unethical practices. The guidelines rightfully prohibit AI-generated or manipulated patient images, voices and testimonials. But section 8.1(i) prohibits advertisements that create “unnecessary demand” for medical procedures or promote “fear-based marketing”. Without objective criteria, such expressions leave considerable room for subjective interpretation and inconsistent enforcement.
Hospitals may publish factual details of services, charges, accreditation and doctors’ credentials. Yet Section 8.1(iii) restricts advertising professional achievements and success rates, and Section 8.1(v) prohibits promotional “before and after” surgical photographs, except for specified scientific or educational purposes. Such blanket restrictions risk regulatory overreach, particularly when authentic, appropriately contextualised images could help patients understand surgical outcomes. Section 9.2 also restricts the use of doctors’ photographs for self-promotion, including on letterheads and signboards. These restrictions apply only to registered medical practitioners under the NMC’s jurisdiction.
Why the information asymmetry?
Patients rarely possess the same medical knowledge as those treating them. Even amid an abundance of AI-enabled health information, choosing a surgeon or assessing a hospital’s safety record remains difficult. Verifiable professional achievements, including the number of surgeries performed, years of experience and treatment outcomes, could help patients make informed choices. While such figures can be misleading without context, they are fundamentally different from unsubstantiated claims to be the “best” or to guarantee success, which the guidelines already prohibit. Rather than restricting genuine professional accomplishments, requiring their accurate and transparent disclosure could better serve patients’ right to informed choice. The answer may lie in better disclosure, rather than less information.
Is commercialisation unethical?
The guidelines seek to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, while Clause 8.1(ii) restricts promotion, suggesting commercialisation of medical practice. But in India, profit-making healthcare is lawful, as section 2(c) of the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, recognises privately operated hospitals, and section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, enables lawful commercial enterprises, including hospitals. Government policy also permits 100% FDI in hospitals.
Article 19(1)(g) protects citizens’ freedom to practise a profession or conduct business, subject to reasonable restrictions. In the case Tata Press v. MTNL (1995), the Supreme Court recognised commercial speech under Article 19(1)(a), including the public’s right to receive information, while permitting restrictions on misleading advertisements. The current guidelines appear to treat commercialisation itself as a problem, without clearly distinguishing legitimate business interests from practices that mislead or exploit patients.
Are government schemes exempt?
Central and State government schemes undertaken in the larger public interest are exempted, and can advertise. Flexibility for vaccination drives and other health programmes is understandable. But the exemption is broad. Safeguards should remain equally important whether a campaign is run by the government or a private hospital. Patients seeking private healthcare may independently praise or criticise doctors. But the guidelines remain silent on hospitals and practitioners using unsolicited patient testimonials for promotion. What if a patient voluntarily posts an account and a hospital subsequently shares it? The distinction remains unresolved.
Other unclear aspects
Graded penalties are intended for violators, starting with a warning and mandatory ethics training for the first violation, and increasing to a 6- to 12-month suspension for subsequent violations. At the same time, repeated offences could lead to removal from the register for one to three years. State Medical Councils will enforce these provisions after issuing show-cause notices and considering doctors’ explanations. Appeals can be made to the NMC’s Ethics and Medical Registration Board.
The guidelines remain unclear about who can initiate complaints and the evidence required. It addresses genuine concerns, but its broad and ambiguous provisions may create confusion over compliance and leave considerable room for subjective enforcement, particularly affecting smaller hospitals. Protecting patients from misleading advertisements and commercial exploitation is necessary. However, treating commercial intent itself as inherently suspect serves little purpose. Clearer distinctions between legitimate professional communication and unethical promotion would better serve both patients and healthcare providers.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

A three-year long study in Bengaluru of over 10,000 frontline workers has brought to light reduced lung function among BMTC bus drivers, traffic police, pourakarmikas and construction workers — sections most exposed to polluted air.
The study, done by the VAAYU Occupational & Environmental Respiratory Illness Clinic (VOERIC), screened 4,517 BMTC drivers, 3,285 traffic police personnel, 2,169 construction workers and 379 pourakarmikas.
Vulnerable sections face highest health risk
All the groups that were screened showed higher-than-normal prevalence of early lung-function abnormalities.
Among the occupations, pourakarmikas were found to have the highest proportion of workers with the PRISm pattern, an indication of reduced lung capacity. Around 45% of them showed indications of reduced lung function.
BMTC workers and traffic police followed, with 29.5% and 28%, respectively, showing reduced lung function. Among construction workers, 15% showed a PRISm pattern.
Around 2.6% of BMTC drivers, 2.3% pourakarmikas, 2.1% construction workers, and 1% traffic police personnel reported signs of obstructive airflow.
The survey also found that 88.2% of the BMTC drivers never used a mask, as was the case with 55% traffic police, 37.9% construction workers, and 16.3% pourakarmikas.
Comorbidities
The subjects were also analysed for comorbidities, and the results revealed a grim situation, with high levels of obesity reported among the sections.
Pourakarmikas had the highest proportion at 62%, closely followed by BMTC drivers, 60.7% of whom were found to be obese/overweight. For traffic police, the figure stood at 51.3%.
The figures are much higher than the India reference figure of 28.6%.
The study also flags that diabetes prevalence among BMTC drivers was 18.2%, higher than the Indian average of 11.4%. Among traffic police personnel, the prevalence was 14%.
The physically active nature of the work and the relatively young demography among the construction workers translated to lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases. The average age of construction workers was found to be 31.3± 10, 98.3% of whom worked for more than 8 hours daily.
The concerns with higher incidences of diabetes, uncontrolled blood pressure, overweight and obesity across occupational groups has reinforced the need for a comprehensive approach to worker health including cardiometabolic screening
“While the findings demonstrate a significant burden of health abnormalities, further longitudinal research is required to establish the extent to which occupational exposures contribute to specific respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes. VOERIC plans to start this as cohort along with government support,” a statement from VOERIC said.
“Air pollution is considered the new tobacco. It is an emerging risk-enhancing factor for heart attack and brain stroke,” said C.N. Manjunath, leading cardiologist and Bengaluru Rural MP, at a round table where the results from the study were published.
Speaking about the importance of reducing traffic congestion, scientific garbage disposal and adoption of necessary measures during road construction to reduce dust, in tackling air pollution, he acknowledged the importance of policy intervention backed by data.

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.
Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.
Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.
Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.
The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).
'Nigerian patient did not travel to Congo'
In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.
The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).
Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.
U.S. introduces new protocol for all travellers
United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.
Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

Cundy 'no spring chicken' but nears 20-year unbeaten run
- Published
Four laps, flat out, from a standing start. Legs and lungs screaming, lactic acid building.
The kilo, track cycling's one-kilometre time trial, has a punishing reputation.
And yet Jody Cundy has been putting himself through it for decades.
"At the end of it, your legs don't want to pedal. You're fighting everything," he tells BBC Sport. "But when you get it right, it's really cool."
Cundy is king of the kilo. At the Para-cycling Track World Championships, he has been unbeaten in the event since 2006.
If he wins again at this year's edition - which starts on Thursday in Apeldoorn, the Netherlands - it will mark his 20th straight year in the rainbow jersey.
Not bad for someone who has just turned 48 years old.
"It's a fairly dominant run," he said. "There have been some moments where I thought it wasn't going to happen and somehow I've pulled something out of the bag.
"But I am getting older and the competitors are getting younger. It's going to be very hard to keep that unbeaten run.
"As much as I would love to do it, the people I have to race this year...I'm in trouble."
Some of that "trouble" comes from within the Great Britain squad.
Archie Atkinson, 22, was eight years from being born when Cundy won his first Paralympic gold medal - as a swimmer - at Atlanta 1996. Atkinson was just two when Cundy first became world champion as a cyclist, after switching sports.
"One of my first races was against him," said Atkinson. "That felt pretty special.
"This guy was Paralympic champion, world champion and held a world record at the time."
But Atkinson is catching up. Last year he beat Cundy at the National Track Championships, only to be beaten in turn by Cundy at the World Championships a few months later.
"I want to win," Atkinson said. "But if he wins, it's historic. There aren't many people who can win for 20 years."
In addition to his world titles, Cundy is a six-time cycling Paralympic champion - two of those victories coming in the kilo, which he won at the 2008 and 2016 Games.
Such is Cundy's standing in the squad that his team-mates call him "captain".
"It feels like I've earned a bit of respect from being here for so long," he said. "I try to be the person everyone looks up to.
"But I know at some point somebody's going to have to take my place and I'll be walking away from the sport."
When Cundy will walk away is anyone's guess.
He says he doesn't have a plan for his retirement, but he knows that qualifying for the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles will be difficult.
"If I'm still performing at the very top level and that means that they want to take me, because I can go win in LA, then I shall be there and I'm there to be counted," he said.
"I'm realistic in the fact I'll be 49 when it comes to LA and I'm no spring chicken any more.
"What we do afterwards I really don't know, whether it's in sport in some way, shape or form.
"It's 31 years I've been in elite sport. If I go away and take all of that knowledge away with me, I feel like I'm kind of cheating the system a bit.
"So there's part of me that wants to come back and help - whether it's in a coaching role or a managerial role, or even further up in governing body roles and trying to influence the UCI [cycling's world governing body] and the IPC [International Paralympic Committee] - to make cycling better than what it actually is."
The UCI, Cundy says, has "let the sport down" by the lack of Para-cycling track competitions it hosts outside of the World Championships and Paralympics.
At the upcoming Worlds, Cundy and Atkinson are among a 24-strong Great Britain squad - but it is the first time the team will have raced at a UCI track event since the last edition of the Worlds in Brazil last year.
"When it comes to track cycling we have one race a year, the World Championships, and then every four years we have a [Paralympic] Games. That's really not good enough," he said.
"When I first started we used to have competitions, we used to travel and go race in places. Now you go 12 months without seeing anybody.
"You see a start list and you don't know who half of the names are on it. You don't know whether they're going to be fast, slow, whether they're any good. There's not really any results or rankings to follow."
The UCI did not respond to a request for comment.

How Kane defied doubters to become world's best
- Published
Harry Kane has taken the scenic route to the Ballon d'Or - a road littered with doubts and diversions, but one that eventually led to the ultimate destination: being crowned as the world's best player.
The 33-year-old's glory at the London Palladium on Monday is fitting reward for an exemplary career that has seen records fall at his feet for England, Tottenham Hotspur and Bayern Munich.
Kane is England's top goalscorer with 91 goals. He has 125 England caps, joint-highest with Peter Shilton. He is Spurs' record scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances. He scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025–26 season.
This is the Kane of recent vintage, the world-class striker and complete footballer who beat Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe, as well as Spain's teenage Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal, to the sport's biggest personal honour.
Kane's humility has seen him described as an 'anti-superstar' and his achievement has been commended both inside and outside the football world.
One post on social media from Kane as he celebrated the greatest moment of his career said it all: "Work hard in silence. Let success be your noise."
And yet, Kane's journey was not always smooth.
It was one that started with loan moves around the lower divisions with Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City before he developed into a great for club and country.
The same Kane sat on the bench on loan at Leicester City – alongside future England team-mate Jamie Vardy – when the Foxes lost a dramatic Championship play-off at Watford in May 2013.
Kane went through hard schools and hard times away from his more familiar environment at Spurs, joining Orient on loan as a 17-year-old in January 2011, playing 18 games with nine starts and scoring five goals.
He joined Millwall in similar circumstances a year later, with some behind the scenes at Spurs fearing the traditionally hostile atmosphere at the New Den might intimidate the teenager, but he acquitted himself well, scoring nine goals in 24 starts.
Former Spurs manager Tim Sherwood said: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there'.
"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him'."
Kane made his Spurs debut in August 2012 before a spell at Norwich City, where he failed to score in three starts and suffered a serious foot injury.
It was an unhappy time but Chris Hughton, the former Spurs defender who was manager at Carrow Road, said: "What I saw in him was a desire to do well. Did I see him having the mobility and flexibility he has in his game now? Probably not. He was a very good finisher. He would stay out after training for half an hour every day, left foot, right foot."
Next stop was Leicester City between February and May 2013, when he made five starts and scored two goals, a stint best remembered for that dramatic Championship play-off game when Troy Deeney scored for Watford to send them to Wembley seconds after Anthony Knockaert's penalty was saved by Manuel Almunia.
Kane was not even selected in Leicester's starting line-up, only being sent on after 61 minutes. And who was alongside him on the bench? Vardy, who later won the Premier league with the Foxes and played alongside Kane for England.
He later admitted this was a time of self-doubt, saying: "That was probably the time in my career where it was the hardest - I was 19 and I was thinking, 'If I can't play for Norwich or for Leicester, even in the Championship, then how I am going to get back and play for Tottenham?'"
- Ranking England's Ballon d'Or winners - how does Kane compare?

It is testimony to Kane's strength of character, even as a youngster, that he not only returned to Spurs but left for Bayern Munich in August 2023 as one of their greatest ever players.
Even at Spurs, Kane's superb record always carried the qualification that he never won a trophy, a stick used to unfairly beat a player whose remarkable consistency and approach marked him down as the consummate professional.
Kane has put that right spectacularly at Bayern, winning the Bundesliga twice, the move propelling him to the level of global superstar, giving him the profile and platform to win the Ballon d'Or - the first English player to win the trophy since Michael Owen in 2001 and the fifth overall.
Former England midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport recently: "He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career."
There is still that one space on his roll of honour, namely success with England after losses in two Euros finals and two World Cup semi-final defeats, but who would bet against Kane being fit and motivated enough to have one last crack at Euro 2028 in the UK and Ireland.
Kane is now at the peak of his powers and fitness, not just a goalscoring machine but the complete player capable of dropping deep into midfield to play the sort of breathtaking defence splitting pass exemplified by Alphonso Davies' goal against Arsenal in the recent Champions League game.
One of Kane's illustrious predecessors in England's number nine shirt, Alan Shearer, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "It was so well deserved because he hasn't had things all his own way. He's had to go round it the hard way. He had to start off the hard way by someone telling him, 'You're not quite good enough, you're going to have to work a lot harder to get to where you want to'.
"He did that. He went out on loan and worked harder than anyone else. He's got to the very, very top and now he's the best player in the world and that's what dedication does for you. It's a message to everyone.
"Harry said it in his speech - that if you're told you're not good enough, then go and try again and work harder. He did that and look where he is now. He's been scoring goals at a phenomenal rate for so many years now and he deserved it."
Shearer added: "I think the best thing for me is how humble Harry is. Footballers are like movie stars nowadays. You see them walking down the red carpet and some of them are in sunglasses when it's pitch black and eight o'clock at night. Harry is just normal, as normal as they come."
Once the celebrations die down, it will be back to business for the humble superstar, with Bayern playing Magdeburg in the German DFB Pokal second round on Wednesday before the big home fixture against Borussia Dortmund on Saturday evening.
Kane's career has not been without its obstacles but he remains as focused as ever to conquer whatever is placed in front of him by Bayern Munich and England.

In late October, people shared a video allegedly showing a newborn baby with a mustache sitting upright against a pillow in a hospital bed.
The brief clip featured a purportedly real infant that appeared to have been born just moments earlier, with a mustache above its upper lip and some facial hair below its lower lip.
For example, on Oct. 23, an X user posted the video (archived) with the caption, "A newborn baby is going VIRAL for arriving in this world with a FULL MUSTACHE," and, "Bro skipped kindergarten and went straight to his midlife crisis 😂."
Users shared the video on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived) and other social media platforms. Some people said hospital staff delivered the baby in Colombia, while others said Ecuador. Snopes readers emailed to ask whether such a baby truly had been born.
A review of comments under social media posts found people making jokes about the baby being born already retired, as well as referencing the mustachioed baby Pubert Addams from "The Addams Family" and comedian Guillermo Rodriguez from "Jimmy Kimmel Live!"
Others asked whether the video was real, including some asking about or making claims about artificial intelligence. Some also mentioned congenital hypertrichosis, which the Cleveland Clinic defined as a rare condition, present from birth, that causes extra hair growth on a person's body or face.
In sum, we found the video displayed at several signs of either being created or manipulated with AI, including inconsistent hairs and other facial features, an AI content label on a very early TikTok post and a duration exactly matching a common AI video length. Therefore, we rated the clip as fake.
Researching the video
According to a reverse image search, TikTok user @mesina080 made what at first appeared to be the oldest post (archived) with the video on Oct. 20.
Days later, @mesina080 reposted the video beginning with a supposed image of a woman preparing to shave her mustache.
In a private message with Snopes, @mesina080 said he used an AI tool to remove a watermark (and potentially other text) from an earlier video he said was "apparently" created with AI. He did not send a link to that earlier video.
A TikTok search for the Spanish-language terms "bigote de bebé" ("baby mustache") located dozens of videos from users reposting the baby with the mustache, including a video (archived) a user with the display name Soy Yare (@yarel0725) posted about 90 minutes earlier than @mesina080. That user watermarked the clip with her name. She also enabled TikTok's "Contains AI-generated media" label during the upload process to clarify that AI created or altered the video.
The clip lasted exactly 10 seconds and ran at 24 frames per second with no added individual frames, a common duration of AI-generated videos. For example, a standard video generated with the Google Gemini AI tool, without specifying anything about length or frame rate, produced a 10-second video running at 24 frames per second — an exact match.
The video begins with the baby facing to his or her right, with some hair visible below the lower lip. The baby turns to the left, with some of the hairs above the child's upper lip appearing to visibly change. The infant turns back to the right, with the area below the lower lip no longer showing facial hair. Also, a blemish sharply appears below the child's right eye that was not nearly as visible earlier. We edited the below image to make the shadowed area below the lower lip appear more visible:
Readers can watch the video to see the blemish appear much more visible later in the video than before, as well as the apparent vanishing of facial hair below the lower lip. (@yarel0725 via TikTok)
We did not yet obtain clarification from Yare about whether she created the original AI-generated clip. Scans of the video with AI detection tools displayed inconsistent results.
Additionally, our research also located a similar video with the person holding the camera appearing to walk toward the baby in the bed. That clip first appeared after the one above.
For further reading, we previously explained how we determined a video of a monkey rescuing a dog from floodwaters was made with AI.

Election denial has gone mainstream in the U.S. What does that mean for the midterms?
County clerks prepare to fend off election denial movement empowered by President Trump
Early on a Wednesday morning in October, a dozen people gathered in a wood-panelled room in Barry County, Mich., to be trained as poll workers for the U.S. midterm elections.
During the three-hour session, they were taught how to operate a vote-tabulating machine, check photo IDs and process absentee ballots.
But before the session began, Sarah VanDenburg, the clerk in this rural county, thanked them for "helping preserve our democracy."
As the clerk of Barry County, Sarah VanDenburg is responsible for staffing polling stations on election day. (Michael Drapack/CBC)
The 2026 midterms are taking place while an election denial movement, empowered by President Donald Trump, has spent months claiming these otherwise routine tasks are the source of rampant fraud.
And even though there is little evidence to support these claims, they’re being used as a pretext by election deniers — many now in positions of authority — to try to interfere in the voting process.
Trump himself has mused openly about invoking a national emergency measure to alter how votes are counted.
President Donald Trump greets Mike Rogers, a Michigan Republican candidate for Senate, left, on stage during a campaign rally in Port Huron, Mich., on Oct. 25. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Associated Press)
In Barry County, sheriff Dar Leaf has emerged as the loudest voice pushing conspiracies about how elections are run. For the past six years, he has been using his office to circulate claims that foreign nationals hacked voting machines in the county in 2020 to switch votes from Trump to Joe Biden.
More recently, Leaf has been trying to interrogate state election officials as part of a new investigation into claims Michigan’s voter rolls for the 2026 midterms are being deliberately inflated with non-citizens, even though studies have shown non-citizen voting is extremely rare.
"I have a duty to go out and investigate, and I'm not gonna back down," Leaf told CBC News during an interview at sheriff headquarters in Hastings, Mich.
VanDenburg says she tries to maintain a good working relationship with the sheriff, but his beliefs "can make things difficult."
I have a duty to investigate, sheriff says
Leaf is a prominent figure in the Constitutional Sheriffs and Peace Officers Association, which believes sheriffs have ultimate authority in their county and has encouraged its members to investigate unfounded voter-fraud theories.
"It's just getting the sheriffs woke up to what their duties are really supposed to be," Leaf said about the association.
Barry County Sheriff Dar Leaf, seen here at a 2024 Trump campaign event, said he would consider seizing ballots during the midterm elections. (Paul Sancya/AP Photo)
With help from his own deputies, Leaf tried to seize several voting machines in the county in 2021 and 2022 to prove his theory, only to be rebuffed by a judge and prosecutor who determined his claims had no merit.
In an unprecedented move last year, another member of the group, California sheriff Chad Bianco, seized 650,000 ballots from the 2024 election to probe claims of irregularities. A court ruled the seizure unlawful and ordered the ballots returned.
But the prospect of ballots, or voting machines, being seized by pro-Trump officials has alarmed elections observers, who worry such manoeuvres could disrupt oversight and make it difficult to verify results.
Asked if he would consider seizing ballots, Leaf told CBC News, "I would have to have a good reason to seize them. We'd probably seize and then go get a court order."
When election deniers are in charge
For decades, the U.S. Department of Justice monitored local compliance with federal election laws. But under Trump, election deniers now occupy senior positions in the department, which has aggressively sought evidence to support the president’s claims of widespread voter fraud.
For instance, the department is battling 30 states for access to sensitive voter information as part of an effort to find evidence of non-citizen voting.
Earlier this year, the FBI seized ballots in Fulton County, Ga., from the 2020 election. The Justice Department said it was investigating 'irregularities that occurred during the 2020 presidential election in the County,' even though Georgia’s votes in the 2020 presidential race were already counted three times. Each count affirmed Democrat Joe Biden’s win. (Mike Stewart/AP Photo)
The FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have also been tasked with investigating voter fraud, even though most studies suggest it's a rare phenomenon.
Trump has used the premise of widespread voter fraud to justify his attempts to have the White House exert more control over elections and rewrite rules in his favour. Since returning to power, he has ordered the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail-in voting and pushed Congress to pass a voter ID law that would have made it harder for millions of Americans to vote.
But the Constitution gives states, not the president, authority over elections. And courts, so far, have upheld that principle.
Can Trump call a national emergency?
The failure of these efforts, combined with polls suggesting the Republican majorities in Congress are in jeopardy, has led some in the election denial movement to urge Trump to take even more drastic measures, such as calling a national emergency.
Proponents of the measure argue voting machines are so vulnerable to foreign hacking that an emergency would be warranted on national security grounds.
In an interview with Time magazine published earlier this month, Trump was asked about the possibility of declaring a state of emergency. "I don't rule anything out or in," he replied.
Lorenzo Sewell, a Detroit pastor with ties to the Trump administration and several Republicans in Congress, said calling a national emergency would allow the president to order states to stop using vote-tabulating machines and halt mail-in balloting.
Pastor of 180 Church Lorenzo Sewell delivers a benediction after President Donald Trump was sworn in at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 2025. (Saul Loeb/Associated Press)
"But in terms of getting something like this, he needs people. He needs another January 6th, and that's what I'm advocating for, minus the violence," said Sewell, who spoke at Trump’s second inauguration and the Republican convention this summer.
Many legal experts say the idea is unconstitutional and almost certain to be blocked by the courts.
"Our entire constitution is based on the idea that the president has no power over elections," said David Becker, a former elections lawyer with the Department of Justice who now heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research.
Training 'democracy defenders'
State lawmakers and progressive voting-rights groups are nevertheless preparing for a wide range of scenarios on election day, including the prospect of confrontations with armed federal agents or pro-Trump crowds.
"It seems the rhetoric has become more violent," said Autumn Butler, deputy executive director of Michigan United, a Detroit-based social justice organization that's been training "democracy defenders" in de-escalation tactics.
Autumn Butler is deputy executive director of Michigan United, a Detroit-based social justice organization that's been training 'democracy defenders' in de-escalation tactics. (Michael Drapack/CBC)
She recalled how, in 2020, a crowd of Trump supporters attempted to disrupt poll workers counting mail-in ballots in Detroit.
"That's why we have our democracy defenders," Butler said. "These are the scenarios that we're thinking about and planning for."
VanDenburg, the Barry County clerk, is hoping her preparations will help prevent tensions from boiling over on election day.
She recently gave a presentation to the sheriff and his deputies about basic election day rules, such as who can enter a polling station (armed officers are not allowed).
Leaf welcomed the information, saying, "some of those things we've never been taught before."
Those working the polls in the county will mostly be people from the community, which VanDenburg says will lighten the atmosphere.
"You walk into the polling place and you feel warmth. You feel invited, which I think is very important for our voters to feel that way."

Pope says 'there is no such thing as a holy war' in message to religious leaders
Pope Leo XIV has denounced the religious justification for wars raging around the world, saying “there is no such thing as a holy war.”
ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Tuesday denounced any religious justification for wars raging around the world, saying “there is no such thing as a holy war.”
“Only peace is holy,” Leo said in a video-message to a gathering of religious leaders in the Italian hilltop town of Assisi.
The American pope was supposed to have presided over the gathering in person, but had to cancel his participation as he recovers from Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery.
Instead Leo sent a videotaped message that was broadcast to the delegates, who included the Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally, spiritual leader of the worldwide Anglican Communion, as well as Muslim, Buddhist and other Christian leaders.
They were in Assisi, the birthplace of the peace-loving St. Francis, to mark the 40th anniversary of a landmark interfaith peace meeting called by St. John Paul II. That encounter, controversial at the time because it featured leaders of different faiths praying together, spawned a movement of interreligious peace appeals and gatherings.
In his message, the American pope denounced the “troubling revival of war as an instrument of international politics” and its religious justifications by leaders.
“Precisely in these times marked by a culture of power, there is a need to cultivate the spirit of Assisi,” he said. “War can never be waged in the name of God,” he said. “We must rebuild peace everywhere, not prepare for more wars.”
Russia’s Orthodox Church has justified Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as a “holy war” against a Western world it considers has fallen into evil.
Leaders on all sides of the Iran war have used religion to justify their actions. U.S. officials, especially Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have invoked their Christian faith to cast the war as a Christian nation trying to vanquish its foes with military might.
Leo has consistently rejected such justifications as a perversion of religion itself, most stridently in his first encyclical “Magnificent Humanity” in which he said fighting in the name of religion “means attacking religion itself.”
The Assisi gathering came as the Vatican is accelerating its humanitarian efforts for Ukraine following the entry into effect of a localized cease-fire in the devastated southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky. The pope’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution.
Marín de San Martín was planning to visit Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said.
“We want to understand directly the needs and meet with the local people, real people, real faces,” he told Vatican News. “Above all we want to convey to them the Holy Father’s concern and tender care. In their suffering, they are not alone.”
Leo had called for a cease-fire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during an Oct. 16 phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which the pontiff initiated from the hospital where he was recovering from surgery.
Leo followed up three days later, back at the Vatican, with a call to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to the Vatican, Leo noted his appeal for a cease-fire to Putin and “expressed the hope that cooperation between both parties will allow for the delivery of food and medical aid, and for the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.”
The initiatives took place after Italian Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, the papal envoy for the Ukraine-Russia war, finished his third mission to Moscow on Sept. 30 and the first under Leo’s pontificate.
