Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated, but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target.
A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it’s now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level.
The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones.
Focusing on function
Some of the best protein design tools we have available right now work through a two-step process. First, you specify a set of constraints, such as the need to bind another molecule or to have a specific arrangement of amino acids. One AI tool then generates a protein shape that meets those constraints. Once that’s done, a separate tool populates that shape with a specific sequence of amino acids that can ensure the protein folds into the appropriate configuration to match the shape.
Obviously, doing that often requires a fair bit of technical knowledge. If you’re designing a catalyst, for example, then you not only need to know what amino acids are critical to get a chemical reaction to happen, but you have to know where they should be located within a 3D space. That, not surprisingly, requires a fairly sophisticated understanding of protein chemistry and the ability to express that understanding in whatever form that the protein design tools require.
The thing is, if two experts were talking to each other, they wouldn’t need to get that specific. If one said “serine protease,” for example, the other would know a lot of what was implied by that in terms of the specifics of the reaction mechanism. We need to get specific when communicating with an AI tool because, while our current generation of tools are great at working through the 3D arrangements of amino acids, they’re kind of stupid about the functions that those 3D arrangements enable.
In the work of the team behind the new tool, called Pinal, this doesn’t necessarily have to be the case. We have databases full of millions of protein sequences tagged with notes about the functions those proteins perform. With the proper training, the researchers reasoned, it should be possible to just use the same terminology in those tags to get a system that outputs a sequence that performs exactly like what you’re looking for.
Proteins plus language
Pinal, on some levels, works quite like the standard tools, following a two-step process of building a backbone for the protein and then filling in the details of the amino acids that populate that backbone through a separate process. But there are very significant differences—beginning with what you need to do to start the process.
Rather than specifying some details of a few amino acids in the design product, you simply tell the system what you want. “The first stage is handled by T2struct, a text-to-structure module that translates a natural language prompt into a structural blueprint,” as the system’s developers describe it. T2struct doesn’t output a 3D shape, either; it simply produces a linear array of tokens that correspond to the spatial relationship between each amino acid and its nearest neighbors and assign a probability to each.
That gets handed off to a system called SAProt-T, which uses a combination of the original text and the output to T2struct to construct the sequence of amino acids in the final protein design. Here, the probabilities generated earlier matter, since SAProt-T performs a global re-evaluation. According to the authors, this avoids the risk of “overlooking a slightly less probable structure that can accommodate a far superior functional sequence.”
How do you develop a system that can do all of this? The researchers decided the best way was to use massive amounts of data. For each set of tags that describe a protein’s function, they fed the tags into an LLM and had it provide a plain-language description and used both the tags and the description as part of the training. They used protein sequences from three different databases, paired with structural information predicted by AlphaFold; just one of these databases contained 800 million keyword–protein pairs.
It’s noteworthy that AlphaFold is not 100 percent accurate in its predictions, so if you’re trying to generate something related to a relatively obscure protein, this could be a problem. But many common proteins have structural data available, which presumably would ensure AlphaFold made informed predictions.
In any case, apparently enough of the structural data was right for the training to work.
Functional proteins
To test Pinal, the researchers asked it to design four very different proteins: a fluorescent one, two enzymes, and one that takes part in a large multi-protein complex. While the details vary a bit from case to case, there was a similar process for each; we’ll use the fluorescent protein as an example.
The classic example of a fluorescent protein, which won its discoverer a Nobel, is GFP, the green fluorescent protein. Pinal was asked to produce 50,000 proteins that could fluoresce like GFP. This massive list was then filtered down by a number of criteria. For starters, the researchers rejected anything with a sequence that looked like a known fluorescent protein. But they selected for a couple of key features found in GFP: the ability to form a barrel-like structure, and the presence of a key amino acid that can be chemically modified to enable fluorescence.
In short, they wanted it to be a bit like GFP in general, but not very similar in terms of the specific amino acid sequence. That filtering left them with a high-priority list of just 29 candidate proteins, all of which were made in E. coli. A grand total of one of them fluoresced.
All the other examples were done similarly: start with a massive list, narrow it down computationally, then test a few dozen designs, of which only a few would work.
It would be tempting to dismiss this as a horrifically low success rate. But remember that a lot of the suggestions that were most likely to work would look a lot like known GFP proteins, and so be weeded out. The researchers also didn’t even bother to test whether things that didn’t form a structure similar to GFP might work, so they may have rejected a huge range of alternative fluorescent proteins based on that.
Not just proteins
Last week also saw the introduction of something very similar but focused on DNA sequences. A collaboration of the AI company Hugging Face, the Zhongguancun Academy, and the University of Naples “Federico II” introduced what they’re calling Carbon X, an open-weight model that can run on local hardware. It is based on a human-language model called Qwen3-14B but was retrained using DNA, followed by reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning.
The re-training (technically termed mid-training) required a careful balancing act: “A low learning rate preserves English but leaves DNA at chance, and a high one learns DNA but forgets English.” But the result is a single model that can speak both DNA and English and translate between them. So, like large genome models, you can prompt it with a DNA sequence, and it will attempt to predict sequences that might come after it in a typical genome. But you can also prompt it with a mix of DNA and natural language, asking it things like “what would the consequence of changing this G to an A be?”
While the team has not released a publication describing the behavior of the system, their internal performance suggests it’s quite good, being competitive with large, specialized commercial models like GPT-6.1 Sol. That said, it also includes a few cautions. The system is not especially good at noting specific positions, especially on longer sequences. It can also be prone to hallucinations if the prompt isn’t specific enough. So, the usual cautions when using an AI tool definitely apply.
Hugging Face points out two major reasons why Carbon X might be a better option than commercial models, even for tasks where the commercial models tend to perform a bit better, both of them related to the fact that Carbon X can be run locally. The first is simply cost; the company’s demonstration video was done using a MacBook, so it can be run repeatedly on relatively affordable hardware. The second is that there are many situations where, for proprietary or privacy reasons, people will not want to share the inquiries they’re making with a commercial entity.
Keeping it plain
It’s easy to think this is dumbing biology down so anyone with the slightest bit of knowledge can start making custom proteins and viruses. That’s not entirely accurate. They can easily get the sequences out of the tool. But they will then likely need to use a lot of specialized tools to screen through these in order to find sequences that are more likely to be functional. And then there’s the issue of testing them, which requires a well-equipped biology lab and trained specialists.
Biologists have clearly not been taken out of the equation.
In many cases, this may solve ongoing issues faced by experimental biologists. In the post-genome era, there have been lots of questions that are best answered via computers. But a lot of tools made to get these answers were made by bioinformaticians who did not go out of their way to make their tools approachable. Many biologists can understand a relatively English-ish phrase like “find me all the enhancers that control the expression of this gene.” But far fewer will know which combination of tools are needed to answer that question, much less how to configure them.
Giving those biologists a tool that can answer these questions without the need to consult multiple software manuals has potential to accelerate research. But it may take a few years before it becomes clear that biologists find this capability useful.
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.

- Versions of a post claiming to state a list of "facts" about the history of Social Security have circulated online for over a decade.
- This supposed list of facts is so pervasive, the Social Security Administration debunked the claims within it on the administration's website.
- We have rated this list overall as mostly false because every claim is largely or entirely inaccurate, except for two.
- Former President Franklin D. Roosevelt — who signed the law creating Social Security — did, in fact, put the program's money in a trust fund separate from the government's general budget. However, claims that former President Lyndon B. Johnson reversed that decision are inaccurate. Social Security has always been in a separate, independent fund and still is as of this writing.
- Democrats did, in fact, increase taxes on Social Security annuities under former President Bill Clinton, but only for higher earners.
In late 2026, readers asked us about posts claiming to share a long list of "facts" about the history of Social Security, including five supposedly broken "promises" about the program and a Q&A section about the Democratic Party's supposed impact on the public benefits program.
Snopes readers referenced posts on LinkedIn and Facebook. These posts claimed that when former President Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced the public benefits program, he allegedly promised voluntary participation, far lower tax rates, tax deductible-eligibility and a Social Security fund separate from the general government budget.
The Q&A section of the posts blamed the Democratic Party for supposedly breaking these promises and providing benefits to immigrants.
Here's one example: 
HISTORY LESSON ON YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY CARD:
Just in case some of you young whippersnappers (& some older ones) didn't know this. It's easy to check out, if you don't believe it. Be sure and show it to your family and friends. They need a little history lesson on what's what and it doesn't matter whether you are Democrat or Republican. Facts are FACTS.
Up until the 1980's, Social Security cards expressly stated the number and card were not to be used for identification purposes.
Since nearly everyone in the United States now has a number, it became convenient to use it anyway and the "NOT FOR IDENTIFICATION" message was removed.
Franklin Roosevelt, a Democrat, introduced the Social Security (FICA) Program. His promises are in black, with updates in brackets.
1.) That participation in the Program would be completely voluntary [No longer voluntary],
2.) That the participants would only have to pay 1% of the first $1,400 of their annual Incomes into the Program [Now 7.65% on the first $90,000, and 15% on the first $90,000 if you're self-employed],
3.) That the money the participants elected to put into the Program would be deductible from their income for tax purposes each year [No longer tax deductible],
4.) That the money the participants put into the independent 'Trust Fund' rather than into the general operating fund, and therefore, would only be used to fund the Social Security Retirement Program, and no other Government program [Under Johnson the money was moved to the General Fund and spent], and
5.) That the annuity payments to the retirees would never be taxed as income [Under Clinton & Gore up to 85% of your Social Security can be taxed].
Since many of us have paid into FICA for years and are now receiving a Social Security check every month — and then finding that we are getting taxed on 85% of the money we paid to the Federal government to 'put away' — you may be interested in the following:
Q: Which Political Party took Social Security from the independent 'Trust Fund' and put it into the general fund so that Congress could spend it?
A: It was Lyndon Johnson and the democratically controlled House and Senate.
Q: Which Political Party eliminated the income tax deduction for Social Security (FICA) withholding? 
A: The Democratic Party.
Q: Which Political Party started taxing Social Security annuities? 
A: The Democratic Party, with Al Gore casting the 'tie-breaking' deciding vote as President of the Senate, while he was Vice President of the US
Q: Which Political Party decided to start giving annuity payments to immigrants? 
A: That's right! Jimmy Carter and the Democratic Party. Immigrants moved into this country, and at age 65, began to receive Social Security payments! The Democratic Party gave these payments to them, even though they never paid a dime into it! 
Different versions of this copypasta — copied-and-pasted text shared online — have spread for years. The claims within have been debunked not only by independent fact-checkers, but by the Social Security Administration itself. In fact, these claims contain so many inaccurate details that our peers at FactCheck.org said in 2009 that they believed a near-identical version of the post circulating online "must be an intentional and malicious effort at disinformation."
Given that almost every single supposed "fact" in the above post is largely inaccurate — but there are a few details based in varying levels of truth — we have rated the overall post as mostly false. 
Below, we broke down each claim made in the post and gave each its own rating, primarily relying on the Social Security Administration and the original Social Security Act of 1935 that Roosevelt signed into law.
(For further reading, we also previously looked into a list of supposed Social Security "fun facts.")
Roosevelt's supposed promises
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised that participation in Social Security would be completely voluntary.
RATING: Mostly False
All employees who are covered by Social Security are subject to the Federal Insurance Contributions Act tax, or the FICA payroll tax, which funds Social Security and Medicare.
"Like all taxes, this has never been voluntary," said the Social Security Administration. "From the first days of the program to the present, anyone working on a job covered by Social Security has been obligated to pay their payroll taxes."
According to the Social Security Administration, however, when Roosevelt passed the law, "only about half the jobs in the economy were covered by Social Security." As such, people could technically choose to work a job that did not pay FICA taxes, which would make them ineligible for Social Security benefits. Nevertheless, there's no record of Roosevelt promising that participation in the program would be "completely voluntary," contrary to claims.
As of 2026, an estimated 94% of workers are covered under Social Security.
There are several exceptions to mandatory participation in Social Security, such as for some employees of state and local governments, who might be able to voluntarily choose Social Security coverage under certain conditions.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised participants would only have to pay 1% of the first $1,400 of their annual incomes into the program.
RATING: Mostly False
The tax rate on employees is listed in the Social Security Act of 1935 as 1% on the first $3,000 of earnings from 1937 to 1939. The rate then would increase on a regular schedule up until the end of 1948, when it was 3% on the first $3,000 of earnings.
Section 801 clearly lays out the tax rates:
INCOME TAX ON EMPLOYEES
SECTION 801. In addition to other taxes, there shall be levied, collected, and paid upon the income of every individual a tax equal to the following percentages of the wages (as defined in section 811) received by him after December 31, 1936, with respect to employment (as defined in section 811) after such date:
(1) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1937, 1938, and 1939, the rate shall be 1 per centum.
(2) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1940, 1941, and 1942, the rate shall 1 1/2 per centum.
(3) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1943, 1944, and 1945, the rate shall be 2 per centum.
(4) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1946, 1947, and 1948, the rate shall be 2 1/2 per centum.
(5) With respect to employment after December 31, 1948, the rate shall be 3 per centum.
Meanwhile, Section 811 defines "wages" as everything paid to an individual up to $3,000.
We have rated this claim as mostly false because the 1% tax rate figure in the claim was somewhat accurate for the program's early years — even though the maximum taxable amount claimed in the rumor is inaccurate. Furthermore, Roosevelt did not expressly promise a permanent 1% tax rate, per the law.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised the money the participants elected to put into the program would be deductible for income tax purposes.
RATING: False
In truth, Section 803, Title VIII of the original 1935 law that Roosevelt signed expressly forbids making employees' Social Security payments tax deductible (emphasis ours):
SEC. 803. For the purposes of the income tax imposed by Title I of the Revenue Act of 1934 or by any Act of Congress in substitution therefor, the tax imposed by section 801 shall not be allowed as a deduction to the taxpayer in computing his net income for the year in which such tax is deducted from his wages.
Since the claim made is the opposite of the truth in this instance, we have rated it as false.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised the money participants paid would be put in an account independent from the general government fund.
RATING: Mostly True (but misleading)
The Social Security Administration called this idea "basically correct."
However, the list of "facts" in question claims that this was a broken promise and that under former President Lyndon B. Johnson, "the money was moved to the General Fund and spent." Below, we rate that claim, which shows up in the Q&A section of the post, as false.
That's because the government's independent Social Security trust fund has never been "put into the general fund of the government," the Social Security Administration said.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised Social Security annuity payments to retirees would never be taxed as income.
RATING: Mostly False
According to the Social Security Administration, while Social Security benefits were not originally taxable income, that had nothing to do with the Social Security Act of 1935, "nor anything that President Roosevelt did or could have 'promised.'"
In truth, Treasury Department issued a series of administrative rulings after the law already passed determining that Social Security benefits would initially not be taxable income.
In 1983, under former President Ronald Reagan, a Republican, Congress changed the law to authorize the taxation of Social Security benefits (see the section titled "TAX TREATMENT" for a detailed explanation from the Social Security Administration about how the Social Security Amendments of 1983 changed U.S. tax code).
Since Roosevelt was president when the Treasury Department's administrative rulings went into effect — but he made no such promise about taxable income, nor did he personally sign such a rule into law — we have rated this claim as mostly false.
Evaluating more of the post's claims
CLAIM: Former President Lyndon B. Johnson and the Democratic Party took Social Security payments from the program's independent trust fund and put the money into the general fund so Congress could spend it.
RATING: False
As we previously stated, the Social Security Trust Fund has always been a separate, independent account.
This claim likely comes from confusion about how the Social Security Trust Fund is treated in federal budget accounting, the Social Security Administration said.
In 1968, the Johnson administration changed the way the federal government presents its budget by creating a "unified budget." This was simply a framework for presenting all of the federal government's finances together in order to make the budget less confusing.
Presenting everything as a unified budget did not actually change the operations of the Social Security trust fund. The way Social Security is presented in relation to the federal government's budget has undergone changes since Johnson's time, but it ultimately doesn't change how the federal government actually deposits or withdraws money from the fund.
We have rated this claim as false because Johnson did not take money from Social Security's independent trust fund, nor did he put it in the general fund so Congress could spend it.
CLAIM: The Democratic Party eliminated an income tax deduction for Social Security (FICA) withholding.
RATING: False
As stated above, Section 803, Title VIII of the original Social Security Act prohibited income tax deductions for Social Security (FICA) withholding. As such, there was no income tax deduction for the Democratic Party to eliminate.
CLAIM: The Democratic Party enacted taxes on Social Security annuities.
RATING: Mostly False
Taxes on Social Security benefits began in 1984 under Reagan, who signed the Social Security Amendments of 1983.
Those amendments, which were aimed at saving the Social Security program from insolvency, passed on a bipartisan vote and came from a bipartisan commission's recommendations. (Reagan even praised the "bipartisan spirit" in which the amendments were passed.)
"The basic rule put in place was that up to 50% of Social Security benefits could be added to taxable income, if the taxpayer's total income exceeded certain thresholds," the Social Security Administration said.
At the time, Reagan presented the amendments and the new taxes as a compromise to ensure the Social Security system continued: 
Time and again, benefits were increased far beyond the taxes and wages that were supposed to support them. In this compromise we have struck the best possible balance between the taxes we pay and the benefits paid back. Any more in taxes would be an unfair burden on working Americans and could seriously weaken our economy. Any less would threaten the commitment already made to this generation of retirees and to their children.
Since Democrats were involved in the efforts to save Social Security in the 1980s by taxing annuities — but these taxes happened under Reagan and were overwhelmingly bipartisan — we have rated this claim as mostly false.
CLAIM: The Democratic Party increased taxes on Social Security annuities, with former Vice President Al Gore casting a "tie-breaking" vote in the Senate.
RATING: Mostly True 
In 1993, Congress increased taxes on Social Security benefits through a single provision in a massive budget bill called the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act, which former President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, signed into law.
Section 13215 of the bill increased the taxes from the 1983 amendments from 50% to 85% for "higher income" beneficiaries (see Page 164 of the bill).
After its passage, Clinton said the act "created real fairness" in the U.S. tax code by placing more tax burden on higher earners and implementing tax cuts on low-income working families.
As vice president, Gore did, in fact, cast the tie-breaking vote, given that Republicans were universally against this legislation at the time (as were a few Democrats).
CLAIM: The Democratic Party and former President Jimmy Carter passed a law giving Social Security annuity payments to immigrants, who don't pay into the program.
RATING: False 
Noncitizens in the United States who have Social Security-covered jobs — in other words, almost every job in the country — must pay Social Security payroll taxes.
That even includes people who are working in the U.S. without authorization or those working in the country temporarily.
In fact, a 2013 report from the Social Security Administration found that immigrants in the country illegally paid a net $10 billion to the Social Security trust fund in 2010. More recently, an independent report from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy found "undocumented immigrants paid $25.7 billion in Social Security taxes" in 2022. (It is worth noting that some immigrants are also in the country legally but cannot legally work in the United States.)
Immigrants who become citizens or legal residents can qualify for Social Security only to the extent that they have worked and paid into the system — the same as for citizens.
When the Social Security program began, there were no restrictions on payments to noncitizens, according to a Congressional Research Service report. Restrictions for certain groups of noncitizens came later.
It's unclear where the claim about Carter came from. The Social Security Administration said this claim likely confuses the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program with Social Security. SSI is a federal welfare program that some immigrants can qualify for, but it was an initiative of former President Richard Nixon, a Republican, not Carter.

Fast bowler Mitchell Starc did not know Australia’s premier batsman Steve Smith would not take part in the decisive third Test against South Africa at Newlands on Tuesday until he went to warm-up ahead of play.
Smith tested his neck injury in the nets on Tuesday morning but was still experiencing discomfort, captain Pat Cummins said at the toss.
“He wasn’t happy with how his neck was feeling, so we had to look elsewhere,” Cummins said.
Smith’s absence meant he would not feature at the ground where he was embroiled in the 2018 ball-tampering ‘Sandpapergate’ scandal, with much of the pre-match focus centred on how Australia’s most experienced batter would cope with the occasion.
“I did not know he was not playing until I went out to warm-up today,” Starc told reporters after the day’s play. “He has been battling that neck since last week.
“I don’t actually know what happened with that and I have not asked. He seems upbeat enough, but I don’t know what he has had done.”
After winning the toss, Cummins opted to bowl, a rare decision at Newlands that might have been taken with the reshuffle of the top six batsmen after Josh Inglis learnt just before the start he would replace Smith.
The move initially appeared to have backfired as South Africa made a strong start. However, Starc produced a masterful spell with the second new ball late in the day, finishing with figures of six for 72 as the host was dismissed for 329 on the stroke of stumps.
“I am not in that pay bracket,” Starc said when asked if he agreed with the decision to bowl first. “My opinion doesn’t matter. It is what it is. At one point it looked like we were bowling a fair bit tomorrow, so it was good to bowl them out today.
“There was clearly not as much swing and sideways movement as we thought might be on offer (early in the day). But we found different ways to be effective and if you delete that first session, I think the last two were back on what we expected.”
It was another see-saw day in a series that has already seen plenty of twists and turns.
“These are two very good cricket teams. At times it is going to get away from you, at times you will wrestle the momentum back, which we did in the second half of the day,” Starc said.
“I expect more swings through the test match as we now need to go and bat and they have a very good (bowling) attack.”

Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up
- Published
Jose Mourinho has done it again.
The Real Madrid manager celebrated Kylian Mbappe's late winner at Barcelona on Sunday with a trademark knee slide, as he maintained his midas touch over their bitter rivals.
Mourinho has become just the third Real boss to go six El Clasicos in a row without defeat - 13 years after he last led Los Blancos in this fixture.
Four wins and two draws in his past six matches in charge of Real Madrid against Barcelona put him up there with Miguel Munoz (1962 to 1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001 to 2003) as Real managers who have gone six in a row without defeat against the old enemy.
It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions
And more importantly for Mourinho, Mbappe's double in Real's 2-1 win ended Barcelona's nine-game unbeaten domestic run with a crucial Clasico victory at the Camp Nou.
A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho's side to within three points of their rivals.
"In my view, Real Madrid do not play to win at the Camp Nou, Real Madrid play to win La Liga," he said.
"We could win with luck, but we won with calmness and with all merit," he said. "It's a very strong group. Everyone works very hard. Everyone was ready to win.
"The credit goes to the players. When you win, the credit goes to the players. But when you lose, the blame falls on you. And that's why we see coaches being sacked from their positions every week."
The Portuguese, who returned to Real 13 years after his first stint in charge this summer, has now won six and lost six El Clasicos.
He said: "I've learned that I have an extraordinary group, with the quality and mindset to play.
"In midfield, having a mix of talents gives us more than just having two players with similar characteristics. This mix of talents gives us balance when defending and quality when we go on the attack.
"We've beaten several teams by four or more goals, but this is Barca, and the players put on a great performance. We need to continue like this and don't go over the moon after this win."
Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he didn't want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team lacked fresh legs after a demanding few weeks.
"We missed the freshness," he said. "It's not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat.
"In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn't on our side.
"I can see that today we were not fresh and this is what we have to change."

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”

The BCA Stadium in Kotambi is a special venue for Pratika Rawal. It is where she was introduced to international cricket two years ago against the West Indies.
She made quite the first impression with 134 runs in her first three games. It was a sign of things to come as she went about piling on the runs from one series to the next. Even in a tough World Cup campaign, which ultimately ended with a major injury to her ankle, she ground out some valuable runs, including a century against New Zealand.
But the volume of runs was never the issue with Pratika. It was the rate at which they came in.
Back in Vadodara for an ODI series against Zimbabwe, Pratika’s ODI game looks visibly different. While she was scoring at a strike rate of 84 in 2025 and managed just 79 runs in three games against Australia earlier this year at an even lower rate of 75.96, in Vadodara, she leads the scoring charts in the ongoing series against the Lady Chevrons with 161 runs in two games at a much-improved 98.77. Her century in the first game even came at a sprightly 104.16.
“The more matches I have played over the years, the more I am understanding the game. So, it’s basically an adaptation of that game, adaptation of my batting and adaptation to how the bowlers are bowling to me,” she told reporters ahead of the third ODI here.
There is a marked change in her approach, particularly in the PowerPlay. After being the steady hand that allowed Smriti Mandhana to unlock her quickscoring ways, Pratika is focusing on her own boundary hitting skills.
“I have worked on that as well, to be able to find more boundaries in the PowerPlay because there are only two fielders outside. You can actually get an advantage and hit a lot of boundaries. When you see Smriti batting at the other end, you feel there’s a lot to learn. So I try to replicate what she does when she is in her best version. Hopefully, I will get there as well.”
The numbers are telling. Before the Zimbabwe series, her PowerPlay strike rate was around 77. In the first two ODIs against the Women in Red, not only is Pratika unbeaten in the first 10 overs, but she’s also striking at 104.
Role clarity goes a long way in securing a batter’s focus firmly on their process. With Shafali Verma’s explosive quality, particularly in the PowerPlay, available for the team to utilise, Pratika needed to buck up. But it helps that the murmurs about batting position and shuffling are not ones the dressing room has in its space.
“There were no conversations inside the dressing room about the batting order to be very honest,” she explained.

“Smriti and I knew that we were going in as openers and I think Shafali knew as well that she was going in one down. That’s the same batting order that we followed in the Australia tour as well. I went with a clear mindset that I’m opening for the Indian team. There were no doubts about that.”
That clarity was important given she was fresh from an initiation to T20Is that did not go as smoothly as she would have wanted. Handed a debut in the Asia Cup, the 26-year-old returned scores of 22,10, 4 and 20.
She didn’t make the cut for the T20Is in the Zimbabwe series, and had time to gear up for the One-Dayers.
“The first thing I did after going home was to bat for a longer duration because it’s a longer format. To be able to have that patience even when they bowl a flighted ball, to just stay there and push it for a single and try to build your inning — these were some points I worked on back home. Honestly, when you bat for a longer duration, you get that sense of confidence. You get that feeling that you are timing the ball well and everything else just works out your way.”
Her century came on the first anniversary of another ton, an important one, against New Zealand in the 2025 ODI World Cup.
“It wasn’t a perfect innings, and as a batter you have to learn from that. But it was one of those days when the ball went where I wanted it to. Luckily, it turned out really good today,” she had said after that knock. She only leaned into that comfort with a commanding half century that dug India out of trouble when it was left stumped at 19 for 2.
While working on her strokeplay, taking it deep into the innings is another element Pratika would want to stay on top of, more so now when her opening partner navigates the added pressures of captaincy.
In 28 innings, Pratika has a cluster of dismissals in between the 19th to 30th over, with only two past the 42nd over (when the game goes that long). Should India bat first on Wednesday, the Women and Blue and the steady opening bat from New Delhi will have their chance.

About 60,000 Microsoft employees have a choice to make: take a buyout and leave at the end of the year, or stay.
Eligible employees have until early December to decide. Offers reviewed by Business Insider vary by level, location, and length of service.
For US employees at levels 64 and below, the cash offer is one week of base pay for every six months of service; at levels 65 to 67, it is two weeks for every six months. The offers also include continued stock vesting and health insurance.
Buyouts are a reasonably common offering for corporations looking to cut costs, but deciding whether to take one can be difficult. Business Insider spoke to two HR experts to ask which factors employees should weigh and which questions they should ask before signing.
Read their top tips below:
Work out what the offer is really worth
"The number is important," Marjo Miles, founder and principal consultant at The Ember Effect, told Business Insider. "But really, there’s more than that number."
Employees should check what happens to their stock, paid time off, health coverage, and any bonus or commission due after they leave, Miles said. They should calculate how long the payout would cover household expenses after tax and deductions.
Deborah Saneman, CEO of workforce management and HR technology company Würk, told Business Insider that employees should price out replacement health insurance: how long coverage lasts, what they would pay monthly, and whether the company covers any of the premium.
She also recommended checking which shares would vest after their exit. "The headline number is only part of the picture, so get the details in writing," she said.
Plan for a longer job search
"Whatever somebody thinks their job search is going to take, double it in your mind and plan for that," Miles said.
She suggested using the time before the deadline to explore options. "Instead of deciding today, maybe start your job search today, she said.
Contacting people in their network and applying for roles could give employees a clearer sense of their prospects before they commit to leaving.
Saneman said employees should ask about career coaching, outplacement, or training. "A payout covers your bills, but help with the search itself can shorten the runway," she said.
Consider what staying could look like
Turning down a buyout does not guarantee job security, Miles said, though she cautioned against assuming layoffs will follow. Companies could leave vacant roles unfilled or take other steps to meet a savings goal.
"There are a lot of different ways that organizations can strategically get to their goal without just immediately doing a reduction," she said.
Saneman also cautioned against predicting what Microsoft or any other company might do next. "The benefit of a buyout is that it's on your own terms and gives you time to plan your next steps," she said. "A layoff may not."
Miles suggested asking how departing colleagues' work would be redistributed and what support would be available.
Saneman said employees should consider their longer-term plans: "The right choice is the one that fits where you want your career and your life to go, not just the one that looks best on paper."
Questions to ask before taking a buyout
Business Insider asked Saneman and Miles to share what questions they'd advise employees considering buyouts to ask. Read their four key questions below:
Would I be eligible for rehiring?
"Microsoft is a large organization, and professional paths may cross again in the future," Miles said. That may not make or break the decision, but it is worth knowing.
Will the payout be a lump sum or continued salary?
This can affect when the money arrives and how health insurance and other benefits are handled.
What happens to my bonus or commission?
Employees should check whether they will receive any payment due after their exit date and have the answer documented by HR.
What help will I get finding another job?
Saneman suggested asking about career coaching, interview preparation, and training to build new skills.

King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour.
The king arrived in the Bahamas to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.
His visit comes amid renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for the atrocities of transatlantic slavery and engage in reparations talks.
Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.
In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.
“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”
He said the Chogm leaders would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.
But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.
“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.
“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.
“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – a full and formal apology – and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”
Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.
She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”
The chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.
Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.
Charles is to travel to Guyana on Thursday where the president, Mohamed Irfaan Ali, recently called for the monarch to take the next step and offer to apologise.
The king follows the guidance of his ministers, and it is understood the government has not advised him to offer an apology or reparations, in keeping with established policy.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will join Charles in Antigua for the gathering of Commonwealth leaders.
Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.
A year later he described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to “deepen my own understanding of slavery’s enduring impact”, in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “At the request of host governments, the king’s programme will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future that are having a transformative effect on the region, as it confronts the challenges of today.
“For his majesty, this tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past. This will therefore also be reflected in differing ways and words during the tour, as you would expect.”
Additional reporting by Press Association

First, they saved the cow. Petunia was suffering from a bovine form of maple syrup urine disease, a life-threatening condition unusually prevalent in Pennsylvania’s Mennonite community.
At the local veterinary hospital, Petunia was given a novel gene therapy. Today, she is a healthy 5-year-old heifer.
The doctor behind this procedure wanted to save the calf, of course. But his mission was bigger — Kevin Strauss is building a biotech company by and for the people he treats inside a wooden, mortise-and-tenon frame medical center. The goal is to develop innovative gene therapies to treat the unique set of rare diseases that afflict Amish and Mennonite people.
Jason Mast has an inside look at the new company, including its effort to resurrect treatments abandoned by pharma or left to gather frost in an academic freezer, often because there are too few patients for a company to generate profit.
Our roundup of the big European cancer conference
My colleague Adam Feuerstein and I are leaving Madrid after a packed four days at the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual meeting. Selecting which readouts to cover is a form of triage given the massive amount of research being detailed (if you think we missed something game-changing, let us know), but one highlight in terms of outcomes didn’t come from some new drug. Rather, it was the combination of Amgen’s Imdelltra and AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi showing that it greatly extended survival in difficult-to-treat small cell lung cancer — and showing the potential of paired approaches.
Other highlights:
- Yes, the big readout was Merck and Moderna’s cancer vaccine, and yes, the wind got a bit taken out of the presentation’s sails with the embargo break. But it’s still a milestone in cancer research. Here’s our deep dive into what the results mean for melanoma care, and what they could mean for moving cancer vaccines into other tumor types. And don’t miss Adam chatting to Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel about the impact for the company, and where it goes from here. (We also got some early data from a vaccine designed to prevent tumors in an inherited condition that leaves people at much higher risk of cancer.)
- Scientists figuring out how to target KRAS led to a major advance in pancreatic cancer, as you’ve probably heard. Now more KRAS-targeting drugs are coming, often going after specific mutations. Roche unveiled strong data from divarasib in non-small cell lung cancer, and Incyte showed promising results from INCB161734 in pancreatic cancer.
- Three years ago at ESMO (coincidentally the last time the conference was in Madrid, so a real hardship assignment for me), I wrote about how antibody drug conjugates were all the rage. That continues to be the case, with important readouts from Merck, AstraZeneca, GSK, and beyond. One thing I’m thinking about going forward: These drugs in theory should be safer than the standard chemotherapies they’re designed to replace, but some of them carry quite serious side effects themselves. With so much money pouring into ADC design, is there a way to reduce rates of those adverse events? — Andrew Joseph
Too many emergency departments can’t handle child patients
A few years ago, parents rushed their baby to a small rural hospital. But the facility didn’t have pediatric specialists, pediatric nurses, or a children’s intensive care unit. As the little boy’s condition worsened, the hospital’s staff scrambled to identify a facility that could take him. But every children’s hospital in northern California was overwhelmed. No one had room for one more.
The baby died of RSV. And the problem has only gotten worse since then, write two pediatric care experts in a new First Opinion.
“In this new normal, community hospitals across the country are transferring children to dedicated pediatric centers not just because a child is critically ill, but increasingly because smaller hospitals have quietly lost the ability to manage even common conditions,” they write. “The nation’s relatively few children’s hospitals can’t accommodate every sick child, much as we would like to. We now routinely turn sick children away and hope one of our colleagues somewhere else will have a bed.”
What’s the solution? Read on.
The Washington news you need this week

A possible treatment for brain-eating amoebas, found in the sea
Brain-eating amoebas are the stuff of zombie novels and spooky season. They are also, unfortunately, real-world parasites found in warm freshwater. Infections caused by N. Fowleri are hard to treat and nearly always fatal. But researchers have isolated a compound that could help stop the disease.
The substance was taken from a marine bacterium, and has been able to kill multiple strains of N. Fowleri faster than the current treatment. There is much work to be done before this discovery can translate to medicine though. Researchers say their next focus will be studying whether the compound can cross the blood-brain barrier.

Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
Many student voters studying outside their hometown face a key decision before they even get a ballot: Should they register to vote where they go to school?
A Supreme Court ruling in 1979 affirmed the right of eligible students to register in the communities where they live during the academic year. But close to a half-century later, some people continue to question why students can vote in their college towns.
That issue resurfaced in discussions about changes Montana made last year to its requirements for residents who want to register to vote. After a student advocacy group sued, a state judge blocked the new restriction for now. That leaves the previous rules in place for Montana students who want to register to vote, including for the midterm elections through Election Day.
Now, as the wait continues for the judge's final ruling, some experts on student voting see the case as a reminder of common misunderstandings about the rights of some of the country's youngest voters.
Why out-of-state college students are like owners of multiple homes
Voting in the U.S. is tied to residency, and state and local governments determine who qualifies as a resident who can register.
To make sure certain voters, such as eligible students, are not discriminated against, federal law sets ground rules for residency requirements, explains Michael Hanmer, a professor of government and politics at the University of Maryland, whose research has focused on student voters.
"You can't apply different standards to different groups of people, so college students need to be treated the same as anybody else in the mix here who might be new to a particular place," Hanmer says.
All eligible voters have a right to cast a ballot somewhere. And like owners of multiple homes, many students are able to choose which of their residences to be that somewhere for registering to vote. In the legal world, it's known as their "domicile."
"It's defined as the one singular, fixed, permanent, principal home where one intends to return, although she may not currently reside there," explains Yael Bromberg, an attorney who co-edited the book Youth Voting Rights: Civil Rights, the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and the Fight for American Democracy on College Campuses. "In the case of a student who may not know where she might live after graduation, that determination of domicile is highly personal and an individualized assessment."
How Montana's new law could stop thousands of eligible students from voting
In Montana, a U.S. citizen who is 18 or older and has been a state resident for at least 30 days is generally eligible to register to vote there.
Last year, Montana's Republican-controlled legislature passed a new restriction for "temporary" residents in an "educational program." Under the revised state law, they could only register in a Montana county if they intend to make the county or the state their permanent home at the end of their program.
GOP state officials argue that restriction does not apply to students at colleges and universities in Montana. That interpretation, they claim in a court filing, "would render the word 'temporary' meaningless, because no one understands obtaining a two, four, or eight-year degree as a temporary endeavor."
So far, Missoula County Judge Jason Marks is not buying that argument. In February, he found the restriction against student voters likely violates Montana's constitution.
After holding a hearing this month, Marks is now preparing his final ruling for the lawsuit brought by student advocates at the Montana Public Interest Research Group. MontPIRG claims the change to Montana's residency rule could force thousands of students to lose the ability to have a say at the ballot box about how their communities are run.
Why out-of-state student voters should be aware of other state requirements
At a public hearing last year, some of the restriction's supporters said student voters from outside Montana should not be able to affect the state's elections.
But Hanmer at the University of Maryland doesn't see Montana's law clearing legal hurdles.
"I would be surprised if this attempt to restrict students from voting if they're in Montana just for educational purposes holds up," he says.
Still, Hanmer points out student voters who do have the right to choose where to register should keep in mind that, in some states, that choice may come with other requirements.
"If they want to follow through and vote in that new state, then they might have to engage in some additional activities that could be costly in terms of their time," Hanmer says. Certain states require a new resident to, for example, get a new state ID or change their car registration. "They can impose these restrictions," Hanmer adds, "but they impose them on all new residents, not just college students."

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

How much of Antonelli's success is down to his ability? - F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is one step closer to becoming the new F1 world champion after winning the United States Grand Prix from pole position.
The 20-year-old Italian, who leads team-mate George Russell by 123 points in the standings, will secure the title in Mexico City on Sunday by finishing ninth or higher.
BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race in Austin.
- Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet' 
  - Published1 day ago
This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achieve the same success. There is a theme throughout the season. How much of that is down to driver ability, driving style etc and how much is down to car set-up and strategy. Is George better than this or has he reached his limit? - Julian
The dominant theme of the 2026 season has been the degree to which Kimi Antonelli has stepped up his game after a mixed rookie season that contained some definite highs, but also quite a few difficulties.
In doing so, he has overwhelmed George Russell, who has accepted and is more than willing to say that Antonelli has simply done a better job than him this season.
Antonelli's performances this year have lived up to the billing with which he came to F1 - that he could be the sport's next generational talent.
He has had some luck, and some of his wins have turned on fortune - safety cars in Japan and Madrid, for example.
But he has also performed at a level of consistent excellence, and produced some absolutely standout performances, most obviously Monaco, Monza and Austin.
The Mercedes has on average been the best car, but Antonelli is the only one of the team's two drivers who has always been a factor. He fully deserves the world title that he is almost certain to clinch this weekend in Mexico City.
As for Russell, he has fundamentally used driving style as an explanation for his relative struggles, saying the previous cars suited his, and the new ones Antonelli's. He has won only three races compared with Antonelli's nine.
On Sunday, team principal Toto Wolff said Russell had struggled in Austin to get the right set-up on the Mercedes with the new upgrade package, which has been problematic since it was introduced in Malaysia.
Wolff said: "George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category and merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year.
"This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles and he struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us.
"We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.
"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all about the intelligence, the ability, the determination."
Driving style and set-up are genuine reasons for a driver to struggle in certain circumstances.
However, it's also a case that the absolute elite, the all-time greats - drivers such as Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso - tend to find a way to be at the top of their game regardless of the car's behaviour.
The worry for Russell right now is that if Antonelli is at that level - and it looks as though he has the potential to be, given his performances in only his second season - he will have his work cut out to beat him consistently in the future.
So he needs to regroup over the winter, come back next year and prove he can get back on to Antonelli's level.
With Lewis Hamilton's intentions clear of staying in F1 until there is an African Grand Prix, which I think will most likely be with Ferrari, what does that mean for the young talents who desire to drive for Ferrari? Will it be at least another four to five years before we see new drivers replacing either or both Lewis and Charles Leclerc? - Liam
Lewis Hamilton repeated in Austin last weekend that, ideally, he would like to still be racing when Formula 1 returns to Africa.
"I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," he said.
"So, yes, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."
Whether he can manage to stay that long is another question.
Formula 1 has said the African Grand Prix in Rwanda will be held in the "early 2030s".
The aim is for that to be in 2030 but it's not clear whether the new track will be ready by then.
Even if they make that deadline, will Hamilton still be racing? He will be 45 at the start of 2030. That's the same age as Fernando Alonso is now, and he is still going strong.
Hamilton's answer alludes to his current contract, which it is believed lasts until the end of 2027. So he would need to do another one of three years to make it to 2030.
As he says, if he is still performing at the level he is now by the middle of next year, why not? But as yet it's not clear what Ferrari will think about that.
Hamilton's presence - and the long-term contract held by team-mate Charles Leclerc - does raise questions about Ferrari's driver academy.
First and foremost, those questions surround Oliver Bearman, who is yet to finalise his new contract with Haas for next season.
Bearman has had a strong season and a new deal is believed to be pretty much a formality - driver and team have expressed their desire to stay together, and the Briton was talking in a BBC 5 live interview at the weekend very much as if he would still be a Haas driver next year.
But Bearman has higher ambitions than staying at Haas for the rest of his career.
If Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be at Ferrari for the next four years, Bearman would have every right to be asking the team what that means for him.
If he isn't going to get into the senior team, what can they do to further his career? Do they let him go, so he can pursue his ambitions elsewhere, or do they allow him to do that while still maintaining links?
These questions become even more pressing for Bearman now Brazilian Rafael Camara - also a Ferrari young driver - is joining Haas for 2027.
Bearman needs to beat the Brazilian if he is not to face an existential threat to his future as a potential driver for a top team.
What's been happening with Alex Albon this season? Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz seems to have the better of him, and the car doesn't look to be in a good place. - David
Of the two Williams drivers, in a team that is struggling, Carlos Sainz has had the better season.
But it's not as stark as it perhaps appears just looking on the surface.
Sainz leads Albon by two points in the championship, and while the qualifying comparison is skewed heavily towards Sainz on a head-to-head basis at 13-5, the time gap between them is 0.115 seconds.
As if Albon was not already having a rough season, to top it he incurred the wrath of Fernando Alonso in Austin after the two collided on the first lap, leaving both with damaged cars.
Alonso said: "The quality of the drivers in the lower third of the grid is very low, as we saw today with Alex."
Williams are in such a state this year that comparing the drivers should be treated with a degree of qualification.
The car has been slow, and the team have struggled with consistency between parts, as well as quality and degradation.
In other words, two parts that should perform the same have not always done so, and some of them wear out and lose performance quicker than others.
Of course that works across both drivers but it does make comparisons difficult.
Albon was asked about the comparison with Sainz in qualifying in Monza last month.
He pointed out that the crash he had in Canada when he hit a groundhog had been costly because there was a new engine in the car that weekend, which was written off. That meant he had to run an old engine longer than ideal.
And he alluded to Williams suffering from the same issues with varying engine performance that happened in the early days of the new engine rules at Mercedes and McLaren.
"There's a few things," Albon said. "In the beginning of the year, it was very battery-dominated.
"If you think even just the George and Kimi situation, that's the manufacturer side of it having issues. So you can imagine it's not just them two that have had problems.
"There's been a few qualifying sessions where the corners have been good, but you don't see it in the lap time. It's on the stopwatch.
"And then we're also going through our own issues as a team. And that's not just on my side. There's also a side where to say that both cars are performing in the same way would not be true. We've been fighting some inconsistencies in the cars that's been there since the beginning of the year.
"We're much better now at getting on top of them. If you look at the last four or five weekends, we're actually very close in terms of performance. But it's taken a while to get there."
Do you foresee a world in which live F1 coverage ever returns to free-to-air telly in the UK or is it now stuck behind a paywall for eternity? I've now taken a different career path but becoming an engineer in F1 was my ultimate ambition when I was applying for university in the early 2010s, inspired by BBC's live coverage. - Ian
In the UK, the current situation is that Sky has exclusive rights to broadcast F1 behind a paywall, while Channel 4 has highlights on free-to-air television, with live coverage of the British Grand Prix.
Sky has the rights until the end of 2034, after it struck a new deal for a larger fee earlier this year.
That came in the wake of Apple buying the US rights starting from this season.
At the same time, the television market is in flux as streaming becomes increasingly prevalent as a means of consuming content.
In that context, as well as the wider sports broadcast situation, it's hard to imagine a situation where F1 could return fully to free-to-air television.
The wider picture is it is still on free-to-air in some countries - Brazil as an example.
But F1 would also argue free-to-air does not always mean more people getting sight of the sport, depending on how it's promoted in various ways, and viewing habits are not the same in all countries.
Social media output is also an important consideration. At the same time, F1 is a business that exists to make money.
