International distributors continue to fall for “Ulya.”
The Latvian Oscar submission for Best International Feature Film has closed North America (New Mountain Films), France (Destiny), Italy (Invisible Carpet), Slovakia (ASFK), former Yugoslavia (Five Star Distribution), Estonia (Hea Film), Lithuania (GPI), MENA (Teleview), Finland (Cinema Orion), Poland (1989) and Brazil (Belas Arte).
The black-and-white film, directed by Viesturs Kairišs, will open the 30th edition of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival. It premiered at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section. Produced by Ego Media (LV), Allfilm (EE), Staroń Film (PL) and Tremora (LT), it’s sold by B-Rated International.
Inspired by the life of legendary basketball player Ulyana Semjonova, born in 1952, “Ulya” is not a typical biopic.
“I don’t think I could ever make a nice, typical biopic. My interest lies in arthouse films. I wasn’t really thinking about sports either. I wanted to tell a Werner Herzog-esque story about a giant girl living in the countryside,” Kairišs told Variety.
Semjonova was known for her size; she stood at seven feet tall. But it also made her a bit of a recluse.
“I’ve been wondering how to get into her head. I wanted it to be very, very subjective. To stick to her point of view, we used what we called ‘crazy cameras’ and slightly out-of-focus shots. Finding the landscape of her inner soul was a very concrete task.”
It was not Kairišs who came up with the idea of making a film about Semjonova. It was the long-held dream of his lead, Kārlis Arnolds Avots.
“When I became the artistic director of the Dailes Theatre, I was looking for actors and he was outstanding. During our first meeting, when I asked him to join our ensemble, he said: ‘You know, I would like to play Ulyana Semjonova.’ Then I forgot all about it,” recalled Kairišs.
“In theatre, it’s not unusual for men to play women. It goes back to Shakespearean times. A few years later, he played in my film ‘January’. At one point, while I was resting, I heard Kārlis talking to our DP, explaining this idea to him again. That’s when I realized: It’s a film!”
Other collaborators still needed convincing, though. “Everyone wanted us to make a standard biopic. I understand it. It could be a good film, but it wouldn’t be my film. We set out to make a film about a girl and we just had to believe in it.”
As proved by a photograph of Semjonova with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, added at the end of the film, she actually gave them her blessing. She passed away in January, 2026.
“She trusted us. It must have been strange to have us come over and say: ‘And a boy will be playing you.’ But it quickly became clear why it made sense,” said Kairišs.
“I actually saw Kārlis yesterday. He’s been filming [the Viking series] ‘Bloodaxe,’ so he has a long beard and he’s really big right now. But he always felt close to her somehow. He knew how it felt to be treated as a ‘giant’.”
Or simply as an outsider. To Kairišs’ surprise, “Ulya” has managed to connect with all kinds of viewers, regardless of their size. “Everyone is struggling with something they want to hide, but it’s probably the best part of who they are,” he said.
“We had incredible reactions everywhere in Latvia. This film is a blockbuster – we’re already the second most-watched film in history. It was the same at Cannes, Rome and Los Angeles. None of my previous films have received this kind of response. Even my daughter said to me: ‘It’s about me, too.’ We touched upon something that’s very modern and very universal.”
Kairišs added: “There’s so much pressure today to look the same and like the same things. We live in times that try to kill all the difference. Everyone struggles with their identity or feels like a ‘freak’. We just have to learn to trust this freak and embrace it as the best thing about us, rather than trying to get rid of it.”

Man Utd stick with Carrick - inside a turbulent 48 hours at Old Trafford
- Published
When Michael Carrick disappeared down the tunnel after Manchester United's loss to Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the support from fans for a legendary player turned to hostility and anger at the current squad.
The atmosphere afterwards was said to be emotional.
Carrick was the last to leave the stadium and, as usual, patiently posed for selfies and signed shirts for the fans who remained on what had been a foul day weather-wise, and an awful one on the pitch.
Asked in his post-match news conference if he expected to be in charge for Saturday's trip to Chelsea, Carrick said: "I'm not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I'm carrying on as normal."
Few felt that was sustainable. Even Carrick's coaching team wondered whether they would survive.
And yet, that is what has happened.
United have decided Carrick and his players will have the chance to turn the present situation around. No timescale has been put on this, but Carrick will be in charge at Chelsea, with his team 16th in the table.
They have a crucial Champions League match against Roma three days later, then a Premier League encounter with in-form Aston Villa before a two-week international break.
No-one from Manchester United is saying so, but that would be the most obvious time to decide if a change of coach is required.
Waiting for a decision that never came
On Monday morning, when it was widely anticipated an announcement terminating Carrick's tenure would be made, a senior figure at United said calmness and a clear head would be needed to navigate the turbulence around Old Trafford.
Carrick had been treading water since the crushing 4-1 defeat at Como on 21 October - one of the worst European nights in club history.
Respected United fan and United We Stand fanzine editor Andy Mitten, who interviewed chief executive Omar Berrada on behalf of the club last June, described the performance as "an affront to the name of Manchester United".
In addition to the catastrophic nature of the performance, captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick's tactics and the inability of his coaches to spot what was going wrong.
Fernandes' comments came a week after defender Lisandro Martinez said he had expected more investment in the squad and - turning attention to Jason Wilcox - "more from our technical director".
It painted a picture of a squad out of control, posing an immediate dilemma for the United hierarchy.
Feeling it would look reactionary and impulsive to remove Carrick based on the negativity of one game, United stuck with the 45-year-old for the Bournemouth match - only for that to turn sour thanks to a performance that, arguably, was worse than the one in Italy.
Fernandes played no part and was dropped to the bench. Afterwards, the Portugal star liked an Instagram post which included the caption: "Never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care".
Late on Sunday night, BBC Sport was led to believe a final decision to sack Carrick had not been made, and the judgement would stretch into Monday.
There was no decision then, either. The United players who started against Bournemouth were given the day off but bizarrely, Fernandes and Carrick were both at Carrington. Fernandes was having pre-planned treatment while Carrick watched a closed doors Under-21s game.
Also at the training ground were Berrada and Wilcox, discussing what the immediate future should look like. Sources say it is inconceivable minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family would not have been part of those discussions.
It was early evening before it became clear there would be no update on Carrick's future. His arrival at Carrington at 07:30 GMT on Tuesday was a sign he would take training as normal and, along with Fernandes and several other players, Carrick signed autographs and posed for photographs with a group of fans invited to the training ground that day.
Four hours later, United sources confirmed he would be in charge at Stamford Bridge.
'We all want to put it right'
The current predicament at the club is seen as not being entirely Carrick's fault.
Senior figures at the club feel United's players - a squad they think are capable of qualifying for the Champions League - are underperforming badly and should shoulder some of the blame.
There does seem to be a general desire to help Carrick out. One player told BBC Sport: "The feeling is that we all want to put it right. Players, staff, everyone."
It is not known if the "we" includes Fernandes, and BBC Sport has not been made aware of what, if any, conversations have taken place between the captain and his boss.
Obviously, it is easier to get rid of one manager and his backroom team than an entire squad of players - and if results do not turn around, Carrick will pay the price.
One former senior United official told BBC Sport: "Ordinarily, Michael would have gone. The last two performances were unacceptable and team discipline is broken. Not doing it is fascinating and risky."
Cynics may argue the main reason Carrick is still in a job is because of the inability to secure a replacement before the Chelsea game. Additionally, some of the coaches current Under-18s boss Darren Fletcher called on to help him during his spell as interim manager in January are now part of the senior set-up.
As highlighted by BBC Sport on Monday, Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann were among the options explored by United as they weighed up whether to make a change. Any decision to appoint Howe would trigger a multi-million pound compensation payment from his former club Newcastle.
BBC Sport has also been told former Chelsea boss Antonio Conte is willing to have a conversation about the job, although there has been no direct contact.
That trio are all out of work - as is Kieran McKenna, who worked with Carrick as part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at United and then left for Ipswich.
Aston Villa's Unai Emery also has strong backing at United, but the club are realistic about their chances of tempting the Spaniard from Villa Park.
What about Berrada and Wilcox?
Wilcox's future has also come under intense scrutiny.
One source close to United feels it is inevitable the former Blackburn and Leeds player will eventually lose his job if a third managerial change in as many seasons is made.
There is sympathy with Wilcox, who did not set the summer transfer budget. Others say Ratcliffe has provided significant funds for transfers since he took charge of football affairs in early 2024, as well as injecting £300m of his own money into the club.
While disgruntled fans may point to the recruitment of teams such as Brentford and Brighton as proof good players can be signed without paying astronomical fees, options for bigger clubs such as United were said to be scarce during the summer window.
Nevertheless, it has never been explained why it was decided to focus on bolstering the midfield last summer, rather than address clear personnel issues at left-back and central striker. Injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko have made that issue even more acute.
Another senior figure in the game told BBC Sport both Wilcox and Berrada may be vulnerable, suggesting Ratcliffe could be considering a wider overhaul of senior staff.
For now, though, minds are focused on Stamford Bridge, with Carrick due to speak to the media on Thursday.

Cyclone Arnab makes landfall in Andhra Pradesh; trees uprooted, power supply disrupted
Gusty winds with speeds of 125-135 kmph have been reported in Kakinada, Konaseema and West Godavari districts and will continue over the next three hours
Severe cyclone Arnab made landfall on the Andhra Pradesh coast between Kakinada and Yanam of Puducherry early Wednesday affecting the entire coastal Andhra with destructive winds and torrential rains, disrupting normal life, authorities said.
According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the process of the extremely severe cyclone making landfall began on Tuesday night in Konaseema district and Narsapuram areas in West Godavari district.
A bulletin released by AP State Disaster Management Authority chairman Prakhar Jain at 6am on Wednesday said the landfall process of the very severe cyclone Arnab was continuing, with its “eye” located approximately 30km from Narsapur, 55km from Yanam, 70km from Kakinada and 90km from Machilipatnam.
“Gusty winds with speeds of 125-135 kmph have been reported in Kakinada, Konaseema and West Godavari districts and will continue over the next three hours,” Jain said.
According to reports being received in the control room at the state secretariat, uprooted trees, fallen electricity poles, damaged roads, inundated low-lying areas and widespread power outages were reported from Srikakulam in the north to Bapatla in the south.
Visakhapatnam district recorded the highest rainfall, with 200.20mm reported by midnight on Tuesday. Kothavalasa in Vizianagaram district received 162.75mm.
Sea waves in the Kakinada and Yanam regions reported to have risen to the heights of 1.5 to 2.5 metres, while reports from affected coastal stretches indicated waves surging much higher in some locations.
Road, rail transport hit
As many as 63 trains were cancelled and 15 others rescheduled in view of the deteriorating weather conditions. The Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (APSRTC) cancelled 160 services in Visakhapatnam district.
The government has imposed restrictions on night-time travel in Visakhapatnam and several other districts from Tuesday night as a precautionary measure.
Road connectivity was disrupted at multiple locations, including stretches of National Highway 16 between Kathipudi and Ongole, where traffic movement came to a standstill, according to reports from the affected areas.
Visakhapatnam affected by heavy rain and winds
Visakhapatnam bore the brunt of heavy rain and powerful winds, with seawater advancing significantly towards the city. Uprooted trees blocked roads and damaged vehicles. Electricity supply was disrupted across the city.
Extremely heavy rainfall was reported in Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Srikakulam, Parvathipuram Manyam, Anakapalli, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Kakinada and East Godavari districts.
The situation remained tense in coastal settlements as residents faced the combined threat of heavy rain, strong winds and rising sea levels.
Coastal damage reported in Kakinada and Konaseema
The coastal areas of Kakinada and Dr BR Ambedkar Konaseema districts were among the worst-affected regions as Cyclone Arnab intensified on Tuesday night.
What began as light rain in the morning developed into torrential downpours accompanied by powerful winds by nightfall, bringing normal life to a standstill. Waves surged along the coast, with reports from affected stretches indicating heights of five to eight metres.
At Kothapatnam near Uppada, a protective wall constructed with boulders was severely damaged by the force of the waves. Several motorcyclists travelling along coastal roads lost their balance amid the powerful winds and spray from the sea. Six people sustained minor injuries.
Uppada–Kakinada Beach Road damaged
Large stones placed as part of coastal erosion-control measures were broken apart or dislodged and scattered across the road, further obstructing movement.
Hundreds of electricity poles collapsed in Kakinada and Konaseema districts, while numerous hoardings were brought down by the winds. Several mobile towers were also tilted or damaged. With power supply to many towers interrupted, mobile communication signals failed in several areas.
At Allavaram, seawater reached the compound wall of an ONGC plant. Several tin-roofed sheds were blown away in villages, while poultry farms suffered extensive damage.
Yanam also witnessed the collapse of trees and electricity poles at several locations. A rehabilitation centre set up for evacuated residents was inundated, with water entering the entire ground floor. Officials shifted the occupants to the first floor to protect them from the rising water.
Residents moved to relief centres
Authorities had moved people from low-lying areas in several mandals of Kakinada and Konaseema districts to relief and rehabilitation centres as the cyclone’s impact intensified.

In West Godavari district, several trees were uprooted in Narsapuram, while power supply disruptions plunged the town and neighbouring villages into darkness.
Around 3,000 people from Chinna Lanka, PM Lanka, East Thallu and Vemuladeevi villages were shifted to rehabilitation centres as a precaution against the cyclone and possible coastal inundation.
Coastal districts remain on high alert
With Cyclone Arnab’s landfall process expected to continue until the early hours of Wednesday, coastal districts remained on high alert. The combination of destructive winds, torrential rainfall, high waves and seawater intrusion had already caused extensive damage to transport infrastructure, electricity networks, roads, homes and agricultural fields.
Evacuation operations were under way in vulnerable coastal and low-lying settlements, while electricity department personnel were engaged in restoration work.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.

The Indian Institute of Technology Bombay on Friday said its researchers have developed a low-cost device that can screen for anaemia and sickle cell disease using a drop of blood.
A research team from the Department of Chemical Engineering, led by Mahesh Tirumkudulu, has developed a simple, low-cost point-of-care approach that uses the length of a blood smear (the distance that a drop of blood spreads across a glass slide) to detect anaemia, and detect and monitor treatment for sickle cell disease. IIT Bombay said.
Prof Tirumkudulu's team built their own automated device to have a uniform method of creating a smear. Under these controlled conditions, the researchers observed that blood from different people gives different smear lengths, and this difference holds useful information.
Prof. Tirumkudulu explained that more viscous blood spreads less easily and, therefore, produces a shorter and thicker smear under the same conditions.
Once the team confirmed that the method could sense small differences in blood viscosity, they decided to investigate whether those differences could help identify disease. It was found that anaemia lowers red blood cell concentration and haemoglobin, while sickle cell disease makes red blood cells rigid.
The researchers said their patented automated smearing device can be manufactured cost-effectively. Also, the test itself requires only a pipette, glass slides, an inexpensive chemical, vials for the sickling treatment, and a ruler or imaging device to measure smear length, they added.
"This makes our technique particularly useful in places where conventional diagnostic laboratories are difficult to access, and it doesn't require any special expertise to use," said Dr. Mahrukh Mir, a former PhD scholar in Prof Tirumkudulu's lab, and the first author of the study.
The researchers pointed out that blood viscosity cutoffs vary for various groups of people because certain genetic differences affect how blood reacts when oxygen levels drop.
Also, the anaemia test could miss identifying some patients when the usual link between viscosity and anaemia does not hold, such as in a rare condition called hyperviscosity syndrome, where blood plasma is unusually thick.
Currently, the technology is licensed to Rheoheme Private Limited, an IIT Bombay startup, and the team is now working with the National Institute for Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur, in Madhya Pradesh and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur, toward regulatory approval, while exploring extending the device to measure clotting time and glucose levels.
"Our initial aim was to understand the physics of spreading blood drop, and that led to the medical applications," added Prof Tirumkudulu.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway (R) has warned Eli Lilly to discontinue its practice of requiring hospitals to provide claims data to receive discounted medicines under a federal program, a sign that more states are pushing back against such moves by drugmakers.
In an Oct. 26 cease-and-desist letter sent to the company, Hanaway maintained that Lilly has “broken” its promise to sell its medicines under the 340B Drug Pricing Program to eligible hospitals in the state. As a result, she contended the drugmaker has made “false and misleading statements” and violated state law.
Hanaway pointed to University of Missouri Health Care, which operates seven hospitals in the state and, she maintained, recently agreed to provide claims data. Yet Hanaway said Lilly denied the health care system discounts on its medicines anyway, and asked the drugmaker to end its new policy by Nov. 26.

I've been singing the praises of merino wool in these pages for over five years. Most people have come around to the fact that merino wool is a super fiber; it's both sustainable and quite remarkable in its capabilities. Merino wool somehow manages to be comfortable in 95-degree heat, and it'll insulate you against below-freezing temperatures. Unlike synthetic fibers derived from petroleum, merino wool resists odors and is naturally breathable. What's not to love? The price.
Merino wool isn't cheap. That's why I love these merino T-shirts from Quince: They're just $42.
The Quince All-Season T-shirt is 100 percent extra-fine merino wool with a 165-gsm weave, which is perfect even on the warmest summer days where I live. (Admittedly, I think the hottest it got this summer was 92 Fahrenheit). I like the relaxed fit here as well. It's neither skintight technical nor overly loose and baggy. It fits like a T-shirt is supposed to. That's what Quince does well in a number of categories: offer a solid, no-nonsense, competitively priced merino wool T-shirt that fits well and feels great. As an added bonus, Quince offers free shipping and free returns for 365 days. I haven't actually tested either—I haven't needed to, my Quince T-shirt is still going strong after two years of use. But there are plenty of customer reviews on Reddit suggesting the company does honor that offer.
Not sold on the idea of a wool T-shirt? I understand. When I started testing merino, I too had visions of lumberjacks in plaid and itchy sweaters someone's grandma had knitted. None of that is merino wool. Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool, which has evolved to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures and is comfortable to wear next to your skin.
One wool myth that's not just a myth is care. Merino isn't cotton. Quince's care instructions for the All Season T-shirt say to wash it in cold water and lay flat to dry. The latter is important, as hanging merino wool to dry will stretch it out (because of the water weight). Can you throw it in the dryer? Yes. I have, for testing purposes only. It will shrink, and it will wear it out much, much faster, but you can do it.

Bank of Canada expected to hike interest rate 25 points as inflation ticks upward
The Latest
- The Bank of Canada will announce its latest interest rate decision at 9:45 a.m. ET, with most economists predicting a quarter-percentage-point hike.
- The increase would bring the bank's benchmark rate to 2.5 from 2.25 per cent.
- The bank's governor Tiff Macklem had kept the interest rate at 2.25 for seven consecutive meetings. A hike would mark the bank's first rate change in a year.
- Canada's annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September, largely driven by surging energy prices due to the war in the Middle East.
- Macklem faces a difficult balancing act: raising interest rates could help slow inflation, but could also weaken growth in an already struggling labour market.
- The announcement is accompanied by the bank's latest Monetary Policy Report, which will include forecasts for inflation and economic growth.
Updates
- October 28 A chilly housing market already Abby Hughes Even ahead of the interest rate decision, some housing market experts say the potential for a rate hike is already having an impact. Home sales have been sliding in Canada. The Canadian Real Estate Association said sales dropped 7.7 per cent in September compared to the same month last year. "Things are pretty slow right now," said John Pasalis, president at Move Smart Realty. Pasalis says fixed mortgage rates have been climbing as bond yields have risen, while variable rates tied to the Bank of Canada's rate have stood still as the central bank has been on hold. But he added that the prospect of a rate increase has also made some potential home buyers wary, and pushed them to the sidelines. Pasalis expects one or two rate hikes might not have a big impact on the housing market, since consumers have already somewhat come to expect that. But the potential for more hikes in the future could leave even more people choosing not to buy a home. "Two rate hikes in the next six months is one thing, but four rate hikings obviously is a much … bigger story," Pasalis said. "I don't think we're there. But again, I think if the sentiment shifts in that direction, then that's going to impact buyer behaviour."
- Could today start a cycle of rate hikes? Abby Hughes It's rare that central banks make interest rate moves as a one-off — often, they'll go on a cycle of either raising rates or lowering them in consecutive rate decisions. Some economists are predicting that will be the case this time around. For example, David Doyle, head of economics at Macquarie Group, is expecting the central bank will raise interest rates today, and then keep raising them through 2027 by 125 basis points. That would raise the overnight rate to 3.5 per cent. Others disagree. Andrew DiCapua, principal economist at the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, says despite the inflation factor, the Canadian economy is weak right now. It shed about 100,000 jobs in recent months and outlooks for economic growth overall aren't great, either, he noted. "The economy doesn't need that slowing. We don't need to hit on the brakes," DiCapua said. Instead, he says if the bank does raise rates today, it would "send a message" that the bank is taking care of inflation, and predicts the bank would then wait to see if further rate hikes are truly necessary.
- U.S. Fed interest-rate decision also coming Verity Stevenson Canada's central bank isn't alone in grappling with whether to continue holding its benchmark rate steady or raise it to slow inflation — the U.S. Federal Reserve faces a similar dilemma ahead of its rate decision later today. The Fed is widely expected to hold rates steady after raising them last month. Markets anticipate at least two more hikes by mid-2027 in the U.S. as inflation remains elevated with the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Falling oil prices lifted investor sentiment Tuesday with U.S. stock markets opening slightly higher. But analysts have warned that persistent inflation, heavy government and corporate borrowing, and uncertainty surrounding next week's midterm elections continue to weigh on financial markets. Some analysts also suggest the Fed's influence on markets is being overshadowed by other factors. "I don't think the Fed is entirely in the driver's seat in today's market. Increasingly, the bigger story is the AI-driven investment cycle and what happens to risk sentiment around it," Christian Hoffmann, head of fixed income at Thornburg Investment Management, told Reuters. "In recent trading, capital has moved out of some AI-related trades and into bonds in what looks like a flight to quality, and flows like that can overwhelm relatively small changes in Fed expectations." -With files from Reuters
- How far should the Bank of Canada go? Philippe de Montigny No matter what happens today, most economists expect the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates before the year is up. But they disagree over when that increase will happen and by how much rates will go up. Before every rate decision, the C.D. Howe Institute's monetary policy council weighs in on where interest rates should go over the next year. The organization brings together leading economists from the country's big banks, universities and financial markets. Take a look at their latest recommendations: Most of that council — with the exception of Scotiabank's Jean-François Perrault — are actually calling on the Bank of Canada to hold rates today, as they see "little evidence of broader price pressures" beyond energy. Looking forward to October 2027, their opinions somewhat diverge, with rates ranging anywhere from the current level of 2.25 per cent all the way to 3.25 per cent.
- A look at recent rate decisions Abby Hughes Ahead of today's decision, let's take a look at how we arrived here. At its last meeting in early September, the Bank of Canada held its rate at 2.25 per cent. That move was widely predicted by economists in advance, so it came as little surprise. It also marked the bank's seventh hold in a row, keeping the trend-setting interest rate at 2.25 per cent. The bank has stayed there in part because of the tariff environment — Macklem cited "unpredictable" U.S. trade policy as a source of uncertainty in his January decision. But the threat posed by rising oil prices has crept up since the U.S. and Israel struck Iran in late February. Pricier oil has led to inflation, and combatting inflation usually requires rate hikes. At first, Macklem said the central bank was monitoring the situation in the Middle East but "looking through" the increased cost of energy in April, and said in June and July there was little evidence of high oil prices spilling over into higher prices for other things, like food. Inflation is now at 3.1 per cent. That's almost entirely because of sky-high energy prices which inflation data showed still aren't flowing over into the rest of the economy yet. But the longer energy prices remain high, the bigger that risk becomes as Macklem has warned at past meetings — and economists say the bank might not want to wait around too long to see how bad things get before taking action. And at a meeting in Thailand, Macklem made comments about oil inflation driving up prices at home. A number of economists changed their predictions in the days after those comments, and many now predict a rate hike today.
- Why this interest rate decision matters Verity Stevenson Canada's economy has shown resilience in the face of punishing U.S. tariffs, but new import bans on a range of Canadian products are creating further drag. Accounting firm Deloitte has lowered its growth forecast for next year by 20 per cent. Despite inflation on the rise due to energy costs and a struggling labour market, the Canadian economy has shown resilience. Those price pressures have remained relatively contained. Excluding gasoline, inflation was actually eased to 2.2 per cent in September, down from 2.4 per cent in August. But Macklem has warned that persistently high energy prices could push inflation higher more broadly. Economists say the central bank may be looking to get ahead of those pressures, even if that means raising borrowing costs for Canadian households and businesses at a time when economic growth remains sluggish.
- Economists predict Macklem will raise rate Verity Stevenson Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of the Bank of Canada's latest interest rate announcement. Nineteen of 34 economists surveyed by Reuters from Oct. 21 to 23 said the central bank will hike its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent. A majority also forecast one more rise before March. The prediction by economists comes amid surging energy prices and an uptick in inflation. The decision for Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem isn't a straightforward one this time around, though. Inflation climbed slightly above the bank's target range of one to three per cent in September to 3.1 per cent, but Canada's economy has been showing some signs of weakness. The labour market shed 68,000 jobs in September, according to Statistics Canada. We'll bring you developments, analysis and reaction as the bank announces its decision.

A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.
The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.
The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.
Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the DIA assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified Defense Intelligence Agency assessment of threats to the United States in space.
Catch and release
The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020 with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.
The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Authorities have evacuated at least 89,000 people from vulnerable coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab intensified over the Bay of Bengal and was expected to make landfall early Wednesday, AP reported.
The India Meteorological Department classified Arnab as a "very severe" cyclonic storm, warning of heavy rainfall and strong winds along the east coast. The storm's outer bands began affecting parts of Andhra Pradesh late Tuesday, with officials saying the expected landfall had moved earlier than initially forecast.
Prakhar Jain, a senior official with Andhra Pradesh's disaster management authority, said the cyclone could reach the coast between 2 am and 4 am local time on Wednesday. He warned of heavy to very heavy rainfall in several districts and called for heightened vigilance during the critical hours before landfall.
Quick answers to key questions
Cyclone Arnab was expected to reach the Andhra Pradesh coast between 2 am and 4 am on Wednesday. The storm was forecast to cross the coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam.
Authorities moved residents from low-lying and flood-prone coastal areas because the storm was expected to bring very heavy rainfall and strong winds. Officials warned that winds could reach 140 kmph at landfall.
Authorities evacuated at least 89,000 people from vulnerable coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh. In neighbouring Odisha, officials planned to evacuate around 48,000 people from areas likely to be affected.
The state established more than 2,000 cyclone shelters across 20 districts, secured over 30,000 fishing boats and deployed nearly 1,100 medical teams. Emergency alerts were also sent to residents’ mobile phones.
Residents were advised to monitor weather updates and be ready to move to safer places. They should use safe shelters and avoid taking shelter under trees during lightning.
Authorities placed all coastal districts in Andhra Pradesh on high alert and began moving people from low-lying and flood-prone areas to safer locations. Some train services were also cancelled as heavy rain and gusty winds began affecting parts of the coast, AP reported.
The cyclone was moving at around 20 kmph, Jain said. Officials warned that wind speeds could reach 140 kmph at landfall, accompanied by extremely heavy rain and strong gusts across parts of the coastal region on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The state's disaster management authority said more than 12 million people live along the cyclone's expected path.
Authorities have established more than 2,000 cyclone shelters across 20 districts and are sending emergency alerts to millions of residents' mobile phones. More than 30,000 fishing boats have been secured along the coast, while nearly 1,100 medical teams have been deployed to provide emergency assistance, Jain said, according to the PTI.
In neighbouring Odisha, officials planned to evacuate around 48,000 people from areas likely to be affected by the cyclone.

Exit polls project no clear winner, as anti-Netanyahu bloc leads but Likud remains biggest party
Exit polls from Israel’s major TV stations have projected that a majority of Israelis have voted against Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest party.
The Channel 12 exit poll shows that the bloc of Jewish-led parties opposing Netanyahu has the biggest bloc, and is projected to win a total of 52 seats, compared to 50 seats for the parties supporting Netanyahu.
It also projects that Netanyahu’s Likud party will win 24 seats in the Knesset, while Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is projected to win 22 seats.
Neither bloc is close to a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset without the support of the Palestinian-led parties, which also oppose Netanyahu and are projected in that poll to win a total of 18 seats, a record number for them.
Israeli voters issue sharp rebuke to Netanyahu - snap analysis
So, Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is indeed projected to lose its parliamentary majority.
If the exit polls are correct, his Likud party narrowly comes out as the largest party by a projected one or two seats, but this still represents a loss for the party of 25% of its seats compared to the last election in 2022. And what is more, Netanyahu’s coalition bloc is projected to win only 50 seats this time around, a loss of 14 since the 2022 election.
Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc, meanwhile, is projected to win 52 or 53 seats, and therefore also remains short of the 61 Knesset seats needed to make a majority. The former IDF chief would thus have to try to form a government with the support of the Israeli Arab parties, who are projected to win a staggering 17 or 18 seats, though it is unclear whether that would alienate some of his political allies. Eisenkot himself had ruled out such an arrangement before the election, but there is precedent for a deal still being made in what will no doubt be intense negotiations to come.
By contrast, analysts have argued that if the exit polls are correct, there is no clear pathway to power now for Netanyahu, unless he could somehow convince centrist parties to join his coalition. If not, he would also of course stay on in a “caretaker” capacity while opposition parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Israel foreign minister says opposition celebrations 'premature'
Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar has said that opposition celebrations were “premature” after initial exit polls in this historic election projected a slight edge over Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc but still short of a majority.
“The celebrations on the left are premature. The smugness of the biased commentators – ridiculous. One thing seems quite clear: [Netanyahu’s] Likud is the largest party in Israel,” he said on X, posting a video showing Likud’s first election win in 1977.
Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats
Emma Graham-Harrison
Israel’s election was too close to call on Tuesday night after a historic turnout by voters for an election described by some as the most consequential in the country’s history, and marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters.
Exit polls published on Tuesday evening suggested that the opposition bloc of parties led by the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin, edging out Benjamin Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition despite the prime minister’s Likud emerging as the largest party.
The result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called.
After a day in which Israelis streamed to polling stations across the country, exit polls suggested Netanyahu’s ability to command the loyalty of a large core of Likud party voters remained undimmed despite his rejection by large numbers of his Israelis.
The predicted haul of up to 18 Knesset seats for Israeli Arab parties is likely to make them the kingmakers in what seem certain to be protracted talks to form a new government, with Netanyahu likely to fall short of the support required to form a new coalition.
The exit polls – if they prove accurate – suggest a struggle for either Likud or Eisenkot’s Yashar to find a road to a majority in the 120 seat Knesset. Likud’s projected showing, not for the first time, appears to have defied predictions in the run up to the vote.
What is clear, however, is that Netanayhu no longer has a claim to a mandate with his political fate in the balance.
Former Israeli prime minister and Beyachad (Together) party canddiate Yair Lapid has said that Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc has been told “to go home” in this election.
He wrote on X:
Don’t let anyone mislead you: the Netanyahu bloc suffered a crushing defeat. It is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home.
At the election night headquarters of the Yashar party, activists cheered the TV broadcast of exit polls showing parties making up the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc were ahead of Netanyahu’s coalition.
“There’s a lot of excitement and a lot of hope for Israel’s future now,” said Itay, a 28 year-old startup founder who had flown back from the US to campaign for Gadi Eisenkot, his first time getting involved in politics.
The excitement felt real, among activists and prospective Knesset members gathered at the National Sports Centre in Tel Aviv, even though Eisenkot’s own party was forecast to come in a couple of seats behindBenjaminNetanyahu’s Likud party.
“I’m really happy,” said Lia, 23, a medical student and activist, adding that she is still waiting for figures from the count, which might give Eisenkot a larger mandate. “I hope we can be even happier when the full results come in.”
The balance of seats in the Knesset are forecast to go to parties supported by Palestinian citizens of Israel in a historic high. Eisenkot has ruled out going into coalition with the Palestinian parties, but they have indicated they might support a minority opposition government.
Itay welcomed the strong Palestinian vote, which he said was a sign to the world that “this is a country where every citizen is equal”, and said he was hopeful deal could be reached to form a working government.
“I’m optimistic with the results everyone can have a shared vision, all the parties can come together. Everyone has to budge, because together we are stronger.”
Voters have ‘dismissed’ Netanyahu’s government, says Golan
The leader of the Democrats party, Yair Golan, has also given his reaction to the exit polls, declaring that Israeli voters have “dismissed” Netanyahu’s government.
He wrote on X:
The public has spoken; it has dismissed the Netanyahu government. We have been granted a historic opportunity to form a government of genuine change in Israel, and we have no intention of letting it slip away. We represent a vast public—people who have been fighting in the streets for four years, joining political parties, and going out into the field to persuade others. We will do everything in our power to ensure that such a government is established.
We are ready to work with all our partners, bridge the gaps, and take responsibility. The public has had its say. Now it is our turn to do the work.
Here are some reactions to the exit polls, which have projected that the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is set to win more total seats than Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition.
Eisenkot says exit polls indicate 'complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu'
Here is Gadi Eisenkot’s reaction to the exit polls. He wrote on X:
Initial exit poll results indicate a complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the “October 7th government” among the Zionist majority and the majority of Israeli citizens.
If these are the final results, it constitutes a victory for the mainstream Zionist majority in Israel.
I will act immediately to carry out the will of the people, to replace the Netanyahu government, and to establish a Zionist government of national mobilisation as soon as possible.
Israel’s Channel 13’s exit poll also projects no clear winner, with the opposition bloc projected to win 53 seats, the Netanyahu bloc 50 seats and the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel 17 seats.
Exit polls project no clear winner, as anti-Netanyahu bloc leads but Likud remains biggest party
Exit polls from Israel’s major TV stations have projected that a majority of Israelis have voted against Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest party.
The Channel 12 exit poll shows that the bloc of Jewish-led parties opposing Netanyahu has the biggest bloc, and is projected to win a total of 52 seats, compared to 50 seats for the parties supporting Netanyahu.
It also projects that Netanyahu’s Likud party will win 24 seats in the Knesset, while Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is projected to win 22 seats.
Neither bloc is close to a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset without the support of the Palestinian-led parties, which also oppose Netanyahu and are projected in that poll to win a total of 18 seats, a record number for them.
Polls close in Israel after historic turnout in election that will determine Benjamin Netanyahu's future
It’s now past 10pm in Israel, which means polling stations across the country have closed after Israelis turned out in record numbers on a high-stakes election day that will determine the future of Benjamin Netanyahu.
A reminder that Israelis waiting in line at polling stations will still be allowed to cast their vote.
Israeli broadcasters are now set to air a set of exit polls, which will provide first estimates of the results. We’ll bring you all the latest on that as those come in.
Polling stations across Israel are set to close in less than 35 minutes, when news tv stations will release their first exit polls giving preliminary estimates of how many seats each party has won.
The first lot of official results then won’t be released until after around 1am local time on Wednesday. And while the exit polls usually provide a reliable indication of how people have voted, they can also vary.
The current coalition is expected to lose its majority, but we won’t expect clear results quickly as the coalition nature of Israeli government means that even small changes in vote share will change coalition calculations. We therefore may not get fuller results until the next day or the day after.
The final tally is expected by 30 October and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on 4 November.
After the final tally is in, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties who can get to 61 seats – and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, meaning Benjamin Netanyahu and his cabinet would remain in place as a “caretaker” government.
The governor of New York, home to the world’s largest urban Jewish community outside of Israel, has said that her job would get “a lot easier” if Benjamin Netanyahu loses this election.
I represent the largest [urban] Jewish population in the world outside of Israel. And I know they’re suffering. A lot of people are anxious about antisemitism, which is sky-high right now …
I went to Israel right after October 7. I saw a lot of pain there. But I actually cautioned the government there, in private conversations, not to overreach.
The world is with you when it comes to the brutal assault by … Hamas on innocent Israeli people. An overreach could change that dynamic, and that’s what’s happened.
We have to have leadership there that understands the security of Israel is paramount - critically important to me, but also the world - but to have a safe Palestinian state as well, which has been talked about my entire life.
I still believe that this can happen. I believe we have to get people of goodwill who can make this happen, and as long as Netanyahu is sitting there, that is not in his interest to do that. It’s just not, and it won’t happen.
Voter turnout as of 6pm local time reached 66.7%, the highest ever by that hour since voting hours were first recorded, the Central Elections Committee said.
That is a 9% increase from the 2022 election at that time and Israel’s highest recorded turnout by 6pm.
Election committee rejects Netanyahu bloc request to extend voting hours
The Central Elections Committee decided not to extend voting hours beyond 10pm, rejecting a request submitted by Netanyahu bloc parties, Haaretz is reporting.
In a statement, the committee said it met this evening and decided “the current circumstances do not justify an extension”.
It added that the high turnout “reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process” and “no need to extend voting hours was identified”.
A reminder that, under Israeli law, the current rules do allow for a voter to cast their vote past the polling time, just as long they arrive at a station by 10pm.
As we’ve been reporting, a record number of Israelis cast their ballots in the first half of polling day, voting at polling stations across the country and in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
By 2pm local time (it is now after 8pm), 44.9% of voters had cast their ballot – the highest turnout since record-keeping began in the 1970s.
It’s been described as an existential moment; a battle for the soul of a nation. With voting under way in Israel today, public opinion is divided on what the future of the country looks like. To his supporters, Benjamin Netanyahu has protected the country in a way no other leader could, taking on Iran, Hamas, Hezbollah and Houthis.
To his critics, Netanyahu is to blame for a catastrophic failure of security, leaving Israel more isolated, traumatised and no safer. Today, his most serious challenge comes from a candidate with little experience in office. Gadi Eisenkot is seen as humble, approachable … and honest. The former chief of staff for the Israeli military is promising a future without corruption. Thirteen months ago, his party didn’t even exist.
But after three years of war and upheaval, it’s clear that the consequences of today’s elections go way beyond Israel’s borders.
In the latest edition of our Today in Focus podcast, Emma Graham-Harrison tells Nosheen Iqbal about the stakes of the election and what it could all mean for the future of Israel – and for the Palestinians living under occupation.

As the protests and hunger strike continues to unfold at Delhi’s Jamia Millia Islamia, students on October 27, Tuesday, reported a near-complete shutdown of normal university activities with the campus has being turned into a fortress surrounded by police personnel and tear gas vans deployed outside the main gate.
Additionally, Section 163 of the BNSS has been invoked, criminalising gatherings of more than four people. A warning sign erected by South-East District of Delhi Police mentions that unlawful gathering or assembly will be dispersed using physical force and legal action will be initiated.
Why are the Students Protesting?
On October 12, two students, Jasim Ali Khan and Ebin Basil, began an indefinite hunger strike to demand the resumption of the student union elections, which have not been held for two decades. The last elected union was dissolved in March 2006 amid allegations of campus violence and disruption. The university has not had a restored, university-wide elected Jamia Millia Islamia Student Union (JMI-SU) since then.
View this post on Instagram
Representatives from various student organisations submitted a memorandum to the vice-chancellor, demanding that necessary facilities, space, and support must be provided to students for their democratic right of free expression and protest. Within the next few days, six more students, Rehan Khan, Rehan Haider, Faizan Ali Khan, Rida Nausheen Khan, Ritik, Altaf, and Abuzar, joined the hunger strike and several students joined the sit-in demonstration around the Mirza Ghalib statue on campus. What followed is severe police crackdown, administrative retaliation, and a state-sanctioned attempt to curb what students described as a peaceful protest for their rights.
‘Students Beaten, Dragged & Detained’
Five days into the protest, around 5:30 am on October 17, Delhi Police personnel arrived in large numbers outside the university gate, and allegedly detained at least 10 students with the aid of the campus security guards. Students alleged that authorities turned off the lights, beat and dragged the protesters out of the campus in the break of dawn in the presence of the chief proctor of the university.
CPI(ML) Liberation alleged that Jamia Millia Islamia administration forcibly removed students on hunger strike from the campus around 5:30 am on Saturday while they were demanding the restoration of the students’ union. In a post on X, the party alleged that campus lights were switched off and students were beaten, manhandled and harassed before being handed over to Delhi Police. It said all detained students had since been released. The students are demanding the restoration of Jamia’s students’ union and the holding of union elections. CPI(ML) Liberation condemned the alleged action and urged the administration to stop what it called repression and restore the union.
— The Observer Post (@TheObserverPost) October 17, 2026
Footage surfacing on social media showed clashes between authorities and the students protesters on the morning of October 17, with videos showing police dragging and pulling students away from the campus.
View this post on Instagram
A video also showed Ebin Basil, writhing in pain, alleging that he had been brutally assaulted by the security guards.
Subsequently, as scenes of utter chaos kept emerging through the day, a large group of students were seen breaking the gate and storming inside the campus even as the police reportedly denied detaining anyone and only removing those attempting to break the gate.
View this post on Instagram
Admin Condemns Slogans, Shifts Classes Online
On October 18, a high-level committee comprising seven university professors was formed to mediate between protesting students, and to convince them to call the demonstration off. During this meeting certain slogans that were painted on walls by students also came under the administration’s scrutiny. These slogans included ‘Restore JMISU’, ‘Reclaim Jamia’, ‘Inquilab Ayega’, ‘Free Palestine’, ‘Free Sharjeel Imam’, and ‘RSS Se Azaadi’ among others.
In a press release published by the official handle of the university on X, the slogans were labelled “highly condemnable and detrimental to the nation’s integrity, security and sovereignty.” The release further stated that the administration has adopted two resolutions. First, to urge the protesters to vacate the protest site and call off their agitation, particularly at the Ghalib statue lawns, which they claimed had been “illegally occupied by the protesting students despite Gate No. 18 being the designated protest site at JMI”. Second, “to repaint the defaced walls and cover the slogans”.
The press release added that the administration had been compelled to issue a notification to shift all classes online allegedly due to the protesters’ resistance to call off the demonstration. “After two hours of efforts to persuade the students to call off the protest…the students continued chanting slogans, shouting that the faculty should “go back” and suddenly began pushing security guards, staff and teachers…even after their demands had been met earlier this week,” the release stated.
Further, the university administration took disciplinary action against Ebin and Jasim. Ebin was rusticated for one academic year and barred from campus while Jasim Khan was barred from campus for six months.
Following the administrative action, students held a press conference on October 18 and expanded their demands beyond the restoration of the JMI-SU — they demanded the withdrawal of disciplinary proceedings against protesting students and an end to further punitive measures. They also demanded the resignation of the chief proctor and security advisor.
Students Vow to Continue Strike, Clampdown Increases
Even as certain hunger strikers gave up due to declining health, the remaining students vowed to continue their hunger strike and sit-in protests. Solidarity for the protesting students poured in from within and beyond the campus, however, the police deployment outside the campus and administrative clampdown also intensified.
“The irony lies in the fact that the same administration that condemned unauthorised police clampdown on students during the CAA-NRC protests in 2019 is deploying that very body against its students in 2026 to suppress the constitutionally safeguarded right of free and independent expression,” Ateerah, a post-graduate student, told Alt News.
On October 23, Congress MP Imran Masood was detained by Delhi Police after he arrived at the university to express solidarity with protesting students.
Water, Electricity, Basic Amenities Cut Off
On October 24 — the 13th day of the hunger strike — through another notice the administration shifted all classes to online mode, shut its gates, suspended canteen services, and restricted access to the Central Library. In what students viewed as an attempt to discourage the protest, electricity and water supply were also cut off in the campus space, students told Alt News. “They have essentially converted our dissent into a question of law and order, to justify police action on a peaceful protest,” said Abdul, another student.
On the same day, a large number of Delhi Police personnel and paramilitary forces were stationed outside the university premises. The protesting students told Alt News that in the afternoon, the proctor’s team, along with university professors and non-teaching staff, had rounded up students who had gathered for a sit-in demonstration within Gate No. 7 of the university premises, at the Ghalib Lawn.
Students alleged use of force on both male and female protestors by the security guards. The protest site was allegedly dismantled, which compelled the protesting students to take shelter within the Political Science building and continue their hunger strike, they added.
View this post on Instagram
Mantasha, a post-graduate student, told Alt News, “The whole affair was an unpleasant reminder of what had transpired within the university premises in 2019. This time, our own professors joined in with the security guards. Some just watched, while others proceeded to manhandle us. Until our 13th day of protest, a solitary female washroom was kept open at night. However, after the protest site was dismantled in the afternoon of October 24, we found that it had been sealed off, leaving us no option but to share the male washroom.”
Students Reject Admin’s Notification
The next day, on October 25, the administration released a notification that said that a student election would be held after 15 days from the date of approval of the constitution of the JMI-SU.
It stated that show cause notices and suspension orders against students during the period of protest would be revoked, and a committee would be constituted to enquire into the actions of the security staff. It also added that students should issue a public apology for any defamatory statement, action, or posts made during the protest against the administration.
However, students expressed their apprehension regarding the notification, pointing out that the date of constitution of the union was unspecified. Those on hunger strike continued their fast, deeming the notification an incomplete victory as all of their demands had not yet been addressed.
They demanded an assurance on the resignation of the chief proctor and the security advisor, and the revocation of all disciplinary actions on protesting students, besides declining to issue a public apology. “The Constitution of the union is to be drafted by December 20, after which it is subject to approval from the V-C. This allows a lot of scope for administrative inaction and complacency, since the approval itself can be indefinitely stalled by the administration,” alleged Abdul.
On October 26, two gates — one in front of the Ibn-e-Sina reading library, and another which serves as a key access point to the campus for residents of the Boys Hostel — were sealed off by the administration, with the suspension of offline classes still effective.
A student protestor, speaking on terms of anonymity, told Alt News, “The gate provides access to facilities serving not only students and hostel residents but also members of the general public, including an Indian Post Office, a public sector bank, an Aadhaar centre, a university health centre and a dental hospital. Restricting access to such essential public services, including medical care for patients with scheduled appointments, warrants immediate reconsideration.”
Less than 24 hours after the administration released the notice, Delhi Police however went on to detain several students for merely attempting to enter the premises of their own university, students told Alt News. Video footage showed police personnel pushing students onto a detention bus.
Speaking to Alt News from the protest site, students alleged that they are not being able to leave the campus given the heavy police and paramilitary deployment in front of the gates. Food and water deliveries are allegedly being intercepted by security guards at the gates, cutting off the basic means of survival for students who have remained within the campus.
“We had earlier put out a message asking for people in solidarity to send in drinking water, but the guards would not let it through. Is this how a university treats its students?” a student, requesting anonymity, asked.

The best ways to tell if someone is using AI glasses
Smart glasses are making unwanted surveillance all too easy, but you're far from powerless against this covert tech.
Smart glasses might be the next big trend in consumer tech, as there's certainly real demand for these gadget-intensive pieces of eyewear. However, there are very legitimate concerns about how these glasses can be used for stalking or other shady activity, especially as the prevalence of public recording comes more and more under scrutiny. If you share those concerns, you might want to keep an eye out for some tell-tale signs of AI glasses.
Of course, it could be a little rude to go around asking random people if they're wearing AI glasses when you're going off a gut instinct. Luckily, most (albeit not all) smart glasses brands have built-in signs of use. If you can't rely on those giveaways, there are some solid-enough reasons for you to be suspicious.
How to recognize whether someone's using smart glasses
Smart glasses are actually pretty easy to recognize at a glance, as their tech-riddled innards often require thick frames, particularly around the temples and the outer sides of the lenses (although this admittedly isn't always the case). That second area is typically where camera lenses are located, while any giveaway ports or grilles might be further back on the design. Most smart glasses also have an indicator light that turns on when they're filming; if you suspect you're being filmed via smart glasses, look for a small LED light.
However, there are reports of a variety of low-cost dupe glasses being sold on sites such as TikTok Shop and Temu that don't have a recording light (as well as audio-first glasses that don't have cameras, such as the Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses), so you'll need to look closer at the aforementioned physical traits. You can also check whether someone you suspect is recording is quickly pressing the temples of their glasses, pausing every now and then to zone out (as if to read text on their glasses' display), or whispering quiet voice commands to themselves. These could be signs of someone interacting with their smart glasses, though there is a small chance they are all completely unrelated.
The apps that can warn you about smart glasses
One of the most recent developments in the arms race against this tech is the arrival of apps that can warn you if smart glasses are nearby. The likes of Nearby Glasses and ZuckOff scan for nearby Bluetooth devices and the identifiers often associated with AI glasses. Admittedly, both of these apps aren't completely reliable. For one thing, there's a chance that anyone wearing smart glasses nearby has turned off their Bluetooth. There's also a risk of false positives. However, both can serve as your first line of defense against nearby smart glasses.
Just because you have a strong suspicion that there are AI glasses nearby, though, doesn't mean you should jump immediately to a confrontation. The best thing to do if someone near you is stirring your suspicions is to move away from the individual and speak to the authorities if you're being followed. If you're hosting a meeting or event that demands a level of confidentiality, it may be worth making a neutral statement about smart glasses not being permitted. In either case, if you need to speak with a stranger about whether they're recording you without your knowledge, do so calmly in a public environment.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."
