In the winter of 2022, two parents carried their sick, coughing baby boy into an emergency room deep in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains. The small rural hospital had no pediatric specialists, no pediatric nurses, and no children’s intensive care unit. But it was hours closer than any hospital that did.
The doctor at that rural hospital recognized immediately that the baby’s condition was beyond their capacity to treat. They called regional children’s hospitals like ours for help. But the winter of 2022 was the peak of the “tripledemic” — Covid, influenza, and RSV striking children simultaneously — and every children’s hospital in northern California was overwhelmed. None of us had room for one more.
There was no single call the team at that hospital could make to locate a pediatric ICU bed. They worked a phone tree, hospital by hospital, asking for an opening. Meanwhile, the baby’s condition worsened. As the team tried to insert an infant-sized breathing tube, the baby died.
That patient’s death and others like it were galvanizing for those of us in on the other end of those desperate calls for help. Saying no to our colleagues and the patients they’re caring for feels horrible.
But the extraordinary crush of the tripledemic has continued. In 2026, the unprecedented pediatric patient crowding of 2022 has become a normal Tuesday.
In this new normal, community hospitals across the country are transferring children to dedicated pediatric centers not just because a child is critically ill, but increasingly because smaller hospitals have quietly lost the ability to manage even common conditions. A 1-year-old with an allergic reaction, a 6-year-old with an asthma attack, a teenager with gallstones — community hospitals once handled these patients locally. Now, as they degrade or eliminate pediatric care, that local safety net is disappearing. The nation’s relatively few children’s hospitals can’t accommodate every sick child, much as we would like to. We now routinely turn sick children away and hope one of our colleagues somewhere else will have a bed.
There is another story from that same winter of 2022. Two parents brought their sick baby girl to a small rural hospital in Washington state’s Northern Cascades. For 12 hours, doctors there tried to find a hospital that could take her. Again, no children’s hospitals had room.
Finally, the emergency physician called Washington’s Regional Medical Operations Coordination Center, or RMOCC — a kind of air traffic control for patient transfers that can match critically ill patients to available beds across a region. The RMOCC pediatrician who answered later recalled the terror in the calling doctor’s voice: “Don’t you know I feel like I am having a heart attack every moment I am caring for this tiny baby? It has been 12 hours. I am terrified she will die here. Why can’t anyone help?”
The RMOCC found a hospital willing to make an exception to its infection-control policies and accept the baby into a neonatal ICU. Unlike the California baby, she lived.
The Washington RMOCC closed last year after budget cuts. It is seeking renewed funding in this year’s budget.
There are many reasons for the collapse of pediatric capacity. Most are fundamentally financial. Hospital bottom lines require high reimbursement, high volume procedures, and expensive, complex treatments. Children’s care often reimburses below the cost of care, meaning that pediatric admissions for common childhood diseases lose money. Hospitals are incentivized to abandon pediatric care in favor of complex adult surgical programs and cancer treatments.
There are three changes in health care policy that could save and restore regional pediatric capacity.
First, Medicaid payments for pediatric care need to reflect the costs of that care. Hospitals can’t be asked to lose money on pediatric admissions and ED visits. Unfortunately, coming cuts to Medicaid seem likely to make reimbursement for children’s care worse rather than better. The incoming Congress must act to preserve and augment funding for pediatric care.
Second, regional RMOCCs like Washington state’s should be a standard part of regional disaster planning and a state and national funding priority. At least 19 states had regional or statewide MOCCs in 2023, though many were open only during surges, and some, like Washington’s, wound down with the end of the pandemic. When a sick child arrives at a rural emergency department, the hospital shouldn’t have to resort to a phone tree to find an accepting specialty facility. A single phone call to a regional air traffic control system for patient movement saves time and lives.
Finally, children’s hospitals need support to be regional resources to the smaller hospitals that depend on them for advanced pediatric care. Incentives for providing telehealth consultations, training, and quality improvement support for community hospitals are essential, as children’s hospitals face the same fiscal realities as their rural peers and cannot provide infinite unfunded support to their communities. Remote support from pediatric specialists can reduce the need for transfers and make local care safer, which could drive down pediatric care costs in the long term.
In pediatric medicine, we like to say that “children are not little adults.” Unfortunately, they are also not what health care executives call “priority populations.”
But children deserve to have quality care available in their own communities. They shouldn’t have to spend hours in waiting rooms and hallways awaiting transfer to overwhelmed regional centers. As pediatric physicians, we’ve gone from seeing the crisis coming to living the crisis every day. So far that crisis has been mostly hidden within the walls of our hospitals, but it’s time everyone know: Our children are out of room.
Jonathan E. Kohler, M.D., is a pediatric surgeon in Sacramento, Calif. Mary A. King, M.D., M.P.H., is a pediatric intensivist in Seattle.

India evacuates tens of thousands as Cyclone Arnab nears eastern coast
Indian authorities have evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern state of Andhra Pradesh as a severe cyclone over the Bay of Bengal is expected to make landfall along the country’s east coast
HYDERABAD, India -- Indian authorities on Tuesday evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern state of Andhra Pradesh as a severe cyclone over the Bay of Bengal was expected to make landfall along the country’s east coast, authorities said.
The India Meteorological Department, or IMD, said Cyclone Arnab strengthened into a “very severe” cyclonic storm and was expected to make landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast by Wednesday morning with gusting winds and heavy rain.
Authorities stepped up preparations and began evacuating people from low-lying and flood-prone areas ahead of its expected landfall. They also canceled some train services as heavy rain and gusty winds had already started lashing parts of the Andhra Pradesh coast, officials said. At least 89,000 people have so far been evacuated in Andhra Pradesh, according to an official statement.
The state’s disaster management authority said more than 12 million people live along the cyclone’s expected path.
Prakhar Jain, a top disaster management official in Andhra Pradesh, said the cyclone was moving at about 20 kph (12 mph). “Extremely heavy rains and strong gusty winds” are likely in parts of the coastal region on Tuesday and Wednesday due to the impact of the cyclone, he said.
Authorities set up over 2,000 cyclone shelters across 20 districts, while emergency alerts were being sent to the mobile phones of millions of residents, Jain said, according to the Press Trust of India news agency. More than 30,000 fishing boats were secured along the coast, while nearly 1,100 medical teams were deployed across affected areas to provide emergency assistance, he added.
In neighboring Odisha, officials plan to evacuate about 48,000 people from areas likely to be affected by the storm.

Quick Answer
The best free alternatives to popular Microsoft apps include LibreOffice for Microsoft 365, ShareX for Snipping Tool, Files for File Explorer, Everything for Windows Search, System Informer for Task Manager, and ImageGlass for Microsoft Photos. These offer more features, better speed, and greater control.
Microsoft bundles plenty of apps with Windows, and you probably use a bunch of them on your PC — some out of personal preference, others because there aren’t enough good alternatives.
Now, there’s nothing wrong with using these apps if they serve you well. But if you find their functionality limited or want a free version, you don’t have to settle. Here are some of the best free alternatives to popular Windows apps that are worth checking out.
Table of Contents
LibreOffice for Microsoft 365
Microsoft 365 is a subscription service that gives you access to Office, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams, alongside 1 TB of OneDrive storage. You can get Microsoft 365 for free, but you need a paid subscription for unrestricted access. However, if you don’t wish to go that route and want unrestricted access to the office suite, LibreOffice is a solid Microsoft 365 alternative worth checking out.
LibreOffice doesn’t require an account or subscription; you can download the app and get started right away. The suite includes three tools — Writer, Calc, and Impress, which are free equivalents to Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, respectively. You also get a vector graphics editor (Draw), a database management system (Base), and a mathematical formulas and equations editor (Math). The app works completely offline and stores all your data locally on the device. It doesn’t have any AI features either, so you have full control over what you do.
ShareX for Snipping Tool
Windows has a built-in screenshot tool called Snipping Tool to help you take screenshots and record the screen. Although Microsoft has updated it over the years to include OCR/text extraction and screen recording capabilities, its functionality is still largely limited compared to many third-party screenshot apps. ShareX is one such app, which is quite popular among power users.
ShareX offers plenty of screenshot modes, including scrolling capture, active monitor, custom, and auto-capture, as well as those you get with the Snipping Tool. Scrolling capture and auto-capture are two standout modes here. The former comes in handy when you want to capture content that extends beyond what’s visible on the screen. On the other hand, the latter lets you automatically take screenshots of a specified area at set intervals, which may be useful when you want to document the steps or monitor some process.
However, that’s not all; ShareX is better than Windows Snipping Tool at a bunch of other things. For example, it supports batch operations and automation capabilities. This allows you to apply edits to a bunch of screenshots at once. Then there are a few extra tools like Imagine Combiner to stitch multiple images, Ruler to measure dimensions, Color to extract color values from elements in your screenshots, and more.
Files for File Explorer
File Explorer is Microsoft’s own file manager for Windows. Although it has largely remained unchanged from Windows 10 to Windows 11, it did receive some noteworthy changes in appearance and functionality. Still, some of its elements, like the dialog box, look archaic. Not to mention, it lacks customizability and many features you otherwise find on its alternatives. This is where Files comes in.
Files is a popular File Explorer alternative that gives you everything you get with File Explorer, along with plenty of other useful features, while blending well with Windows 11 aesthetics. For starters, it supports Miller columns, which makes navigating nested folders easier. Likewise, it has a dual-pane mode for side-by-side file and folder comparisons.
Among other things, Files lets you add color-coded tags to files, view folder sizes at a glance, and preview a bunch of different file types like Markdown and SVG natively. It also offers Git integration for developers and a built-in FTP/SFTP client to manage files on remote servers. Last but not least, Files has a Command Palette, which is essentially a search box pop-up where you can search for files, change settings, and perform a bunch of other actions without digging through different menus.
Everything for Windows Search
Windows Search — the built-in search tool on your Windows PC, which lets you find apps, files, settings, and more- has come a long way over the years. It feels more integrated into the system and gives you options to control the kind of results that appear. Still, Search can feel quite slow, especially on relatively older hardware. It actively scans folders in the background, which increases resource usage. For this reason, it’s best to switch to Everything.
Everything is one of the popular file search tools for Windows. Its biggest highlights are speed and low resource usage. This is partly because of the way Everything indexes files and folders. Instead of crawling folders, it reads the NTFS Master File Table (MFT) — a type of database Windows uses to track files on the drive. This also enables Everything to instantly reflect any changes you make to files on your PC.
Among other things, Everything supports Regex and offers granular search options to help you find exactly what you’re looking for. It also has a handy batch renaming tool built in that lets you rename multiple files at once. Everything also has excellent keyboard-based navigation support, if you prefer that. You can even customize your most-used actions to your preferred keyboard shortcuts.
System Informer for Windows Task Manager
im is a powerful Windows app for monitoring and managing apps and background processes running on your computer. It comes in handy when you want to know what (and how much) resources an app or process is using, manage startup apps, and close frozen apps and system processes. However, it doesn’t support advanced task-management operations and isn’t quite effective at many supported tasks. Switching to System Informer thus makes sense.
System Informer provides low-level control over apps and processes, allowing you to manage them more effectively. It uses interactive graphs to show you all the processes hogging system resources. You can click on any data point for more information. This way, you can see all the past and dead processes to find the culprit. Similarly, the app makes it easier to view, start, and stop low-level system drivers, which is useful when you want to fix system crashes.
For times when you see an unknown background process eating up resources, System Informer lets you learn more about it without leaving the app. Last but not least, System Informer lets you find all processes using a particular file and kill them easily. This can be useful when you’re unable to edit or delete a file because some process is using it.
ImageGlass for Microsoft Photos
Microsoft Photos is the app that your PC launches whenever yoscru open a peenso in File Explorer. It lets you view photos and do basic edits (crop, repair, stylize, and enhance). There’s also cloud integration support to help you view and manage photos from your OneDrive or iCloud account right in the app, along with a bunch of AI features. Honestly, though, all of this feels like overkill for an app meant just to view photos. Not only does it make the interface look cluttered, but it also slows the app down significantly. Hence, the need for alternatives like ImageGlass.
ImageGlass is one of the popular Microsoft Photos alternatives after IrfanView. Although IrfanView is packed with advanced features, it feels dated in today’s time. Add to that the fact that Microsoft Photos is primarily a photo viewer, and ImageGlass starts looking like the better option. It’s fast, thanks to its use of hardware caching, which preloads adjacent images so they load instantly when you use the left or right arrow keys. And unlike Photos, it supports over 90 image formats, including WebP, JXL, and multiple RAW formats, natively. As such, you don’t need to download external plugins or extensions to open images.
Another reason to choose ImageGlass is the clean experience. It’s an entirely local-first image viewer that doesn’t integrate cloud services, nor does it push AI or other unrelated features. The app just lets you open images to view them. That said, you do get basic editing options (rotate, flip, crop, resize, etc.), along with a few other useful tools like a color picker and an EXIF metadata viewer. The app’s UI is customizable too, and you get plenty of themes, layouts, and other options to play with.
Those are some Microsoft apps I’ve replaced on my Windows PC with better alternatives. All of them are free to download and use, though some, such as Files and ImageGlass, offer a paid version that unlocks access to a few additional features. You can visit their website to learn more about these features, and if your workflow demands them, upgrade to their paid versions anytime.

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.
On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.
The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.
In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.
The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.
“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.
The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
Kiran Stacey contributed to this report

By the early 1880s, bacteriology was emerging as a rigorous science. Within the circle of German microbiologist Robert Koch in Berlin, investigators were attempting to isolate specific disease-causing organisms. The logic was to prove that a microbe caused disease, one had to grow it in pure culture, separate it from contaminants, and study its properties systematically. The available solidifying agent was gelatin. It provided a temporary structure to the nutrient broth, allowing colonies to form on the surface. But gelatin was fundamentally flawed: It liquefied at temperatures approaching 37 degrees Celsius, precisely the temperature required to culture many human pathogens. Even worse, several bacteria secreted enzymes that digested gelatin itself. The medium collapsed, colonies merged, and experimental clarity dissolved into formless fluid. For scientists attempting to establish causation of individual species in infectious disease, this was not a minor inconvenience: it was a structural limitation.
Who was Fanny Hesse?
Fanny Angelina Hesse was not formally appointed as a scientist. She assisted her husband, Walther Hesse, who worked in Koch’s laboratory. She prepared materials, maintained cultures, and drew meticulous illustrations of bacterial forms for publication. She was present, not as an investigator, but as a quiet labourer in daily experimental work. It was in that proximity that she repeatedly encountered the gelatin problem. Failed plates, melted surfaces, cultures lost at incubation temperatures. The frustration was practical and persistent. At home, however, she handled another substance entirely. Agar jellies prepared in her kitchen remained firm even in summer warmth. They did not soften as gelatin did. They did not seem to degrade. One evening, in what history records only briefly but imagination can render vividly, the domestic and the scientific converged. The problem of the laboratory and the memory of the kitchen overlapped. She suggested that if agar could withstand heat on the dining table, why would it not withstand incubation in the laboratory?
Before the laboratory
Agar is a complex polysaccharide extracted from the cell walls of certain red algae, mainly species of Gelidium and Gracilaria. Chemically, it consists primarily of two components: agarose and agaropectin. Agarose is a linear polymer made up of repeating units of galactose and 3,6-anhydro-L-galactopyranose, and it is this fraction that gives agar its remarkable gelling property. Agaropectin contains sulfate groups and contributes to viscosity and charge characteristics. The word “agar” is believed to derive from the Malay term agar-agar, meaning jelly.
Long before bacteriologists struggled with melting cultures in Berlin, agar had already lived a quiet life in kitchens. Extracted from red seaweed and known in parts of Asia for nearly two centuries, it was used to set desserts into firm, translucent gels. Unlike gelatin derived from animal tissue, agar did not collapse in warm weather. It held its structure. It was stable. It obeyed heat differently. In the nineteenth century, European cooks encountered agar as an exotic culinary thickener. But in scientific circles, its potential was invisible. The laboratory and the kitchen were separate worlds, divided by sex, habit and hierarchy. No one imagined that a domestic ingredient could resolve a foundational problem in bacteriology.
Thus, Fanny Angelina Hesse’s suggestion to replace gelatin with agar, was out of the box.
Moment of trial
When agar was introduced into nutrient media in Koch’s laboratory, the transformation was immediate and decisive. The medium remained solid at incubation temperatures. It did not liquefy. Most bacteria lacked the enzymatic machinery to degrade it. Colonies appeared as discrete, visible units, each derived from a single organism. For the first time, bacteriologists possessed a surface that was chemically inert, thermally stable, and optically clear. The ability to isolate pure cultures became reliable rather than tentative. Within months, the method was embedded in the experimental practices that led to the identification of the tuberculosis bacillus and other pathogens in the decades to come.
To understand why agar transformed medicine, one must first grasp the idea of culture. A culture medium is an artificial nutrient environment that allows bacteria to grow outside the human body under controlled conditions and at a controlled temperature. Individual bacteria are invisible, but when placed on a suitable medium, such as agar, they form individual visible colonies. This enables laboratories to isolate the exact organism from samples like blood, urine, or sputum. Once identified, the bacteria are tested against different antibiotics to determine which drugs are effective and to detect resistance. Imagine culture is like switching on a floodlight in a dark room. Agar becomes the illuminated stage where hidden microbes step forward, enabling precise diagnosis and rational treatment.
The breakthrough was not dramatic in spectacle. It was a shift merely in material. Yet that shift altered the trajectory of microbiology.
Aftermath and recognition
The scientific practice and literature of the period absorbed agar rapidly, but credit did not travel with equal speed. The technique became standard practice. Petri dishes were designed to accommodate solid media. Textbooks described agar plates as routine apparatus. The name of Koch became synonymous with bacteriological rigour. Fanny Hesse’s contribution receded into footnotes. For decades, the laboratory bench carried her insight without carrying her name. Only later did historians of science begin to recover her role and situate it within the broader narrative of microbiology.
Agar today
More than a century later, agar remains foundational. In every microbiology laboratory, from district hospitals to advanced research institutes, agar plates are prepared daily. Blood agar to detect haemolysis, MacConkey agar to differentiate lactose fermenters, chocolate agar for fastidious organisms. Selective and differential media, all structured upon the same seaweed-derived matrix. Antibiotic susceptibility testing depends on agar diffusion methods. Colony counting for public health surveillance relies on agar surfaces. Molecular biology workflows begin with bacterial colonies grown on agar plates before plasmid extraction or genetic analysis. Even in the era of automated diagnostics and genomic sequencing, agar persists as the primary tool for culturing living microbes.
Today, major production occurs in countries such as Japan, Spain, Chile, China, Indonesia, and Morocco, where seaweed is cultivated or harvested. Beyond microbiology, agar is widely used in the food industry as a vegetarian gelling agent, in confectionery and desserts, in pharmaceuticals as a stabilizer and laxative, and in biotechnology for gel electrophoresis to separate DNA and RNA fragments.
Its properties remain unmatched. It melts at high temperatures but solidifies at lower temperatures, allowing sterile preparation and convenient pouring. It is largely resistant to microbial digestion. It forms a clear, stable gel that supports nutrient supplementation without chemical interference.
Firming up microbiology
Without that transition from gelatin to agar, the systematic isolation of pathogens would have been delayed. The architecture of modern microbiology would have developed more slowly, along a more convoluted path.
Fanny Angelina Hesse recognised continuity between her kitchen and her laboratory. Today, when a microbiologist streaks a plate and waits for colonies to appear, the act is routine. Yet beneath that routine lies the insight of Fanny Hesse. Without her intervention, the discipline might have remained uncertain at its foundation, its cultures unstable, its conclusions tentative.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”

In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.

The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

Aerospace technology startup Parsec Aerospace, founded by former Pixxel engineer Effy John, is in talks to raise around $10 Mn (about ₹95 Cr) in a funding round led by Nexus Venture Partners, sources told Inc42. The funding round is also expected to see participation from existing investors, including Lightspeed Venture Partners, the sources added. The Bengaluru-based startup is developing next-generation engines for aerospace applications and remains in stealth mode. Details about its engine technology, target customers, commercialisation plans, and proposed use of the fresh capital are not publicly available. Queries sent to Parsec Aerospace and Nexus Venture Partners did not elicit a response by the time of publication. John founded Parsec Aerospace after working at spacetech startup Pixxel, which develops hyperspectral imaging satellites and Earth-observation technology. Parsec Aerospace was incorporated in September 2025, according to publicly available corporate records. Rising Investor Interest In Deeptech The funding talks come amid increased capital deployment into India’s deeptech ecosystem, spanning aerospace, defence technology, robotics, and semiconductors. Indian deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals in Q3 2026 compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in the corresponding quarter last year. Funding rose nearly 2.8X, although the number of deals edged lower. Among recent investments, metal additive manufacturing startup ThinkMetal raised ₹27 Cr in a round led by IAN Alpha Fund earlier this month. The startup builds industrial printing systems used to manufacture tools such as moulds, dies, jigs, and fixtures. In September, Aeron Systems raised ₹45 Cr in a pre-Series B round jointly led by Riverwalk Holdings and MGF-Kavachh. It develops inertial navigation and weather-monitoring systems for aerospace, defence, renewable energy, and other industrial applications. More directly in aerospace propulsion, D-Propulse Aerospace raised ₹25 Cr from IAN Alpha Fund earlier this year to develop propulsion systems for defence and aerospace applications.

For a parent preparing for a newborn, a last-minute hospital bag purchase and a carefully planned baby bedding purchase serve very different needs. The former could benefit from delivery within minutes; the latter may involve comparing products, materials and prices before placing an order. For Jaipur-based baby essentials brand Moms Home, understanding this distinction has been central to building its quick commerce business. The D2C brand, which sells organic cotton and bamboo-based clothing, swaddles, bedding and other essentials for children up to five years old, entered quick commerce in early 2025. Within a year, revenue from the channel rose from about ₹1 Cr in FY25 to ₹10 Cr in FY26, accounting for nearly 30% of its ₹35 Cr annual revenue. The FY25 figure, however, represents only the initial months following its launch on quick commerce platforms. The growth has since accelerated. According to figures shared for this story, Moms Home is now selling approximately 45,000 kits a month on quick commerce, with monthly sales approaching ₹5 Cr. But scaling the business has brought its own challenges. Even as revenues have climbed, Moms Home's contribution margins on quick commerce have declined from 20-25% initially to 10-15%. The brand has also had to navigate unpredictable product demand across cities, delays in platform warehouse replenishment and the risk of unsold inventory. For cofounder Kumar Vaibhav, the experience has reinforced a distinction that is becoming increasingly important for D2C brands: getting listed on quick commerce platforms may expand distribution, but it does not guarantee that products will sell, let alone profitably. In an exclusive conversation for The Quick Commerce Code by Inc42 and Nitro Commerce, Vaibhav discussed how Moms Home reworked its assortment, packaging and inventory operations for quick commerce, the role of brand trust in driving sales and the challenges of sustaining growth as the channel matures. How Moms Home Found Its Place On Quick Commerce Moms Home's quick commerce expansion came after several years of building its presence in India's babycare market. Founded in 2018 by Vaibhav and Bhupendra Agrawal, the company emerged from the founders' experience with organic textiles. They identified an opportunity in baby essentials, where they believed much of the existing product offering was concentrated on conventional clothing rather than a wider range of products made with organic cotton and bamboo. The brand initially focussed on products such as bamboo muslin swaddles, baby socks and blankets, building its presence on ecommerce marketplaces from 2019. According to Vaibhav, instead of rapidly introducing dozens of products, the company concentrated on establishing a handful of bestselling SKUs before expanding into adjacent categories. Its bamboo muslin swaddle, for instance, accumulated around 10,000 customer ratings on Amazon, according to the founder. The company subsequently expanded through its own website and invested in parent communities and creator-led marketing. Rather than relying exclusively on celebrity endorsements, it worked with mothers and parenting influencers to build awareness and product credibility. This groundwork would later become relevant to its quick commerce strategy. In November 2023, after raising its Pre-Series A funding, Moms Home was considering opening five to six exclusive retail stores. But the founders were also tracking the expansion of quick commerce beyond groceries and everyday FMCG products. By late 2024, platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto were beginning to show greater interest in categories including newborn essentials and baby gifting. Moms Home saw an opportunity to reach consumers through a channel where instant availability could influence purchase decisions. However, entering these platforms was not immediate. Vaibhav said the company spent approximately six months approaching quick commerce platforms, during which its sales performance and product portfolio were reviewed regularly. It eventually secured listings on Blinkit and Zepto in early 2025, followed by Swiggy Instamart in August that year. "Initially, the platforms took a bet on us because we were already one of the go-to brands in a newborn category. But no one knew for sure how the category would perform on quick commerce," Vaibhav recalled. The company's early presence was limited to around 20 SKUs. More importantly, it soon realised that the products generating consistent sales on ecommerce were not necessarily suited to quick commerce. Bulky and relatively expensive products, such as quilts, bedding and larger bundles, continued to perform better on conventional ecommerce platforms. Quick commerce consumers, on the other hand, showed stronger demand for newborn kits, baby shower kits and other curated essentials that could address more immediate purchasing needs. Rather than simply transferring its existing catalogue, Moms Home began developing a separate assortment with different packaging, product combinations and price points. Its newborn kits were priced at approximately ₹699-₹899, while larger baby shower and hospital bag kits generally fell within the ₹700-₹1,500 range. These kits combined products such as baby clothing, swaddles, towels, caps, mittens and other essentials. The company was also responding to a broader shift in how consumers used the channel. Although many kits were marketed as gifting products, Vaibhav said customer interactions revealed that 50-60% of purchases were made by expecting or new parents for their own use, while approximately 30-40% were intended as gifts. This meant the products were serving two different purchase occasions — planned babycare requirements and gifting — despite being sold through the same quick commerce catalogue. The distinction also helps explain why Moms Home's average order value (AOV) on quick commerce stands at around ₹900, compared with approximately ₹700 on traditional ecommerce. For Moms Home, quick commerce was not necessarily a channel for lower-priced purchases. Customers were willing to spend more when the product assortment matched a specific need. That finding shaped the company's next challenge: ensuring that the right products were available in the right locations without accumulating excess inventory. Why Managing Assortment And Inventory Became The Bigger Challenge For Moms Home, getting listed on quick commerce was followed by another five to six months of learning how to operate within the platforms' supply chains. The company had to understand purchase orders, warehouse appointments, goods-receipt processes, replenishment schedules and the differences in demand across platforms and cities. Vaibhav said the initial assortment revealed how unpredictable product performance could be. Even when Moms Home introduced 20-30 products, only around 10-12 would gain meaningful traction in a particular market. Products that sold well on Blinkit did not necessarily perform similarly on Zepto, while preferences varied between cities. The company therefore had to continually reassess its assortment rather than depend on a fixed set of bestselling products. Warehouse operations presented another problem. According to Vaibhav, products sometimes had to wait seven to eight days to be accepted into fulfilment centres, even after appointments had been scheduled. Such delays were particularly difficult for a business that depended on having fast-moving products continuously available. The challenge was compounded by the company's product model. Unlike brands built around a relatively small number of standardised FMCG products, Moms Home sells clothing, gifting kits and other baby essentials across different designs, sizes and combinations. Pre-assembling large quantities of kits created the risk that certain products would remain unsold if customer preferences shifted. To address this, Moms Home changed how it managed inventory at its factory. Instead of storing large quantities of finished gift kits, the company began holding individual components — including caps, mittens, booties and clothing — in multiple designs and assembling kits according to demand. This allowed it to change product combinations without committing all its inventory to finished kits that might not sell. The company also used additional discounts to clear older inventory, although Vaibhav acknowledged that recalling products after they had moved through the quick commerce distribution network was difficult. The objective was to maintain flexibility while ensuring fast-moving products could be replenished quickly. Vaibhav believes products on quick commerce should ideally move through inventory within seven to ten days, with platforms increasingly prioritising brands that demonstrate consistent sales velocity. But Moms Home's availability data suggests that operational efficiency remains an area requiring attention. An analysis by Zodiac AI by Nitro Commerce found that Moms Home's Blinkit catalogue recorded average on-shelf availability of 72.2% during 11-13 October 2026. Availability varied across markets, from 65.1% in Mumbai to 80.6% in Hyderabad. The analysis also found that 87% of listed products were available to buy at the time of tracking. These figures measure different aspects of availability: buyability indicates whether a listed product can be purchased, while on-shelf availability captures how consistently products are available across the observed locations. The three-day snapshot does not establish the company's performance over a longer period. Nevertheless, it points to the complexity of maintaining inventory availability across a growing distribution network. For Moms Home, the next stage of scaling will depend not only on adding more products and entering new cities but also on improving the consistency with which those products reach customers. There is another challenge, however. Greater distribution and faster inventory movement do not automatically translate into better margins. The Economics Of Quick Commerce: Growth Comes At A Cost Moms Home's rapid expansion has coincided with a narrowing of contribution margins on quick commerce. According to the company, its contribution margins across Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart initially ranged between 20% and 25%. They have since declined to approximately 10-15%. The company has not provided a detailed breakdown of the factors behind this compression, making it difficult to isolate the impact of platform charges, advertising, discounts, fulfilment expenses or changes in product mix. Nevertheless, the decline raises an important question about how economically sustainable the channel remains as brands expand their presence. Vaibhav believes one of the biggest mistakes emerging brands make is assuming that listing products on quick commerce will automatically generate sales. For products that lack brand recognition or clear differentiation, gaining visibility can require significant spending on platform advertising and promotions. He also questioned the effectiveness of paying substantial marketing fees to platforms when products have not demonstrated consistent demand. In his assessment, platforms ultimately prioritise products that sell quickly and generate repeat purchase orders. "Just being available on quick commerce won't make your product fly," Vaibhav said, arguing that product-market fit and pricing are more important than presence alone. His argument is particularly relevant to babycare, where purchasing decisions can involve a higher degree of consideration than the speed of delivery might suggest. According to Vaibhav, only around 10-15% of Moms Home's quick commerce sales come from customers discovering and purchasing the brand directly on the platform without prior familiarity or research. He estimates that approximately 70-80% of purchases involve consumers who already know Moms Home or research the brand through Google, Instagram, reviews or other channels before ordering. These are the founder's estimates rather than independently measured customer acquisition figures, but they offer an important perspective on the role quick commerce plays in the purchasing journey. For a brand selling baby essentials, delivery speed does not necessarily eliminate the need to establish trust. Moms Home's existing presence on marketplaces, its parenting communities, customer reviews and its appearance on Shark Tank India have helped create awareness beyond quick commerce apps. The channel, therefore, benefits from demand that may have originated elsewhere. This distinction also complicates how brands should assess the profitability of quick commerce. If customer awareness is built through spending on marketplaces, social media and the brand's own website, the economics of sales on quick commerce cannot necessarily be evaluated in isolation from those investments. At the same time, Vaibhav believes the platforms themselves are becoming more selective. He recalled instances where platforms introduced several brands within the same category, only for a handful to sustain sufficient sales momentum. His assessment is that discounting and paid visibility cannot indefinitely compensate for weak product-market fit. For Moms Home, that makes the combination of product relevance, customer trust, inventory availability and pricing central to its quick commerce strategy. It also makes the decline in contribution margins an important metric to watch as the brand pursues its next phase of growth. Can Moms Home Sustain Its Quick Commerce Growth? Moms Home's wider financial performance shows how quickly its business has expanded alongside quick commerce. The company generated ₹9.5 Cr in revenue in FY23, ₹12.5 Cr in FY24 and ₹17.65 Cr in FY25. It reported a profit after tax of approximately ₹29 Lakh in FY25. Vaibhav said revenue nearly doubled to ₹35 Cr in FY26, with quick commerce accounting for approximately ₹10 Cr of the total. He also claimed that the company was EBITDA-positive at around 5% in FY26. The growing contribution of quick commerce has reshaped the company's revenue mix. A year earlier, the channel accounted for only around 5% of Moms Home's business. Its share has since risen to approximately 30%, while ecommerce marketplaces account for roughly a third and the brand's own website contributes around 25%. The balance comes from retail, B2B and other partnerships. Importantly, Vaibhav said ecommerce revenue has continued growing in absolute terms even as its share of overall sales has declined. This suggests that quick commerce has become a significant additional growth channel, although the company has not disclosed enough customer-level information to determine how much of that growth is incremental rather than shifted from existing channels. The company's distribution footprint is also expanding rapidly. Moms Home is now present in approximately 80 cities on Blinkit, 40 cities on Swiggy Instamart and 20-25 cities on Zepto. It has a portfolio of around 300 products, and close to 100 are listed on Blinkit and approximately 50-60 on each of the other two platforms. However, Vaibhav pointed out that being present in a city does not mean a brand is available across every dark store in that market. As the company expands, it is concentrating on four growth levers: entering more cities, increasing dark-store coverage within existing markets, expanding the assortment and improving average order value. Smaller cities are becoming increasingly relevant to that strategy. Tier II and III markets currently contribute approximately 40% of Moms Home's total revenue, with Lucknow, Bhopal, Guwahati and Nagpur among the markets showing traction, according to Vaibhav. The company expects quick commerce to contribute as much as 50% of overall revenue within the next 15-18 months. However, growing dependence on these platforms also brings strategic risks. Vaibhav expects quick commerce companies to increasingly develop private-label products, following a trajectory already seen in conventional ecommerce, where platforms such as Amazon, Myntra and FirstCry have developed their own brands. For Moms Home, one response is to continue strengthening its direct relationship with consumers. The brand is exploring logistics partnerships that would allow it to store fast-moving products closer to customers and offer faster deliveries for orders placed through its own website. This could give Moms Home greater flexibility in how it serves customers while reducing its reliance on third-party platforms for fast delivery. The company has also moderated its earlier ambitions for exclusive offline stores, although it continues to sell through selected babycare retail outlets. On the funding front, Moms Home previously raised more than ₹5 Cr, with Mistry Ventures among its investors. It also received a ₹75 Lakh investment offer from Vineeta Singh on Shark Tank India in 2025. Vaibhav said the company was in discussions to raise another $3 Mn, although the latest status of the proposed round has not been established. For FY27, Moms Home is aiming to generate more than ₹35 Cr in quick commerce revenue. Beyond this, the founders want to expand Moms Home into a wider babycare business. Vaibhav said the company would consider entering categories such as hardline products and cosmetics over the next three to four years, but only after scaling its existing baby essentials business towards ₹200 Cr in revenue. The immediate challenge, however, is more operational and financial. Moms Home has demonstrated that consumers are willing to buy relatively high-value babycare products through quick commerce platforms, provided the assortment and buying occasion are right. It has also shown how a brand can use existing consumer trust, customised products and flexible inventory management to expand rapidly in a category that was not traditionally associated with instant delivery. But as its quick commerce business grows, maintaining product availability and protecting contribution margins will be as important as adding new cities, dark stores or SKUs. For Moms Home, the next phase will test whether the model that helped it scale quickly can also deliver stronger operating efficiency as quick commerce becomes an even larger part of its business.

Cyberattacks targeting companies through publicly accessible websites and apps have more than doubled from last year, according to Macnica, a major Japanese cybersecurity company.
There have been 216 cases involving confirmed or suspected data breaches reported so far this year, or 2.6 times the total for all of last year.
Finding vulnerabilities in individual websites has traditionally required considerable time and money, but advances in artificial intelligence are believed to have made it easier for attackers to identify weaknesses.
At a ministerial meeting on cybersecurity held Monday, officials presented an analysis showing that attackers are increasingly scanning web-based systems to find entry points and steal personal information in a short period of time. A government official said AI was likely being used in these attacks.
According to Yokohama-based Macnica, publicly reported cases of data breaches rose sharply from this summer, with 101 cases in October alone so far.
Recent cases of cyberattacks through websites and apps include software company Sourcenext, which is suspected of experiencing a breach involving about 22.5 million customer records, and Skyticket, a travel booking website that also reported the leakage of large amounts of customer information.
These attacks exploit weaknesses directly in websites and apps, allowing hackers to access information without first breaking into a company’s internal network.
In some cases, attackers log in as legitimate users and attempt to view other customers’ information that they should not be able to access.
Targets are also becoming more diverse. While e-commerce sites previously accounted for a particularly large share of incidents, attacks now affect a wider range of services, including membership websites and booking platforms.
Data breaches or suspected leaks have been reported at everyday services such as library catalog search systems, sightseeing train seat reservations and university facility booking systems.
Vulnerabilities specific to individual websites cannot necessarily be fixed simply by updating commonly used software.
Yutaka Sejiyama of Macnica said attackers were exploiting blind spots in security measures and stressed that companies need to identify and fix weaknesses in their own systems.
Hiroshi Tokumaru, a director at EG Secure Solutions, a Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm, noted that security measures are often given lower priority for websites that do not handle confidential information or financial transactions.
As AI advances, attacks that were previously too time-consuming to be worthwhile are becoming easier to carry out, he said, adding that the balance of power between attackers and defenders has shifted.

- The claim that a Catholic priest in Ecuador stole $2 million in church funds then died when a crucifix fell on him during a livestreamed Mass is unfounded.
- The claim spread on social media following the Oct. 17 death of Father Patricio Sánchez Molinari. The original source of the theft allegation remains unclear.
- Although the priest's death was real, Snopes found no credible evidence supporting the alleged theft. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil told Snopes there was no evidence to support the accusation and that it didn't receive any complaints of financial mismanagement involving Sánchez or his parish. The Archdiocese also confirmed that Sánchez was responsible for the parish's finances.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the Redemptorist congregation, Our Lady of Perpetual Help Parish and Ecuador's Prosecutor General's Office and await their responses.
In October, social media users claimed that a Catholic priest in Guayaquil, Ecuador, who died after a large wooden crucifix fell on him during Mass had previously stolen $2 million in church donations.
For instance, one Threads post claimed, "Catholic Priest Killed by Giant Cross During Mass After Stealing $2 Million in Donations."
(Threads user @the_awaken1814)
"LET THIS TRAGEDY BE A WARNING TO ALL WHO THINK GOD ISN'T PRESENT IN THESE TIMES," the user wrote above a video showing the crucifix falling on the priest during livestreamed Mass.
The allegation also circulated on Facebook and Instagram, with some people suggesting the priest's violent death was a form of "divine punishment." Snopes readers also contacted us to ask whether the incident really happened and whether the accusations were true.
In short, the strange circumstances of the Rev. Patricio Sánchez's death were real and documented on video, but the allegation he stole $2 million in donations beforehand wasn't supported by credible evidence. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil rejected the allegation in statements to Snopes.
What happened to Sánchez?
On Oct. 17, 2026, Sánchez was celebrating Mass at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church when a large wooden crucifix mounted behind the altar detached from the wall and struck him. The Associated Press reported on the incident, citing confirmation from the Archdiocese.
The incident was captured during a livestream of the Mass, a recording of which remains available on Facebook (archived):
The Archdiocese of Guayaquil announced a memorial Mass for Sánchez on Instagram, scheduled for Oct. 18:
Sánchez was 52 years old and belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, commonly known as the Redemptorists. According to an obituary published by the congregation, Sánchez served Catholic communities in several Ecuadorian cities before becoming parish priest at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church in Guayaquil.
In an Oct. 21 article, Spanish newspaper El País interviewed parishioners who recalled Sánchez's work in the community, including activities supporting children and young people.
The exact reason the crucifix fell wasn't clear in the immediate aftermath of the incident. On Oct. 19, Metro Ecuador reported that the cause had not yet been officially established. On Oct. 20, Ecuadorian newspaper El Comercio reported that Sánchez's relatives wanted authorities to investigate the circumstances of his death.
What did the Archdiocese say?
Snopes contacted the Archdiocese of Guayaquil to ask if it was aware of the theft allegation, whether there was evidence supporting it and if whether the archidiocese had ever received complaints about financial misconduct involving the priest.
In a message to Snopes, communications manager Steven Pincay said:
There is no evidence to support the claims made in this video. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil has not received any accusations or complaints of mismanagement of funds within the Perpetual Help Parish or by Fr. Patricio Sánchez, CSsR., who was the administrator and responsible for the finances of said parish.
In a separate message, the Archdiocese said it did not endorse the allegation, which it claimed was "maliciously disseminated by a YouTuber to gain views, regarding the death of Fr. Patricio Sánchez, CSsR." The Archdiocese didn't identify the YouTuber and we have reached out for more information.
Where did the theft allegation come from?
The exact origin of the $2 million theft allegation remains unclear. It was circulating online by Oct. 18, one day after Sánchez's death. We found no evidence it had circulated before his death.
On Oct. 18, Christian News & Investigative Reports published an article addressing the rumor, saying it found the accusation on social media. The following day, Kenyan news outlet K24 Digital reported the allegation was spreading online but remained unsupported by credible evidence.
On Oct. 20, a more elaborate version of the story appeared on a website called Cross Message. In addition to claiming Sánchez stole $2 million, the article alleged "some people also pointed out that church members had previously seen him driving expensive luxury cars and living in a mansion, raising serious questions about where his wealth came from." It also claimed a wooden cross he held during an earlier Mass developed cracks, which some believers supposedly interpreted as a warning from God.
The article didn't identify the sources of these allegations or provide evidence to substantiate them.

On September 29, 2015, a memo went out from Swasthya Bhawan, the West Bengal Health Department’s headquarters in Salt Lake, to every medical college principal and every district’s chief medical officer of health. Its subject was a concern the Union Health Ministry had raised about rising Caesarean sections rates, especially where the operation was not medically needed.
The memo enclosed a statement the World Health Organization (WHO) had issued that April. It suggested that chief medical officers, who license private clinics, carry out periodic “prescription audits” of Caesareans in private and government facilities.
At the time, the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2015-16) had found that about one in four births were Caesareans in West Bengal (23.8%). The latest sixth round (NFHS-6, 2023-24) puts the figure at 44.5%, close to double that level, against 27.2% for India. In Kolkata and North 24 Parganas it was found to be 67.5%, meaning about two of every three babies were born via a C-section.
Why the concern
A Caesarean section saves mothers and babies when labour goes wrong. It is also, however, major abdominal surgery, with slower recovery rates and higher risks of infection and bleeding, and it leaves a scar that can complicate later pregnancies.
The WHO statement said that across a population, Caesarean rates above 10% are not associated with fewer deaths of mothers or newborns. While the WHO does not recommend a specific rate, the increasing numbers of Caesarean births in West Bengal, and more widely in India, deserve attention.
The opening of the gap
The NFHS’s first three rounds, from 1992-93 to 2005-06, found West Bengal close to the national average when it came to C-sections, at 10.2% against 8.5% by the third NFHS round.
The State then pulled away. Its rate reached 32.6% in NFHS-5, for which West Bengal was surveyed in 2019-21, and by NFHS-6 (2023-24) the gap with India had widened from 1.7 percentage points in 2005-06 to 17.3.
The climb has also grown steeper. The rise of 13.6 points between 2005-06 and 2015-16 took a decade, while the latest 11.9 points came in four to five years.
The data cannot reveal how many of West Bengal’s operations were necessary, though it does show when and where the rise happened.
Prevalence of C-section delivery, West Bengal
| Survey Round | West Bengal (%) | India (%) | Difference (% points) | Change in WB (% points)) | Change in India (% points) | 
| NFHS-1 (1992–93) | 3.3 | 2.5 | +0.8 | — | — | 
| NFHS-2 (1998–99) | 10.3 | 7.1 | +3.2 | +7.0 | +4.6 | 
| NFHS-3 (2005–06) | 10.2 | 8.5 | +1.7 | −0.1 | +1.4 | 
| NFHS-4 (2015–16) | 23.8 | 17.2 | +6.6 | +13.6 | +8.7 | 
| NFHS-5 (2019–21) | 32.6 | 21.5 | +11.1 | +8.8 | +4.3 | 
| NFHS-6 (2023–24) | 44.5 | 27.2 | +17.3 | +11.9 | +5.7 | 
Source: NFHS reports
Private vs. government
Of every 10 women who give birth in a private facility in West Bengal, 9 nine now have a C-section (87.7%). In 2015-16, the year of the memo, the figure was 70.9%. West Bengal’s numbers are also significantly higher than current the national private-sector rate, 54.1%.
While numbers in the government sector are lower, they are also on the rise: government facilities performed C-sections in 28.8% of the births they handled, up from 18.8% in 2015-16 and 1.7 times the national public-sector figure of 16.9%. In Kolkata, the share of births in government facilities delivered by C-section rose from 32.4% in NFHS-5 to 59.1% in NFHS-6.
The move to private care
Births are also increasingly moving to private facilities. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 their share of the total rose from about 19% to about 29%, even as the public share fell from 72.4% to 65.8%.
These private facilities now perform almost 6 in 10 of the State’s Caesareans (57%). Had births stayed where they were at NFHS-5, the same arithmetic would give a rate of about 38%. The move into private care accounts for more than half of the 11.9-point rise, about 6.6 points, and higher rates in government facilities for most of the rest, about 4.1 points.
The pattern holds outside cities as well. In rural West Bengal, 88.1% of births in private facilities are Caesareans, slightly more than the urban figure of 86.8%.
A belt around Kolkata
On a district map, the highest rates form one contiguous belt in the south of the State. Kolkata and North 24 Parganas are at 67.5% each, Hooghly at 66.6%, Nadia at 62.9%, Purba Medinipur at 59.1% and Howrah at 58.5%.
Urbanisation alone does not account for the belt. Purba Medinipur, a coastal district where 11.6% of people lived in towns at the 2011 Census, has a higher rate than industrial Paschim Bardhaman (48.1%), where 81.6% did.
Purulia, on the Chota Nagpur plateau in the West, has the State’s lowest rate at 21.6%, followed by Jhargram (27.4%), South 24 Parganas (28.5%), Maldah (29.9%) and Bankura (30.1%). Every district except Purulia is above the national average of 27.2%.
A low district average, however, can also obfuscate women in remote blocks who need an emergency Caesarean and cannot get one. Almost every birth in the two districts with the lowest C-section rates now takes place in a health facility (95.7% in Purulia and 97.7% in Jhargram, against 94.9% for the State), so what matters here, is whether those facilities can perform a Caesarean when one is needed. Block-level hospital records would show how often they do.
Behind the rise
Explanations for the rise need records the survey does not hold. The first concerns money.
Swasthya Sathi, the State’s health insurance scheme, was launched in 2016 and opened to every resident on December 1, 2020. It covers up to ₹5 lakh per family a year in government and empanelled private hospitals. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6, the share of households with at least one member covered by a health insurance or financing scheme rose from 33.7% to 88.2%.
The timing matches the shift to private care. West Bengal was surveyed for NFHS-5 before the scheme became universal, and the births counted in NFHS-6 straddle the change. A scheme that pays for care in private hospitals would be expected to move births into them. The same years brought the COVID-19 pandemic. By May 2020 the State had set aside 69 hospitals for COVID-19 patients, 16 government-run and 53 privates. The disruption fell on both sectors, and the survey cannot separate its effect from the scheme’s.
Whether the scheme’s payments also tilt private hospitals towards surgery is a question its claims records could settle. They would show what share of delivery claims are Caesareans and how package rates for normal and Caesarean births compare.
Another explanation feeds on itself. A woman with a previous Caesarean can safely try labour only where an emergency operation can follow at once, which most district hospitals in India cannot promise. Each first operation therefore tends to bring a second, and the rate keeps rising over years.
Additionally, more women of childbearing age today are overweight or obese (34.6%, up from 22.7%), and more have 10 or more years of schooling (40%, up from 32.9%). An analysis of NFHS-5 data links both to higher odds of a Caesarean.
What the memo asked for
The 2015 memo already proposed periodic audits by the officials who license private clinics. The WHO statement it enclosed put forward a common method for such audits, the Robson classification. It sorts women into 10 groups by details such as how labour began and the baby’s position, so that hospitals can be compared fairly.
Published for each hospital, including every private hospital empanelled under Swasthya Sathi, the results would show where Caesareans are common among low-risk women, the group most likely to have unnecessary operations.
Fewer unneeded operations also require labour wards that can manage a normal birth safely at any hour, and protocols that let suitable women attempt a vaginal birth after a Caesarean. In Purulia and Jhargram the task would have to run the other way, to keep emergency surgery within reach.
What is needed now
The first step is for the State to say whether the audits suggested in 2015 were ever carried out, and what they found. Caesarean audits must then become routine in government and private hospitals alike, under the health department’s supervision. Swasthya Sathi can check each Caesarean claim against the medical reason recorded for it and devise methods to ensure hospitals are given no reason to prefer surgery.
Every woman who needs a Caesarean should get one without delay, and no woman should have one when there is no compelling medical reason behind it.

Ghanaian twin brothers and US woman plead guilty to $9m romance scam
- Published
Twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media.
The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure their victims into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana.
The 22-year-old twins, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie from Hawaii face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year.
Between July 2024 - April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9m (£6.7m).
While many of them were from Ohio - where the charges were brought - other victims were located in 24 other US states, as well as Germany and Austria.
As part of the plea, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit pieces of jewellery which investigators seized during their arrest, including luxury watches, rings, chains and earrings.
The three accused go by several names:
- Jamal Abubakari, also known as Jamal Abubakar and Arrangement
- Kamal Abubakari, also known as Kamal Abubakar and Lancaster
- Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman
In recent months, US authorities have stepped up their crackdown on criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa which seek to defraud elderly Americans.
Earlier this month, FBI Director Kash Patel said it had made hundreds of arrests after dismantling a scam centre in Ghana.
In June, a Ghanaian social media influencer known as Abu Trica, whose real name is Frederick Kumi, was extradited to the US to face trial for allegedly running a romance scam that defrauded elderly Americans of more than $8m (£5.9m).
He targeted victims through social media and online dating platforms, and is accused of requesting money or valuables under false pretences such as urgent medical needs.
The case against Kumi is being prosecuted under the US Elder Abuse Prevention and Prosecution law. He denies all the charges against him.

Cyclone Arnab starts landfall process along Andhra Pradesh coast, triggers heavy rain and strong winds
Authorities remain on high alert as rescue and relief teams continue to take precautionary measures to minimise the impact of the severe cyclonic storm.
Cyclone Arnab's landfall process started along the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday around 1:10am, bringing strong winds and heavy rainfall to several areas, the Indian Meteorological Department said.
In its bulletin issued at 1.10am on October 28, the IMD said Arnab’ was moving westwards over the west central Bay of Bengal, close to the Andhra Pradesh coast and Yanam, at a speed of 10 kmph.
IMD estimated the storm’s intensity at 125-135 kmph, with gusts reaching 150 kmph.
The storm is expected to cross the coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, south of Yanam, between 2 am and 4 am. Winds are likely to gradually weaken after landfall.
Track live updates on Cyclone Arnab
Authorities remain on high alert as rescue and relief teams continue to monitor the situation and take precautionary measures to minimise the impact of the severe cyclonic storm.
Andhra Pradesh and Odisha had stepped up preparations on Tuesday ahead of the expected landfall of very severe cyclonic storm Arnab, with thousands of people moved to safety, nearly 4,000 cyclone shelters readied and at least 50 trains cancelled across the region.
Air travel impacted
Air travel was also affected, with at least 21 flights cancelled at Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam airports on Tuesday. The cancellations affected services to Chennai, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam and Kadapa. An official said 15 flights scheduled to operate from Vijayawada airport on Wednesday had also been cancelled.
