Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While US users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google’s voluntary Registered App Stores program. Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year.
App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google’s store does.
“In March, we announced the Registered App Stores program to give third-party app stores a more streamlined way to reach users while maintaining the safety and security of the Android ecosystem,” said a Google spokesperson. “Eligible app stores outside the US can now apply to register their stores ahead of the new simplified installation experience rolling out to users later this year.”
The Android Registered App Stores program was initially Google’s backup plan. After losing its appeal of Judge James Donato’s verdict, Google was faced with a number of remedies, like allowing third-party billing and sharing app catalogs with rival stores. The most dramatic shift was the court’s requirement that Google distribute third-party stores within Google Play.
Google and Epic, having patched things up following the trial, attempted to settle the case in a way that gave Google more control. Registered App Stores were intended as a replacement for hosting the stores in Google Play, provided they could adhere to a baseline level of trust and safety. Google intended to use this program in the US and internationally, but the companies withdrew the settlement when the court signaled it would not be approved.

Max Dowman red card: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta explains his reaction to 16-year-old after sending off in Carabao Cup exit to Fleetwood Town
Max Dowman was sent off in Arsenal's defeat to Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup and Mikel Arteta appeared to say something to the 16-year-old as he went down the tunnel; that drew criticism from Paul Merson but Arteta has explained what he said to the 16-year-old
Tuesday 27 October 2026 23:58, UK
Mikel Arteta has explained his reaction to Max Dowman as the 16-year-old went down the tunnel after being sent off in Arsenal's shock Carabao Cup exit to Fleetwood Town.
Moments before Arsenal exited the competition on penalties to the League Two sidee, Dowman was sent off for violent conduct for allegedly lashing out at Fleetwood defender Harrison Neal. The pair challenged for a couple of 50-50s before a brawl broke out.
Dowman then went down the tunnel and Arteta appeared to lean towards and say something to the teenager as he walked past. That treatment of the youngster was criticised by Paul Merson, who felt the Arsenal manager should have put an arm around him.
Asked what he said to Dowman, Arteta told reporters: "It was something that we discussed before the game." Arteta refused to go into any more detail on that when pressed on it.
On Sky Sports co-commentary duty, Andy Hinchcliffe said the red card was harsh on Dowman and Arteta replied: "I haven't seen it with the camera. You can't really see what happens. The decision was made by the referee and that's it.
"And even with 10 men, we have three big chances to score the second goal."
Asked if the incident is something Dowman has to learn from, Arteta replied: "We knew when we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate."
Merson questions Arteta reaction
Reacting to the incident, Merson said: "If that's [Viktor] Gyokeres, who's an experienced international, he [Arteta] isn't doing that - but he does that to a 16-year-old kid?
"He's not the last person to get sent off for Arsenal, nor the first. If it was me, I'd have put my arm around him. It's still 1-1, they're still in the game.
"We all say things in life we wish we hadn't and if he [Arteta] could have that back, he'd do it differently."
Fellow Sky Sports pundit Jobi McAnuff said: "I can't understand the reaction. Arteta probably feels it was petulant, naive which I think it is.
"It is frustration from Dowman, but when you see the reaction from Arteta... we have to remember he's 16.
"Yes, he's a fantastic talent, but he will make mistakes along the way. I didn't like the reaction at all."
He added: "Dowman is potentially the future of Arsenal. Arteta didn't get that quite right."
Arteta has no complaints about Arsenal effort in defeat
Speaking after the game, Arteta was graceful in congratulating Fleetwood for the shock victory - but did not think his Arsenal players showed a lack of fight against the League Two side.
Instead, Arteta was frustrated that his side did not show a more clinical edge - putting 19 shots off target, with Kai Havertz the most guilty of missing three or four top opportunities.
"First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through to the next round in the manner they've done it," Arteta told Sky Sports.
"A really sad day for us. I cannot fault at all the attitude of the players, I haven't seen anybody not doing what is required at this level but we had so much of the ball, had so many chances, so many shots and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to penalties, you have to capitalise on that. We didn't and football is about that.
"It wasn't to do with attitude otherwise I would be here fuming. I'm sad, we're all sad.
"We have a responsibility to represent this badge in the best possible way. It was nothing to do with effort, application or determination to go and win it, but we lacked other things to create much bigger margins.
"With what we produced, it should have showed in the scoreline."

Police say assailant killed after attacking guard outside Israeli Embassy in Belgrade
Serbian police say an unidentified assailant attacked a guard with knives outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade and was killed just after midnight Wednesday
BELGRADE, Serbia -- Serbian police said on Wednesday that an unidentified assailant attacked a guard with knives outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade and was killed just after midnight.
Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said that police were treating the incident as a “terrorist attack” and had raised the terror threat to the highest level and stepped up police presence at key locations.
Dacic said that “a minor, so far unidentified … shouting Allahu Akbar, attacked the member of Gendarmerie and attacked him with two knives.” He added that the police officer “liquidated” the assailant in “self-defense” and was lightly wounded.
Dacic said that Serbia's security agencies had been monitoring the attacker, who he said was a supporter of the Islamic State group. Dacic said that “he kept the black flag in support of the Islamic State on his Instagram” account.
Wednesday's attack comes just days after Serbia held a key early parliamentary election on Sunday in which long-ruling former President Aleksandar Vucic was defeated by a youth-led movement after almost two years of protests against him. But Vucic and his allies still control the police as the new government is yet to be formed.
Israel also held its parliamentary vote Tuesday that exit polls said produced no clear winner.
In June 2024, an attacker with a crossbow wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade. The assailant was shot and killed by a guard.

The woman was attacked on Saturday and her death was confirmed on Tuesday

A zookeeper who spent nearly all of her 40-year career at the Beekse Bergen Safari Park in the Netherlands has died from wounds suffered following a leopard attack.
The woman, whose name has been withheld in accordance with Dutch privacy law, passed away on Tuesday, the park in the southern Dutch town of Hilvarenbeek said.
She had suffered serious wounds to her head and neck on Saturday while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards. The woman began working at the zoo when she was 17.
“Her passing deeply affects us all, and we sympathise intensely with her family, friends, and loved ones,” the zoo said in a statement, which was made together with her family.
An investigation is underway to determine why the woman was in the enclosure with the leopards. Zoo staff are typically not permitted to be in the same space as predatory animals.
According to the zoo, the woman was able to alert colleagues via a walkie-talkie that she had been hurt.
An ambulance and a trauma helicopter were dispatched to the park at around 11am local time on Saturday.
The woman underwent emergency surgery, but her condition worsened on Sunday evening and the zoo had said they did not expect her to survive.
The death of the Dutch zookeeper comes a little over two weeks after a man was mauled to death by a tiger in Yorkshire, England, after entering an enclosure at a wildlife park.
An initial post-mortem examination recorded multiple traumatic injuries as the cause of William Chapman’s death, a hearing at Doncaster Coroner's Court was told.
The inquest heard that Mr Chapman had a history of mental illness and a diagnosis of schizophrenia. He had experienced previous bouts of psychosis, the hearing was told.
Coroner's officer Caitlin Brookes said that his family had expressed “a number of concerns” in relation to his contact with mental health services.
Mr Chapman had been under adult mental health services in Doncaster but was “highly functioning and independent with no care requirements”, the inquest heard.
Ms Brookes said the Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS Foundation trust had launched an investigation following Mr Chapman's death.

Bomb blast near Colombia’s border with Venezuela injures at least 4 police officers
An attack with explosives near a bridge on Colombia's border with Venezuela injured at least four police officers in Cucuta
BOGOTA, Colombia -- A bomb exploded Tuesday near a bridge that crosses Colombia's border with Venezuela, injuring at least four police officers in the Colombian city of Cucuta, officials said.
Norte de Santander provincial Gov. William Villamizar said on X that police were investigating who was responsible for the attack.
The explosion was set off in front of the local branch of Colombia's tax collection agency near the Francisco de Paula de Santander International bridge. Footage of the aftermath showed a truck and several motorcycles that were damaged by the blast.
The attack comes as Colombia’s conservative government changes the nation’s security strategy and takes a more confrontational approach towards gangs and rebel groups.
After being sworn into office in August, President Abelardo de la Espriella cancelled peace talks with the nation’s remaining rebel groups, alleging that negotiations had yielded few results over the past four years, with armed groups using ceasefires with the government to strengthen their grip over rural areas.
De la Espriella, who goes by the nickname of “the Tiger,” has also re-established joint task forces aimed at protecting oil pipelines, and promised to tackle the cocaine trade by spraying coca fields with herbicides, a practice that was suspended in 2015 over health concerns.
Early on Tuesday morning, De La Espriella supervised an operation against gangs in Medellin, in which the government said it captured 135 people suspected of trafficking drugs and running human trafficking rings. In a video shared by De La Espriella’s office Tuesday, the president scolds some of the suspects captured by police.
“The party is over,” he tells a suspect. “You will see how hard the Tiger bites.”
Critics have accused De la Espriella of using law enforcement operations for propaganda purposes, and have expressed doubts about the capacity of Colombia’s armed forces to disarm rebel groups solely through the use of force -- without eventually returning to negotiations.
In Cucuta, next to the border with Venezuela, authorities are investigating the murder of a former deputy mayor, who was assassinated on Monday night while on his way home. In September, an attack on another police station in the border city killed a civilian and injured eleven people.

Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!

New Delhi: India and Mexico have formally launched negotiations for a preferential trade agreement (PTA), signing the terms of reference that define the scope and framework for talks aimed at expanding bilateral trade and investment, according to a press statement from the commerce ministry. The move is part of India’s broader efforts to forge bilateral trade deals to bolster exports at a time when geopolitical conflicts have forced a realignment of global supply chains. Bilateral merchandise trade between the two countries stood at about $7.83 billion in FY26, with India recording a trade surplus of around $3.62 billion. India's exports to Mexico were $5.73 billion, down 0.38% from the previous year, while imports fell 26.59% to $2.11 billion, according to official Indian trade data. Automobiles were India's largest export category to Mexico, accounting for around $1.92 billion. Other important categories included auto components, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and chemicals. Crude oil accounted for about three-fourths of Mexico's shipments to India. The terms of reference cover market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, dispute settlement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, and trade remedies, the commerce ministry said. The proposed agreement aims to create new business opportunities, enhance investment flows and strengthen supply chains by leveraging complementarities between the two economies. The initiative follows an understanding between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Canada in June 2025 to deepen bilateral ties. During a visit to Mexico by commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal, Indian and Mexican officials met to discuss expanding trade and investment. Agrawal held talks with Mexico’s undersecretary of foreign trade Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez Romano, who represented economy secretary Marcelo Ebrard Casaubon. Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters and investors because of its links to global value chains. Sectors identified for potential cooperation include automobiles, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, medical devices and advanced manufacturing. The two sides also discussed the possibility of organising a Mexican business mission to India in the first quarter of 2027. The proposed visit would facilitate business-to-business meetings, help identify commercial opportunities, and strengthen ties between businesses in the two countries. The negotiations mark a step towards a broader economic partnership, with both sides seeking to expand market opportunities and strengthen commercial engagement. The recent conversation over the merchant discount rate on select UPI transactions raised the question of who pays for the digital convenience that millions of people enjoy. Hospitals may soon face a similar problem for strengthening their privacy even if no separate “privacy charge” appears on a patient’s bill.
Protecting digital patient information will require secure systems, trained personnel, and continuous compliance. Parliament enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 in response to this need. The Act consists of 44 sections in nine chapters plus one Schedule. The government notified its Rules on November 13, 2025, with the Sections pertaining to provisions for consent managers set to kick in from November 13, 2026. The rest of the substantive obligations will start to apply from May 13, 2027.
Unusually difficult places
The Act is a general framework to protect digital personal data across sectors, including healthcare. In healthcare, the Act recognises that clinical consent and data consent are different. For example, a person agreeing to undergo a medical scan does not automatically mean they have agreed to every later use of the same scan, no matter how useful the hospital or doctors deem the scan data to be. While facilitating this distinction, the Act also makes room for data-processing during emergencies and specific medico-legal and public health situations.
Under the DPDP Act, the patient is the data principal (or owner) and the hospital — which usually decides why and how some information will be used — is the data fiduciary. Some external software, cloud, and/or data-processing company will serve as the data processor.
That said, hospitals are unusually difficult places in which to ensure compliance with a general data-protection law. Unlike banks or regional transport offices, hospitals continuously create information of an intimate nature. For example, healthcare workers record a patient’s clinical notes, nursing observations, diagnostics and laboratory results, ventilator readings, and prescriptions — all within hours.
At the same time, several professionals will need to access different parts of that record at different times. If access is too tightly controlled, patient care may suffer; on the other hand, unrestricted access can result in significant breaches of privacy. So the Act needs to facilitate the lawful processing of consent with reasonable security safeguards, grievance handling processes, and of course the correction or erasure of data where permissible.
Failure to take reasonable safeguards can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore.
Compliance costs
In the same vein, compliance requires hospital information systems with role-based access, facility to encrypt or mask data as necessary, systems to generate and preserve audit logs, backups, vendor contracts, breach response protocols, staff training, and a clearly identified person who is responsible for data governance.
Entities designated data fiduciaries must also appoint a statutory data protection officer, and smaller hospitals will need a privacy or data management lead in practice.
Further, information rarely stays within the hospital, since a cashless claim can send diagnoses and reports to an insurer or a third party administrator. Laboratories, radiology platforms, cloud vendors, and telemedicine services will create additional routes for the same record. Even low-cost WhatsApp-based workflows that became popular because they were convenient will have to be examined for compliance and security.
Healthcare may therefore need specific DPDP provisions, either explicitly or eventually as a separate Act, to cover sector-specific uniqueness, such as small hospitals and large hospitals separately, as clinical care is more than a commercial transaction.
Lesson from Chandigarh
U.S. estimates show the cost of complying with the famed Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, to be around $5 per patient a year in 2008. Estimates for 2025 suggest the cost of $498 per affected record.
In a 2023 study, researchers from India and Norway estimated that adding an integrated information and communications system to an urban primary health centre (PHC) would expand the centre’s annual economic budget by 17.7%. But when the researchers applied the same model across 400 PHCs, the incremental cost fell to about 6% per PHC. The reason: common development and infrastructure costs were shared.
The finding offers an important policy clue: the government should not expect every small hospital, diagnostic centre, and/or PHC to independently purchase the same privacy tools, legal templates, and so on.
That said, the harder problem is that India has legislated faster than it has trained the people who must make the law work. Medical education teaches confidentiality and ethics, but there is no uniform DPDP-oriented National Medical Commission curriculum or standard course materials that span medicine, nursing, allied health, hospital administration, and healthcare IT training.
The vendor side faces the same problem: behind every software workflow is a human being who configures access, checks claims, handles support or views data. And an untrained person handling data in a hospital can pave the way for a major breach due so little as to one leaked password. So data literacy has to become a core healthcare competency.
Building an ecosystem
The National Health Accounts 2022-23 released this year estimated the out-of-pocket expenses on healthcare to be 43.4% of total health expenditure. There is a nontrivial chance that the new costs of complying with the DPDP Act will be passed on to patients as well.
Ahead of the November 13 date, the Indian government should step in by enabling a shared infrastructure through the Unified Health Interface of the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. It could provide model consent and vendor agreements with affordable cybersecurity support, and healthcare-specific implementation standards.
User data is routinely commoditised today, and passing a law assuming compliance and waiting for complaints or litigation will not suffice. As the DPDP Act comes into effect, the government must finance, build, and sustain an ecosystem that allows every health worker to comply and patients to be able to better access care.
Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. Views expressed here are personal.

Top Vatican official says pope's cancer diagnosis a 'game-changer' for the papacy
A top Vatican official says that Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis is “a bit of a gamechanger” for the Vatican
ROME -- Even though Pope Leo XIV is recovering well from lung cancer surgery and is going ahead with a big trip to Latin America next week, the diagnosis is “a bit of a game-changer” for the Vatican and Leo’s still-young papacy, a top Vatican official said Tuesday.
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, said there had been a temptation to think that Leo was a “Superman, a Superpope” after he was elected in 2025 and “hit the ground running” following the drawn-out illness and death of Pope Francis.
“The fact that he has fallen ill with, in many ways, one of the most common illnesses of our age means that he is a poor mortal like the rest of us. And I think that that is going to change how we see him and possibly how he sees himself as well,” Gallagher told reporters at the Italian foreign press association.
“Even if the operation has gone well, and everybody (says) there are grounds for considerable optimism, I think it is a bit of a game-changer at the same time,” Gallagher said.
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 after doctors found a tumor, later diagnosed as adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Subsequent tests indicated no further treatment is necessary, and Leo has been slowly resuming his daily activities.
The Vatican this week confirmed Leo would go ahead with his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, without any changes to the program. The published trip itinerary is challenging even for a healthy pope, with a dozen flights and two helicopter rides covering 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles), the longest of Leo’s pontificate.
Asked why Leo didn’t postpone the trip so he could recover further, Gallagher said the pope simply wanted to go. Leo spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru, where he has citizenship, and has made clear his close attachment to its people and his former diocese of Chiclayo.
“All of the medical advice is very positive, from a clinical point of view, so he feels he can go,” he said.
Gallagher, a British veteran of the Vatican's diplomatic service, also predicted that the Chicago-born Leo would in the “not-too-distant future” visit his native United States. But he said the outcome of next month’s midterm elections might influence whether the trip comes in 2027 or later.
The Vatican generally tries to avoid papal trips to countries in the throes of national election campaigns to avoid allowing the governing powers to use the pope for political benefit. U.S. presidential elections are scheduled for November 2028.
Preliminary discussions on an eventual U.S. trip have included timing it to coincide with the U.N. General Assembly gathering in the fall, or alongside a possible stop in Mexico, though Gallagher stressed that no firm plans are in place.
“He’s, I think, quite keen to visit the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe at some point,” Gallagher said, referring to the immensely popular pilgrimage destination where past popes have visited.
Gallagher also said it was “highly likely” that Leo would travel to Australia in 2028 to close out a big church meeting in Sydney, the International Eucharistic Congress. Other big trips expected are to South Korea in August 2027 for World Youth Day.
Gallagher, who served as foreign minister under Pope Francis as well, shared some insights about working with Leo after the sometimes turbulent Francis pontificate, which was characterized by the Argentine pope's spontaneity, grand gestures and occasional diplomatic gaffes.
Leo, he said, is pensive, thinks things through and is “not impetuous.” The math major pope can read a spreadsheet and is extremely well-informed, asking follow-up questions, such that when Gallagher meets with him each Wednesday evening to brief him on pressing foreign policy issues, “nearly everything I say he knows already.”
At the same time, Leo is tight-lipped and holds his cards close. Gallagher revealed he didn’t know about Leo’s planned surgery until the pope announced it to the world on Oct. 11 at his weekly Sunday blessing. He said he still doesn’t really know what the pope is thinking down the line.
“I think he’ll stick to his plan. And he will stick to revealing his plan, because he’s not the sort of personality who shares a lot in what he’s thinking of doing in three or four years’ time,” he said.
Gallagher said what has struck him most working with Leo is his serenity, focus on preaching the Gospel and dealing with issues as they come along. And he rejected speculation that the Italian-centric Vatican bureaucracy would eventually have its way and thwart his agenda.
“I don’t think the Curia will eat him up. I think if there’s any indication of that, he will demonstrate that he too has an appetite,” Gallagher said to laughs.

While plant-derived kababs may still struggle to replicate the taste and texture of meat from a tandoori joint, they may contain relatively more protein in a form that the body can absorb, according to a study presented on Monday (October 26, 2026).
In a collaboration between the CSIR–Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (CSIR-IHBT), Palampur, and the Good Food Institute (GFI) India, a non-profit that promotes alternative proteins such as plant-based, fermentation-derived and cultivated meat, scientists investigated whether protein bioavailability (meaning protein in a form that’s nutritively useful to the body) of traditional meat was the same as that of plant-based meat.
Tests on five cooked plant-based products — two burger patties, a nugget and two seekh kebabs — showed higher bioavailability percentages than their chicken counterparts, according to the findings presented at a press conference on Monday (October 26). The plant-based kebabs scored 80.8% and 86.1% against 38.8% for chicken. The nugget scored 61.2% against 43.4%, and the patties recorded about 57% and 58% against 21.2%.
The findings do not mean plant-based meat is healthier, but only that they are nutritively comparable, as ‘healthier’ is a subjective term, Dr. Padma Ishwarya, senior scientist at GFI India, told The Hindu. “It’s too much of a vague term. It’s too broad a term…for health, we need to do further studies.”
The chicken products held more crude protein and released more amino acids, the building blocks of protein, during digestion, and Dr. Ishwarya said more products and samples would be tested in the next phase.
The work has not yet been published as a journal paper. “It is a report that is hosted on our website, but it is very much peer-reviewed,” Dr. Ishwarya said in a conversation with The Hindu. Two experts reviewed it, she said, and it was an overview and that detailed manuscripts would follow.
The team used an in vitro method that simulated digestion in a laboratory. Samples went through a two-minute salivary phase, then a stomach phase with digestive enzymes at pH 2 to 3, and then an intestinal phase. The method follows INFOGEST, an internationally harmonised protocol, Dr. Ishwarya said.
The team added an ultrafiltration membrane chosen to mimic the pore size of the human intestine. Whatever passed through the membrane was deemed bioavailable, and only free amino acids were measured. Each sample was adjusted to start with 40 milligrammes of protein.
Animal studies remain the gold standard, she said, but are tedious and require ethical clearances. The simulated method is faster and more reproducible. The team plans to conduct tests across laboratories next year so that NABL-accredited labs can use the method.
Plant-based meat, Dr. Ishwarya said, is made “specifically for biomimicking animal-derived meat”, unlike crisps or cereals, which are plant-based foods. It is made from soya, pea or wheat gluten, mostly soya, and shaped by extrusion, a process in which material is pushed through a die under heat and pressure. She said it contains no synthetic chemicals beyond ingredients such as spices and texturisers.
The study examined only protein. An earlier analysis in 2024 of about 120 products in the Indian market, she said, found that saturated fat and sodium levels were comparable to those in animal-derived products, leaving room for reduction. Plant-based products also supplied dietary fibre, which animal-derived products do not.

U.S. President Donald Trump held a series of October rallies across battleground and deeply conservative states in an attempt to bolster the Republican Party's chances in the 2026 midterms.

Donald Trump suggested Venezuela would become the 51st state of the United States on Tuesday as the president showed off a tanker he claimed had “one million barrels of oil on it” from the country, nine months after deposing its president.
At a campaign rally in Corpus Christ, Texas, Trump touted a US oil deal with Venezuela, which the US attacked in January, capturing its long-serving leader Nicolás Maduro.
Trump claims the agreement – struck with the South American country’s interim government, which is backed by Trump’s administration – will cover “billions” of barrels of oil.
Venezuela “will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe some day soon it’ll become a prosperous 51st state,” Trump said at the podium on Tuesday. “That’s possible.”
Venezuela is on a growing list of countries and territories Trump has spoken of acquiring, including Greenland, Canada and Mexico.
With tens of millions of Americans set to vote in next week’s midterm elections, Trump’s aggressive foreign policy – including his controversial war on Iran, and tariffs on goods from much of the world – have challenged his popularity, according to opinion polls, with his approval ratings falling to record lows.
But on Tuesday, the president sought to point to the Venezuela operation as an example of his success. US fuel prices, which surged after the start of the Iran war, piling pressure on Americans’ cost of living, “will soon come plummeting down”, he claimed in a social media post.
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” he said at the rally, pointing out the ship off the Texan coast. “The oil provided is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer.”
Moments before Trump took the stage in Texas, he claimed on his Truth Social platform: “By unleashing Energy Dominance from Alaska, all the way down to Venezuela, I have made the Western Hemisphere the Energy Capital of the World.”
The deal has also drawn skepticism as critics complained that the Trump administration has not pushed a transition to democracy in Venezuela, where elections have not been held since Maduro was detained by US forces and taken to New York to face criminal charges after a raid on his Caracas residence.
The urgency of the oil agreement stems from Trump’s opting into the war with Iran in February. Gas prices have shot up nationwide after Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a passageway for 20% of the world’s oil supplies.

A group of 21 news publishers has reportedly challenged India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act in the Supreme Court (SC), arguing that the law could undermine investigative journalism and expose journalists’ sources. The lawsuit, filed on October 6, argues that the law’s provisions on consent, data erasure and government access to information could restrict news reporting and force publishers to remove factual stories. The case is scheduled to be heard on October 27, according to a Reuters report. The challenge comes nearly a year after the Centre notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 in November last year. The broader DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules establish a framework governing how organisations collect, process and protect individuals’ digital personal data. The Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents the publishers, has argued that the law does not provide a specific exemption for journalistic activities. According to the confidential filing, the association reportedly said that the absence of such safeguards could compromise press freedom and investigative reporting. The DNPA’s members include Mukesh Ambani-owned Network18, Gautam Adani-owned NDTV, the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group. Publishers Vs The DPDP Act A key concern raised by the publishers is the requirement to obtain consent before processing personal data. The DNPA has argued that requiring journalists to notify the subjects of investigations and seek their consent could allow them to destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses. The association has also flagged provisions allowing individuals to withdraw consent and request the erasure of their personal data. According to the filing, the absence of a public-interest safeguard could force publishers to remove or substantially redact factual news reports. The publishers have further raised concerns about provisions empowering the government to seek information from organisations handling personal data. They argue that these powers could expose confidential journalistic sources and discourage whistleblowers from sharing information about corruption, corporate wrongdoing and electoral malpractice. The filing also challenges the government's power to restrict access to information in the public interest, arguing that the provisions could curtail press freedom. The DNPA has sought the quashing of several contentious provisions of the law, most of which are scheduled to come into effect from May 2027, Reuters reported. The association has also argued that the government has granted broad exemptions to the state without extending corresponding protections to the press. What The DPDP Framework Provides The DPDP Act, enacted in August 2023, establishes obligations for processing digital personal data. The later DPDP Rules, notified in November 2025, provide a phased implementation framework, giving organisations up to 18 months to comply with specified requirements. The framework requires platforms to obtain consent for processing personal data, provide clear information about its use and implement security safeguards. It also gives individuals rights to access, correct, update and seek the erasure of their personal data, subject to the applicable provisions. The latest case marks one of the most prominent challenges to the DPDP framework so far, raising questions about how India’s data protection requirements will interact with press freedom and investigative reporting. The Act provides for financial penalties of up to ₹250 Cr for failing to implement reasonable security safeguards. Other violations, including certain breaches of obligations relating to children’s personal data, can attract penalties of up to ₹200 Cr. However, the publishers argue that the framework does not adequately account for the requirements of investigative journalism, particularly when reporting involves personal information collected in the public interest. The government has maintained that the framework protects citizens’ privacy while supporting responsible data processing.

Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at rape and sex assault trial
Russell Brand says allegations of sexual misconduct have had a “devastating” impact on his life
LONDON -- Actor-comedian Russell Brand said allegations of sexual misconduct have had a “devastating” impact on his life, as he testified in court Wednesday at his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault.
Brand entered Southwark Crown Court alongside his wife, Laura Gallacher, telling reporters that “today is the day for truth and justice.”
Brand, 51, stood in the witness box and took the oath, then gave his full name: Russell Edward Brand. He answered “no” to each of the charges: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Questioned by his lawyer, Ian Winter, Brand said the allegations had a “devastating” impact, with friends and colleagues abandoning him. He said no one with relevant evidence had been willing to testify in court on his behalf.
“My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations,” he said.
Brand said he even was forbidden from staying with his baby son in hospital after anonymous allegations of sexual misconduct were made against him in a newspaper and a TV documentary in 2023.
“The reason given by Great Ormond Street Hospital when my son was receiving open heart surgery and subsequent treatment was due to the material published,” he said.
Over the past two weeks of the trial, prosecutors have set out their case and the jury heard from six women who accuse Brand of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors that Brand was “ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator.”
As the defense attorney asked Brand about each of the alleged incidents, which his accusers said took place in locations including a hotel room, the offices of MTV and the toilet of a London bar, he denied forcing women to do anything against their will.
“Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself,” Brand said.
Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
- Published
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
What is a plenum?
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
What is on the agenda this year?
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

Shooting is underway in Venice on “Upgraded 2,” the sequel to Amazon MGM Studios’ buzzy 2024 rom-com “Upgraded” that, as announced, is set to star Leslie Bibb alongside Camila Mendes.
Mendes is returning to the franchise as Ana Santos, an intern at a New York City auction house who feigns a higher job status after she is upgraded to first class on her flight to London. During the flight, she impresses a wealthy young Englishman named William who is connected to the high-society art world, played by Archie Renaux.
In the sequel to the modern-day “Cinderella” tale, on which cameras started rolling in Venice on Oct. 21, Ana is now seemingly seeking to make her mark at the Venice Biennale art exhibition, the world’s oldest contemporary art fair. Becca Gleason, who is helming the sequel — taking over from “Upgraded” director Carlson Young — has been shooting on the terrace of Ca’ Giustinian, the Biennale headquarters that overlook the lagoon’s Grand Canal; in the neo-Gothic Palazzo Franchetti near the Accademia bridge, which serves as a Biennale exhibition space; and at the luxurious Moro Venice restaurant. So far, there are no indications on what Bibb’s role is.
Luke Roberts and Justin Matthews, who penned the first film, also wrote the screenplay for the sequel.
Besides Venice and the Biennale, “Upgraded 2″ will have a decidedly Italian flavor. Following 12 days of shooting on the lagoon, principal photography will move to Rome where 33 more days of shooting are planned, according to Italy for Movies, the country’s national portal for film and TV production locations and incentives. The production designer is Italy’s Luca Tranchino (“Prison Break,” “Domina”). The Italian company serving as executive producer on the sequel is Colorado Film.
Producers on “Upgraded 2″ include Mike Karz and Bill Bindley for Gulfstream Pictures, Mendes and Rachel Matthews for Honor Role, Lena Roklin for Luber Roklin Entertainment and Piers Tempest for Tempo Production.

Ecommerce major Meesho reported a 68% decline in its consolidated net loss to ₹132.5 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹411.4 Cr in the year-ago period as its revenue growth outpaced increase in expenses.However, net loss remained largely unchanged from ₹132.8 Cr in the June quarter.
Operating revenue rose 34% YoY and 11% QoQ to ₹4,131.6 Cr. Including other income of ₹127.4 Cr, Meesho’s total income stood at ₹4,259 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 31% from ₹3,254.9 Cr a year ago.
Meesho incurred exceptional expenses in the last year quarter which it didn’t incur this year, leading to the sharp annual reduction in loss. In Q2 FY26, Meesho incurred exceptional expenses of ₹45 Cr towards a business combination and a vendor dispute settlement, besides a ₹64.4 Cr tax charge related to the business combination. Neither charge recurred in the quarter under review.
Before exceptional items and tax, its loss narrowed by 57% to ₹123.3 Cr from ₹285.5 Cr a year earlier.
Meanwhile, Meesho’s total expenses increased 24% to ₹4,382.3 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹3,540.4 Cr. (The story will be updated soon)

Pune: The owner of Mor Pankh Sarees in Chandan Nagar has alleged that two persons misappropriated ₹1.59 crore from her business, diverted stock to other outlets and used her shop's Goods and Services Tax (GST) registration to procure goods worth ₹33.91 lakh without her consent. The complaint also alleges threats to her husband, unauthorised access to business social media accounts and destruction of CCTV footage.
According to the complaint filed by Mohini Autade, Poonam Shirale and Manoj Shirale were involved in the business and were expected to share its profits. However, when Autade sought details of the shop's financial transactions, they allegedly failed to provide a satisfactory explanation.
The shop's chartered accountant, Sangram Bhoite, reportedly told Autade that he could not complete the accounts as the purchase and sales records and employee details had not been provided. After examining the available accounting entries, he found that ₹1.59 crore was reflected as cash in hand for the period from August 2025 to July 7, 2026.
When questioned about the amount, the two allegedly claimed that the money was with market traders but failed to provide details or supporting records. Autade suspects that the funds were diverted to Mor Pankh Fashion, an outlet in Wagholi.
The complaint further alleges that stock was removed from the Chandan Nagar shop and goods worth ₹33.91 lakh were procured for Mor Pankh Fashion in Wagholi and Phulrani Sarees in Alandi using her shop's GST number without authorisation.
The dispute allegedly escalated on July 7, when Poonam and Manoj Shirale, accompanied by Poonam's brother Rahul Patil, visited the clinic of Autade's husband, Dattatray Autade. They allegedly threatened him during an argument and took away a mobile phone used for online business transactions. The two also allegedly refused to restore access to the shop's social media accounts.
Poonam is further alleged to have livestreamed on social media and claimed that the Chandan Nagar shop was closed and its phone numbers were switched off. Autade alleged that the statements misled customers and damaged the business's reputation. The complaint also alleges that CCTV footage was destroyed and the shop's assets and digital accounts were misused.
Police have registered a case in connection with the allegations.

Former Bengal minister Indranil Sen arrested in Kolkata over alleged financial irregularities in Durga Puja preview shows
The investigation centres on alleged financial irregularities involving the Mass Art Society, an organisation headed by Indranil Sen’s wife.
Former West Bengal tourism minister Indranil Sen was arrested by Kolkata Police on Wednesday after being questioned by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in a case linked to alleged financial irregularities involving Durga Puja preview shows.
The probe centres on massArt (Mahanirban Road Mass Art), an organisation associated with Sen’s wife, Madhuchhanda Sen, which organised Durga Puja preview shows at selected pandals in Kolkata. The ED has alleged that the organisers sold tickets priced between ₹1,749 and ₹5,499, with more than one lakh tickets issued in 2023 and 2024.

According to the ED, the proceeds were allegedly siphoned off through cash withdrawals or recorded as miscellaneous expenses. The agency has also alleged that more than ₹3.8 crore in cash was deposited into the bank accounts of Sen and his proprietorship concern, Octave Records, during his tenure.
The ED further said nearly ₹30 lakh was transferred from Octave Records to former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee through banking channels. Sen reportedly described the payment as “royalty”. However, the agency did not specify what the payment was for or allege any criminality in the transaction.
The case is being investigated under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). The ED had questioned Sen for around 10 hours and searched 15 premises in Kolkata linked to him and his associates as part of the investigation.

My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people.
 
John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999.
 
Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008).
 
Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

On 22 October 2026, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur admitted that “face-offs” with Chinese forces had taken place at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. Following the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated on 23 October 2026 that the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) becomes “disturbed” when Chinese troops diverge from established patrolling patterns.
In this context, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming to show Chinese soldiers confronting and inspecting Indian soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing a confrontation in Arunachal Pradesh, where Chinese soldiers are intercepting and restricting the movement of Indian troops.
Fact: While the reports have confirmed face-offs between Indian and Chinese forces along the Arunachal Pradesh border, this video actually depicts a counter-terrorism mock drill conducted in Karnataka in April 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led to the original footage (archived) uploaded on the ‘Jagdamba Motors’ Instagram page on 30 April 2026.
The full-length video clearly shows shop signboards, such as “Jagdamba Tools” and “Balaji Tiffin, Tea Centre & Chat”, written in Kannada, indicating that the video was shot in Karnataka, not Arunachal Pradesh.
Furthermore, we contacted the phone number displayed on the “Jagdamba Tools” signboard and spoke with the owner, Sohan Singh Rajput. He confirmed that he recorded the video outside his shop near Devanahalli, Karnataka, in late April 2026, and that it actually depicts a mock drill conducted by Indian forces. We also found some other videos (here and here) of Indian forces participating in exercises at this exact location.
Moreover, the official Indian Army Fact-Check handle clarified that the footage shows an old counter-terrorism mock drill conducted near Bengaluru, Karnataka, and is not a confrontation between Indian and Chinese soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh.
To sum it up, an old video of an Indian counter-terrorism mock drill in Karnataka is being falsely shared as a recent confrontation between Indian and Chinese soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh.

In late October, with Election Day less than two weeks away, a post on Threads (archived) about the purported experience of a volunteer at the polls captured social media users' attention. According to the post, the volunteer's training focused on what to do if federal agents, such as officials with U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement or the Department of Justice, intimidate voters at election sites.
The post read:
I've been volunteering at the polls for the last 6 years and I just finished the training for Nov. 3rd.
Six years ago the training covered what to do if some MAGA instigators tried to disrupt voting. Training for this election focused on what to do if DHS, DOJ, ICE, or the Military attempted to intimidate voters.
In 6 years we went from random private citizens to our very own government trying to block our constitutional right to vote.
That is f…ing horrifying.
Users shared the post on other social media sites, such as Facebook (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent us emails asking whether the claim was true.
There are nonprofit, voting-oriented organizations that have been training polling-site volunteers on what to do if federal agents are present and intimidate voters. Therefore, we've rated this claim true.
We attempted to reach out to the Threads user who made the original post to ask more about her experience, but were unable to direct-message her via the social media platform.
To be clear, someone does not have to be an election worker — such as someone who counts votes — to volunteer at the polls. Republicans and Democrats alike have volunteers who monitor polling sites, and nonprofit organizations, particularly those focused on voting concerns, also have volunteers active at voting locations.
For example, Hands Off Our Vote, which is supported by various civil rights organizations and community groups, keeps a toolkit for people and groups to use to host trainings that will "equip volunteers with the skills to handle federal interference (including ICE/ feds at the polls)."
In a report detailing ways it and other organizations may handle armed federal agents at polling sites, the Brennan Center for Justice — a nonprofit group focused on democracy and criminal justice — said civic engagement organizations are providing guidance to volunteers monitoring polling sites on what to do, "such as documenting and reporting agents' activity while avoiding confrontation."
Civic engagement groups in the Chicago area prepared volunteers for potential federal immigration action during the primaries, according to local news reporting from March.
The Save America Movement, which has previously documented ICE operations in various American cities, is participating in Vote Safe, a project between multiple organizations designed to decrease voter hesitancy in minority groups intimidated by the potential of federal agents at polling sites. According to the Save America Movement, it plans to train and have "teams of local activists, volunteers, veterans, and faith leaders stand alongside voters at polling locations, serving as a visible deterrent against intimidation."
According to reporting from NPR, Living United for Change in Arizona has trained what the organization has called "constitutional observers" to monitor polling sites. NPR reported that the group wants people on the ground in the case ICE agents are at polling sites.
Snopes reached out to the group through Facebook Messenger to confirm the group has been training volunteers on what to do if federal agents are at polling sites. We'll update this story if we receive a response.
For further reading, Snopes has fact-checked a number of rumors about voting ahead of the midterms, including a claim that voting machines in Illinois were flagging Republican picks as unpopular.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023), with effect from October 17. The move has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.
The MSMER-2023 was withdrawn with immediate effect through a notification dated October 14, published in the Gazette on October 17. There is no single new regulation replacing MSMER 2023. Instead, the requirement for medical colleges to submit Annual Disclosure Reports (ADRs) will continue under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and other applicable regulations, the NMC said.
Rules on penalties, enforcement removed
The withdrawal comes close on the heels of a nationwide agitation for greater accountability in the undergraduate medical entrance examination.
Healthcare activists and medical education experts have raised concerns about three key areas that may fall through the gaps with the withdrawal of these regulations: the alleged removal of specific penalties under MSMER-2023, including fines of up to ₹1 crore for specified violations and personal fines of up to ₹5 lakh for faculty and administrators submitting false records; the verification of colleges’ annual disclosures on faculty, infrastructure, clinical facilities, and patient load; and the removal of the specific procedures and timelines for enforcement and appeals laid out in the MSMER-2023.
‘Patients at risk’
Bejon Kumar Misra, consumer rights activist and founder-director of the Patient Safety and Access Initiative of India Foundation (PSAIIF), said the withdrawal raised concerns about transparency, accountability, and the quality of medical education.
While the NMC Act, 2019, provides statutory powers for inspections and enforcement, Prof. Misra said that withdrawing a detailed regulatory framework without clarifying equivalent safeguards creates uncertainty over how institutional deficiencies and false disclosures will be addressed.
“Medical colleges cannot be judged merely by their buildings, equipment, or number of approved seats. The real measure of medical education is the competence of graduating doctors, the availability of qualified faculty, adequate supervised clinical exposure, and their ability to deliver safe and ethical patient care,” he said.
Prof. Misra has also written to the Union government, warning that misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk. He urged the Union Health Ministry and the NMC to clarify the enforcement mechanisms that will remain in place and to ensure that medical education standards are independently verifiable.
‘Dilution of regulatory oversight’
Babu K.V., an ophthalmologist and medical activist, said the withdrawal could dilute the penalty framework. He explained that by denotifying the stronger MSMER 2023 September regulation and retaining the June regulation, some clauses have been deleted.
“Like the clause 8(2)c, which states that monetary penalty not exceeding ₹5 lakh [will be imposed] for the faculty/Head of the Department (HoD)/Dean/Director/doctor submitting false declaration/documents/records (including patients’ records). Further, they can also be charged or penalised for misconduct under the Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations in vogue,” he said.
“This is the key regulation ,where the individual doctors are made accountable and hence deleting it is dilution of regulatory oversight,” Dr. Babu explained, refuting the NMC’s argument that there is no dilution of regulatory oversight.
‘Eliminates duplication’
However, a senior NMC official told The Hindu that the decision had been “misinterpreted”. The withdrawal followed a review by the Commission’s legal team, which recommended streamlining regulatory powers and removing overlapping responsibilities, the official said.
The Commission functions through four autonomous boards, of which two set standards for undergraduate and postgraduate medical education. Another assesses and rates medical colleges and undertakes institutional inspections and regulatory action, while the fourth oversees medical registration, professional conduct, and ethics.
The NMC maintains that the move eliminates duplication without diluting standards, and that its inspection and verification powers remain intact.
Not retrospective
The Gazette notification provides that the withdrawal will not affect actions already taken, approvals granted, or rights, obligations and liabilities accrued under MSMER-2023. Applications, proceedings, appeals and inquiries pending before the withdrawal will continue to be dealt with under the regulations, insofar as applicable. Matters arising after the withdrawal will be governed by the NMC Act and the statutory and regulatory provisions then in force.
India had 846 medical colleges, 1,39,864 MBBS seats and 86,360 postgraduate medical seats, according to government data cited in August 2026. “With medical education expanding, the key question is whether the regulatory framework that remains can ensure that colleges meet prescribed standards and face effective action when they fail to do so,’’ Dr. Babu said.

Australian sunscreen brands face stricter rules after safety scandal
- Published
Australian sunscreen manufacturers will be subject to stricter rules in the wake of a safety scandal that saw popular brands pulled off shelves.
The reforms, announced by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) on Tuesday, include stronger testing and quality requirements for specific ingredients.
This comes after a bombshell report last year by consumer advocacy group Choice which found that some popular sunscreens did not provide the level of protection their manufacturers claimed.
The new proposed regulations are "about making SPF claims more reliable" and giving the agency "faster access to evidence when concerns arise", Robyn Langham, the TGA's chief medical adviser, tells the BBC.
"Australians expect the SPF on the label to be backed by robust evidence," she said in a statement over email.
"These proposed reforms put that expectation at the centre of sunscreen regulation, with stronger testing requirements for the finished product consumers buy and repeat testing throughout its time on the market."
Under the new regulations proposed by the TGA, cosmetic sunscreen brands will also be limited in the skin protection factor (SPF) claims they can make.
This is to ensure "clear distinction for consumers" between sunscreens that are mainly made for UV protection and cosmetic products where UV protection is a secondary function.
Suppliers would also be required to provide their SPF testing data to the TGA when they list a sunscreen, and keep periodically testing the product throughout its shelf life.
Under current regulations, it's not mandatory for sunscreen manufacturers to provide testing data to the TGA unless requested.
The TGA said the reforms would be "implemented in stages, with further consultation where required".
The Choice report, published in June 2025, found that 16 of 20 tested sunscreens - including several premium, expensive brands - failed to live up to their advertised SPF rating.

One product, Ultra Violette's Lean Screen Skinscreen, which was voluntarily recalled last year, was marketed as having an SPF of 50+ but was found to offer only SPF 4.
The scandal sparked massive backlash in Australia, which has the highest rate of skin cancer in the world.
More than a dozen products were pulled from shelves or had their sales suspended as a result of the scandal.
The TGA proposed sweeping reforms to the sunscreen industry earlier this year, which included plans to make sunscreen labelling simpler and more oversight at testing labs.
Its statement on Tuesday said that changes to labelling would be made after further review and consultation.
Choice welcomed the reforms, saying in a statement on Tuesday that it was "pleased to see" the stricter rules proposed by the TGA.
However, the group pointed out that the TGA has not proposed to "routinely monitor and evaluate test results".
Choice also argued that that sunscreen test results should not be provided only to the TGA - as proposed by the regulator - but rather made publicly available and routinely monitored, "in the interest of transparency and public safety".

For more than 160 years, a humble ginkgo tree raised from seed in Geelong’s botanic gardens has been the backdrop to “countless local love stories”. Standing beneath it is the most popular spot to get married at the park, its branches forming the backdrop of many wedding photos.
Now, in addition to being the largest ginkgo biloba in the state – and possibly Australia – at a whopping 20 metres tall, it has a new claim to fame. The much-adored Geelong icon has been crowned Victoria’s tree of the year.
The National Trust of Australia (Victoria), which runs the awards, announced on Tuesday that Geelong’s ginkgo beat eight other finalists to the 2026 title, receiving 27% of 4,435 public votes cast. Second place went to the smooth bark apple myrtle in Prahran, while Apollo Bay’s myrtle beech was voted third.
To be eligible, trees have to be listed on the National Trust significant tree register, which recognises 2,500 trees in Victoria for their cultural, scientific, and historic value. More than 40 were nominated this year, then narrowed down to nine by a panel of 12 experts and arboriculturists.
The executive manager of gardens and landscapes at the National Trust Victoria, Justin Buckley, said the ginkgo was a “very popular winner”.
“It’s a really special tree, and very well loved in that area,” he said.
The ginkgo was planted in 1859, just two decades after the township of Geelong was formally established. The seeds were transported from China, rumoured to have been delivered by a ship’s captain making a stop at Geelong’s port.
Since then, generations of botanic garden workers and volunteers have helped it thrive. Not all have been able to see the unusual stalactite-like growths from its trunk and branches, which only occur in much older female gingko varieties, or enjoy its fruit – which has a reputation for being smelly.
Ginkgos, also known as maidenhairs, are among the most ancient trees on earth, dating back to the Jurassic period more than 160m years ago. In Japan, they’re a symbol of hope, longevity and peace, after six survived the 1945 atomic blast in Hiroshima. They were thought to be extinct in the wild for many centuries before being revived.
Botanic gardens supervisor Sheree Parker said the ginkgo was one of the first trees planted in the park and was also its “most visited and talked about”.
“It’s just starting to awaken now after being dormant,” she said. “We’re really excited.
“It’s our most popular destination to get married as well. We have a lot of weddings on this lawn and a lot of couples like to get married underneath the ginkgo.”
The city of greater Geelong staff had been strongly lobbying for the ginkgo to be crowned since the finalists were announced, posting regularly to social media encouraging people to vote.
“As … the backdrop for countless local love stories, she holds a special place in all our hearts,” they said a post earlier this month.
The competition was established in 2016 to celebrate Victoria’s best-loved trees, while also calling for greater protection of green spaces.
A recent urban greening framework, released by Stonnington city council, found over the past decade, more than 17.9 hectares of tree canopy had been lost on private lands in the inner Melbourne suburb alone.
The National Trust is urging the Victorian government to give automatic statutory protection to trees on its register and those of local councils, while also introducing a “retain first” planning principle making tree removal a genuine last resort.
In the past year, the Victorian government introduced uniform protection of canopy trees, but Buckley said it remained “quite limited” and there was “large scope” for significant trees to be removed without a permit.
“The reason we continue to draw attention to trees through this competition is because they really don’t have adequate protection, certainly not the same protection that heritage buildings have,” Buckley said.
“You can’t just think, well, we’ll take this one out, we’ll put another tree in there and everything will be fine. Big significant trees are virtually irreplaceable.
“As we need to accommodate growing populations and more housing … there’s going to be a lot of pressure on trees.”

Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader ends hunger strike after meeting with his brother
Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu has ended a brief hunger strike after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his younger brother
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu ended a brief hunger strike Tuesday after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his younger brother, his lead lawyer said.
Lissu, who survived being shot 16 times in a 2017 assassination attempt and has spent periods in exile citing threats to his life, leads Tanzania’s main opposition party, Chadema.
He faces a treason charge carrying a possible death sentence and has been detained for more than 18 months, with a final judgment scheduled for Nov. 6.
His lead lawyer, Rugemeleza Nshala, told The Associated Press by telephone that Lissu had planned to begin the strike Monday to protest restrictions on court-ordered confidential legal consultations. He postponed it after prison authorities promised private access.
When those consultations failed to take place Monday, Lissu began refusing food Tuesday morning, Nshala said.
“Lissu did not take his tea, breakfast or lunch,” Nshala said. He ended the strike after lunchtime following the private meeting with his brother.
Prison authorities and the government had issued no public statements on the hunger strike.
Nshala said Saturday that prison authorities had, on some occasions, barred access to Lissu altogether. He expressed concern about the health implications of a hunger strike because Lissu relies on medication.
Lissu was arrested April 9, 2025, after addressing a rally calling for electoral reforms ahead of that year’s general election and was charged with treason the following day.
In May 2025, he went on hunger strike to protest being required to appear in court remotely rather than in person.
Presidential candidates from Tanzania’s two main opposition parties were barred from contesting the October 2025 election, which triggered protests and deadly violence.
Chadema announced seven days of mourning ahead of the anniversary of the violence surrounding the Oct. 29 election.
Secretary-General John Mnyika told journalists in Dar es Salaam on Tuesday that the mourning period would run from Thursday through Nov. 4, with party flags flown at half-mast. He called for an independent investigation involving international bodies and independent Tanzanian stakeholders.
An inquiry into the election violence found in April that at least 518 people died. Its chairman, Mohamed Chande Othman, said the toll was likely higher because some families buried relatives without taking their bodies to morgues.
The United Nations had earlier called for an investigation into the killings and reports that police removed bodies from mortuaries to undisclosed locations. Chadema put the death toll at about 2,000, a figure the U.N. said it could not verify amid insecurity and an internet shutdown during the election period.
